Non-destructive Open Fault Isolation in Flip-chip  Devices with Space-domain


Reflectometry


W. Qiu1, J. Gaudestad2, V.V. Talanov2, M.S. Wei1 1Device Analysis Laboratory


Advanced Micro Devices (Singapore) Pte Ltd, 508 Chai Chee Lane, Singapore 469032


Phone: (65) 67969892  Fax: (65) 62339080

10000 Virginia Manor Rd, Beltsville MD 20705, USA   gaudestad@neocera.com


Abstract—Space-domain reflectometry (SDR) utilizing scanning


superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy


is a newly developed non-destructive failure analysis (FA) technique


for open fault isolation. Unlike the conventional open fault isolation


method, time-domain reflectometry (TDR), scanning SQUID SDR


provides a truly two-dimensional physical image of device under test


with spatial resolution down to 30 µm [1]. In this paper, the SQUID


SDR technique is used to isolate dead open faults in flip-chip


devices. The experimental results demonstrate the capability of SDR


in open fault detection.


I. INTRODUCTION


Open and short failures are two common failure modes


frequently seen in assembly back-end-of-line (BEOL) processing


as well as in integrated circuit (IC) testing [1]. With continuously


increasing memory density and shrinking semiconductor device


sizes, failure analysis (FA) is becoming more and more


challenging [2].


Fault isolation is a critical step in the FA flow because it helps


narrow the focus to the suspected area. There are many fault


detection tools available for a short failure, such as scanning


superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID)


microscopy [3], infrared lock-in thermal camera [4], photon


emission microscopy (PEM) [5], and thermal-induced voltage


alteration (TIVA) [6]. However, with regard to open failure


detection, for more than 10 years, time-domain reflectometry


(TDR) has been the only technique available to the


semiconductor industry. Its distance-to-defect accuracy is about


500 µm [7]; hence, to isolate faults in advanced flip-chip devices


accurately using TDR is becoming more difficult.


The recently introduced electro-optical terahertz pulse


reflectometry (EOTPR) system demonstrated its capabilities for


open fault isolation with higher accuracy compared to TDR [7];


however, it also requires waveform comparison among the reject,


golden and bare substrate units to determine the defect location.


In contrast, SQUID space-domain reflectometry (SDR) directly  displays a physical 2D image of an open failure, which provides  real visualization of the defect location. With application of the  appropriate radio frequency (RF) scanning frequency and linear  decay analysis, SDR is able to isolate open fault locations with  better accuracy than TDR. This paper introduces and investigates  SDR linear decay analysis in two open case studies and shares  the respective package physical analysis results.


II.


PRINCIPLES OF SDR AND EXPERIMENT SET-UP


DC and low-frequency signals, normally used in electrical  probing of ICs, cannot pass through the open trace because of the  open defect. However, a continuous wave (CW) radio frequency (RF) signal injected into the open trace from one end propagates  all the way to the open boundary and reflects back, similar to the  pulse in TDR. SDR injects a CW RF signal into the defective  trace and acquires a 2D image of the induced RF magnetic field. At radio frequencies, the open impedance, Zopen (typically in M range), is much greater than the trace characteristic impedance, Z0 (~50), so the open boundary reflects back nearly all the  incident power while no RF power is transmitted past the open (Fig. 1). A superposition of the incident and reflected signals  creates a standing wave [8] in "front" of the open where the zeros (nodes) and extrema (antinodes) remain at the same positions.

The obtained current density image is analyzed as follows. In  the vicinity of the open, the RF current decays linearly; therefore, it can be approximated by a linear fit as shown in Fig. 3. Extrapolating this to the zero-signal level yields the position of  the standing wave node, and thus the location of the open defect. The extrapolation is necessary to mitigate the inevitable noise  floor present in the current image. The open location then is  projected onto an optical image.

III. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


Case study 1: The land-grid array (LGA) flip-chip device  failed its continuity test at automated test equipment (ATE). The  unit was confirmed dead open by curve trace verification, and  TDR analysis indicated the open was located at the package  substrate region (Fig. 4). Usually, the location of an open in a


substrate is hard to determine precisely due to the complexity of  package design layout. Hence, it requires careful examination of  the package design layout to estimate the actual open location. SQUID SDR was applied to this device with 40-MHz RF  scanning frequency and 250-µm SQUID sensor-to-device  distance. The overlay of the RF current density image and the  optical image (Fig. 5) revealed that the open fault is at the  substrate region, which was in agreement with the TDR result. After zooming into the region of interest (ROI), the liner decay  analysis is performed to isolate the open location precisely. The  results (Figs. 6 and 7) clearly show that the open location is at the  corresponding failure copper trace.

A crack vertically crossing the failure trace was observed  under high-magnification optical microscopy (Fig. 8). Further  cross-section analysis was performed on the cracked failure trace. SEM imaging (Fig. 9) showed that the crack initiated from the  top and then propagated to the bottom of the copper trace, leading to the open fault. This case demonstrates that SDR is  capable of locating an open failure with accuracy better than 30 µm, which is one order of magnitude better than TDR.

In order to find out the root cause of the CNW, transmission  electron microscopy (TEM) analysis was performed. The result (Fig. 18) revealed there is a 4.6nm contamination layer on the C4


bump. Energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy analysis  result revealed (Fig. 19) reduced Sn content and increased O  content at the contamination layer. This implies there is oxidation  and this impedes solder wetting during flip chip reflow.

IV. CONCLUSION


The two case studies discussed in this paper clearly  demonstrate the capability of SQUID SDR to isolate an open  fault's location, and it is advantageous compared to TDR in terms  of result presentation and localization accuracy. With its


advantages in open fault isolation, the SDR technique will  become increasingly important in FA applications as IC package  designs become more complex.

Abstract


We have exploited an innovative X-ray tomography system, which is hosted in a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM). The resolution reached by this equipment is closed to 160nm  in 2 dimensions. We imaged Through Silicon Vias (TSV) which have undergone a manufacturing defect and  characterized voids within these interconnections.


Introduction


3D Integration (3DI) is a promising way to improve the  performance of integrated circuits. The main objective of 3DI  is to replace components placed in packages and soldered on  electronic cards by a vertical pileup of chips, in order to avoid  intermediate packages. This technology permits to increase the  devices reliability, the integration level and the performance  and to decrease both cost and electrical consumption [1].


The vertical connection between the chips is ensured by  interconnections of a few micrometers in diameter known as  Through Silicon Vias (TSV) or copper pillars for instance. These objects have a 3D geometry and are large enough to  contain 3D features like voids [2] or intermetallics [3] that  could potentially be a source of failure. It is then necessary to  image and characterize these structures to validate the  fabrication process of the devices and investigate reliability  issues.


Since interconnections have a 3D geometry, it is necessary to  develop and implement suitable 3D nanoimaging tools. There  are many techniques that can provide 3D information, including microtome, Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) coupled to Focused Ion Beam (FIB) [4], electron tomography


[5], atom probe tomography [6] or X-ray tomography [7]. Among these techniques, electron tomography and X-ray  tomography are the less invasive. Electron tomography offers  a nanometer spatial resolution but on samples as small as few  hundreds of nanometers in cross-section. On the contrary, Xray tomography offers a coarser resolution (few tens of  nanometers up to the millimeter) but on thick samples, respectively few tens of micrometers up to few centimeters [8]. We will see in this paper that this technique is well adapted to  image TSVs.


In this context, an original non-destructive 3D imaging  technique to characterize interconnections is proposed: the Xray nanotomography in a SEM. The paper is organized as


follows: first, the system to perform 3D nanotomography on  interconnections is described and then the method to determine  the resolution reachable by this system is explained. Since  sample preparation is an important step of the X-ray  characterization process, the use of a Plasma Focused Ion  Beam (P-FIB) to extract large chunks out of the bulk silicon is  reported. Chunks are then imaged with the X-ray scanner and  3D results are shown. Before concluding, the pros and cons of  this approach are pointed out.


Principle of X-ray nanotomography hosted in a SEM [9-10]


The instrument is a SEM which contains a module to perform  X-ray nanotomography. It consists of 3 main parts, including


(i) the SEM column and the target set that constitutes the Xray source, (ii) the sample stage and (iii) the X-ray detector as  illustrated in Fig. 1. This system has been chosen for its  flexibility: as we will see, it is really easy to choose and  change the radiation energy, to perform tomography at  different scales and to easily switch from the X-ray mode to  the SEM mode since the tomography system is hosted in a  SEM.


The SEM system is a Quanta 450 from FEI; the electron beam  generated by a thermionic electron gun (30kV, 2µA) is  focused on a fixed position of a thin metal target to generate  X-rays. The X-ray wavelengths passing through the sample  depend on the selected metallic target: for instance, the energy  of the primary X-ray emission of a platinum target is about


9.44 keV (L3-M5 transition), while the energy of the primary  X-ray emission of a vanadium target is about 4.95keV (K-L3  transition). Since the high-voltage of the SEM is about 30kV, the energy of X-rays generated by this system is limited to  approximately 10keV. The X-ray spectrum also includes the  bremsstrahlung radiation (radiation coming from the  deceleration of electrons when deflected by a charged particle  of the metal target). A part of these X-rays - defined by the  solid angle between the source and the detector - irradiates the  object, the X-ray beam of this system is therefore conical. The  geometry of this beam implies a natural geometrical  magnification M=R2/R1, with R2 the X-ray source to detector  distance and R1 the X-ray source to sample distance, as shown  on Fig. 1.


The object is mounted on a sample stage which includes a (xy-z-) positioning stage and a rotation stage on top of which 2  perpendicular linear stages make it possible to bring the  sample right on the rotation axis. The positioning stage permits


to change the R1 distance and therefore to adjust the  magnification M.


The X-ray projections of the sample are then collected by a  CCD camera. This X-ray detector is a 1340x1300 pixels (1.7Mpix) direct detection, front-illuminated, deep-depleted  CCD camera with an optimal detection efficiency between 3  and 10 keV. Beyond this range, X-rays are practically not  detected. The metallic targets - with a high precision  positioning system -, the sample stage and the detector (a  Princeton Instruments Pixis XB) are provided by Gatan, Inc.


This tomography system is based on the acquisition of a series  of radiographs while the sample rotates step by step through a  190° rotation (180° plus fan angle [11]). These projections are  then used as an input for reconstruction algorithms. In our  case, the reconstruction algorithm used to obtain a 3D image  of the inner morphology of the device is an Algebraic  Reconstruction Technique (ART) [12].


Figure 1: Synopsis of the tomographic imaging system.


Resolution measurement


First, we explore the current resolution possibilities offered by  our instrument. The resolution of X-ray projections is  improved when the X-ray source size decreases. However, the  lower the electron intensity (and thus the source size), the  lower the Signal to Noise (S/N) ratio. Decreasing the source  size implies decreasing the photon flux and the exposure time  required to acquire radiography would increase.


As X-rays come from the interaction volume generated by the  material-electron interaction, the X-ray source size depends on  three main parameters:


- The atomic number of material used as a metal target. The bigger the atomic number of the metal target is, the smaller the interaction volume will be.


- The focal spot size of the electron beam of the SEM, which adjusts the electron beam intensity. The higher  the electron beam intensity is, the bigger the  interaction volume will be.


- The acceleration voltage. The bigger this voltage is, the bigger the interaction volume will be.


In this paper, only the influence of two first parameters on the  resolution of this system is studied. The acceleration voltage is  fixed at 30kV.


In order to measure the 2D resolution of our equipment, we  used a resolution pattern that includes the Siemens star, which  was manufactured by Xradia company. To realize our study, we first selected a couple of parameters: a metal target and an  electron beam intensity. We then acquired a projection of the  entire resolution pattern to determine coarsely the resolution  reached (Fig. 2). Thereafter, we brought the resolution pattern  closer to the X-ray source to image only a part of the pattern, to determine finely the resolution reachable by this couple of  parameters (Fig. 2).


Figure 2: left, resolution pattern imaged with Au material and  a spot 6, right a zoom of the precedent image imaged with the  same parameters.


To estimate the resolution, the vertical resolution pattern has  been analyzed, as shown on Fig. 3a (this figure is a 90° rotation of the vertical resolution pattern presented in Fig. 2, to  the right). Ten lines of this resolution pattern have been  averaged in order to improve the S/N ratio, the averaged  profile is shown on Fig. 3b. We determined its envelope by  recording its maximal value (red circles) and its minimum  value (blue circles) every 20 pixels, knowing that this signal is  periodic. To monitor the contrast, the ratio R between the  amplitude of the superior envelope of the signal (represented  by the red circles in Fig. 3b) and the mean value of this signal  has been computed:


The value of R is plotted on Fig. 3c. Clearly, R decreases  when the spatial frequency increases.


We define the resolution limit as the value where R is equal to  35%.

This electron beam intensity decreases with the  spot size. In the remainder of this document, the “spot” term  refers to a value proportional to the electron beam intensity.


The acquisition time was chosen according to the S/N ratio. The X-ray accumulation was stopped when a satisfactory S/N  ratio was obtained.


The best resolution was obtained with the couple of parameters  tungsten - Spot 6, it is about 160nm and the duration of the  acquisition was about 35 minutes. The tungsten target can be quite effective to realize a  Computed Tomography scan (CT scan) of a copper object. Indeed, the energy of its primary X-ray emission peak is about

Given the X-ray attenuation length in copper and the potential  spatial resolution of the instrument, copper objects of few tens  of micrometers in diameter with sub-micrometer features are  good candidates for X-ray tomography in a SEM. Interconnections used for 3D integration perfectly fulfill these  requirements. The interconnections analyzed in this paper are  4 TSVs of 10µm diameter which have undergone a  manufacturing defect, they may contain voids which diameter  could be around 4µm. Given the size of these supposed voids  and knowing that the absorption peak of copper is around  9keV, we chose to image these TSVs with a gold target which  primary radiation’s energy is about 9.7keV. This metal has  been chosen in order to obtain a better contrast between  copper and voids. If these TSVs were thicker or if the voids  were smaller, it would have been better to image with a  tungsten target.


The TSVs examined were contained in a silicon wafer where  hundreds of these interconnections are regularly distributed. To perform X-ray nanotomography in our system, the first step  was then to extract a sample out of a wafer. The procedure is

FIB is a V-ion model provided by FEI™. Unlike the  conventional Ga-FIB, the ionic source is generated from a  plasma of xenon ions [13]. Xenon is almost twice as heavy as  gallium and the extracted currents are much higher: approximately 2µA with a P-FIB while we obtain 65nA with a  Ga-FIB. Etching with a P-FIB is therefore until 60 faster than  the etching with a Ga-FIB: for instance, milling a volume of  100µm x 100µm x 100µm of silicon with a Ga-FIB requires

around 50 hours while it only requires 1 hour with a P-FIB.


This instrument is clearly suitable in the context of  characterization of 3D integration devices. Indeed, the  dimensions of the sections to realize and to extract are often  higher than 100µm. The P-FIB thus permits to work quickly  and effectively on “big samples”.


Before taking the sample off the bulk, the top surface is  protected by 3µm thick of platinum (Fig. 5a). Two trenches on  both sides of the region of interest have then been milled (Fig. 5b). Thereafter, the chunk for the lift-out has been prepared by  milling the silicon under and on the sides of the zone of  interest as shown in Fig. 5c. The sample has been then fixed to  a micromanipulator (Omniprobe-Fig. 5d). The remaining side  has been subsequently milled to definitely free the sample  from the substrate (Fig. 5e). 3D results on interconnections


Figure 5 shows the surface of the TSVs we scanned. They  were approximately scanned at a 177 times geometrical  magnification, the magnified pixel size is about 113nm. We  chose to illuminate the gold target with the spot 7 which  ensures a 2D resolution of 235nm and a correct scanning time. We realized a series of 190 projections of our sample at  increments of 1°. Each projection lasted 8 minutes (8 frames), the entire CT scan has therefore lasted around 25 hours.


Figure 6: Projections of the TSVs using a gold target at spot  7, a. Angle=24°, b. Angle=33°.


Figure 6 presents 2 projections of our sample. The voids  contained in the interconnections appear very clearly.


Figure 7: a. Cross section of the 4 TSVs at the level of the  voids, b. 3D representation of the TSVs, c. 3D representation  of the voids (copper transparency).


Figure 7 shows different representations of the obtained  reconstruction. They were performed with the Avizo software. Figure 7a presents a cross section of the interconnections at the  level of the voids. This image has been filtered by applying a  Perona-Malik diffusion filter to the cross section computed by  the ART algorithm. This filter has been used to facilitate the  visualization of voids. By analyzing all these cross sections, we can determine the mean diameter and the mean height of  these voids. They are respectively about 5µm and 34µm. A  void has been segmented using a 3D region growing  algorithm, allowing to determine the effective void volume  which is about 661µm3. Figure 7b is a 3D representation of the  copper while Fig. 7c represents the voids inside the TSVs.


Discussion


X-ray nanotomography hosted in a SEM is a promising way to  image defaults within interconnections. 2D details of 160nm  are visible and it is possible to obtain a sub-100nm resolution  by using thin-foil targets [14]. These X-ray sources will be  examined in a future study. The instrument is versatile and  easy to use. We can easily get a 3D information of an object  by using X-rays and a 2D information by using the SEM  mode. We can easily change the metal target and thus change  the wavelengths passing through the sample.


The instrument has of course some limitations. Since it is  designed to perform high resolution tomography on isolated  objects, it is not really adapted for scanning large objects such


as full 200 or 300mm wafers for instance. It is of course not  suitable to perform tomography on nano-objects; electron  tomography, FIB-SEM tomography or atom probe tomography  are the optimal methods for objects requiring (sub)nanometer  resolution. The system is able to generate 30keV X-rays, which is optimal for sample having a cross-section of few tens  of micrometers – or more or less absorbing objects. For bigger  samples, a higher energy must be used. X-ray tubes can  provide much higher energy (150-180keV) but this is generally  at the expense of the X-ray source size and final resolution. Interesting results have recently been reported using both Xray and optical magnifications, thereby allowing to reach high  resolution with a comfortable working distance [15].  At the  moment, the main limitation of this instrument is the low  photon flux which implies long scan times: between 3 hours  and up to 30 hours depending on the requested S/N ratio. Of  course, X-ray tomography based on 3rd generation synchrotron  sources operates much faster, though at the expense of  accessibility and more complex data processing. Clearly, the  goal of this equipment is not to compete with synchrotron  nanotomography or electron tomography; it is rather a turnkey, easy to use lab nanotomography facility to investigate  isolated samples, and it turns out that 3D integration devices - TSV, copper pillars, etc - are ideal with respect to the system.


Conclusion


Some of the possibilities offered by the X-ray tomography in a  SEM have been analyzed in this study. The influence of  different metal targets and different intensities of the electron  beam on the 2D resolution has been examined. 2D resolution  of 160nm can easily be achieved. The conclusions of this study  have been used to efficiently image copper interconnections. Voids inside these TSVs have been imaged. The next focus is  on improving the 2D resolution by using thin-foil targets and  nano-wire targets.

Challenges for physical failure analysis of 3D-integrated devices


- sample preparation and analysis to support process development of TSVs


Andreas Meyer*, Gabriele Grimm, Michael Hecker, Martin Weisheit, Eckhard Langer  GLOBALFOUNDRIES Dresden Module One Limited Liability Company & Co. KG  Wilschdorfer Landstraße 101, D-01109 Dresden, Germany


* moritz-andreas.meyer@globalfoundries.com


The trend to higher integration of electronic devices  in order to include more and more functions into  ever smaller devices, such as mobile phones or  tablet computers, drives the development of new  packaging technologies for semiconductor chips. The goal is to reduce packaging size and power  consumption while at the same time allowing more  processing power. One of the approaches is to stack  multiple silicon chips on top of each other, i.e. pack  the corresponding DRAM chip directly on top of an  application processor. The electrical connections  between both chips are traditionally established by  wire-bonding from the edge of the upper chip to the  edge of the lower chip. However, this requires  additional space on the chips or could be  undesirable due to circuit design reasons.


An alternative approach is the utilization of  through-silicon vias (TSV) to connect multiple  chips to each other. The electrical connection is  established through Cu-filled holes that run directly  through the silicon substrate of one of the chips.[1] Since the integration of TSVs into semiconductor  manufacturing flows require additional process  steps that may influence the performance or  reliability of the devices, physical characterization  is needed during development, qualification and  manufacturing.


This paper provides an overview of typical  analytical questions and explains sample  preparation and analysis techniques to address  them.


Typical TSV process flow


One approach to integrate TSVs into semiconductor  chips is to include additional process steps into the  manufacturing flow after completion of the middleend-of-line (MOL). At this stage all transistor  structures and similar devices, the so-called frontend-of-line (FEOL), are finished including the local  contacts (MOL). The TSVs are subsequently  formed by a process sequence, similar to the  following:


Lithography and etch for the formation of  the holes into the silicon


_ Deposition of a liner oxide (SiO2)


▼ Deposition of diffusion barrier layers


(TiN/Ti or TaN/Ta)


_ Deposition of Cu-seed layers


_ Electro-chemical deposition of Cu in order  to fill the TSVs


_ Thermal anneal for Cu recrystallization


▼  Chemical-mechanical polish (CMP) to


remove excess Cu and to isolate the TSVs  After this sequence, the process flow for the  backend-of-line (BEOL) continues as usual in order  to form multiple layers of Cu interconnects, the  wiring of the chip. The size of TSVs can be in the  range of several 10 micrometers in diameter and up  to 100 micrometers in depth. Upon completion of  the wafer processing, the silicon substrate is  thinned in order to expose the bottom of the TSVs  where the connection to the next chip is established.


Physical characterization of TSVs


1)  Preparation of cross-sections of TSVs


A typical analysis request is the investigation of  cross-sections of TSVs in order to evaluate certain  process steps in the manufacturing flow, where  images are taken with scanning electron  microscopes (SEM). The task ranges from simple  questions like measuring dimensions of etched vias  or measuring thicknesses of layers to the more  complex analysis of the Cu microstructure, where  grain size distributions and crystallographic  orientations are to be measured. The sample  preparation techniques need to be adjusted for each  task. Since the TSVs are quite large structures, sample preparation can be quite time consuming, ranging up to several hours per cross section.


For the evaluation of etch profiles a simple cleave  through the TSV is often sufficient. Figure 1 shows  a typical image of a cleaved cross-section ofa TSVs  etched into silicon with liner oxide, barrier and seed  layer already deposited. On such samples the


critical dimensions such as width and depth can be  easily measured.


Figure 1. Cleaved cross-section of TSV after  deposition of the barrier and seed layers


For TSVs where the metal fill has happened  partially or completely, the preparation of good  quality cross sections becomes more difficult. The  ductile metal layers will be deformed or ripped out  of the sample during cleaving. Cross sections of  such samples are needed in order to measure the  layer thickness of diffusion barrier layers or to  evaluate the evolution of the Cu microstructure by  electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). There are  multiple ways to prepare such cross sections:


Mechanical polishing


Focused Ion Beam (FIB) milling


Broad-beam Argon ion milling


The first two possibilities have some distinct  disadvantages over the third option. They often  produce artifacts that prevent certain measurements  to be made reliably. Mechanical polishing often  smears the individual materials across the surface, making it difficult to accurately measure the  thickness of thin diffusion barriers. Furthermore it  tends to produce defects in the Cu surface that  compromise the measurement quality in EBSD  investigations. FIB preparation of such large  structures has the drawback that it can take up to  several hours for the preparation of a cross section


of a single TSV. In addition, due to curtaining  effects along vertical interfaces between materials, the diffusion barrier interface can be difficult to  polish by FIB. Such effects can be minimized by  FIB-milling in multiple steps and adjusting the  sample tilt around the image plane normal between  steps. However, this requires user interaction and  increase the preparation time even further.


In contrast to the above, broad-beam Argon ion  milling can produce cross sections of multiple  TSVs at once with up to 1mm of usable cross  section length, while providing a superior quality of  the final sample. Curtaining effects are virtually not  present at all due to the nature of the unfocused  beam and the automated sample rocking under the  beam. Barrier layers are perfectly visible and the  Cu surface is virtually defect free, providing perfect  conditions for the evaluation of the Cu  microstructure with EBSD. Figure 2 shows a TSV  cross section obtained by broad-beam Ar ion  milling.


Figure 2. TSV cross-section obtained by broadbeam Argon ion milling

(glue with two-component epoxy)


Saw with wafer dicing saw close to row of  TSVs

(Settings depend on actual instrument)


In addition to the good quality of the final sample, modern broad-beam Argon ion mills allow the  automation of the process, such that this task can


run unattended, allowing the analyst to perform  other tasks.


2) EBSD investigation of Cu microstructure


As part of the metal filling process, the TSVs  undergo a thermal annealing step in order to  recrystallize the Cu. This is needed to reduce the  resistance of the TSVs and to improve the  resistance against stress- and electromigration  induced degradation. With EBSD, texture and grain  size distributions are obtained simultaneously. Knowledge about the Cu microstructure can help to  optimize CMP processes for more uniformity or to  understand electro- or stress-migration related  degradation effects [2]. The principle of EBSD has  been described in [3]. In figure 5 an inverse pole  figure map is shown. The colors represent the  crystal orientation, i.e. blue grains are <111>-oriented relative to the wafer normal, which means  that the <111>-plane is aligned parallel to the wafer  surface. The cross sections were prepared using the  broad-beam Argon ion milling technique described  above. Only this approach provided the defect free  Cu surface required for EBSD investigations. Figure 3 shows the corresponding pole figures and  figure 4 the grain size distribution.

3) Investigation of post-CMP planarity


An important aspect for the successful integration  of TSVs in regular semiconductor chips is that the  resulting wafer surface in the vicinity of TSVs is  very flat after processing. As highlighted earlier, the TSV sequence interrupts the normal process  flow for semiconductor manufacturing. Upon  completion, the entire BEOL representing the  wiring of the circuitry still needs to be fabricated. Since the process window for lithography with  respect to depth of focus is very limited in  advanced technology nodes like 28nm and below, already height differences of a few tens of


nanometers can cause problems for the photo  lithography of interconnect lines, causing missing  pattern or falling lines. In order to optimize the  CMP process, planarity measurements are  necessary. Several techniques can be applied in  order to evaluate this parameter, namely atomic  force microscopy (AFM), digital holographic  microscopy (DHM)[4] or profilometer scans. DHM  reflects a laser beam from the sample surface, which interferes with a reference beam to produce a  hologram from which a quantitative surface  topography image is calculated. Profilometer  systems are often available as in-fab metrology, while AFM and DHM are typically installed in outof-fab materials analysis labs. Each technique  delivers similar results, while having distinct  strengths:


AFM – highest lateral resolution (~10nm), but limited scan field


DHM – possibility to image large areas up  to several millimeters but comparativly


low lateral resolution (~1μm)


Profilometer – in-fab metrology but low


lateral resolution


For the purpose of this investigation, DHM was  used for the assessment of long-range planarity in  arrays of TSVs and AFM for the investigation of  the planarity and recess of individual TSVs. The  DHM scan in figure 6 shows that the entire surface  of the TSV array is recessed compared to the area  outside of the array.


Figure 6. DHM height profile of an array of TSVs  Figure 7 shows an AFM scan of a single TSV. It  becomes visible that the Cu surface itself is  recessed. Additionally, there is a distinct step in the  oxide surface immediately next to the Cu surface  although the material there is only silicon oxide. When looking for a reason for this step within one  material after CMP, it was found that the step  corresponds to the SiOx liner layer of the TSV. Said SiOx layer has different mechanical properties  as the SiOx used for the FEOL transistor structures


that were processes prior to the entire TSV flow. It  exhibits a higher removal rate, causing the step at  the edge of the TSV.


Figure 7. AFM scan of a TSV post CMP. Local


dishing, protrusion and sidewal defects are visible.


4) Investigation of barrier integrity


TSVs incorporate Cu layers at the FEOL level of  semiconductor chips and below, where such  materials are usually strongly prohibited, due to  reliability reasons. Metal contaminations in the  active regions of transistors can cause severe  performance degradations or failures of electrical  devices. Hence, it is important to evaluate the  integrity of the diffusion barriers of TSVs. The  thickness of the TiN/Ti or TaN/Ta layers can be  measured in SEM or TEM images of cross sections  of TSVs. However, due to the size of the vias it is  tedious to take images of every portion of the  barrier layers. Instead a wet chemical staining  process was utilized for screening different barrier  deposition schemes for potential weaknesses. The  test procedure was as follows:


1. Remove Cu layers inside TSV by selective  etch in ammoniumperoxydisulfate


(APODS)


2. Expose wafer to SiOx-selective etch


chemistry (typically buffered HF etchant)


3. Cleave cross-section and search for holes  in liner oxide layer


Figure 8 shows a cross-section image of a sample  after this test. Weak spots are visible in the upper  part of the via where the barrier layer exhibits a  distinct roughness.


It is important to note that this test may be overly  sensitive for TiN/Ti barrier systems, since the  etchant has a distinct etch rate for Ti. It cannot be  fully ruled out that the test itself weakens the  barrier to some extent. However, since the barrier  function is mostly attributed to the TiN layer, the  test is still useful as a quick test.


Figure 8. TSV cross section after barrier integrity  test


5) Investigation of stress in Si near TSVs


The integration of TSVs breaks the regular  patterning layout of the FEOL of semiconductor  chips. Both the presence of large structures between  sensitive transistor devices as well as the additional  process steps can have an influence on the device  performance and reliability near TSVs. One effect  is the introduction of local stresses inside and close  to TSV structures. Such stresses are not only  critical for reliability and crack propagation  resistance of packaged devices, but can also directly  influence the performance of CMOS transistor  structures due to the impact of mechanical stress on  charge carrier mobility. Therefore, the  measurement of local stress state in such structures  has become essential. Raman spectroscopy can be  used as an appropriate technique to evaluate the  stress distribution around TSVs after different  process steps, i.e. before and after Cu thermal  annealing. Raman measurements were done  utilizing a HR 800 spectrometer (Horiba Jobin  Yvon) with Ar excitation (λ=458nm), 100x  objective (NA=0.9), and grating 3000 grooves/mm. The details of this investigation are discussed in [5]. Figure 9 shows the stress profile across an array of  TSVs before and after thermal annealing of the  sample. A significant change in the stress  distribution from tensile only to compressive near  the TSV and longer range tensile stress further  away from it was observed.


Summary


The implementation of 3D technology in  semiconductor manufacturing provides additional  challenges to the materials analysis community.


Figure 9. TSV stress profile of a sample after


moderate anneal (B, solid black curve), and


after annealing at elevated temperature (C,


dotted grey curve).


Instead of analyzing ever smaller features, suddenly  significantly larger features are to be analyzed. At  the same time these large features contain layers as  thin as 10 nanometers or height differences in the  same range that need to be accurately measured. This work provides a set of sample preparation and  analysis techniques for the comprehensive analysis  of TSVs in support of technology development and  qualification. The toolset ranges from simple crosssection imaging of cleaved samples to the  evaluation of wafer planarity at the end of the TSV  process flow and to the more specific analysis of  the stress field around TSVs. The results provide  valuable insights for designers, integration and  process engineers.

Sample Preparation Strategies for Fast and Effective   Failure Analysis of 3D Devices


Laurens Kwakman


FEI Europe B.V., Eindhoven, The Netherlands


Marcus Straw


FEI Company, Hillsboro, Oregon, USA


Gaëlle Coustillier, Marc Sentis


LP3 Laboratory, Aix-Marseille University - CNRS, Marseille, France  Jens Beyersdorfer, Jan Schischka, Falk Naumann, Frank Altmann   Center for Applied Microstructure Diagnostics (CAM),


Fraunhofer Institute for Mechanics of Materials, Halle, Germany


In this paper different sample preparation strategies for fast  and efficient failure analysis of 3D devices are reviewed and  further explored. It will be shown that a combined workflow  using laser ablation and plasma FIB milling provides best  flexibility to cover most of the FA use cases. Laser ablation  guarantees fast, coarse material removal and the subsequent  plasma FIB milling provides fast removal of any damage or  imperfections induced by the laser ablation, precise navigation  to the region of interest, a high quality surface finish allowing  direct SEM imaging and analytics such as EBSD and, if  required the preparation of a thin lamella for TEM analysis.


Failure analysis and physical characterization of 3D devices  require adapted methods for sample preparation as the device  structures to be analyzed can be embedded in a complex  package (“chip-access”), are relatively large ( > 1000 μm2) and need to be inspected with nanometer resolution. Because  conventional methods have shortcomings (LMIS Ga-FIB is  too slow, mechanical polishing can create unacceptable  artifacts) several analytical equipment suppliers have  developed new technologies and now offer new products  accommodating the growing needs for 3D device Failure  Analysis [1-3]. The FA community has started to evaluate  these technologies [4,5] and although the two basic concepts  each offer distinct advantages, specific limitations have been  identified:


A. The Plasma-FIB (PFIB) platforms offer a 20-50 fold  increase in milling rates enabling excellent quality sample  preparation at precise locations in less than 2 hours provided  material removal is limited to ~ 150x150x150 μm3. Moreover, with PFIB platforms, good quality and large size TEM


lamellae can be prepared. However, for “chip access” including de-packaging and/or removal of one or more dies, plasma-FIB by itself is still too slow to be practical.


B. The LMIS Ga-FIB/SEM platform with (load-lock) integrated ns laser offers bulk material removal rates that are  orders of magnitudes beyond that of the PFIB platforms and  as such provides a fast and efficient solution for de-packaging  and accessing buried dies and interconnects. Unfortunately, the spectacular gains in material removal rates are partially  off-set by additional sample preparation steps that are  required: ns lasers create thermally induced damage that needs  to be removed. Removal of the heat affected zone with a  LMIS Ga-FIB is too slow to be practical if large fields of view  are required for the microstructural analysis. Given the low  milling rate of the Ga-FIB and the relatively poor spatial  acuity of the laser beam, the platform is less suited for time  efficient large area TEM lamella preparation.


To better cover the 3D Failure Analysis application space, a  combined workflow of laser ablation and Plasma-FIB milling  is proposed and in this study further explored. Two workflows  have been considered, one based on an integrated   fs- laser/SEM/(PFIB) solution and the other based on a standalone ns-laser + PFIB solution. While one of the challenges  with laser ablation is to find operating conditions that allow  removal of a variety of materials (silicon, metals, dielectrics  and mould compounds), this study is so far limited to silicon  and copper only.


Laser ablation and Plasma-FIB milling


Laser ablation, (Xenon) Plasma-FIB milling and conventional  LMIS Ga-FIB milling each cover a specific range of material  removal rates but also come with different spatial resolutions (see Fig.1).

The main advantage of laser ablation is its very high material  removal rate (~ 106 μm3/s), however, its limited spatial  resolution poses practical problems when a specific region of


65


interest has to be targeted with sub-μm resolution. The


focused laser spot size is typically in the μm range. Given the


limited depth of focus and focus inaccuracy, care must be


taken when removing material around a region of interest.


At the other end of the spectrum, LMIS Ga-FIB milling offers


excellent spatial resolution with typical (low current) ion


beam spot diameters in the nm range. Material removal rates,


however, are orders of magnitude lower, ~ 20 μm3/s. Thus,


while Ga-FIB systems are ideal for sample preparation of CA


力


advanced (SoC) CMOS devices, they are not really suited for  3D device sample preparation.


Plasma-FIB milling offers an alternative solution optimizing  both material removal speed and spatial resolution, and has  been found to be an excellent technology to facilitate the  analysis of bond wires, solder bumps, TSV’s, Cu pillars or  MEMS devices [1]. In Fig. 2, several Xe Plasma-FIB prepared  samples are shown with clean and smooth X-sectional  surfaces milled within a few nm of the targeted region of  interest (ROI). Bulk material removal is done with an ion  beam current of 1-2 μA and the final surface finish is obtained  using currents in the 10-100 nA range and an automated  sample rocking routine to suppress “curtaining”, surface  roughness that otherwise would develop due to the different  milling rates of the materials present in the sample. Most  samples were prepared in less than 1 hr.


Another important aspect of sample preparation is the ability  to create artifact and damage free material removal and to  ensure that subsequent failure analysis reveals real device  defects and not sample preparation induced defects. Mechanical polishing can cause scratches, delamination, material smearing or grain modifications. Thermal Laser  ablation can cause voiding, delamination, amorphization, grain modifications and phase changes. The extent of the laser  induced sample modifications strongly depends on the  experimental settings such as pulse duration, fluence and


Figure 2: Various PFIB prepared and imaged samples. Top: TSV and metal bond analysis in stacked die device. Middle: Cu-pillar and bump analysis showing voids and cracks. Bottom: analysis of a metal contact in a flexible multi-layer  Cu substrate. sample courtesy: Infineon and Linxens (project  partners in EU ENIAC project JEMSIP-3D), Imec.


repetition rate as well as the heat conductivity of the material  to be removed. The heat affected zone (HAZ) can vary from a  few μm’s to a few nm’s for ns and fs lasers, respectively [6,7].


FIB milling is known to create fewest artifacts and, given its  low rate of energy transfer, produces negligible thermal  damage in silicon and metals [8]. A 1 μA, 30 KeV ion beam  delivers 30 mW to the sample, which when focused in a 1-2 μm spot, corresponds to an irradiance of only ~3 x 106 W/cm2, a value 2-4 orders of magnitude lower than those used for


laser ablation. However, most of the ion beam energy is  transferred into the sample. Based on experimentally  determined sputter rates, less than 1 % is used to sublimate the (Silicon) sample material and TRIM simulations show that ~ 65 % of the Xe-ion energy is converted into phonons. Nevertheless, this energy does not lead to adverse temperature  effects inside the sample beyond the point of ion impact: given the high thermal conductivity of silicon and typically  used metals, thermal equilibrium is established within a  microsecond, a time comparable to the ion beam dwell time  used (~ 1 μs). Finite element thermal calculation results are  reproduced in Fig. 3 and show that for the experimental  conditions (30 mW in ~ 3 μm2 ion beam spot) the silicon  temperature remains below 550 K and, thus, well below the  melting temperature ( T = 1410 K) and drops off to < 350 K  directly outside the ion impact region. Similar calculations for  copper yield a maximum temperature of 420 K (melting point  1357 K). Additionally, it is shown that the maximum  temperature is nearly independent of the dwell time.

Hence, while a PFIB prepared sample is ready for immediate  physical inspection, a laser prepared sample requires  additional preparation steps as laser induced damage and redeposited material needs to be removed to ensure meaningful  physical characterization. For failure analysis, one has to  remove additional material with sufficient spatial resolution to  arrive at the exact defect location. This final preparation step  can be accomplished with a Ga-FIB system but its time  efficiency depends on how much damaged or additional  material has to be removed. For instance, if a ns-laser  produces a 5 μm HAZ and the structure to be inspected has  dimensions of 100 x 100 μm2, at 20 μm3/s the Ga-FIB cleanup would take ~ 45 minutes, effectively neutralizing the time  gained with the initial fast laser ablation.


For SEM analysis of deeply buried interfaces, IC structures  and interconnects, time gains are possible by tilting the sample  and applying only a local Ga-FIB clean-up. However, for  specific techniques, i.e. electron back scatter diffraction (EBSD) or energy-dispersive X ray (EDX) analysis, this  approach creates unwanted constraints due to detector  shadowing. Moreover, the reduced clean surface area limits  the SEM inspection of larger structures and relevant structural  details may remain undetected. Combining laser ablation with  a PFIB for final preparation and surface finish is for these reasons a more attractive approach as both the coarse material  removal and the final clean-up and polishing steps are fast and  effective and required extensions of the milling geometry can  be realized easily.


When considering the characteristics of laser ablation and FIB  milling (speed, resolution, navigation accuracy, induced  damage) different sample preparation strategies can be used  for the analysis of packaged and 3D stacked devices, depending on the dimensions of the structures to be analyzed  and the amount of material that needs to be removed to access  these structures. In table 1 different sample preparation  strategies are compared for different use cases.

As indicated in table 1, different tool configurations can be  considered for sample preparation: classical LMIS Ga-FIB  milling by itself is an insufficient solution as sample  preparation times are simply too long to be practical. A PFIB, either in a single or in a dual beam (SEM/PFIB) configuration, provides an efficient solution for non-packaged, stacked die  devices as long as the features to be analyzed are no more than  100-200 μm below the surface and smaller than a few 100 μm  in size. A dual beam PFIB also provides a means of  performing the physical and/or failure analysis itself, by either  ion or electron imaging and by optional analytical capabilities  such as EDX and EBSD.


For features that are buried in deeper levels (packaged dies, bottom die in stacked device, etc.) or that extend in size  beyond 200-300 μm, laser ablation or mechanical thinning  becomes mandatory as a first sample preparation step. Mechanical thinning involves sample cleavage or sawing, the  first method becomes difficult for stacked devices and the  second method, although feasible, is time consuming and  requires precautions and safety margins to prevent damage to  the devices. For these reasons laser ablation appears to be the  better choice and can come in different “flavors”: photon  energy may range from UV to IR, the laser pulse width can be  in the ns, ps or fs range, and the laser ablation unit can be a  stand-alone unit or be integrated in a FIB/PFIB/SEM system. If integrated, still more options exist with each having specific  advantages and disadvantages: integration in a load-lock or  integration in the main FIB/PFIB/SEM chamber.


Stand-alone ns-laser ablation + PFIB workflow


A stand-alone, atmospheric ns-laser is an easy and accessible  solution, but has a few practical drawbacks including  relatively high sample contamination levels and, compared to  fs-lasers, a larger heat affected zone (HAZ). However, in  combination with a PFIB system this workflow provides a  practical solution for samples that require de-packaging and/or  analysis of deeply buried structures. To that end, in this study  we have prepared Cu filled TSV samples with a ns-laser to  evaluate the extent of damage in the surrounding silicon using  TEM and to measure any changes in the copper crystal  structure inside the TSV with EBSD. The laser prepared  samples were further prepared with a FEI Vion plasma-FIB  system to determine the overall preparation time and to check  the final sample quality.


Experimental conditions


A 193 nm ArF excimer laser, producing 25 ns (FWHM) pulses at a 50 Hz repetition rate, was used to create micro  cavities in well characterized TSV samples at selected  energies of 600 and 750 μJ. The cavities were typically 150-400 μm deep, 250-450 μm square and created at a distance of  10, 2 and -10 μm from the TSV edge (see Fig. 4).

Figure 3: Block of the sample 1 material containing four TSVs (the fifth one is not complete) is sliced and imaged by BSE  detector at SEM beam energy 10 kV. The arrow points in the  direction of FIB milling during 3D tomography data  acquisition and is perpendicular to TSV axes.


SEM imaging time of slices prepared by FIB had to be  optimized too. We have reduced the dwell time to 20 μs per  pixel and increased SEM beam current to 4.8 nA. By using a


special SEM column mode with the reduced spot size at high  currents it was possible to get the same SEM imaging  resolution, while taking advantage of the higher scanning  speed and even higher BSE detector signal than on the  sample 1. As a result, SEM imaging time was 6 hours and  together with the milling time of 4 hours the total analysis time  was approximately 10 hours. Considering that the analysis  volume was increased more than four times, the increase of the  analysis time when compared to the sample 1 (8 hours) is  acceptable. In fact, we have enhanced the throughput of the  method by the factor of three on the sample 2, just by  modifying the procedure. Most probably it would be possible  to optimize it further e.g. by using even shorter dwell time, but  it would be necessary to find a compromise between the  imaging time and the quality of the image, especially when  looking for small voids in TSVs.


ORS Visual™ software [10] was used for data postprocessing  and visualization. Figure 6 shows an example of the obtained  volume rendering on TSVs of the sample 1. Cu crystalline  structure is clearly resolvable, as this information was included  in acquired BSE images.


Figure 4: The block of the sample 2 material containing four  TSVs is attached on the nanomanipulator tip during the liftout procedure. Secondary electron image at SEM beam  energy 10 kV.

3D volume rendering of TSVs from the sample 2 is shown in  Figure 7. The big voids inside TSV’s are resolved very well  and there are two big voids in each TSV (located at top and  bottom), their shape is rather symmetrical. It looks like the  presence of voids is not a significant problem for the  postprocessing of slices, as they are resolved in In-Beam BSE  images clearly and there is no mixing of imaging signals  between neighboring slices.


The voxel size was 260 nm in this work, but based on the  quality of the slices (low curtaining effect), we believe that it  would be possible to analyze defects smaller than 100 nm. For  big blocks of material used in this work, it would require  increasing the number of slices and SEM imaging time several  times, which would not be acceptable for the practical work. Therefore we think that for the analysis of very small defects it  would be better to focus either on single TSV only by  performing lift-out of smaller block, or to keep the block size  but to reduce SEM scanning area on TSVs only (avoid SEM  scanning on Si between TSVs, which gives no useful  information, but makes imaging time significantly longer) during FIB-SEM 3D tomography procedure. These aspects  will be part of further research.

Conclusions


We have shown the possibility of using plasma FIB for 3D  tomography on TSV structures, which are generally too large / impractical to be analyzed by Ga FIB and yet too fine in detail  for more macroscopic tomography methods. The throughput of  the method has been increased using procedures common to  both Ga and plasma FIB applications. The results on both wellfilled TSVs and TSVs with voids were shown. It was possible to  perform high quality 3D volume renderings clearly resolving the  Cu crystalline structure and the shapes of voids as well.


The demonstrated voxel dimension of 260 nm allows analysis of  defects with dimensions in the same range. Furthermore, it is  possible to reduce the voxel size significantly in order to analyze  smaller defects (reduced FIB current and slice thickness  combined with higher SEM resolution). In this situation, however, it would be better to focus on single TSV to reduce the  analysis time, as multiple TSVs require significantly more SEM  imaging time, a large portion of which is spent on large areas of  Si material in between TSVs.


Based on the quality of the surfaces prepared by plasma FIB on  multiple TSVs in this work, we expect that the minimum voxel  size can be reduced below 100 nm, while still keeping the  possibility of much higher throughput when compared to Ga FIB  and better resolution plus material and crystalline contrast  compared to X-ray tomography.


Both, the high resolution and fast analysis time were possible  because of the initial lift-out step only, allowing to rotate the  TSV orientation with regards to the cutting ion beam to get the  optimum milling direction perpendicular to the TSV axis.

22nm BEOL TDDB Defect Localization and Root Cause Analysis


Terence Kane, Yun Yu Wang


IBM Systems Technology Group/Microelectronics Division, Hopewell Junction, New York, USA


For 22nm and below technologies which involve as many  as fifteen back end of the line (BEOL) metallization levels, these leading edge technology nodes pose real challenges in  defect localization and root cause analysis.


Due to scaling, the reduction in copper land cross section  area is accompanied by increased current density and  electromigration failure rates. Time to Dielectric Defect  Breakdown (TDDB) shows an increase in fallout with  successive technology node from 32nm and below. Similarly, the reduced dielectric thickness increases the  electric field stress prompting the necessity for porous, ultra  low k dielectric (ULK) films.


Defect localization is difficult due to the complexity of  these multiple metal layers along with the presence of the  porous, low k dielectric films which exhibit shrinkage or void  formation when exposed to an e-beam/FIB ion beam  > 1keV. Due to the porosity of these ULK dielectric films, they are  especially susceptible to gallium ion implantation.


It has been reported elsewhere that suppressing copper  diffusion at the copper land/cap interface can be achieved by  depositing a thin layer of CoWP and doping the copper seed  layer with manganese [15, 16, 17]. However, a method for  analytically confirming that these approaches for suppressing  the copper diffusion do not affect TDDB  performance/electromigration behavior must be demonstrated.


22nm back end of line (BEOL) technologies involving    fifteen metallization levels and employing ULK dielectric  films at multiple metal layers requires extensive TDDB (time  to dielectric breakdown) reliability testing to determine beta (Weibull slope or shape parameter analysis) and the  calculation of t63 (time to 63% failure) and gamma (voltage  acceleration factor) characteristics to insure electrical  performance. ULK films pose real challenges in defect  localization and root cause analysis.


The TDDB test structures are meant to be sensitive to  defect densities and are not addressable like an SRAM array  with built in self test (BIST).


The entire TDDB structure must be kept electrically intact to  validate that the method for localization is not altering the  subtle electrical leakage characteristics of the defect itself


Root cause analysis of these reliability defects causing  TDDB fallout is essential to yield learning and BEOL process  improvements, including the suppresion of copper diffusion.


Conventional methods of TDDB defect imaging such as  scanning electron microscopic inspection/probing are  problematic since it has been shown that incident accelerating


voltage  electron/ion beams as low as 1kV can cause shrinkage  and introduce voids in the ULK films [1, 2]. Most importantly, the TDDB defect identified by electrically probing the  pads of  these test structures is frequently altered or healed during  attempts to delayer and/or SEM nanoprobe these structures.


While it has been previously reported that incident ion  beam or electron beams can alter the threshold voltage  characteristics of MOS devices, the effect of these incident ion  beams on ULK dielectric films, especially TDDB defect  detection is less understood [3, 4].


Using infrared 1064nm and 1320nm wavelength laser  scanning optical photon methods (LSOP) from the backside of  the die while the pads of the structure are electrically  exercised (similar to the original TDDB stress testing), the  BEOL ULK film stack structure is kept intact and no added  electrical stress or incident ion beam is introduced to the test  site that might cause the defect to “heal”. These methods, including the use of solid immersion lenses (SIL) have been  previously reported [5,6, 7,8, 9, 10, 11]. This way, the fail can  be electrically compared before and after LSOP to insure that  no electrical characteristic of the fail changed during the  analysis.


Figure 1: Vcrit (starting voltage of MOS device degradation  vs. device generations [3]


Figure 1 shows the threshold voltage shifts in MOS  devices reported on successive technology nodes [3].


For the first time, it can be reported that subtle TDDB  type failures at 22nm BEOL technology nodes and below can  be due to defects that cannot be observed during brightfield or


darkfield transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging  but rather detected only during TEM elemental mapping. The  discovery of these types of subtle defects provide important  reliability yield learning as well as BEOL process  improvements.


Most importantly, it can be shown that these subtle TDDB  type failures at 22nm BEOL technology nodes and below are  not related to the methods to suppress the copper diffusion  essential for improved electromigrations performaance and  lower TDDB failure rates.


Without the technique highlighted here to identify the root  cause of TDDB failures in 22nm and below technologies, questions as to a possible relationship between the methods to  suppress the copper diffusion and the root cause of TDDB  failures would exist.


The root cause analysis results presented here  demonstrate there is no linkage between these copper  diffusion suppression methods and root cause of TDDB and  electromigration failures.


Extensive TDDB reliability testing employed on 22nm  back end of line (BEOL) technologies and below are  employed with fifteen metallization levels combined with  ULK dielectric films with specialized test structures. These  structures pose real challenges in defect localization and root  cause analysis.


It has been well documented that an incident ion or  electron beam on these low dielectric constant k films can  cause shrinkage and voids [1, 2, 3, 4].


Even an electron beam as low as 1kV accelerating voltage  is known to cause voids in these ULK films, thereby masking  or healing the TDDB defect.


Just to perform BEOL SEM inspection/nanoprobing to  find the defect, the structure is required to be delayered, with  the real risk of altering the defect to be analyzed.


For these reasons, BEOL SEM nanoprobing/SEM inspection  cannot be employed on 22nm node and below technologies to  find these defects.


In contrast, using a 1064nm or 1320nm wavelength  infrared laser scanning optical photon (LSOP) tool from the  die backside with SIL lenses maintains the integrity of the  BEOL structure. With probes contacting the pads and  exercsing the TDDB test site structure, there is an independent  means of insuring the defect is not altered during the LSOP  localization.


Once the defect is localized, then topdown delayering and  SEM inspection at < 1keV can be performed to identify the  defect followed by TEM cross sectional analysis.


Even with these precautions, shrinkage and void  formation in the ULK dielectric films is routinely observed. However, the localized defect is not affected and can be  analyzed incidental to these secondary effects. The low keV  incident SEM inspection is only performed after the defect has


been localized using the LSOP techniques previously  described [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11].


These leading edge technologies routinely employ  multiple levels of ULK film stacks as part of their BEOL  metallization designs to attain the low dielectric k properties  for device performance


In addition to the multiple levels of ULK film stacks  employed in the BEOL metallization design, these leading  edge 22nm node and below technologies employ two different  methods to suppress the copper diffusion in the copper  interconnects [14, 15, 16, 17].


One method to suppress electromigration diffusion is  through the deposition of cobalt tungsten phosphate (CoWP) on the copper land surface and/or doping the copper seed layer  of the interconnect with manganese, significant improvements  in electromigration performance can be realized.


The second method to suppress electromigration is  by  doping manganese into the copper interconnect liner copper  seed layer via a physical vapor deposition process (PVD) followed by a manganese segregation step to the top copper  surface.


These electromigration performance improvements are  shown by technology node in  Figure 2 [15, 16]

TDDB Representative Failure Analysis


The TDDB defect localized from the die backside with  multiple ULK levels on this large serpentine-comb TDDB  structure is kept electrically intact during LSOP localization  techniques using SIL imaging to insure the defect is not  altered or “healed” during this process.


Figure  6 shows the backside IR image of a localized  TDDB defect from the die backside LSOP techniques with  SIL imaging.


Until the defect location is identified from the backside of  this fifteen level BEOL build TDDB structure involving ULK  dielectric films, the investigator has no idea where the TDDB  failure is located.


Next, this 300μm by 300μm large structure on this fifteen  level BEOL build is next delayered and SEM inspected at the  previously identified site shown in Figure 7. Even with an  overlay of the CAD layout with the LSOP localized site, the  degree of uncertainty of the failing region is still 0.5μm by


0.5 μm in size: very large for 22nm and below technologies.


Figure 7 shows an SEM view taken at less than 1keV of  the localized defect shown in Figure 6 to avoid shrinkage or  void formation in the ULK levels.


Figure 6 Backside IR image of TDDB defect localized in  200μm by 300μm size test macro.


Special precautions are followed to avoid ULK shrinkage/void  formation during this SEM inspection.


Using circuit overlay information in combination with the  backside localized TDDB fail site, any exposure of the ULK


to the incident electron beam, even at sub 1keV voltages can  be minimized.


Previous attempts with SEM nanoprobing to identify the  root cause of these BEOL defects were not successful due to  issues of ULK shrinkage during incident electron beam/FIB  ion beam effects as well as the effects of delayering multiple  BEOL metallaization levels without affecting the electrical  integrity of the structure itself.


Figure 7: Following backside localization of intact BEOL  ULK structure shown in Figure 6, topdown delayering and  low keV ( < 1keV) SEM inspection of same area shows TDDB  defect.


Following this sub 1kEV SEM topdown inspection, the  TDDB defect is next analyzed using transmission electron  microscopy (TEM).


In this case, the TEM of the FIB cut lamella may exhibit  ULK shrinkage and voiding as a result of the incident FIB ion  beam during TEM lamella sample preparation but the original  TDDB defect is not affected.


Figure 8 shows the FIB induced voids and shrinkage in  the ULK dielectric level following this TEM lamella sample  preparation.


The TDDB defect itself is not affected during this TEM  sample preparation using a FIB liftout technique.

No indications of the TDDB defect are disclosed in either  TEM imaging mode.

TEM Elemental Image Mapping


TEM image mapping of the TDDB defect shown in  Figure 10 was able to document and elementally identify the  chemical makeup of the defect. This defect was elementally  identified as copper  bridging the adjacent metal lands and was  not related to the copper manganese or CoWP cap layer


material additions that slow down the copper diffusion  reaction.


Figure 10 (highlighted box) shows the TEM elemental  mapping image where the TDDB defect was not apparent and


09.


where conventional STEM and darkfield TEM imaging in


T


Figure 9 failed to confirm the presence of this copper bridging  defect.


Figure 10: TEM elemental image mapping of TDDB fail site  indicated by box (left) as compared to reference, non failing  area (right).


This example, repeated on other 22nm TDDB defects, demonstrates the LSOP backside approach to localize a TDDB  defect in a ULK BEOL metallization level. This approach  validates the TEM elemental maping technique employed to  find and analyze the defect.


Most importantly, the elemental makeup of the defect, copper, is unrelated to the manganese line doping or CoWP  cap layers employed to suppress the copper diffusion reaction  and improve electromigration/TDDB characteristics.


22nm BEOL Process Yield Improvement


The importance of this TDDB BEOL defect detection  approach is underscored by the emergence of CuMn line  doping and CoWP cap layers to suppress copper diffusion and  enhance electromigration performance for 32nm and below  BEOL interconnects [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17].


Knowing the elemental makeup of the TDDB defect is  essential in improving both yield improvement as well  reliability defect learning.


In addition, knowing the root cause of the TDDB defect


and that it is unrelated to CuMn liner doping as well as CoWP  cap layer deposition further validates these process


improvements for enhancing electromigration lifetimes and


TDDB performance.


The method described here for BEOL TDDB defect  detection complements the analysis performed on  electromigration reliability detractors on 22nm BEOL  hardware.


By understanding the root cause of these 22nm BEOL


TDDB failures, this  technique enhances and complements the


learning obtained from the reliability electromigration analysis  of these BEOL interconnects.


The electro migration performance enhancement for both  CoWP and CuMn alloy additions is due to the suppression of  the copper diffusion on the metal surface and is different  between narrow lines and wide lines [15, 16]. The defect  detection method described here for time to dielectric  breakdown (TDDB) is also applicable for electromigration  defect detection and root cause analysis of the source of these  failures.


The smaller feature sizes associated with advanced  technologies nodes are exacerbated for narrow lines as  compared to wider lines for liner coverage and copper fill  quality. The ability to differentiate defects involving these  interconnects with ULK dielectric films employing these  process improvements cannot be overstated.


The emergence of CuMn additions to BEOL 22nm BEOL  interconnects for enhanced electromigration reliability  performance [12, 13, 14, 15, 16] highlights this method of  TDDB BEOL defect detection for ULK levels.


This technique is also applicable to selective CVD cobalt  capping with PVD Ta(N) and CVD cobalt liners [17].


The ability to localize the TDDB reliability defect in  22nm and below BEOL technologies and  elementally map its  chemical makeup enables the identification of its process  source. In the case cited among others, it has been shown that  the copper manganese additions to the interconnection liner as  well as the cobalt tungsten phosphorous capping layers to  suppress copper diffusion are not related to the TDDB  failures.


Knowing the chemical makeup of these TDDB defects (and by extension to electronmigration type failures) enables  the implementation of the necessary BEOL process fixes to  further improve reliability as well as address process yields.


Most importantly, the elemental analysis unambigusouly  determines precisely what BEOL process step requires  remedial action.


1) Time to Dielectric Breakdown Stress (TDDB) is an  effective method in identifying interlevel and intralevel  failures, especially involving ULK dielectric films of  22nm and below technologies.


Two scans were performed at a speed of 240 μm/s. The  resulting cavities were analyzed with a LEICA DCM 3D  confocal microscope and further inspected with SEM and  PFIB. Typical results are shown in Fig. 5 for a cavity created  with a laser pulse energy of 750 μJ in 156 seconds. The cavity  measures approx. 340 x 255 μm2 and is 180 μm deep. Hence, the laser ablation rate is ~ 1.1 x 105 μm3/s. The cavity shows  significant amounts of re-deposited material and considerable  tapering of the side walls in the upper 80 μm. The latter  relates to the fact that the laser is focused 80 μm below the  sample surface and correlates with the beam broadening at the  sample surface. The objective numerical aperture of 0.52, corresponds with an half opening angle θ of 31degrees which  coincides with the measured (Fig. 5) sidewall slope of ~ 30 0 . In a second series of experiments, cavities were created with  an optimized scanning strategy that included a final laser  ablation step to further prepare the side wall giving access to  the TSV’s. An initial coarse material removal step was used to  create a ~ 450 x 450 μm2, 370 μm deep cavity. Subsequently, a series of 500 μm/s line scans at a lower pulse energy (12.7 μJ) were performed to create a s 150 μm x 50 μm x 150 μm  deep cavity with straighter sidewalls near the TSV. The large  size of the laser machined cavity avoids any shadowing of  electrons during subsequent EBSD analysis. The total laser  preparation time for this two-step approach was ~ 15 minutes.

To summarize these results, the nanosecond laser process used  in these experiments creates damage both in the silicon  substrate and in the Copper filled TSV’s with an estimated  HAZ of ~ 3 μm. From these experiments it is concluded that a  safety distance of ~ 5 μm has to be respected to ensure an  artifact-free inspection of the relevant device structures.


The subsequent FIB milling procedure begins by first  preparing a vertical cross section. Next, the 3 μm thick  damage layer (HAZ) must be removed. A final step prepares  the region of interest with a surface quality sufficient for  structural analysis. In Fig. 11, these steps are illustrated for a  PFIB based process. After in-situ deposition of a platinum  layer of 80 x 60 x 6 μm3 to protect the top of the TSV  structure (15 minutes @ 59 nA and 30 KeV), a coarse  cleaning cross section (180 x 30 μm2) was performed in 10  minutes at 1.3 μA. This was followed by an 8 minute medium  cleaning at 420 nA to arrive at a truly vertical cross-section (150 x 10 μm2). A final cleaning cross section, performed at  59 nA while rocking the sample, took 10 minutes to remove  the surface topography (curtaining).


To appreciate the final sample surface quality, EBSD analysis  was performed on the TSV cross section:

The result is shown in Fig. 12. Excellent indexing across the  entire TSV is observed, even for the small copper grains at the  bottom of the TSV. Despite the non-ideal shape of the laser  machined cavity, significant laser-induced re-deposition, and  the large HAZ produced during laser processing, the PFIB  provides a surface suitable for direct imaging and EBSD  analysis in a relatively short amount of time.


With optimized milling parameters, this final PFIB milling  process takes 43 minutes, which, when combined with the  laser processing time, yields a total sample preparation time of ~ 60 minutes. Compared to a ns laser + LMIS Ga FIB  workflow, the overall FIB sample preparation time is reduced  from 262 to 43 minutes, assuming that with the Ga-FIB these  same steps are performed using a beam current of 65 nA and  an identical amount of material is removed. However, in this  example the laser ablation conditions are not optimized in  terms of cavity wall verticality. Optimizing the laser  processing to produce vertical side walls (by tilting the  sample) further shortens the total processing time by  eliminating the first step discussed above. Furthermore, as less  material has to be removed, shadowing of EBSD signal is  minimized, allowing the FIB milled boxes be reduced from  150 μm to ~ 100 μm. Under these conditions the PFIB and  Ga-FIB preparation processes would require 13 and 28  minutes, respectively.

Integrated fs-laser ablation workflow


A (main chamber) integrated femtosecond laser solution is  significantly more expensive but offers some unique  advantages over a nanosecond laser solution. First, because fslaser ablation is largely a-thermal, very little damage is done  to the sample. Second, navigation to the region of interest and  even fault detection can be performed in a “laser slice & SEM  view” mode with slice steps of less than 200 nm [9]. To arrive  at this spatial resolution the laser parameters have to be  carefully tuned to ensure that the intensity of the beam tail is  well below the ablation threshold of the material. Under these  conditions the ablation rate is in the range of 3 x 103 μm3/s, and volumes of up to 107 μm3 can be removed and inspected  in 3 dimensions in less than 3 hours. Finally, operating under  vacuum helps to significantly reduce sample contamination  due to re-deposition and clean cross sections can be obtained  that can be readily observed by SEM (see Fig. 13).


As with ns-lasers, the fs-laser can also operate at high  fluences, achieving material removal rates of up to 106 μm3/s. To illustrate, Fig. 14 (left) shows a 0.1 mm3 via machined in a  silicon sample in less than 15 minutes using a femto second  laser. Bottom and side walls of laser machined features can be  further cleaned and smoothened using more appropriate  processing parameters as illustrated in Fig. 14 (right). Actual  material removal rates are highly dependent on the material  being processed. For instance, figure 15 shows a 0.75 mm3

Today, no commercial integrated fs-laser/SEM or fslaser/SEM/FIB systems exist, the results presented here are  from in-house experimental platforms. Compared to a  FIB/SEM system with a ns-laser integrated in the load-lock, a  load-lock integrated fs-laser does not offer any advantages  and, thus, has no commercial interest. Integration would have  to be in the main chamber to benefit from above mentioned  slice & view capability and the easy navigation thanks to the  real time SEM observation before and during the laser  ablation process. For this type of integration, some practical  issues have to be resolved as well, the most important being  the potential contamination of SEM/FIB columns and
