during the laser ablation process. Simple engineering  solutions have already been implemented addressing the bulk  of these issues.


Xe-PFIB vs. Ga LMIS FIB milling


二


In conjunction with a first laser ablation preparation step, both  classical Ga-FIB and more novel PFIB milling can be used for  damage clean-up and final sample finish. However, a PFIB  based method offers several unique advantages:


Given its extended ion current range, the PFIB process is  typically 20-50 times faster than a LMIS Ga-FIB process. This  increased milling speed offers an overall, variable sample  preparation time saving which directly translates into  appreciated cycle time and costs savings. Alternatively, at  equal sample preparation time, the PFIB process allows  preparing much larger cross-sectional surfaces for subsequent  analysis and/or relaxing the laser ablation process  specifications in terms of laser placement accuracy, laser  focusing and ablation characteristics (amount of re-deposition, side wall angle). This, in turn, translates into ease of use and  higher sample preparation success rates.


An appreciable benefit of a PFIB milling process, either in  conjunction with, or without a laser ablation process, is its  ability to create a large area TEM lamella in a reasonable time  and with sufficient quality. Even if a laser ablation process  can remove the bulk material around the final TEM lamella  very fast, one has to accept several microns of safety margins  due to the finite laser spot size (> 10 μm) and its limited depth  of focus. Suppose a 50 μm thick lamella region has been  prepared by laser ablation or any other technique (mechanical

In this experiment no milling optimization has  been done and no sample rocking has been applied to suppress  curtaining. Finally, Xe ion induced sample damage is ~ 25% less than that  of Ga ions. Several experiments, including TEM-EDX and  XPS (see Figs. 17 and 18) have shown that for top down  sputtering the damage layer thickness is 54 and 14 nm for 30  and 5 KeV ion energy, respectively, and that ~ 7 and 5 % Xe  is incorporated in these damage layers. For grazing angle  sputtering (TEM lamella preparation case) these damage layer  thicknesses reduce to 18 and 5 nm. TRIM Monte Carlo  simulations confirm these trends and differences between Ga  and Xe ions.

In this study different sample preparation methods for  characterization and failure analysis of 3D stacked or  packaged devices have been reviewed. Plasma-FIB based  sample preparation is ideally suited for the preparation and  analysis of structures such as TSV’s, bumps, bondwires and  UBM layers that are readily accessible and not (deeply) buried  in a package or underneath several stacked dies. Plasma-FIB  lamella preparation for large area TEM analysis is also  possible. 50 x50 μm2 lamella of ~100 nm thickness can be  prepared in relatively short times (< 2 hrs). When Xe-ions are  used the damage layer is approximately 25% less than that  obtained with classical LMIS Ga-FIB milling.


For analysis of packaged devices and buried devices or  interfaces, chip access requires a first step of bulk material  removal that, in view of material removal rates and the  volume to be removed, is best done with a laser ablation  process. Such laser process step, however, needs to be  combined with a more site specific FIB milling process step  not only to remove laser induced damage and re-deposited  material but also to further approach the region of interest that  given the relatively poor spatial resolution of lasers cannot be  done with the laser step alone.


It is shown that an (inexpensive) stand-alone ns laser set-up  can be used effectively for the coarse material removal and  that the HAZ zone in silicon is limited to ~ 3 μm. If the laser  created trench respects a distance of > 5 μm with respect to Cu  filled TSV’s, no significant changes in Cu grain structures  occur as evidenced by EBSD measurements. When  generalizing this argument, one can conclude, or safely  assume, that a stand-alone ns laser ablation + PFIB workflow  provides an efficient means for sample preparation if one  respects sufficient spatial safety margins: 500 x 500 x 300 μm3 cavities can be prepared within 15 minutes by laser  ablation and a PFIB finish of a full 500 x 300 μm2 X-section  can be realized within ~ 50 minutes when assuming a 10 μm  laser cavity-ROI safety distance.


It is concluded that a PFIB is a very useful tool to facilitate  Failure Analysis of complex packaged or stacked devices in  conjunction with a laser ablation technique: in view of sample  preparation time constraints, a laser + PFIB based process is  faster than a laser + Ga-FIB process and more importantly, is  more flexible in dealing with laser process imperfections as  relatively large amounts of materials (re-deposited materials, HAZ etc.) can be removed in times still compatible with  today’s FA lab targets.

Fast and Precise 3D Tomography of TSV by Using Xe Plasma FIB


Tomáš Hrnčíř and Lukáš Hladík


TESCAN, Libušina třída 21, Brno, Czech Republic   tomas.hrncir@tescan.cz, Tel. +420 547130468


3D tomography of TSVs was performed by combining Xe  plasma FIB milling and lift-out techniques. This approach  allows analyzing the structure of TSVs in detail using a  method faster than the usual 3D tomography by Ga FIB and  more precise than X-ray tomography. Both well-filled TSVs  and TSVs with voids were analyzed and the results were  compared. The analysis procedure was optimized in order to  reduce the analysis time and to increase the throughput. The  lift-out of the analyzed block of material was performed to  obtain 90º angle between TSV and the ion beam axes, which is  critical to reduce the curtaining effect and which allowed to  increase FIB beam current significantly, reducing the analysis  time.


The Xe plasma ion source integrated on TESCAN FERA3  plasma FIB-SEM instrument offers an extremely high milling  and material removal rate, which is important in many  application fields, such as failure analysis in the semiconductor  industry (e.g. through-silicon vias or flip chip cross sectioning) or MEMS fabrication and analysis [1]. The high resolution of  SEM column complements the intrinsic advantages of the Xe  plasma ion source. SEM allows observation of the sample  during the milling process by utilizing two separate specially  designed backscattered electron detectors and a precise endpoint detection based on SEM or FIB image information. Coupled with advanced control software, a series of complex  tasks can be automated.


One of these automated tasks is FIB-SEM 3D tomography [2]. Traditionally it has been performed by using Ga beam for  sample slicing [2, 3], with a practical analytical volume of  approximately 103 μm3. To obtain the voxel resolution below  10 nm, low FIB current is necessary, which makes the analysis  time of the small volume proportionally longer. For such voxel  sizes FIB has to be operated at probe current below 100 pA


[3], but in that case the analytical volume is limited because of  the increased FIB milling time. Analytical volumes can be  increased by increasing the FIB probe current to units of nA. This allows one to obtain reasonable milling precision (voxel  size ~1003 nm3), while keeping the FIB milling time as short as  possible. However, when the dimension of analytical volume  approaches to ~1003 μm3, Ga FIB milling time becomes


impractical; it can be several days long. Moreover, the total  analysis time is increased by SEM imaging time. Both milling  and imaging processes have to be optimized in order to  achieve the minimum analysis time. Neither process should be  dominant in terms of the time required. In a case where the  image acquisition is too long when compared to FIB slicing  time, scanning speed and the electron beam current should be  increased. This is usually fulfilled by using SEM at an  optimum performance, where the imaging time is short and all  important structures on the sample are still distinguishable. However the limiting factor is usually the FIB slicing time, making increased FIB processing speed most desirable.


Failure analysis at the package level has traditionally relied on  methods like mechanical polishing or broad ion beam etching.  These methods are broadly destructive, difficult and timeconsuming. FIB-SEM 3D Tomography with a Ga beam does  not have these drawbacks; it is site specific, but as mentioned  in the previous paragraph, is too slow for volumes approaching ~1003 μm3. The dramatically increased current of Xe plasma  ion beam and also approximately 30% higher sputtering yield  of Xe ions as compared to Ga ions [1] allows to use powerful  FIB 3D Tomography method, while still maintaining the  advantage of traditional FIB operations.  These advantages  include limited sample damage and the ability to analyze  multiple sites of interest within a relatively small sample area. The plasma FIB method yields sufficient data density to locate  even a small failure site within the analyzed volume while  extending the FIB 3D tomography technique to much bigger  volumes.


Alternative 3D methods to FIB-SEM tomography of TSV  include confocal microscopy [4], which only allows surface  imaging and  X-ray tomography, which has the significant  advantage of being generally non-destructive in the region of  interest, but has a spatial resolution limit under best conditions  on the order of several tens of nm [5]. Minimum size of a  distinguishable void in TSV is around 100 nm [6], so X-ray  tomography is not suitable for analysis of nano-sized defects.  In this case, FIB is an appropriate technique. Another  advantage of FIB-SEM 3D tomography against X-ray  tomography is the possibility to obtain precise information  about the crystal orientation and the material contrast, depending on the detector used for SEM imaging.


FIB-SEM 3D tomography of TSV structures is a typical task  where the analytical volume is greater than what would be


practical for a Ga FIB instrument. Despite the limitations, this  task has been performed using a Ga FIB [7], although  requiring very long analysis times. As already mentioned, this  problem can be easily overcome by using the Xe plasma FIB  with approximately 50 times faster milling rates [1]. However  due to the material composition these samples are difficult for  sputtering by plasma FIB, especially polycrystalline copper  TSVs which show a strong curtaining effect when milled by  plasma FIB at high currents [8].


One obvious method of removal of this curtaining effect is to  perform milling of the sample from two different directions of  the ion beam towards the cross sectioned surface [8]. The  same method is commonly used in current broad ion beam  milling instruments. Even though this is very effective for  simple cross sections of relatively big structures like TSV, it is  unfortunately not very suitable for 3D tomography where it is  necessary to mill up to several hundreds of slices with the  well-defined position and identical thickness. It is definitely  more precise to perform the slicing without the movement of  the sample stage (tilting), as the stage movement would  introduce significant errors of the slice position and thickness. As the stage precision can generally be worse than the slice  thickness, it would complicate post processing of acquired 3D  data and cause hardly correctable distortions on the rendered  volume. Generally, milling from two different angles is  practically very challenging for creating equidistant and welldefined slices with the thickness in the order of tens or  hundreds of nanometers, as the depth of the curtaining can be  higher than the slice thickness. The depth observed by AFM  on 150 µm deep TSV with the diameter 50 µm (polished by  plasma FIB) was around 2 µm [8]. Therefore it would be much  easier to perform 3D tomography by milling from one  direction only and to reduce the curtaining effect by using  another method.


Another possible method is using the gas injection system  during the milling, which has shown to be very promising but  still requires further study. Simultaneous gas injection during  the milling process can significantly reduce the curtaining  effect. This effect depends upon both the gas type and the  sample material but can be quite difficult to tune for the best  performance on a TSV sample. Because of these difficulties, we have chosen the former method, which is more  straightforward on TSV samples.


To minimize the curtaining artifacts while milling from one  direction only, the choice of that milling direction is crucial. The angle between the ion beam and TSV axis should be 90° for the best result, like this TSV could be sectioned with the  ion beam advancing along TSV axis or from the side of TSV [7, 9]. When applying this optimum milling angle and by using  the fast plasma FIB, FIB-SEM 3D tomography can be applied  on TSVs and the information about TSV geometry, filling  quality and Cu crystalline structure can be obtained, while the  analysis time could be significantly shorter than when using  state of the art Ga FIB instrument.


There are several methods how to prepare TSV sample for FIB  milling at the optimum milling angle.  For example it is  possible to cut or cleave the sample close to TSV or to  combine these methods with the mechanical polishing [4,5]. However the preparation can be completed inside plasma FIB  system using the lift-out technique. The advantage of this  technique is that the analyzed volume can be separated from  the sample and the result of 3D tomography is not influenced  by the effects of the sample, e.g. dependence of the image  signal on the depth or redeposition of the sample material. By  using plasma FIB for the preparation of a TSV block and for  the lift-out, we can take advantage of its fast milling rate and  avoid using macroscopic methods like cutting or cleaving, which create a larger damage profile and require additional  tools.  Importantly, the analyzed volume can also be oriented  in the required direction during the lift-out process easily.


Results and discussion


The block of the material with the volume approximately  1003 μm3 was removed from the sample by using plasma FIB  milling and welding to the nanomanipulator tip by platinum  deposition (Figure 1). The preparation time was approximately  3 hours for the milling at the FIB beam current of 1 µA, followed by approximately 30 minutes for the lift-out and  subsequent attachment of the block to the surface of a clean Si  sample by another platinum deposition and final cut to release  the nanomanipulator (Figure 2). Next, the sample was removed  through an automated load-lock, rotated to the appropriate  direction for FIB milling (Figure 2) and inserted back at this  different orientation.


Figure 1: Extracted part of the sample 1; the block containing  four TSVs is attached on the nanomanipulator tip during the  lift-out procedure. Secondary electron image at SEM beam  energy 10 kV.


Two examples of 3D tomography applied to the typical TSV  structures will be discussed. On the sample 1 TSVs were wellfilled, while on the sample 2 there were relatively big voids  inside the Cu filling material. The length of one TSV was  100 μm and the diameter was 10 um for both samples. For  both samples, we have selected a group of four TSVs for the  lift-out and 3D tomography process, located on a rectangular  pattern. The length of TSVs and their distance in the pattern  determined the volume for the analysis.


In the case of the sample 1 (well-filled TSVs), the distance  between TSVs in the pattern was 40 µm. Dimensions of the  analyzed sample block after the lift-out process was  approximately 140x100x90 μm3 (Figure 1 and 2), which was  enough to contain four TSVs. FIB probe current was set to  50 nA at beam energy 30 keV, cubic voxel edge 260 nm and  voxel resolution of the whole analyzed volume (which was  covering the block and its vicinity) was 768x768x339. All  slices were acquired automatically by 3D tomography data  acquisition routine installed on TESCAN FERA3 XMH  instrument. Total analysis time was 8 hours, of which milling  time was 5 hours (339 slices, each one 260 nm thick) and SEM  imaging time 3 hours. SEM images were saved at a pixel dwell  time of 32 μs and pixel resolution of 768x768 (total saving  time for one image was approximately 30 seconds at SEM  probe current 550 pA).


Figure 2: Block of the sample 1 material containing four TSVs  is attached on the surface of Si sample. The arrow points in  the direction of FIB milling during 3D tomography data  acquisition. Secondary electron image at SEM beam energy  10 kV.


Backscattered Electron (BSE) detector and In-Beam  Backscattered Electron (In-Beam BSE) detector (placed inside


SEM column) were used for SEM imaging simultaneously. Both BSE and In-Beam BSE detectors are based on YAG  crystals and provide a distinct material contrast and crystalline  contrast on copper as well (see Figure 3 for a typical BSE  image during the slicing process of sample 1).


In the case of sample 2 (TSVs with voids), the distance  between TSVs in the pattern was 100 µm, which was 2.5 times  longer distance than on the sample 1. To be able to fit four  TSVs into the analyzed block, the block size had to be  increased to approximately 230x170x150 µm (Figure 4). As  the slice quality on the sample 1 was perfectly acceptable at  FIB probe current 50 nA and it was necessary to analyze the  bigger block on the sample 2, we have increased FIB beam  current to 300 nA. This allowed decreasing of FIB milling  time significantly. On the sample 1, FIB milling time was  5 hours (339 slices). On the sample 2, we have kept the slice  thickness, but we have increased the number of slices to 573. In spite of this increase of the analyzed volume and the  number of slices, we were able to reduce FIB milling time to  4 hours only while the quality of slices was still acceptable and  comparable to what we have obtained by milling at FIB probe  current 50 nA. Quality of slices on sample 2 is shown in the  Figure 5.

I. Introduction


With increased competitiveness in semiconductor industry, maintaining profitability is a challenge. With more players in


IESRRSSSI


量


OOD


the market, foundries experience a shortening life span to


口


enjoy the high premiums of being the first source. This trend


Connect Rx


is expected to worsen and hence it is critical to achieve faster


日


卯


product time to market. One critical step in the yield learning


唱


cycle is to carry out physical failure analysis (PFA) to provide  understanding of defect mechanisms in the manufacturing  process. However, the whole PFA process with delayering,


爸


Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Focused Ion Beam (FIB) analysis can amount to a long turn-around time. With  limited resource in the lab, the PFA throughput can often be  the bottle neck for yield improvement.


To improve PFA turn-around time, selecting good candidates  is a prerequisite. With the help of layout-aware scan diagnosis, potential defect locations (i.e., diagnosis candidates) can be  effectively isolated. More recently, volume diagnosis  techniques [1] have been developed to analyze the whole  population of diagnosis candidates, and identify the ones that  represent systematic issues. However, even with volume  diagnosis, many a time a large amount of diagnosis candidates  can be identified – that is, much more than what can possibly  be processed in the PFA lab. Thus, it is critical to carefully  select which candidates are most suitable for PFA, to ensure  successful PFA. Carefully selecting candidates can also reduce  the PFA processing time and improve throughput. Conventionally, this selection is simply based on a simple set  of rules of thumb, which can capture some of the important  aspects for the “ease of PFA”, but is not always enough to sift  out the best candidates.


In this work, we argue that the cost of PFA processing should  be directly taken into account while making the PFA candidate  selection. With a focus specifically on open failure candidates, we take an extra effort in defining the ease of PFA processing  by closely modeling the PFA processing flow and make  detailed estimation of the processing cost involved in every  step. Hence, each potential PFA candidate is evaluate by its  potential processing cost, even before any actual PFA  processing is carried out and the ones with the lowest  estimated cost is the one we choose for PFA. With this costmodel based PFA selection at its heart, we come up with a  comprehensive methodology of diagnosis candidate selection  for open failure candidates. Conventional candidate selection  criteria, volume diagnosis indicators and the cost model are all  taken into account in this flow. With the help of such a


procedure, we can quickly identify the potentially easiest  candidate and achieve shortest turn-around time without  compromising the learning to be gathered from the PFA.


The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2  discusses the general PFA procedure to process open failure  candidates in logic circuits, highlighting the highly regular  steps that can be repeated for each layer in each candidate. Then, in Section 3, we review the common practice in PFA  candidate selection before proposing our comprehensive  selection flow that aims to filter out the easiest candidate in  terms of processing cost. Section 4 evaluates this methodology  by several case studies. After discussing potential future work  in Section 5, we conclude this paper in Section 6.


II. The PFA Procedure


With the help of layout-aware scan diagnosis, various defects  in a chip can be effectively isolated by software simulation  based on the collected test fail log, the design net list and test  patterns. The potential open failure locations, or open failure  PFA candidates, can be exported in the form of net traces, which contain a set of polygons for each metal and via layer  where the open failure may happen. One of such an example is  visualized in Figure 1, where a suspected failure net is  highlighted in the layout.


For open candidates, a typical process flow for failure analysis  is shown in Figure 2. The FA process starts with carefully  reading the diagnosis report. Then the trace files are loaded  into a layout viewing/analysis tool to allow for the topographic  analysis of the failing net. Based on the analysis of the wire  connection scenarios, the normal voltage contrast at each layer  can be predicted and listed in a table as a reference for the  subsequent layer-by-layer inspection. The layer-by-layer


Figure 1. Logic diagnosis candidate call-out by scan  diagnosis


inspection contains a sequence of sample de-processing, SEM  inspection and decision making. The inspection usually starts  from the top metal layer of the net, and is repeated as a cycle  until the failure location can be pin-pointed. As we de-process  down each layer, the passive voltage contrast (PVC) can be  checked for indication on the interconnectivity of the  underlying layers. In general, a metal line connected to the  active layer (RX) will show up as relatively bright in PVC, those connected to gate (PC) will show up as grey, and those  floating will show up as relatively dark [2]. This type of  voltage contrast is caused by the difference in the easiness for  the electrons to flow from the substrate to the exposed metal  parts to compensate the e-beam induced positive charge. In both cases, by following the suspect-area narrow-down  procedure, PFA analysis can be completed very quickly. One  may contend that the above two cases are ideal since the  suspect area quickly shrinks after a single cycle of delayering  and PVC inspection. It is true that for a different candidate, we  may well end up with a lot more cycles of repetitive  delayering and inspection. Wouldn't it be nice if one can  estimate, ahead of time, how quickly the suspected area can be  reduced during processing and then select candidate based on  this knowledge? We believe this is possible, thanks to the  highly regular steps of the PFA process on open candidates. In  the next section, we aim to demonstrate that with a little bit of  effort, not only can we gain valuable understanding about the  difficulty of each PFA candidate before actual processing, but  also outline all the possible scenarios to help guide the  decision-making during the PFA process.


III. Open Failure PFA Candidate Selection Flow


From the previous section, we can see that the PFA procedure  is complicated and may be time consuming. Thus, it is highly  critical that one make informed choice on which candidate  should be selected for failure analysis. In this section, we first  review the common practice for PFA candidate selection, before introducing our comprehensive candidate selection  flow.


A) Common Practice


Conventionally, once scan diagnosis is completed, one can  take all the candidates and make some manual filtering for  PFA candidates based on a set of reasonable criterion, such as: 1) High diagnosis score. High diagnosis score means that the  isolated candidate, if failing, can better explain the failure


M5


No


behavior of the circuit. It is always recommended to carry out


V4


Abnormal


V4 Under-etch


M4


PFA on candidates with higher diagnosis scores for better


V3 M3


VC


chance of finding the defect.


2) Shorter net length. A net call-out that covers a smaller


physical area is usually easier for delayering and SEM  inspection.


3) Fewer suspects for the defect. In scan diagnosis, for each  defect, it is common that multiple suspects can be called out  for a single defect. This can be due to insufficient information  from the test fail logs generated by the test pattern, or simply


0盲日


DRB


because that all the suspects will cause the same failing  behavior as shown in the test fail log. If too many suspects are  highlighted, the chance for finding the defect on each suspect  will be lowered.


4) Targeted failure mechanism. With the help of volume  diagnosis, based on a population of diagnosis reports, an  overview of the failure mechanisms can be generated. Hence it  is usually more meaningful to pick candidates that are  representing a specific, dominant mechanism.


All of these are helpful tips to start with. However, what is  missing is the consideration for the inherent difficulty of  processing the candidates -- that is, in the PFA processing, how fast we can zero in to the defect and identify it. This  essentially means that with the conventional flow, the actual  PFA processing time is largely up to sheer luck during the FA  process. This is especially inefficent at the beginning of a  technology node, when the number of possible PFA candidate  is far more than that can be possibly processed with a realistic  bandwidth.

B) Comprehensive PFA selection flow


Hence, we propose a more comprehensive methodology to  carry out PFA candidate selection. The overall flow is as  shown in Figure 6. On the diagnosis side, we rely on state-ofart layout-aware scan diagnosis to provide physical open  suspects, highlighted as sub-sections of a net. Then, volume  diagnosis techniques are adopted to focus on representative  failure mechanisms. Within the pool of candidates for the  failure mechanism of interest, we first apply a set of  conventional filtering criterion as described in the previous  subsection to reduce the total number of possible candidates. Afterwards, the processing cost of each candidate is estimated  based on a carefully constructed cost model. Then the  candidate with the lowest potential processing cost is selected  for PFA.


C) The Cost Model


At the core of the above PFA selection flow is a cost model  that strives to estimate the cost to process a candidate before  any actual PFA is carried out. One major challenge to estimate

In this work, we propose to do a  thorough evaluation of all the possible situations and calculate  a statistical expected cost for each sample. Hence, suppose the  total processing cost for each situation is ck, where k refers to  the k-th situation, and Pk is the probability for the actual defect  to be the k-th situation, the expected cost of the i-th sample Ci  can be calculated as:


k=1


Here, each situation refers to the case where the open defect  lies in one section of a metal line or via. For each FA sample, there is a finite set of possible situations, which can be  analyzed by layout analysis. For example, in Figure 3, there  are a total of 5 metal open situations (M3, M2a, M2b, M1a, M1b) and 4 via open situations (V2a, V2b, V1a, V1b). Hence  the expected cost of this sample is a weighted sum of the cost  in each of these 9 situations, and the weight is the probability

Situation Cost ck


For each specific situation, the location of the defect is already  known by assumption. Thus, we estimate the total processing  cost by emulating the flow of PFA processing, as described in  Section 2.  Because the flow includes repetitive delayering and  SEM inspection for each layer and an optional final step of  FIB cut, we express the estimated cost as:


l=1


where L is the total number of layers, Dl and Sl are the  delayering cost and SEM inspection cost for layer l, respectively. Usually, both Dl and Sl depend on the size of the  area of interest at that layer -- the larger the size, the higher the  cost is. Other fixed costs for processing a layer l like plasma  cleaning, sample cleaning and mounting are lumped together  as a fixed cost Fl.   If FIB cut is needed for the sample, the  cost is represented by Bk. Note that for each sample, typically  only one time of FIB cut is necessary at the end of the flow, and the cost of FIB is also usually related to size of the area of  interest.


For each situation, it is straight-forward to simulate the PFA  process for every layer from the top metal of the net. Given  the size of the area of interest (AOI) at a specific layer, the Dl


and Sl can be estimated, together with the potential PVC  situation. Since the PVC situation is definitive, one can further  narrow down the area of interest and proceed to delayer to the  next level. Note that each delayering step always stops at the  via layer so that the PVC of both the via and the under-lying  metal can be checked together. By repeating the sequence  until no further narrow down can be carried out -- usually by  reaching a layer where all the VC is dark, the sample has been  narrowed down to the minimal possible. If the failure  mechanism is still unclear, progressive FIB cut will be


adopted. This completes the situation cost simulation.

Relative Failure Probability


The other key aspect in estimating the expected processing  cost of a sample is to estimate the probability for each  situation to be the real failure situation. That is, we need to  analyze the relative failure probability for each of the possible  open location k. Since the defect location can be either on a  metal section or a specific via, we define Pk as:


Such a relative failure probability is essentially a normalized  ratio between the failure probability of the hypothetical defect


∑Ph=1


location (i.e., a metal segment or a via) and the sum of the  failure probability of all possible defect locations. Naturally Pk  sums up to 1. Here, a metal failure rate fl is assigned for each  metal layer l, while a via failure rate fv is assigned for each via  v. In our model, we assume the failure probability of a metal  segment is proportional to its length. Here, slk is the run length  of the defective metal segment lk. For candidate sample i, Lli is  the total run length of the net on metal layer l and Nvi is the  total number of Via v in the net.


The absolute failure rate fl for metal layer l and the via failure


L


rate fv for via v are fabrication process dependent variables and  hence can be estimated based on the physical properties of


Ck=∑(Dt+St+Fi)+Bk


each layer (e.g., metal width, via size, metal pitch, etc.), known process issues, PFA paretos and other existing  knowledge.


D) Optimal Candidate Selection


With the situation cost and relative failure probability models, one can statically calculate the expected processing cost (Ci) of any diagnosis candidate i. And by simply sorting Ci, the  best candidate for PFA processing can be selected.


It is important to note that the cost-model based selection only  handles the PFA processing cost and is orthogonal to certain  FA selection criteria like diagnosis score or dominant failure  mechanism. It however naturally incorporates physical aspects  like net length. Still, it is always feasible to adopt the  conventional FA filtering criteria first before leveraging this  cost model to make a final decision, as illustrated in Figure 6.

M4_1 will show up as grey. Based on the grey PVC, one can  arrow down the area of interest to the left side of the M4_1  polygon. This dramatically reduces the area of interest by  more than 9x from (4.5x2.55um2) to (2.54x0.5 um2). Afterwards, the process is repeated to delayer to expose  M3/V3 layer. In this case, M3_3 will show up as bright, as its  connection to RX is intact, while  M3_1/V3_1 will be dark as  they are floating. Note that in this step, the VC of M3_2 is  irrelevant as it is outside of the AOI, though it should be grey  as it is connected to PC. Because both M3_1 and V3_1 are  dark, and assuming only one open defect is present, we can  make the conclusion that V3_1 is not the culprit and the  subsequent AOI can be further narrowed down to V2_1/M2_1. As V2_1 and M2_1 are  on a single line, FIB cut can be  carried out to identify the root cause. Similar process is  repeated to fill up the table for all the other possible situations. It is interesting to note that once constructed, this Table 2 can  also be used as an aid to the FA engineers to guide their  processing and decision making in the actual PFA process.

V. Future Work


The case studies presented in the previous section  demonstrated that even manual execution of the proposed PFA  selection flow is capable of providing insights into the  difficulty of each potential PFA candidate and can help  improving the selection. However, such a flow is obviously  tedious and time consuming. What makes it most attractive is  the prospect of automating the whole flow in software. As the  PVC situation is definitive and only base on the physical  topology of the net polygons, it would be easy to devise an  algorithm to work off the physical representation of a design (e.g., LEF/DEF). The fact that the PVC driven candidate  processing can be formulated in a regular table in Table 2 is  proof that a software implementation is feasible. In that way, one can quickly scan through hundreds and thousands of  candidates and it will significantly improve the efficiency of  the analysis.  This will be the focus for our next steps.


VI. Conclusion


In this paper, we proposed a comprehensive PFA candidate  selection algorithm for open failure candidates. Leveraging the  physical design information that comes with layout-aware  diagnosis, the PFA de-processing flow is thoroughly emulated  to provide an accurate estimation for the processing cost of  each diagnosis candidate. Such estimated cost of each PFA  candidate sheds light onto the potential processing difficulty  of the candidate and is used to narrow down the best  candidates for efficient PFA processing. Case studies show  that the cost model closely matches with real world PFA turnaround time and the authors are working towards automating  the full flow in software to further improve the efficiency.

This paper presents two case studies, based on 32nm SiliconOn-Insulator (SOI) and 28nm bulk Si technology, on finding  the root cause of nanometer scale short failures using Passive


Voltage Contrast (PVC), Active Voltage Contrast (AVC) and  Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM). PVC/AVC is used


as precision localization technique that is critical for a  successful FA-TEM analysis. Combining planar TEM sample  preparation and high sensitivity Energy Dispersive


Spectroscopy (EDS) mapping, a small residual filament, which is not visible even at high resolution TEM, is found to


short two metal lines. The effective usage of voltage contrast  and TEM provides the need of high throughput, high  precision, and high resolution in the advanced FA lab that


serves leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing.


As semiconductor technology continues to advance to smaller  dimensions and more complex circuit designs, it is becoming


more challenging to perform a successful Failure Analysis (FA). In the competitive foundry business, high throughput is


expected along with high quality FA results. PVC/AVC has  been widely adopted in FA lab as an effective way to localize  the defect [1]. Compared to other localization techniques,


voltage contrast is fast and simple to use and yet it provides  accurate defect location to an individual contact or device for


subsequent TEM analysis. Test macros presented in this paper  are designed for yield learning and they consist of many  repeating structures. One of the challenges working on this


type of structures is that even the short failures could have the  electrical resistance as high as millions of ohms, which is


difficult for other fault isolation techniques such as Laser  Scanning Microscopy (LSM) or Photoemission Microscopy (PEM). Moreover, the defect area identified by LSM or PEM


is often in the range of microns. One of the critical  requirements for TEM analysis is to obtain a thin lamella,


typically around 100nm. In order to perform TEM analysis on  a nanometer scale defect, the defect location has to be known  precisely. In this paper, we present two case studies, one is


based on 32nm SOI and the other one is based on 28nm bulk  Si technology, both cases are short failures that were found by


using voltage contrast and TEM techniques.


Case Study 1


Test data on 32nm SOI technology showed increasing  defectivity at M1 level, more M1 short failures were seen on


the test macros that do not have CA (contact) underneath M1. The goal of this FA is to find the root cause of M1-M1 short  and understand how it is related to CA processes.


Figure 1a is the layout of the comb/serp structure. M1 lines


from comb and serp run parallel to each other and they are  separated by ultra-low-k dielectric material. When 1V was


applied between serp and comb, a 1.5E-7 amp leakage current  was detected.


FEI’s Dualbeam Focus Ion Beam (FIB) system 450s is used to  conduct PVC. This tool provides both high resolution SEM


imaging at accelerating voltage as low as 500V, and high  resolution FIB imaging at beam current as low as 7.7pA. To


successfully FIB mill M1 lines that are less than 50nm, excellent FIB imaging capability is essential. Using low beam  current is also very important as the M1 is exposed to FIB,


which could potentially destroy the defect if it lies on top of  the M1 lines. PVC can be done by either SEM or FIB


imaging. To minimize the FIB damage, SEM PVC was used  with low beam energy and current, while a high kV but low  beam current FIB was chosen to cut M1. Selective Carbon


Mill (SCM) was used to enhance the FIB milling and imaging  contrast. FEI’s Osiris, equipped with Super-X system [2], is


used for TEM analysis. The key advantage of this new EDS  system is higher elemental sensitivity, which allows the  detection of nanometer scale defects.

Although M1 line is not connected to ground, the line is long


enough for the electron charge to dissipate so that both comb  and serp lines are contrasted as bright. By keeping one of the  lines intact and FIB milling the other line via bisection


method, the M1-M1 short was finally localized within 3um, as  shown in Figure 1b. However, SEM inspections at various


conditions (2, 5, 20kV at both SE and BSE mode) did not  reveal any abnormality. Without knowing the exact location of  the failure, a planar TEM sample was prepared using the insitu lift-out technique. Compared to cross-sectional sample, the planar sample is thinned parallel to M1, which leaves the


isolated M1 lines entirely intact over a large area (~4um x  7um). Surprisingly, no defect was observed under either bright  field TEM or dark field STEM mode, see Figure 2a. Thanks to


the highly sensitive Super-X system, a small residual Titanium  filament was detected by EDS mapping, as shown in Figure


2b. The location of the short is exactly between the PVCisolated M1 lines.

Based on this FA, it was determined that the defect was  introduced from the previous CA processes, because of the  oxide CMP uniformity issue, the region without contacts was  polished faster which creates recessed area for the  subsequently deposited Titanium filament.


Case Study 2


As one of the top yield limiting defects in 28nm bulk Si  product, CA (contact) to PC (gate) short was submitted for


failure analysis. The test structure is comprised of two M1  combs interweaved among each other with thousands of CA  contacts leading to RX (ground).  Beneath the two M1 comb


structures is a nest of PC lines that run alongside all of the CA  contacts in order to test the short between PC and CA. Figure


3a shows the layout of this structure. After removing M1, PVC was first attempted at CA-PC level. In bulk Si  technology, all CA contacts are connected to ground, which


are contrasted as bright in FIB image. All PC lines are floating  and they show the dark contrast. Because of CA-PC short, PC


lines are contrasted as bright as CA contacts. In theory, once  the PC lines are isolated by FIB, the contrast will change from  bright to dark if the isolated portion is not shorted to CA. At


the end, CA-PC short can be found around the bright PC. However, FIB isolation within the long, bright PC proved to


be difficult. This is primarily due to how dense the CA  contacts are along the PC line. Figure 3b shows the isolated  PC line through typical PVC methods.

Since the early beginning of the integrated circuits, electromigration is a reliability issue of first interest. In 3-dimensionnal structures, electromigration is responsible for  the formation of voids in lines connected to the Through  Silicon Via (TSV). To our knowledge, this paper presents the  first in operando electromigration experiment in a Scanning  Electron Microscope (SEM) performed for 3D integration. The experimental protocol, including sample preparation and  temperature regulation, is detailed. A current of 25 mA is  injected in a structure heated at 350 °C for about 900 h. The  evolution of voids is monitored and explained. Void growth  occurs step by step, so that the microstructure may be assumed  to play a major role in the depletion mechanism. The behavior  of the electrical resistance is analyzed using the SEM  micrographs.


Development orientation of the microelectronics


3D integration is a solution that may enable to overcome the  limits of the conventional microelectronics. Through Silicon  Via (TSV) is one of the main technologies explored for the  compact stacking of chips. TSV role is to connect the BackEnd Of Line (BEOL) on the front side of a chip to the  ReDistribution Layer (RDL) on the back side. Whereas the  characteristic dimensions of conventional microelectronics  interconnects are of the order of hundreds of nanometers, it  has to be multiplied at least by a factor of ten for 3D  integration. Three main types of process flow are possible, depending at which stage the TSV are processed. In our case, they are processed after the Front-End Of Line (FEOL) and  the BEOL, and are named TSV last. It has to be noticed that  the thermal budget, hence the residual stress state through the  different dilatation coefficients, depends on the process. The  stress state impacts the materials properties, such as the atomic  diffusion coefficients.


Many physical phenomena can induce the failure of a  technology; therefore as 3D technologies become mature, their  reliability has to be studied.


Electromigration issues


Electromigration (EM), among other degradation mechanisms, may cause failure. It consists in the displacement of atoms by  momentum transfer from electrons. As always, the diffusion  mechanism is accelerated by temperature. For the 50 previous  years, EM has been extensively studied, first in the aluminum  lines and then in the copper interconnects. Black‘s law [1] gives the relation between the Mean Time To Failure (MTTF) and parameters like the current density (j), the temperature (T) and the energy needed for the diffusion of atoms (activation  energy, Ea), which depends on the diffusion paths:


(  MTTF = Aj-nexp(  )


(1)


For copper lines of the BEOL, the microstructure is a main  parameter [2], even if its importance varied with the shrinkage  of dimensions. EM mechanism is strongly dependent on the  interface between copper and the metallic barrier or between  copper and the passivation layer [3]. The crystallographic  grain orientation [4] has also a key role in the kinetics of  degradation.


The macroscopic consequences of EM are the formation of  voids and, sometimes, extrusions. As vacancies accumulate, the difference of volume between them and the atoms induces  a local tensile stress. Voids nucleate if the tensile stress  reaches a threshold. Conversely, the accumulation of atoms  builds-up the compressive stress and then extrusions form if a  critical stress value is exceeded. The voids growth induces an  increase of the electrical resistance value with the possibility  of opening the circuit. Blech [5] proves that the stress gradient  induces a metal ions backflow, which compensates more or  less the electromigration flux. In both cases of voids or  extrusions, the functionality of the device is lost or at least  distorted. Nowadays, the observation of extrusions is unusual  due to the mechanical limitations.


Furthermore, displacement of copper in area where the current  is near zero is observed in BEOL, with the mechanical stress  acting as a driving force. It is called reservoir effect. This  phenomenon is used to enhance the lifetime of the devices, since the metal ions in the reservoir replace the ions that are  removed at critical sites (above/beneath vias) [6].


Previous studies on electromigration in TSV


With 3D integration, technologies with different scales  coexist. Characteristic dimensions are in the order of hundreds  nanometers for BEOL, micrometers for RDL on the other side  of the chip, and tens of micrometers for 3D interconnects. Reliability issues are expected at the junctions of these  different technologies.


Frank et al. studied the technology of TSV last high density. They prove that killer defects are always located above or  beneath the TSV, never inside it [7]. This is explained mainly  by the small current densities due to the large section of the  TSV. It is also possible that the relatively small height of the  TSV allows Blech effect to occur. Indeed, interconnects are  immortal if the product of the current density j by the length L  is lower than a critical value [5]. For the studied technology  j.L is about 500 A/cm², which is almost an order of magnitude  less than the critical value (3000-4000 A/cm² for copper [8]). Moreover, the ends of metallic lines (such as RDL) connected  to TSV are sites of current crowding. The section shrinks  indeed from 7 µm² to 2.3 µm². Furthermore, the TiN barrier (Fig. 1) blocks the diffusion of copper atoms from the TSV to  the line. For these two reasons, the ends of the lines connected  to TSV are sites of maximum Atomic Flux Divergence (AFD), which are known to be sites of the appearance of defects [9]. The localization of the void at the top level or at the bottom  level depends on the polarization of the structure. In upstream  configuration, the void is located above the TSV, while in  downstream configuration the defect is located beneath the  TSV. Intuitively, in the upstream configuration, the electrons  wind moves the copper atoms above the TSV, and due to the  barrier, none of atoms of the TSV comes to fill the vacancies.

Figure 1: Up- and downstream configurations with  corresponding zone of voiding above or beneath the TSV.


Frank et al. also prove that the mechanism of degradation  depends on the copper line thickness [10]. Under a certain  threshold, after the nucleation, the void spans over the whole  thickness of the line and then grows above the section of the  TSV (or beneath depending on the polarization). If the  thickness is higher than the threshold, the failure is due to a  slit-void, right above (or beneath) the TSV.


Among other significant works on this subject Tan et al. [11] use the theory of Sasagawa et al. to obtain the site of  nucleation of voids. Studies are based on more detailed  models [13], which have already proved their relevance for  dual-inlaid copper lines. Recently, Orio et al. develop a model  based on the analysis of Frank et al. [14]. Except the studies of  Frank et al., most of the works are based on modeling or  simulation.


SEM in situ experiments


Most of the literature on interconnects reliability deals with  the characterization of the samples after failure, or after  interrupted stress test. Works bring to light that in situ or in  operando experiments allow a better understanding of the  failure mechanisms. For example, Besser et al. [16] study the  behavior of voids in aluminum lines and observe the healing  and the coalescence of voids. More recently, Meyer et al. [17] performs such an experiment on dual-inlaid copper lines. Thanks to an EBSD (Electron BackScatter Diffraction) detector, Meyer et al. point out the role of the grain orientation  in the electromigration mechanism. It is crucial to notice that  the dimensions of the structure studied by Meyer et al. are  more than one order of magnitude smaller than the 3D  structures.


In situ experiments require a specific sample preparation to  allow exploitable micrographs while keeping failure  mechanism unchanged. Another key step for electromigration  in situ experiments is the method used to heat the sample and  to maintain the temperature constant.


Purpose


The objective of this work is a better understanding of the EM  mechanisms in 3D structures. The study rests especially upon  the observation of the defects evolution. Then, the experiment  will be used to calibrate and validate a multiphysics model (in  development). Finally, the industrial objective is the  enhancement of the technology.


Organization


First in this paper, the set-up and the methodology used to  perform the experiment are explained. Then, results are  presented, like the voids evolution kinetics. The analysis of the  SEM micrographs points out the impact of the voids evolution

Experimental set-up and test structure


This section describes the method developed to perform in  operando electromigration experiments, especially of  interconnects above TSV.


Description of the set-up


All tests are performed under high vacuum, in the chamber of  a JEOL 7500F Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM). The  chip with the test structure is stuck in a DIL 16-pin package. Electrical connection between the device and the package is  achieved by aluminum wire bonding. A Keithley 2402a  module injects the electromigration test current (25 mA, direct  current, in this experiment) and measures the Device Under  Test‘s (DUT) resistance with a 4-point method. The resistance  value is automatically saved with a home-made LabVIEWbased acquisition software.


Set-up, heating and temperature control


Temperature has a critical effect on atomic diffusion and  therefore on electromigration rate. Therefore, the temperature  in the experiments has to be carefully controlled.


Heating the sample by Joule effect with an adequate stress  current would result in heterogeneous temperature in the test  structure, due to the temperature sensitivity to singular points (local electric resistance). Moreover, managing independently  temperature and current density allows, if needed for statistical  studies for example, a reliable extraction of the parameters of  Black‘s law. It is hence decided to include in the test structure  an independent heating system, which can furthermore be used  to reach temperatures higher than working temperatures. Highest temperatures (350 °C, but possible up to 500 °C) are  used to accelerate the failure mechanism. The objective is to  maintain experimental times within reasonable bounds, partly  because the SEM is unavailable for other users for the whole  time of the experiment.


Heating of the sample is achieved by the injection of a high  current in a resistive tantalum filament, placed in the ceramic  which supports the sample (Fig. 2). The ceramic sample  holder is fixed on the native stage and is designed to suit the  dimensions of the DIL 16-pin package, in which the DUT is  placed and wire-bonded. The temperature is monitored with  two thermocouples. One is located between the ceramic and

Figure 2: Zoom on the set-up at the sample holder level.


Tests have been achieved with a feedback control of the  temperature with an on/off switch. The principle was to  alternate phases where the current flows with phases where the  current is stopped. The system was monitored by a  temperature controller connected to a thermocouple. This


method induced small fluctuations of the temperature due to  the on/off alternating and hence fluctuations of the DUT  resistance. Further tests prove that without the control, under  constant heating current, the temperature remains stable  enough, ±1 °C around the set-point. The temperature drift is in  the range of 0.5 °C/10 h, similar to [17]. Thanks to our  previous works and the Thermal Coefficient of Resistance (TCR) value estimation, the initial test temperature is also  confirmed by the resistance value.


In the experiment reported hereafter, the DUT is heated at  350 °C by a constant current of about 5 A.


Test sample and procedure


The objective of the experiment is the observation of the  formation and evolution of a killer defect in a 3D structure. Therefore, the defect has to be observable and easy localized. The following structure has been designed to meet these  requirements.


The test structure is made of a bottom metal level (MBOT), ended on one side by one TSV and on the other side by four  TSVs (Fig. 3). The TSVs connect MBOT to the top metal level (MTOP), which is the current source line of the anode (I+) and  of the cathode (I-). Both metal levels are Cu-damascene level, 350 nm thick. MBOT is 4 µm wide and current source lines are  14 µm wide. The current density is about four times higher in  the single TSV than in each on the four TSV side, so that  defects are much more probable on the single TSV side. As  explained in the introduction, the voids appear above or  beneath TSVs, depending on the polarization. To start with the  easier case regarding the sample preparation, the upstream  configuration is chosen, leading to the nucleation of the killer  defect above the single TSV.


For more details about the process, the geometry, etc. of the  structure, the reader is invited to refer to [18].

An in-depth analysis of the SEM micrographs shows that after  the nucleation, in a first time, voids grow along the perimeter  of the TSV (Fig. 7-a to e). As free surfaces, such as voids  surface, are always main diffusion paths [19] and considering


the current flow direction, this voids evolution is intuitive. While void 3 is getting closer to void 2, the current flows  mainly between voids 1 and 3 (illustrated by the arrow on  Fig. 7-c) and passes above void 3. This explains why the latter  evolves in this direction. As a consequence of the voids  growth, the whole perimeter of the TSV is depleted (Fig. 7-f). Then, the current flows again in all directions, through the TiN  barrier.


After the coalescence of the three voids, the growth of the  resulting void occurs in two steps. First, analysis of all the  micrographs shows that void growth is globally isotropic. Afterwards, once the void has reached the ends of the line, the  geometry aspect induces a more linear directional evolution.  The analysis of the intermediate SEM micrographs highlights  that the different voids behave differently, until the end of the  experiment. For instance, void 2 remains unchanged from the

Resistance evolution


The electrical resistance value is the main parameter  monitored during electrical reliability tests. A relative  electrical resistance value increase of 10 % is a standard  failure criterion, even if this threshold has no physical  meaning and not always functional consequences. As the goal  of this experiment is a better understanding of all the  phenomena, the failure criterion is not taken into account.


Figure 10 shows the evolution of the resistance over time. Four main stages can be distinguished on the curve. First, the  resistance remains constant for around 220 h. Then, a slow  rise with a small step (less than 1 %) is observable. After that, one can notice a sudden jump of around 10 % in 10 h. Finally, resistance increases quasi-linearly, with a ramp of about  47 mΩ/h.


As the micrographs were taken regularly, it is possible to  relate the evolution of the resistance to that of the voids. Voids  can be electrically detected at about 250 h, meaning that  before Fig. 7-c, voids have no impact on the resistance. Especially, nucleation is not detectable with only the  monitoring of the resistance value. On Fig. 7-d, where around  75 % of the TSV perimeter is depleted, the effect of voids on  resistance is still quite negligible (less than 1 %). From these  observations, one can conclude that the current crowding has  no significant effect on resistance. Once the whole perimeter  of the TSV is depleted, electrons flow through the TiN barrier, which is more resistive than copper. The difference of  resistivity explains the sudden jump of resistance. While the  void grows, the conduction path in the metallic barrier  increases, hence the resistance rises too. This analysis  corroborates the assumptions of Frank et al.


Figure 10: Evolution of the resistance over time. Inserts a-f  refer to the micrographs of Fig. 7.

Considering previous studies [14], the linear increase of  resistance after the jump is not expected. In these studies, the  circular growth of the void leads to a logarithmic increase of  the resistance. The reason for this difference is currently not  known. As the in operando experiment has been carried out  once only, new experiments have to be realized before  conclusions can be drawn.


Diffusion pathway


On SEM micrographs, the grey level depends on the materials  and on the thickness crossed over by the electrons of a  considered material (up to a certain threshold). Hence, the  difference in the grey levels (contrast) proves that the  thickness of depleted copper is not uniform. Darker is a void, thicker it is, with darkest level being the full depletion of the  thickness. Based on this hypothesis, voids shape (particularly  at the beginning of the experiment) fits with previous  observations [20] (Fig. 11). Based on this hypothesis, voids  shape (particularly at the beginning of the experiment) fits  with previous observations [20]: wider at the Cu/SiN interface  than at the Cu/TiN interface. It means that the first is the  weakest interface and the main diffusion path, before grain  boundaries or Cu/TiN interface. This study confirms results  already proved for 3D structures [21] and copper dual-inlaid  structures [22].


Figure 11: Schematic cross-section view of the void shape.


Moreover, Fig. 12 shows that the tail of the islet (undepleted  copper) is thinner than the islet. As this tail is bounded with  the bottom of the line, it means that copper is depleted first at  the top. This observation confirms hence that Cu/SiN interface  is the main diffusion path.


Tail


Figure 12: Copper islet (sample tilted at 45°).


Observing Fig. 7, void 1 seems to follow the end of the line, which is a Cu/TiN interface. Nevertheless, on intermediate  micrographs, it appears that in fact, the void grows from the  TSV to the TiN barrier. However, there is an open question  concerning the nucleation of void 1. Does it start along the  TiN barrier, or above the TSV but with a growth towards the  barrier? Since no micrograph is available just after the  nucleation, it is impossible to know the exact role played by  the Cu/TiN interface in the nucleation of void 1.


Role of the microstructure


In the literature of electromigration, especially in the BEOL, the influence of the microstructure is abundantly studied [2]. It  is reasonable to assume that as for previous technologies the  local microstructure of the materials plays a major role on the  electromigration. This is corroborated by our study.


The evolution of the voids shape is an argument in favor of the  main role of the microstructure. After the coalescence, the  void evolution is revealed to occur step by step (Fig. 13). It is  assumed that each step is a grain with a special orientation. This means that at equal current density, the current flows  through preferential grains. The depletion by preferential  orientation can explain that void 2 does not evolve (Fig. 7-a to  c), depending on the orientation of grains at its surrounding.  66 h

double origin. First, comparing a previous test under similar  conditions (but not in operando, Fig. 14-a) and the present  experiment, it can be noticed that the center of the TSV is in  both cases not depleted. Hence, it can be reasonably assumed  that the geometry of the TSV has an effect. This hypothesis is  supported by the low current density (Fig. 8). Secondly, the  islet is observed to be in the vicinity of void 2 (Fig. 7-f). Previously in this paper, it was assumed that void 2 stays  unchanged due do the orientation of grains around it. Therefore, it may be assumed that the islet, or the part of the  islet which is not at TSV center (its top part in Fig. 14-a and  its right part in Fig. 14-b), is a single grain with a particular

It is also interesting to notice that the copper islet which  appears by copper deposition (Fig. 7-h) occurs precisely at the  location where the nucleation of a fourth void could be  expected. Before Fig. 7-g, it seems that there is no copper at  the islet location, but one can assume that a germ remains, too  small to be observable.


Due to the difficulty in further isolating the defect location  within the bright PC line, additional methods needed to be  investigated in order to isolate the CA contact causing the


bright contrast. To remedy this issue, active voltage  contrasting is used at M1 level to help identify a row of


contacts that could be causing the short. A Kleindiek  ProbeWorkstation installed inside FEI’s Dualbeam FIB 450s


is used to conduct AVC at M1 level. The M1 comb structure is  first segmented through FIB cuts. Then the pad leading to the  underlying nest of PC lines is probed and brought to a


potential that induces an active contrast. With the nest of PC  lines being actively contrasted, the segmented area of the M1


comb structure in which the CA-PC short resides will also  contrast. Figure 4a shows an area within the macro structure  that contrasts brighter than the rest of the macro. With a


general area of the macro isolated at M1 level, the contrasting  area will then be further segmented. This will in turn isolate


each individual M1 line from one another within the  contrasting area. The active contrast method on the nested PC  structure will be repeated, this time one individual M1 line


will be isolated. Figure 4b shows a single M1 line which  actively contrasts bright in relation to adjacent lines. The die is


then deprocessed further to CA-PC level by removing M1. The isolated M1 line can be referenced at CA-PC level  through layout and counting methods.


Figure 4a: M1 comb structure was segmented through FIB  cuts near the arrows. Active contrast was seen in bracket  area. Figure 4b: M1 comb structure was then cut to isolate  every runner within the active contrast area, a single M1 line  was actively contrasted bright in relation to adjacent lines.


With the die at CA-PC level, PVC is conducted to isolate the


bright PC line. The isolated lines at both M1 level and PC  level provide the ability to effectively address a single failing


contact with a row (M1 level active contrast) and column (PC  level passive contrast), as shown in Figure 5a. The precise  localization makes it possible to perform high resolution TEM


analysis. Because of the small CA dimension and spacing, tiny  defects could be blocked from the sample projection effect.


Figure 5b is a STEM image of CA-PC short defect. EDS  analysis revealed that the defect is composed of Nickel and


Germanium. Several other locations confirmed this CA-PC  short defect is due to Nickel encroachment.


Figure 5a: A single contact was isolated. Figure 5b: STEM  image showed the PC-CA short is due to Nickel  encroachment.


Two successful FA cases are discussed in this paper. Voltage


contrast was used as a simple, fast and effective method to  provide accurate defect location for TEM analysis. In the first  case, a small residual Titanium filament could only be


detected by Super-X EDS analysis on a planar TEM sample. In the second case, a single failing contact was found by  combining AVC and PVC. Active contrast at M1 level


provided a row address and passive contrast at PC level  provided a column address. Nickel encroachment defect is


then found. The combination of voltage contrast and TEM is  proven to be very effective in finding nanometer scale defects.

[2] P. Schlossmacher, D.O. Klenov, B. Freitag, and H.S. von  Harrach, “Enhanced Detection Sensitivity with a New  Windowless XEDS System for AEM Based on Silicon  Drift Detector Technology”, Microscopy Today, Volume 18, Issue 04, July 2010, pp 14-20.


Defect Isolation Tools Accelerate the Failure Analysis Process


Adam Winterstrom*, Kevin Meehan*, Ralph Sanchez and Rich Ackerman *International Rectifier


Teseda Corporation


Temecula, CA, USA


Portland, OR, USA


This paper presents case studies that highlight the use of  new scan technologies and techniques to quickly test, diagnose, localize and isolate the root cause of the defects  demonstrating that the solution meets the rapid and  constant changing demands of industry.  Cases include; a) a device that is seemingly passing functional test, but not  scan test with emission, b) a device with emission  requiring resolution to its location and c) a device having a  timing issue that does not have emission.


Traditional Techniques Meets Scan


The devices diagnosed were primarily designed as a single  chip solution for complete inverter controlled appliance  motor control applications. It consists of a collection of  control elements, motion peripherals, a dedicated motion  control sequencer and dual port RAM to map internal  signal nodes.


Traditional techniques to locate physical defects in digital  integrated circuits include static observation techniques  such as emissions microscopy and static bias laser  stimulation techniques.  These include Optical Beam  Induced Resistance Change (OBIRCH), Voltage Bias  voltage sensing Amplifier (VBA), and Thermally Induced  Voltage Alteration (TIVA).  With continued growth in  diagnostic tools and applications using scan technology, new tools are being added to enhance failure analysis  laboratories methodologies [1] [2].  Both hardware and  software scan diagnostic tools, together with equipment  commonly used in failure analysis laboratories were used  to diagnose the motor control devices.


The new scan diagnosis methods were incorporated as part  of the overall diagnosis flow depicted by the methodology  depicted in Figure 1.  After initial inspection the devices, whether field returns or production test failures, are tested  to recreate and capture all the failures.  The failures, captured as mismatches in the scan chains, are mapped  against the physical design in the diagnostic software.  The  scan based diagnostic software physically identifies  mismatching scan cells resulting from ATPG test by  mapping them with the XY coordinates in reference to the  device.  The logic observed by these scan cells can be  traced to localize the defect.  Logic cone and pruning


techniques in the software are used to isolate the location  of the failure which in turn is the suspect defect.


Confirmation of the suspects are determined through both  nondestructive and destructive means in failure analysis.   The compact scan test hardware is easily placed within the  chambers of FA equipment, such as XIVA and photoemission equipment.  Once situated in the chamber, the  test hardware stimulates the device for emission. The  diagnostic software was also used in finding the physical  location of the actual emission as well as aiding the FA  engineer in determining the best placement for FIB points. FA destructive techniques for the device become a lower  risk with higher success in revealing the actual root cause.  This approach quickly localized the defect and established  an enhanced FA methodology to isolate the root cause for  final confirmation. The time reduction of localization and  isolation was dramatically reduced from what is typically  several months to a number of days.


External Visual Inspection


All the samples were subject to initial nondestructive  failure analysis techniques, such as X-RAY and C-SAM  inspections, to examine the interior details of the devices.  X-RAY radiography was used to detect any wire sweep  and other wire bond problems, die attach voids, package  voids and cracks. C-Mode Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (C-SAM) was used to detect any delaminations between  package interfaces such as Plastic-to-Leadframe, Plasticto-Die, Plastic-to-Die Attach, Die Attach Voids and  Internal Cracks. No anomalies were detected in either of  these inspections.


Sample 1 Diagnosis


Electrical Verification and Test


In the first sample examined, initial verification confirmed  normal leakages and switching during the functional  testing in the device.  However running the ATPG test on  the hardware system revealed scan test failures, as  summarized in Figure 2.  97 scan cell failures at room  temperature and 135 scan cell failures at 70°C were  captured. In both tests, at different temperatures, the  failures were captured in the same scan cells, showing a  consistency in the defect behavior.

Scan Test Debug


The scan debug software drives the hardware system and  starts the analysis process with the failing device by  highlighting the logical representation of the scanned  register reporting failure by way of instance names .  Figure  3 illustrates the summary of the scan cell mismatches with  their instance name,  i.e., pwm_cnt_32x_reg[0-15].  The  test results indicate that 14 of the 16 bits  of a register are  mismatching.  The proximity of the register identifies the  logical register index numbers, 0 - 15, and the correlated  index numbers of the scan cell index numbers of the scan  chain the register is embedded in.  The scan debug  software provides the pattern and statistical data such as  number of times the mismatch occurs in each scan cell of  the register.


Given this information, it is surmised that the logical  information provided in the scan debug software results  that the physical location of the register scan cells are in  close proximity.  From the results of the ATPG testing, it  can be concluded that the scan cells are working properly  due to the fact that the first pattern is typically the integrity  test that checks the connectivity of the scan chain.  The  mismatching values occur later in the ATPG test after the  initial integrity test.  Thus the scan cells are correctly  reporting the defect behavior in the logic of the design.

The tracing of logic was done within the diagnostic  software to further get a fix on the defect candidate with  the XY coordinates.  This established the area localization  of the defect.


Cone Tracing


Knowing that the ATPG integrity test pattern executes and  returns results correctly indicates proper functionality of  the scan chain operation.  As such, the ATPG test also  indicates proper shift and capture of the scan data.  Further, high confidence that the scan enable and clock are  operational is assessed.


By tracing from the d inputs of the mismatching scan cells, cone tracing for each of scan cells can reveal commonality  of nets and cells in their paths.  After tracing into a couple  of the mismatching scan cells, a common net (n_401) is  input to the driving cell (an AND gate) for each scan cell. Figure 5 illustrates this finding (the small component cells  are the AND gates and the highlighted trace is net n_401. The findings of the cone trace effectively leads to the  convergence of a single net (n_369) and cell (a NAND  gate), Figure 6.

Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Analysis


With XY coordinates determined, FIB pads were made at  the output signal of the cells with emission sites.  The  emission site cells (Site 1 = nand4i_adn_4 and Site 2 = adfull_adn_apr_2) are highlighted, Figure 8, in the  diagnostic software as well as the output net path for the  cells.   Repeating the ATPG test for stimulus in the  photoemission procedure, the scan test was paused at  specific cycles before the capture point of the scan pattern.


Doing so keeps the scanned input pattern constantly  propagated through the logic to stimulate the defect for  emission. Measurements of the logic states of the block  outputs were taken, reported in Figure 9.  It was confirmed  that the nand_4i_adn_4 cell had the incorrect logic value. The input B of nand4i_adn_4 was resistively shorted to  Vdd which would not allow input B to be pulled down to  VSS.  This behavior ultimately resulted in mismatches that  were captured in the scan cells.

Sample 3  Diagnosis


Dianosis of a Timing Issue Without Emission


Sample 3 was a case in which no emission occured during  the photoemission step of the flow.  The inital steps  of the  flow for inspection and testing, as in the other previous  samples, were again performed.  The test results from this  device isolated a segment of the scan chain that was failing  with 7947 mismatches.  The mismatches were within a  constant range of scan cells in the scan chain, scan cell


index 2169 through 2200.  In looking at the failing scan  results, the behavior of the mismatching values captured  were unlike a stuck-at behavior.  The captured results from  the propagated values of the shifted stimulus pattern were  inexplicable when taking into consideration the logic paths  leading to the capturing scan cells.  What would be  expilicable for a stuck at value given  the stimulus was not  being captured.


Taking a closer look at the shift operation of the test data  reveals what appears to be a shoot-thru type effect on the  captured results of the mismatching segment of the scan  chain, Figure 16. Tracing the scan chain in the diagnostic

software revealed lock up latches within the mismatching  scan cell segment of the chain, Figure 17.


The initial suspect was a narrow path between nets  sysclk2x_L6_N1, the buffered clock to the scan cells, and  sysclk2x_L5_N1, the signal feeding the buffer.  However, no visible evidence could be seen.  When the  sysclk2x_L6_N1 clock further traced, it was discovered  that clock buffering distribution had clock tree segments  going to scan cells bound between the lock up latches. The  five different sub-trees of the clock going to the scan cells  also have an enable to control the clock pulse for capture. With probe points now placed on the driving buffer output  of suspect sysclk2x_L6_N1 clock net path, the clock  waveform revealed to have a 20ns delay from the source  clock input, Figure 17.  sysclk2x_L7_N1 is the buffered  sysclk2x_L6_N1, which is then in turn gated several times  with independent enables.  Thus it can be explained how  the delayed edge of the clock affects not only capturing of  data, but also the shifting effect of the captured data.  The  input shift data seems to be correct since the mismatching  scan cells (after capture)  are near the beginning of the  scan chain.  Hence, the effect of the defect occurs during  the time of capture and transistion into the shift operation  of the scan chain.


The driving buffer of sysclk2x_L6_N1 was then fibbed for  a probe point between the two adjacent inverters of the  buffer, Figure 18. The input to the buffer, sysclk2x_L5_N1, shows no significant difference between  the contol (good) device and the failing device.  However,


comparing and overlapping the control and failure  waveforms after the first inverter of the buffer to the input  of the buffer, sysclk2x_L5_N1, it was here that clearly  determined that the output of the first inverter was  the  source of the delay.  The delay is then propagated to the


output of the buffer and subsequently to the mismatching


scan cells.  The delays measured at the probed points are  as follows;
