Technique Differentiation


These scan techniques present a different approach for the  failue analyis lab.  Defect isolation is kept in a physical  environment where analyis is performed on the phsical  layout of the design.  All data is in reference to the  physical views of the device.  The algorithms are  interactive search techniques.  The effort is performed  totally independent of simulation and mandatory design  modeling providing the autonomy needed for fast and  complete “confirmation” of the defect.  Most importantly, the presented techniques enable the diagnosing engineer to  rationalize to the root cause.


The case studies presented concluded with successful  completion of finding root cause of the defect.  The first of  the three cases included defect islolation with the new  methodology with FA confirmation using emission  techniques.  The second sample demonstrated the usage of  parts of the flow to confirm the exact location of the  emission.  The third and final sample uses the flow to find  a timing issue in the case where no emission is achieved.  The diagnosis time for each of the three devices was  within a period of one to three days per device.  The  confirmation stage of the defect is now the longest lead  time of the dianosis process.


Product lines are now introducing more and more devices  with scan and mixed mode operations. Along with this is  having the need for a scan diagnosis environment that is  not only contributing, but is also non-intrusive to the FA  flow.


The importance of having complete failure data from scan  testing done on the device rather than just typical pass/fail  results from production test provided insight on the defect  behavior of the device when analyzed and debugged.  The  hardware system also played a dual role when it was  configured within the chamber of photo emission  equipment to stimulate the defect for emission.  Localizing  failure candidates in real-time with diagnostic software on  the front end of the FA flow and then probing for the  defect proved to be an efficient manner to which root  cause could be found.  The correlation of the emission sites  with the localized areas in the early procedure gave way


for the FIB and TEM efforts, all of which contributed  towards establishing the new diagnostic flow.


The authors wish to extend thanks to the EAG lab for their  fine efforts in the TEM analysis which was a contributing  factor towards confirming  root cause.


Reservoir effect


With this experiment, the reservoir effect is observed two  times. First, whereas voids 2 and 3 coalesce, void 1 starts to  evolve between the TSV and the end of the line (Fig. 15). Since there is no conduction pathway at this place, the current  is assumed to be near zero. Then, after 409 h of test, copper is  deposited above the TSV and forms an islet, while the copper  line is fully depleted in this area. The islet grows over time (Fig. 7-g and h).


Figure 15: Reservoir effect at the end of the line.


Volumetric depletion rate


In the BEOL, the drift velocity is an interesting parameter


[23]. It is measured directly from SEM micrographs, as the  void growth is in the direction of the line. In the present case, the void growth is globally multidirectional and anisotropic.


Therefore, the drift velocity cannot be estimated. Instead, a  volumetric depletion rate, which represents the depletion of a  volume of copper per unit of time unit, is calculated.


Figure 16 represents the evolution of the volumetric depletion  rate. The volume is obtained by measuring the surface (top  view) of the voids on the SEM micrographs and multiplying it  by the thickness of the void. It is assumed that the void either  spans over the whole thickness of the line or half the  thickness, depending roughly on the difference in contrast. The volumetric depletion rate is then calculated by dividing  the volume by the stress time.

This defect, which was not present at the beginning of the test, grows over time, following again the perimeter of the TSV (Fig. 22-b). Post-mortem Focused Ion Beam SEM (FIB SEM) observations prove that the defect is a thickening of the copper  line (Fig. 23). Figure 23 and Fig. 24 reveal also the existence of two kinds of  voids beneath the four TSVs. The first (type 1, full circles) are  assumed to have nucleated at the Cu/SiN interface. They were not  observed by Frank et al. for this copper thickness, maybe due  to the difference in time scale. Defect


Defects near the aluminum pads


Aluminum pads are sites of high atomic flux divergence, due  to the change in material and mainly due to the current  crowding. On the cathode side, electrons leave the pad and  push away copper atoms. The pad is made of aluminum; therefore copper atoms are displaced but not replaced inducing


voids nucleation and growth (Fig. 25). By transparence, voids  are also observable beneath the pad. The calculations have not  been done yet, but it is certainly possible to prove that the  amount of missing copper is about the same quantity as copper  in excess above the four TSVs.


On the anode side, electrons flow towards the pad, where  copper atoms build-up at the interface, leading to the  formation of extrusions (Fig. 26). The extrusions explain, at  least partially, where the copper from above the single TSV  goes. The total volume of depleted copper is indeed about  60 µm² whereas the volume of the two extrusions and the  deposited islet is respectively around 30, 20 and 3 µm², i.e. about 53µm².


Al pad


Figure 25: Voids at the  interface with the Al pad (@ 620 h).


Figure 26: Extrusion at the  interface with the Al pad (@ 620 h).


In this paper, a methodology to perform an in operando SEM  electromigration experiment on structures with TSV was  presented. The aim of this work was a better understanding of  the electromigration phenomenon and of the voids evolution  kinetics.


The observations mainly focused on the killer defect. SEM  micrographs and post-mortem analyses brought out that the  Cu/SiN interface is the main diffusion path. The main role of  the microstructure has been confirmed through the step by step  growth of the voids, the undepleted copper islet or the nonevolution of a void.


Events from the SEM micrographs perfectly match the  evolution of the electrical resistance. The impact of the voids  on the resistance is observable, and each evolution of the  resistance can be referred to a specific step in the evolution of  the voids.


Secondary defects have been observed at different position of  the structure. These defects have a negligible impact on the  failure, but their study reveals interesting mechanisms, such as  voids life (growth, displacement and then shrinkage and  disappearance).


The results have to be confirmed first with new experiments, especially the resistance fast linear increase stage, which has  not been reported previously. The following step is  experiments with inverse polarization (downstream), but the  sample preparation has to be studied. In the future, the in


operando protocol will also be used for other technologies, such as TSV middle, direct bonding, etc.


On the other hand, the present results deserve more  investigations to better clarify the role of the microstructure (grain orientation). Experiments with EBSD (electron  backscatter diffraction) or synchrotron beam characterizations  are planned. All these results will be used to calibrate a  multiphysics model, which is currently developed and could  bring more insight into the complex coupling of electric flow  and diffusion.

The Application of Magnetic Force Microscopy for Detection of   Subsurface Anomalies in Semiconductor Device Wiring Levels


Phil Kaszuba, Frank Alwine, Leon Moszkowicz, Randy Wells


International Business Machines, Essex Junction, Vermont  pkaszuba@us.ibm.com, 802-769-1043


Subsurface wiring level anomalies in VLSI semiconductor  devices are extremely difficult, if not impossible to analyze  without de-processing the device to expose suspect wiring.  Magnetic Force Microscopy (MFM) is a scanning probe  technique that requires minimal sample preparation and has  the capability to sense magnetic fields in proximity to thin  film conductors with high lateral resolution [1]. In this study, multiple VLSI device conductors were intentionally modified  and then the magnetic field around the energized conductors  was analyzed using MFM.  An overview of the technique and  results of the magnetic field analysis are discussed.


A critical issue facing the semiconductor industry as device  sizes shrink and functional complexity increase, is the inability  to adequately and accurately analyze subsurface current  carrying conductors.  Defects or anomalies in wiring levels  can lead to short term or long term device failure. Analysis of  the magnetic field around a current carrying conductor enables  a better understanding of problematic or potentially  problematic areas which may have failed or are susceptible to  failure.  MFM is a scanning probe technique which has  demonstrated the capability to detect magnetic fields around  thin film conductors.  Other techniques such as Liquid Crystal  Thermography [2] and Scanning SQUID Microscopy [3] are  capable of current analysis based on the thermal signature or  magnetic field respectively, but both methods have limited  spatial resolution. MFM is a near field technique that has  shown to be effective in analyzing magnetic thin films [4] and  current carrying conductors [1, 5].  In this paper we present  results of a study in which the MFM technique was optimized  for detection and analysis of the magnetic field around a thin  film current carrying conductor and we present the results of  MFM analyses on intentionally modified thin film conductors  using the optimized configuration.


Magnetic Force Microscopy


MFM is a scanning probe technique that detects and creates an  image representative of a sample’s proximal magnetic field.  The sensing element is a silicon Atomic Force Microscope (AFM) probe which has been coated with a ferromagnetic  film, e.g., Cr-Co.  The probe tip is magnetized, thereby


creating a dipole which responds to the forces encountered  when in the presence of another magnetic field. The probe is  raster scanned over a surface and an image is created  representative of the magnetic field near the sample surface.  Typical radii of curvature (ROC) at the apex of MFM probe  tips range from 40-75 nm [6].  In practice, MFM data  collection is a two pass scanning probe technique.  For each  line of data that comprises a full field image two ‘raster’ passes are made over the sample surface prior to indexing a  predetermined distance in the orthogonal axis to repeat the  next ‘two pass’ raster.  In the first pass, using Atomic Force  Microscopy, a ‘line’ of topographic data is collected and  stored.  In the second pass, the tip is raised to a predetermined  elevation, e.g., 10-1000 nm above the sample surface.   Again  the tip is raster scanned across the sample, using the  previously acquired topographic data to maintain a constant  elevation above the sample surface.  The cantilever is  oscillating at its resonant frequency (f0) and the dipole at the  end of the cantilever responds to the magnetic forces proximal  to the sample.  If the forces encountered are repulsive (with  respect to the tip dipole), f0 increases with a corresponding  positive phase shift (φtip) in the mechanical tip oscillation.  Conversely, an attractive force results in a decrease in f0 and a  negative shift in φtip.


Equipment


All AFM and MFM data were collected using a commercially  available scanning probe microscope.   Standard silicon probes  were used for the acquisition of topographic data and a variety  of MFM probes were used for magnetic field analysis.


In order to thoroughly investigate and understand the  application and optimal conditions for performing MFM on  patterned circuits for the detection of wiring level anomalies a  systematic approach was taken to include studies of:


1. Current detection sensitivity


2. Probe selection


3. Sensitivity optimization


4. Modified test structures

Current Detection Sensitivity


Establishing a thorough understanding of the current detection  sensitivity of MFM is important in understanding the  limitations of the technique.  Since the magnetic field strength  around a current carrying conductor is proportional to the level  of current passing through the conductor, a series of  measurements were taken in which the oscillation phase  change of the MFM probe was recorded while varying the  current density (J) in the conductor.  The separation distance  between the probe tip and the dielectric layer on the wire was  held at 200 nm.  Figure 3 shows an example of the magnetic  field around the conductor while passing a DC current of 6.9  mA.

Peak to peak magnetic field data were collected and recorded  in degrees of phase change (φtip) and averaged (Fig. 4).

Another critical factor affecting the ability of the MFM to  respond to magnetic forces is the separation distance between  the probe and feature of interest, given that the field strength  decays as a function of distance nominally with a 1/r  relationship (however the high lateral resolution of the MFM  causes a slight deviation from 1/r as shown in Figure 6).  This  is especially important when the feature of interest lies  beneath a passivation or insulating layer, e.g., a semiconductor  device interlayer dielectric.  To better understand the system  response as the separation distance increases, a series of MFM  scans was performed at varying heights above the passivation  layer on top of the conductor.  Current flow through the  conductor was held constant at 8.75 mA (J= 29.48 mA/µm2).

Computed Tomography as Failure Analysis Insurance


Gerald M. Martinez

TCS Space & Component Technology, Torrance, CA, USA  jmartinez@telecomsys.com


Failure analysis of electronic components is almost always  destructive, and there’s no going back once a destructive step  is performed. Or, that’s the way it used to be, before the  development of some of the more sophisticated nondestructive  techniques such as computed tomography (CT). This paper  presents a case study of an optocoupler, the suspected failure  of which could not be confirmed until the last day of the  month-long analysis, when the cause of failure was  conclusively determined by a CT model captured weeks  earlier.


AQ0750A


6N140A/883B 8302401EA


The well-established best practices of component failure


SGP


analysis typically require both nondestructive and destructive


50434


analysis techniques. Of course, we perform as much


nondestructive analysis as could be meaningful, but generally,


we end up having to perform analytical steps that are


progressively more destructive to learn the information


necessary to determine the root cause of failure, its scope, and


corrective actions. With each destructive step, we analysts ask


ourselves, “In pursuing this evidence, am I destroying other


evidence that may be useful or vital?” – and then proceed to 4HX.do as we must. This paper suggests the use of computed tomography (CT) as an insurance policy: a way to  permanently document the detailed construction and any


physical anomalies that may be present in a device as


received, which can be used to recover crucial information


which would otherwise be permanently lost in the course of


destructive analysis. Information captured in the CT model of


an as-received suspect device can later result in the payoff of


conclusively determining the cause of a failure, which is often


worth far more than the up-front cost of performing the CT.


Background


A suspect upscreened 6N140A/883 optocoupler made by  Avago Technologies (Figs. 1 and 2) had been mounted on a


vo甲新228目on


circuit board. The failure was reportedly observed after this


board was connected with two other boards, and testing found


that this optocoupler had no output. Electrical probing *reportedly found that there was an open circuit between pins 7


and 8, the anode and cathode respectively of the light-emitting 文日


立


diode (LED) that serves as the channel 4 input. After the part Nw岳ni。2


was removed, this channel 4 LED was found to have a slightly


higher VF (forward voltage) than the other three channels, and  channel 4 was reported to have a lower CTR3 (current transfer  ratio, or gain, at 5 mA) than the other channels.


Two additional samples were returned at the same time, because they reportedly both exhibited out-of-family (high) post-burn-in +25ºC VF readings of 1.51 V and 1.57 V “asshipped.” These devices were reportedly never installed or  tested by the customer. These two samples were not analyzed; they were only electrically tested for correlation purposes.

Analysis


The suspect device was thoroughly inspected with a lowpower (7X to 40X) stereoscope. No anomalies were observed.


Curve Tracer Diode Characterization I


The input LEDs of all four channels were tested with a curve  tracer for forward voltage (VF). All diodes exhibited VF  readings between 1.4 and 1.5 V at a test current of 1.6 mA. No  indications of intermittency or degradation were noted.


Automated Electrical Testing


In order to verify the present condition of the devices, all three  were sent to the same test facility that had been used for the  upscreening of the lot. Automated testing was performed at +25ºC, -55ºC, and +125ºC. All samples were well within  specification limits.


These return data were compared with the upscreen burn-in  data recorded 2½ years prior. The +25°C data for all three  parts are presented in Table 1 below. Several observations  were made:


 All VF values were in family with those of the other two  parts. In none of the tests was the VF of channel 4 higher  than any VF of other channels.


 In the return testing, the channel 4 CTR performance of  all three parts degraded as the test currents increased. For  CTR1 (tested at 0.5 mA), all four channels performed  similarly. For CTR2 (tested at 1.6 mA), the channel 4  readings were consistently lower than for the other three  channels. For CTR3 (tested at 5 mA), the channel 4  currents were at least 39% lower than all other channels.


 Only in the return testing did the suspect device exhibit  the most severe degradation of the CTR3 (hFE3), by  approximately 48%, from 4.22 to 2.20.


 In the return testing, both sample parts showed similarly  low CTR3 parameters; in fact, the CTR3s of both samples  were even lower than that of the suspect device.


 In the return testing, the CTR3s of all three parts were  much lower for channel 4 than for the other three  channels.


Review of Original Radiographs


The original x-ray film of the lot was reviewed. No anomalies  were observed for the suspect device.


Real-Time X-Ray


The circuit paths between pins 7 and 8 (channel 4 LED) and  between pins 10 and 11 (channel 4 detector) were examined  by real-time x-ray imaging in an effort to find any possible  physical discontinuities. None were found (Figs. 3 and 4).


Figure 3: X-ray of the device as received. Pin 1 is at the bottom  left, and the channel 4 detector is in the chamber at the right.


Figure 4: X-ray detail of  the channel 4 LED  solder attachments. The  attach indicated by an  arrow had a large void  at its top right corner, but otherwise appeared  solid.


Computed Tomography I


The device was then subjected to CT [1, 2]: a detailed threedimensional model of the device was captured, which was  used to create virtual images and cuts of the circuit paths from  pin 7 to the LED, pin 8 to the LED, pin 10 to the detector, and  pin 11 to the detector. Detailed images of all conductor  interfaces were captured and examined, and all interfaces were  seen to be solid and intact. Included among these were  detailed images of the channel 4 LED and detector die  attaches, which were solid and intact, showing only minor  voiding. See Figs. 5 through 11.


Figure 5: Overall CT image of the suspect device, with the  metal lid and all ceramic digitally removed, so that all


conductive paths and the detector dice can be seen. Pin 1 is at  the lower left, so the channel 4 circuit is at the right.


Figure 7: CT image of the channel 4 detector die attach, as in  Figure 6, but with everything above the plane of the die


surface and below the plane of the substrate metallization  digitally cut away.


Figure 8: CT image of the LED die attach, as in Figure 6, but  with everything above the plane of the die surface and below  the plane of the substrate metallization digitally cut away. The  LED’s gold-germanium solder connections (bottom left and  bottom center) are also seen to be solid, with minimal voiding. Figure 6: Detail of the channel 4 circuit, showing the top of the


detector traces (upper half of the photo) and the underside of the


LED traces (lower half of the photo). A portion of the channel 3


circuitry is visible at the left.


Scanning Acoustic Microscopy


The device was imaged by C-mode scanning acoustic  microscopy (C-SAM) through the underside of the package. This technique [3, 4] successfully imaged the die attaches of  all four detector dice and the gold-germanium solder attaches  between the small LED substrate and the device package. All  four detector die attaches and all eleven gold solder attaches  were seen to conduct sound properly, indicating that they had  wetted properly and were mechanically intact. See Fig. 12.


Curve Tracer Diode Characterization II


Per the customer’s request, curve tracer testing of the LEDs  was repeated to check their VF behavior. All tested well within  specification, with results as previously observed.


Internal Inspection


The seal around the lid was cut with a sharp knife, and the  device was delidded. An inspection found no anomalies, though at this time, the LEDs were not visible, and only the  bond wires and bond pads of the detector dice were visible. Since the potting material was soft and gelatinous, a  nondestructive bond pull of 2.4 g was performed on the  detector bond wires through the potting material. All wires  from all four channels were tested, and all passed the test.

channel 4 detector vias (arrows), with all ceramic and pins 9  through 16 digitally removed, so that these vias could be  seen. Both appeared intact.

(black arrow) dice, along with their bond wires and die


attach fillets. Note that the silicon detector die is virtually  invisible in this image, as silicon has a very low x-ray cross  section. The LED die is visible, because it is made of gallium  arsenide phosphide, which images well in x-rays. Images  optimized to show the silicon dice well show the other


materials poorly.


Figure 12: C-SAM scan focused on the plane of the gold-germanium solder attaches between the small substrate and the rest of the


package. The eight dark square shapes along the bottom of the image indicate good sound conduction across the solder joints.


Figure 15: Overall optical view of the channel 4 detector  die. High-magnification examination found no anomalies.


Figure 17: The channel 4 LED circuit on the underside of the  small substrate. The upper two solder joints were the anode


and cathode connections to pins 7 and 8, respectively.


Curve Tracer Diode Characterization III


Per the customer’s request, curve tracer testing of the channel  4 LED was repeated at this time while the device was  physically tapped to check for intermittency. The channel 4  LED was connected to a curve tracer now with both polarities  monitored, and VF and VBR (breakdown voltage) were both  measured. The device was then tapped first with a fingertip, then with the side of a metal tweezer to induce a stronger  mechanical shock. No intermittency was observed. The device  was then cooled to about -45°C with a freeze spray and then  carefully heated with a heat gun while continuity was  monitored, and again, no intermittency was observed.

The potting material was removed by immersion of the device


in an industrial solvent for about two hours at room

removed: the device was set on a 540°C hot plate to melt the


gold solder, and within a few seconds, the small LED


substrate was removed. All of the LED dice, the detector dice,


and the bond wires could now be inspected. Both dice were


examined at high magnifications to ensure that even the tiniest


dark spots observed on the dice were surface particles or


cosmetic defects rather than electrical rupture sites. See Figs. +

Nondestructive Bond Pull Testing


All eight LED wires were subjected to nondestructive bond  pull tests at 2.4 g, and all passed.


Electrical Probing


OM


Per the customer’s request, the VF parameters of all four LEDs  were electrically probed on the removed small substrate. All  LEDs still met specification, with none out of family.


Per the customer’s request, the electrical path between each  LED pin and its internal bond pad was probed. The resistances  of pins 1 through 7 ranged from 89.7 mΩ to 112.9 mΩ, but  the resistance of pin 8 was 1.763 Ω (Table 2).


Inspection of the package at this time found that several pairs


of adjacent pins were now externally shorted together by  bridges of apparently molten silver-colored material. Pins 11, 12, and 13 were shorted together, as were pins 14 and 15, but  the thickest bridge of material was between pins 7 and 8 (Figs. 19 and 20). Wet-film x-rays of the package at this time could  not resolve whether these new bridges of material could have  extruded from between ceramic layers of the package due to  the high-temperature exposure experienced by the device  during removal of the LED substrate. Energy-dispersive x-ray  analysis found the bridging material to be lead-tin solder. Although these bridges would not have affected these  electrical measurements, their presence was seen as an  indication that the physical integrity of the dual in-line  package (DIP) may have been compromised during the  analysis.


Destructive Bond Pull Testing


Destructive bond pull testing was performed on all 12 detector  wires, which broke at forces ranging from 7.89 g to 12.86 g. The channel 4 detector wires broke at 7.89, 10.01, and 11.34  g, all far exceeding the minimum requirement of 2.5 g.


Microcircuit Die Probing


The channel 4 detector die was probed, as was the channel 3  detector die for comparison. Each detector die is made with  three bonds connected to it, and two more unused bond pads  are available for probing, giving a total of five bond pads on  each detector die that could be probed (see Figure 18). With  the wire bonds disconnected, all combinations of the five bond  pads were electrically characterized with a curve tracer. All  breakdown characteristics and forward turn-on voltages were  recorded, and all curves were photographed. Comparison of  the channel 3 and the channel 4 diode characteristics revealed  no differences – there was no indication of opens, shorts, electrical leakage, “soft knees,” premature breakdowns, or any  other anomalies.


Additional Electrical Testing


Per the customer’s request, a destructive physical analysis  sample from this lot was retrieved for probing of the electrical  path between each LED pin and its internal bond pad, for  correlation with the subject device. The resistances for all of  pins 1 through 8 ranged from 57.0 mΩ to 113 mΩ.


Figure 18: Overall optical  view of the channel 4 LED  die.


Figure 19: Pins 5 through 8 at the stage in the analysis after  removal of the small substrate. These external solder bridges  were observed during inspection immediately after Electrical  Probing.


Figure 20: Pins 9 through 16 as seen after Electrical Probing.


Cross-Sectioning


Because of the high pin 8 resistance reading observed during  probing, the suspect device was sawed in half so that one  piece contained pins 5-12, and the other contained pins 1-4  and 13-16. Each half was mounted separately in epoxy resin  and cross-sectioned transversely – one half to the pin 8 via  and the other half to the pin 1 via, which is routed and  constructed similarly to the suspect pin 8 via (Figs. 21 and


22). The cross section of the pin 8 via found that the via was  solid and intact, as were its interfaces to the metallized  conductive traces. A large, wide crack through the ceramic  was seen extending vertically between the via and the pin; this  crack was filled with the epoxy used for the cross-sectioning  mount and extended to both the top and bottom surfaces of the  ceramic package (Figs. 23 and 24). The presence of mounting  epoxy in the crack indicates that the crack was present prior to  mounting and was not induced during cross-sectioning. The


conductive path between pin 8 and the via was intact

Computed Tomography II


Now that a suspect anomaly had been found, it was necessary  to determine whether the ceramic crack had been induced  during the destructive analysis process (such as during the  540°C LED substrate removal process) or had been present  when the device was returned to TCS. To make this  determination, the 3D computer model of the device that was  acquired prior to any destructive testing (see Computed  Tomography I) was revisited. Previously, the CT imaging had  been directed toward examining all conductor interfaces along  the channel 4 circuit paths, and the ceramic packaging  material had been ignored; in fact, it had deliberately been  image-enhanced to be transparent, so that the metal  conductors could be studied. Now, the 3D computer model  was image-enhanced to bring out the details of the ceramic, particularly in the pin 8 area. A hairline ceramic crack was  now seen in the same location and following the same path as  was seen during actual cross-sectioning – virtual cross  sections showed the crack extending between the top edge and  the underside of the package, passing through the pin 8  metallized trace. See Figs. 25 through 31.

FIB-STEM Cross-section and EDS Analysis


FIB-STEM cross-sectioning of the emission site showed  electrostatic discharge (ESD) damage on the DFET (Fig. 6). The cross-sections show material movement in a small section  of the AlGaAs layer and the InGaAs DFET channel. EDS  analysis of the damaged area showed that the indium from the  DFET channel has diffused into the spacer and the gate (Fig. 7). This diffusion allowed the gate to be closer to the channel, which in essence is similar to transforming the small section  of the DFET channel into an EFET2 (wherein the drain is  connected to VMODE0 and both the gate and source are  connected to the base of the Q1 HBT).


In this configuration, the channel is pinched off as long as the  drain is at a higher potential compared to the gate-source  node. Once the drain is more negative than the gate-source  node, the channel starts to conduct. This corroborates the I-V  curve observed when the VMODE pin was probed with  respect to the base of Q1 HBT. Defect Simulation


An experiment was performed in order to simulate the defect  as well as determine which type of ESD stress caused the  failure. A total of fifteen passing parts were used for the  experiment. Five devices were used for each type of ESD  stress3 (MM, HBM and CDM). For each type, the voltage was  increased until the VMODE0 pin failed. Afterwards, the I-V  curves were compared to those of the original failing devices. For the MM stress, the VMODE0 pin started to fail at -150 V. For the HBM stress, the device failed at -2.1 kV. However, both stresses did not yield the same I-V curve for the  VMODE0 pin. Finally, for the CDM stress, the VMODE0 pin  failed at 750 V and the I-V curve looked the same as those of  the original failures. The five devices that were subjected to  the CDM stress were then tested using the production test. As  expected, the devices failed the same parameters as the  original failure.


As a design correction, a 500 Ω resistor was added between  the VMODE0 pin and the DFET. The device did not fail the  CDM stress even at voltages up to 2000 V.


hutSo 1383 as Curer. 0000


Multiple GaAs PA devices were submitted for analysis after  failing different reliability stresses. Fault isolation revealed  ESD damage on a DFET connected to the VMODE0 pin. The  ESD damage converted a small portion of the DFET channel  into an EFET and resulted in the device to be stuck in high  power mode. Simulation of the failure showed that most likely  the defect was caused by CDM stress. A design change of  inserting a resistor between the VMODE0 pin and the DFET  made the device more robust against CDM stress.

Marginal RF Gain Investigation and Root Cause Determination


Keith Harber, Steve Brockett


TriQuint Semiconductor, Inc., Hillsboro OR USA  Keith.Harber@tqs.com


This paper outlines the failure analysis of a Radio Frequency  only (RF-only) failure on a complex Multimode Multiband  Power Amplifier (MMPA) module, where slightly lower gain  was observed in one mode of operation. 2 port S-parameter  information was collected and utilized to help localize the  circuitry causing the issue. A slight DC electrical difference  was observed, and simulation was utilized to confirm that  difference was causing the observed S-parameters. Physical  analysis uncovered a very visible cause for the RF-only  failure.


Radio Frequency (RF) chips and wireless networks are an  ever-expanding market, as are the number of frequencies  which they serve. RF Power Amplifier Modules (PAMs) utilizing GaAs power amplifier (PA) die are becoming more  complex, as they are optimized for these different frequencies  and different markets. A further complexity factor is the  consolidation of functionality into MMPA modules, which  integrate the various bands into single module units designed  to provide one RF solution. This integration often means the  implementation of multiple GaAs PA die into a module, with  various other functions, generally control and switching  functions, handled by other semiconductor die that may also  be GaAs, Si, or SOI-based. After including output matching  networks for the various PA die (implemented both at the  packaging level and in surface-mount device (SMD) components), a typical MMPA module may end up serving 4  different frequency bands, at 3 different power levels per  frequency, and include 4 different GaAs PA die (with 2 or  more GaAs, Si, or SOI die), 14 SMDs, and four laminate  inductors.


While failure analysis of GaAs-based RF modules might be  thought to be straightforward, since the use of GaAs often  means much larger physical scales than those in the state of  the art Silicon-based die, there are challenges which  counteract that one advantage. As previously mentioned, the  increasing integration of multiple components (multiple die / different technologies, SMD components, and packaging  complexity) into a single functional unit provides a  localization challenge for failure analysis. Localization  becomes even more difficult in the case of an “RF-only” failure (a failure which occurs only in RF parameters such as  power or gain), for the simple reason that it is quite rare that  RF signals can be successfully utilized in an FA lab  environment. Given that a subtle modification of wire bond  placement can impact RF performance, it does not take much


imagination to consider the impact of probe points, probe  needles, noise, harmonics / oscillations, etc. on RF  performance and the subsequent difficulty introduced for FA. Rather than stimulating an RF-only failure with RF and trying  to observe the failure to perform the analysis, the analyst must  critically review test information on how the part failed with  regard to RF performance, determine if any further RF  characterization may be helpful, and then begin to assess the  failing RF circuitry effectively using only DC techniques. An  analyst must be armed with logic, and an attention to detail  when analyzing RF-only failures, for a subtly different DC  parameter may have a large impact in the RF world—or, it  may not have any impact at all. As with any technology, carefully orchestrated physical analysis techniques must be  employed to find the failure root cause1; unplanned or  haphazard execution of physical analysis approaches can  preclude subsequent analysis work or destroy the cause of the  failure when potential causes are not considered in advance.


This paper outlines the failure analysis of an RF-only failure  on a complex MMPA module, where slightly lower gain was  observed in one mode of operation, and serves to highlight the  challenges of analysis for RF-only failures.


Failure Details


During room temperature testing, one mode (Medium Power, MP) of Low Band (LB) Wideband Code Division Multiple  Access (WCDMA) amplifier operation on a handful of  MMPA modules returned by a customer were observed to  have a consistent failure, displaying only a subtle ~0.7 dBm to  1 dBm lower RF output power than expected. The fail units  were from different assembly batches, with different assembly  dates. Engineering hand test and automated test showed the  failure to be consistent in the lower RF gain. The stability and  consistency of the failure units pointed towards a repeatable  issue with the units themselves, and not variation in test  fixtures, test systems, or test evaluation of the RF gain in the  failing mode. In addition, no other parameters other than RF  gain failed during testing.


Failure Analysis


Commonly performed failure analysis “triage” activities  including package optical inspection, pin curve-tracing, and  X-ray inspection2 (both 2D and 3D) provided no insight into  the failures, as might be expected given the subtlety of the  observed failure. Figure 1 shows the 2D X-ray of the failing  MMPA part, providing an idea of the complexity of the  module.


Figure 1: 2D X-ray view of a failing MMPA, showing the  multiple GaAs die (both PA and control), SMD components, and laminate components.


With no practical ability to perform analysis while exercising  the failure, the schematics for the MMPA were reviewed with  the failing test results in mind. A functional block level  schematic for the failing RF tests of the MMPA is shown in  Figure 2.


Figure 2: Block level schematic for RF tests failing on MMPA. Green components outline the expected RF path for the failing  LB MP WCDMA mode, while blue components are those  which could impact the RF performance in that operation  mode.


Given multiple failures, one unit was deprocessed by polishing  to the first laminate layer, thereby providing electrical access  to the surface mount devices (SMDs) shown in Figure 1, and  the individual pads of the die of interest for the failing mode. Probing of the SMD components was performed to compare  with nominal values and component tolerances. No suspect  components were identified. Simple curve-tracing of first  laminate connections to the die of interest was performed to  examine the possibility of resistive pad connections on either  die. No issues or possibilities for the fail cause were noted on  either die.


The unit was then decapsulated to allow inspection and  microprobing access for both the control / switch die and the  LB WCDMA PA die. After decapsulation, close inspection of  both die revealed no anomalies. Both DC and functional  microprobing was then performed, looking at all aspects of  both die and how they were utilized during the failing mode. Voltage regulation and drive levels from the control die were  checked and found to be satisfactory. Functional operation of  the control die switch transistors, both input and output, were  verified. DC levels and quiescent currents associated with the  LB WCDMA PA die were checked at multiple locations, and  curve tracing of bias lines on the PA die showed no obvious  issues. In summary, a first order analysis could find no notable  DC parametric which would account for the RF-only failure  which was observed.


With no obvious DC electrical anomaly discovered, further RF  characterization of an additional failure unit was performed in  an attempt to provide further understanding and localization of  the failure cause. 2 port S-parameter characterization of the  MMPA in the failing mode was performed, and identified a  difference in the S11 (input reflection) response of the fail unit  as compared to a reference device, as shown in Figure 3.


Figure 3: S11 response of fail units (red traces) compared to  reference units (green traces).


With the completion of the S-parameter measurements  showing an issue with the input side of the unit, analysis could  confidently focus on the input path side of the functional block  diagram, where the S11 measurement would be affected.


Detailed parametric analysis on every element on the input  side of the RF input path of the unit was performed. Control  die switch transistors were re-verified, with measurement of  the Ron performed. Control die bias levels were also reverified, and microprobing in the PA circuitry was re-done, with a high level of scrutiny on circuit elements which were “visible” to the S11 measurement.


A subtle parametric difference was observed in the  measurement of an input matching circuit inductor resistance  on the fail unit LB WCDMA PA die, as shown in Figure 4. The inductor was DC-blocked, and so would not provide any  obvious DC parametric signal. In addition, the inductor was  implemented in parallel with a resistor; first order analysis, after verifying a low inductor resistance (i.e., no open or  resistive vias), had focused on measurement of the parallel  resistor, physically making further measurement of the  inductor resistance impossible. On a reference unit die, the  inductor measured ~ 8 Ω. However, on the fail unit die, the  inductor resistance measured ~ 25 Ω. Four-point resistance  measurement of the inductor confirmed the subtle difference  in resistance noted by curve tracing.


Figure 4: Close scrutiny of components which would affect  S11 in the failing mode led to the identification of an  anomalous inductor resistance (~25 Ω, red trace) when  compared against a reference inductor (~8 Ω, green trace) on  the input RF match circuit on the LB WCDMA PA die.


The observed DC difference shown in Figure 4 was the only  item noted which would match expectations from test and  characterization results, given its location in the circuit on the  input side of the failing mode. However, certainty of this  parametric difference as the cause for the failure was desired  prior to proceeding with any physical analysis. In an effort to  obtain certainty, RF simulations for S11 response was  performed utilizing the measured inductor resistance values. Results are shown in Figure 5, and are overlaid against the  measured characteristics shown previously in Figure 3. The  near-match between measured and simulated characteristics


provided good confidence that the anomalous resistance of the  inductor was causing the failure.


Figure 5: Simulation results (dashed lines) of the added  resistance observed on the inductor shown in Figure 4 are  overlaid against the measured S11 response of fail units (red  traces) and reference units (green traces) shown previously in  Figure 3. Simulation results closely match measurements.


Physical Analysis


With an electrical cause for the RF failure determined, physical analysis of the inductor was undertaken. A summary  of the inductor construction is shown in Figure 6.


Figure 6: Inductor construction is shown above; upper images  show layout views of the three metal layers used to construct  the inductor, with the lower image showing the resulting  inductor on the die.


Sequential FIB cross sections with SEM inspection were  performed, focusing on the single likely point of added  resistance in the inductor—the via between Metal 2 and the  paired Metal 1 / Metal 0. Close inspection of the via was  performed, but revealed no obvious issues at the via.


Liquid crystal analysis was performed on the inductor with a  second unit. Interestingly, no single point of higher thermal  emission was identified, consistent with the FIB cross section  results. A review of the metal layer resistance differences due  to thickness suggested the resistance difference could be due  to an issue with one of the lower metal coils.


Polishing of the inductor was then performed so that the lower  metal coils of the inductor could be examined. While the  electrical effect of the failure was subtle, physical analysis  showed the defect very clearly. An area of Metal 1 was  missing, thereby disconnecting one of the paired coils of the  inductor, as shown in Figure 7.


Figure 7: Removal of the upper coil on the inductor revealed  an open in the lower Metal 1 coil. The open completely  explained all aspects of the failure which were observed.


Logical next steps were taken, verifying missing Metal 1 in  the same inductor coil on an additional fail unit. Interestingly, and quite surprisingly, the missing Metal 1 was at a different  physical location on the same inductor coil. Physical analysis  of yet another of the failures revealed missing Metal 1 on the  same inductor coil, but also at a different physical location. Given the consistency of the RF failures, it was obvious that  missing Metal 1 in the inductor was the cause of the failure, as  it would create a consistent anomalous inductor resistance.


Investigation into the part history revealed that  implementation of the failing tests had been improved slightly  between initial testing of the parts (which passed) and  subsequent test of the units on their return (which had slightly  failed for low RF gain). No defects were observed on the  Metal 1 mask of the GaAs die (nor expected, given the  varying location of missing Metal 1 on the inductor), which  suggests that the multiple failures were due to individual  random defects in processing.


Thanks to Steve Brockett, Tarun Juneja, Vivek Dixit, Jule  Cunningham, Pat Hamilton, Varun Juneja, Carl Stuebing, Matt  Salove, Wayne Jung, Bill Roesch, Khanh Lieng, Brad Silvers, and other analysts in the TriQuint Failure Analysis group for  their help and insight during the analysis work and the  subsequent publication process.


[1] Microelectronics Failure Analysis Desk Reference, 5th  ed., ASM International, 2004.


[2] Microelectronics Reliability 47 (2007), "Field returns, a  source of natural failure mechanisms", pp. 1156-1165, W.J. Roesch, S. Brockett.


Anamnesis in Failure Analysis - How a System-Related Approach Can Save


Failure Analysis (FA) Time, Shorten Learning Loops and Reduce Cost


Peter Jacob


Empa Swiss Fed Labs for Materials Testing and Research, CH-8600 Duebendorf, Switzerland  and


EM Microelectronic Marin SA, CH-2074 Marin-Epagnier, Switzerland


Peter.jacob@empa.ch


Anamnesis is known as an important method for pre-diagnosis  in medical sciences. In device failure analysis (FA) it is not so  far used, yet – especially with regard to system- and  application-aspects. As a consequence, a lot of useless rootcause-related FA efforts are done on device level, while the  root cause is on system level. Introduced by an illustrative case  study, the benefit of a suitable anamnesis is shown as well as  the way to do it – by posing the right questions before FA  starts. Many FA efforts can be saved or optimized and  frequently, a sound anamnesis already may lead towards the  root-cause conclusion.


Most of actual FA cases start and end on device level, frequently not knowing about the circumstances under which  the device has failed. Findings as molten metal, oxide  breakdown etc. finally result in the diagnosis “Electrical  Overstress (EOS)” which, however, in the vast majority of  cases doesn’t allow to draw conclusions on a root cause or  corrective actions. FA of the future, however, must look  beyond the chip level and include system- and application  aspects. However, such approach needs a culture- and  paradigm change in failure analysis: On system level, a lot of  contributors in the production chain are afraid to get passed  the buck – thus providing 8-D-“smoke grenades” instead of  communicating existing problems frankly and cooperatively  working on related technical solutions (which are sometimes  done in a hidden manner and kept confidential).


Anamnesis


In order to reduce doubtful conclusions and useless  conclusions, a list of questions and linked aspects has been  worked out which allows redirecting the F/A effort from the  beginning into a device-related, an application-related or a  system-related way. In many cases, already statistical results  allow to exclude a variety of in principle possible failure  mechanisms.


The paper introduces into the topic using a small case study of  an opto-coupler, followed by a Schmitt-threshold detector. The


output of the optocoupler delivered bad, flat pulse edge  steepness, resulting in an inacceptable threshold detector  output. The device has been sent to us together with a report of  the electrical characterisation, demanding for physical FA. It  was not easy to obtain the application circuitry from a third (system level) party involved. They claimed that after having  replaced the optocouplers by those of another vendor, the  problem had disappeared. After physical FA on “defective” samples had not shown any useful evidence, we reconstructed  the application circuitry in our lab and re-analyzed the  problem electrically, using known good, known bad samples  and also samples of a second-source-vendor. It turned out that  an external resistor, determining the operation point of the  output amplifier, has been selected at a border value, which  sometimes results in good and sometimes in non-reproducible  outputs after the threshold detector (fig. 1). Redimensioning of  this resistor made the circuitry properly working even with  known “bad” devices.


To generalize this and other cases with similar histories, a  check list has been developed which should be discussed with  any requester of FA support.


This list includes the following Q&A aspects: Failure  evidence/ statistical work, circuitry evaluation vs. device  specification, operation environment, secondary damages, EMI and ESD impacts, supply- and signal stability, derating  issues, user-related impacts, evidence of PCNs, device origin (fake evaluation) and others.


Figure 1: The optocoupler (left) delivered incorrect output  pulses, resulting in a loss of some pulses in the subsequent  threshold detector (right). While the optocoupler had been  sent to us for FA, the real root cause was a wrong  dimensioning of the external circuitry resistor R, which  determines the working point of the integrated amplifier, resulting in bad pulse shapes.


Practical Experiences


The anamnesis approach has been tested at Empa in the last  two years in a wider variety of FA-requesting customers. Most  of them came from the wide scope of industrial electronics as  wind-/ solar power control unit manufacturers (both powerand microelectronics) , process equipment control electronics, medical electronics, building control electronics, aircraft- and  automotive electronics, LEDs and watches. Most of these  companies didn’t produce the semiconductors by themselves  but were producers of subsystems or even of the final product. In few cases as power electronic modules, LEDs and one ICwafer manufacturer, we deal with real device manufacturer  clients. All companies were long-term customers with a good  and close relationship beyond the scope of actual common  projects in FA and reliability. Above all, the intensive pre-FAanamnesis gave significant benefit for all parties involved  since nearly always aspects came into discussion, which had  not been considered, yet. The pie-chart in fig. 2 shows the  most important topics.


Figure 2: Pie-chart of device failure root causes, found by  careful anamnesis, followed by investigations on system level. This chart didn’t consider real device-production-related root  causes (wafer & pre-assembly), which contribute about 1/4 of  overall failure root causes appearing in the field


Let’s have a look into the details of fig. 2. We start with the  major contribution of sportive specifications versus missing  derating. On both side of component manufacturer and  component user, economic pressure increased significantly in  the recent years. As a result of component miniaturization and  competition, components meanwhile are specified more and  more along the borders of their real capabilities. For instance, a capacitor specified for 16V today is at risk already at 20V  spikes, while in former times, even 24V spikes would have  been survived for long time. On the opposite side, many users  don’t have the economical reserve to design-in some derating (as was done in former times). This pair of scissors is now  going to close more and more and frequently results in field


failures. A focal point is given by capacitors, where this effect  can be observed in all classes (electrolytic capacitors, foil  capacitors and also ceramic capacitors) [1]. On semiconductor  devices, the reduced space available for protection circuitry  means that less energy (of voltage spikes) can be bleeded off  without destruction, resulting in enhanced EOS failures with a  misleading, ESD-similar failure texture [2].


This leads us to the second frequent category, which we called “missing overvoltage/ spike protection”: the hit list of this  category is headed by missing protective diodes for sensitive  MOSFET circuitry in heavily exposed circuitry as it can be  found in all combinations of micro- and power electronics. Typical scenarios can be found in solar- and wind-power plant  rectifiers, light railway- or trolley bus electronics etc. Also  circuitries with (sometimes hidden) inductive components  missed to design-in useful protective circuitry against  inductive response voltage spikes. A special category within  this problem field is that of LED-circuitries and –matrixes, where the LEDs should be protected against reverse-bias  voltage spikes by means of a serial diode. LEDs are rather  sensitive against reverse bias voltage spikes and far the worst  is the fact that they don’t fail functionally by this but suffer  significant lifetime reduction [3].


Looking now towards functional circuitry failures, the third  place on the hit list, we are talking about a lot of very  individual (but also sometimes systematic) circuitry failures. Generally it can be stated that today’s circuit design frequently  relies on simulation results and math, applied without a circuit  design veteran’s gut instinct of what really can happen in a  circuitry. A few examples may better illustrate that category: If  an optocoupler is used in a circuitry, it should be controlled in  a manner, that, if the system is off, the optocoupler should be  so, too. We had problems on locomotive electronics, where  optocouplers were on duty when the locomotive has been  parked overnight, resulting in dedicated early life failures. Also in optocouplers, we’ve seen critical dimensioning of  feedback-circuitry: in order to balance the long-time  decreasing LED emission of the optocoupler, a second  integrated receiving photodiode has been used to measure the  LED emission and to re-power up the LED towards a constant  signal output. If such circuitry is used from the beginning  already close to the maximum ratings, the lifetime is  dramatically reduced, too. Another example are hidden  inductivities in DC-DC-converters, which may respond by  voltage spikes in case of sudden load changes. If the circuitry  around doesn’t consider this, sensitive devices may fail. A  third example is given in a three-phase EMI-catching Yconnection of three capacitors: If the neutral (center point) is  floating, the voltage may deviate by capacitance deviations  and reach critical voltages in one of the phases (if no voltage  derating of the capacitors took place).


The example takes us to EMI-related failures, which is  frequently by long cable connections. Every subsystem (delivered by one manufacturer) has been successfully tested  on EMI robustness. But when integrating these subsystems  into a big system, for instance a long trainset with long cable  connects and high voltage around, devices of one of the  subsystems may fail due to coupled pulses. In the RF band,


even dedicated cable length may generate resonance cases  which cause systematic device failures. In such cases, it is  more or less absolute useless for root cause finding, if the  subsystem manufacturer sends the failed device to an external  FA lab asking for root cause analysis…The failure category  increased recently with upcoming new combinations of microand power-electronics as for instance in wind- or solar-power  generators and traction current rectifiers. These applications  are frequently also exposed to thunderstorm lightning and  unstable state of connected power networks, which add-on  related risks.


Cooling and thermal equilibrium problems are the next  category of failures. A very trivial but most frequent issue is  the component placement on PCBs, where often heatgenerating components as for instance power semiconductors  are placed neighbored to heat-sensitive components as for  instance electrolytic capacitors. In power electronics, sometimes big power devices are not mounted on heat sinks if  they are just used in an emergency case to redirect excess  power for a few seconds. However, if they are exposed to  continuous reverse bias voltage, intrinsic small leakage may  power up their internal temperature locally towards a critical, self-accelerating degree, thus causing long-term failures. Also, frequently LED-cooling of high-power LEDs is  underestimated, especially if they are pulse-driven.


If we look to the smaller categories of fig. 2, the following  topics can be highlighted:


Environmental impact problems are related in many cases to  relatively new applications as electronics for windpower plants  or solar energy. In these fields, application-specific  standardization of requests to electronic devices is still at the  beginning. New and hard environmental superimpositions as  combinations of salty humidity, vibrations and power cycling  as on off-shore windpower plants meet with high voltage and  high power and overburden many components (Figs. 3, 4). In

Closure


Now that the crack was known to have been present prior to  this analysis (i.e., it was not induced during the analysis), fractography could be performed. The main findings were that  the fracture that caused the failure was not a fast (instantaneous) fracture, such as might have been caused by  an impact. No material defect, such as an inclusion or void, was found. The origin of the fracture could not be found, implying that the origin had most likely already been crosssectioned away earlier in this analysis. As a result, it could not  be determined whether the crack was initiated by a material  defect or an externally applied stress, such as a thermal  overstress.


There are at least three possible root causes of the crack:


 A crack may have already been present when the device  was first delivered by Avago, possibly propagating later. The extensive electrical testing conducted in this  investigation has demonstrated that it passed all electrical  testing at ambient, hot, and cold temperatures, even with  the crack present. This would be considered a test escape, with the device eventually intermittently failing after the  stresses of installation and under the different mechanical  stresses of being mounted on its circuit board.


 The crack may have been induced during normal  installation or rework because of a latent defect in the  ceramic. If no excessive thermal or mechanical stresses  were applied to the device during installation or rework, then the package should not have fractured unless there  was a material defect in it, such as an inclusion, microcrack, or large, irregular void. No evidence of such  a defect was found, though it is noted that a portion of the  crack had already been cross-sectioned away prior to the  fracture analysis.


 The crack may have been induced by excessive thermal  or mechanical stresses during installation or rework, though based on the fractography results, a mechanical  overstress is less likely. Ceramics are known to be  sensitive to both thermal and mechanical shocks, and this  device was reportedly installed by a hand-soldering  process.


It is noted that the observed fracture did extend to both the top  surface and the underside of the device, suggesting that if it  was preexisting, it may have been noticeable to an inspector – at Avago, TCS, the test lab, or the customer’s facility – who  was performing any inspection of the part prior to installation. If any cracks had been seen prior to delivery, this part should  have been rejected. However, it is also noted that in the  condition in which this device was received for analysis – with some residual coating material on the top and bottom  surfaces – the crack was not seen during TCS’s external visual  inspection steps.


Avago Technologies has stated that they manufactured  approximately 100,000 6N140A parts that year, and they have  been manufacturing four-channel 16-pin optocouplers for  about 30 years. If there had been a crack or other defect in this  device package – perhaps already present when Avago  procured the package from package manufacturer NTK  Technologies – this would be considered an extremely rare  occurrence. History searches found no manufacturer or  GIDEP alerts for the Avago 6N140 part number, or for any  ceramic DIPs manufactured by NTK. If the crack was induced  by excessive installation or rework stresses, then there would  be no inherent increased reliability risk in the use of any of  these devices. The only increased reliability risk would be a  function of the thermal and mechanical stresses to which the  parts have been subjected since their delivery. TCS therefore  recommended no corrective actions to Avago or the customer.


After exhaustive testing and analysis, at no time was an  intermittent open of the channel 4 LED circuit observed as  reported, though a low current output was observed from the  channel 4 detector circuit. The results of the real-time x-ray, initial CT, C-SAM, internal visual, bond pull testing, and  cross-sectional analyses indicated that all conductor interfaces  were solid and intact. However, a cross-sectional analysis  found that the package ceramic at pin 8 – and a metallized  path embedded in the ceramic – may have been cracked. The  final CT review found that both the ceramic and the pin 8  metallization had already been cracked when the device was  returned to TCS. This crack can explain the reported  intermittent high resistance or open of the channel 4 LED  path. Although the resistance of this path was measured by  TCS to be 1.76 Ω, the finding of a complete fracture implies  that under various mechanical and thermal conditions, the pin  8 path could at various times have had a resistance of less than  one ohm, several ohms or hundreds of ohms (or kilohms), or it  could even have been electrically open. A high enough series  resistance in the channel 4 LED path would cause the LED to  put out less light, which would in turn cause the channel 4  detector to output a low current. This may explain some of the  low CTR3 readings. The package crack is therefore believed  to have caused the originally reported intermittent failure of  channel 4.


When these results were given to TCS’s customer  representatives, they were both relieved and elated. TCS and  the test labs with which we worked had seen no first-hand  evidence that the electrical failure had ever occurred until after  what was supposed to have been the last step in the analysis – the cross-sectional examination. Had it not been for the CT  study performed before destructive work, we would never  have even been certain that a failure occurred. It would have  been easy to write off the observed ceramic crack as having  been induced during LED removal, and its location as a  coincidence. Thanks to CT, we were able to not only verify  the failure, but also identify its possible root causes. CT  effectively served as a nondestructively obtained permanent  record of the physical condition of the suspect device in its  original state as submitted, and the analysis could not have  been successful without it.

automated parametric testing; Jill Hix and Evans Ryan of  SEAL Labs of El Segundo, CA for much of the destructive  analysis work; Dr. Sya Ensha of SEAL for the fractography; Optocoupler Applications Engineer Jamshed Khan of Avago  Technologies for consultation; Senior Component Engineer  Greg Hix of TCS Space & Component Technology for his  help with electrical testing and in coordinating the flurry of  technical tasks; and to our unnamed customer representatives  for their insistence that a failure really had occurred.

Challenges of Small Defect Analysis in Large Analog Power FET Arrays


Eric Cattey


Freescale Semiconductor, Tempe, Arizona USA


The proverbial needle in the haystack – locating a minute


process defect or subtle ESD strike in a large sea of analog


output power FETs can be just that. The premise of this paper  is to discuss failure analysis techniques used to identify these  elusive “needles”, specifically in large array power FET


structures.  Two case studies will be explored in detail – both  of which are 250nm technology devices.


ICs with a significant portion of the die area (>50%) populated  with power FET structures can serve as submicron defect


monitors for the wafer FAB.  Statistically, if a FET related


process defect is to occur, there is a high probability it will


occur in the dominant output FETs.


Figure 1: IC with geometrically dominant power FETs.


Inline defect screening and comprehensive test coverage


contain the majority of manufacturing defects. However, latent  defects resulting in device failure post final test do occur and  require subsequent product analysis. Conveying accurate and


timely failure analysis information back to the wafer FAB for  process improvement is critical.


Analog output power FET structures are often realized as an


array of power FETs connected in parallel, functioning


collectively as a single three terminal device. Common


configurations are high-side and low-side output drivers which  are used to switch electrical loads. The output driver of an IC  fails in an application when the output looses the ability to


fully turn-on (high-side) or fully turn-off (low-side). This


inability is commonly diagnosed during ATE (Automated Test


Equipment) testing as a high Rdson failure. Often, a high


Rdson failure is attributed to some form of gate leakage, either  gate-source or gate-drain. Traditional fault isolation


techniques are typically effective for G-S and G-D leakage


failures, however precise fault isolation becomes more


challenging in FET arrays because there are multiple power


FETs connected in parallel, each power FET with numerous


gate fingers. A gate-to-source leakage path for example, can


exist on any one of the many gate fingers on any one of the


power FETs in the output array. Accurate electrical


localization becomes crucial for finding physical evidence of  the failure mechanism.


Figure 2: Power FET realized as multiple FETs in parallel


Backside techniques are typically preferred when electrically


localizing submicron defects or subtle ESD damage in


multiple large power FETs. However, depending on the ICs


design, layout and packaging constraints, backside analysis is  not always feasible.  Backside functional bias conditions are  often inadequate to properly exercise the leakage source for


fault isolation. Furthermore, the electrical analysis of power


FET gate nodes typically requires topside microprobing,


making a topside approach necessary. Unfortunately, fault


isolation techniques such as OBIRCH (Optical Beam Induced


Resistance Change) can be challenging from the topside due to  thick blanket metallization and multiple backend process


layers that distort or obscure OBIRCH signals.


The following case studies examine various techniques used to


analyze failures in large power FET arrays when design


constraints and other variables hinder electrical fault isolation


and physical analysis.


The first case study involves a topside analysis approach on an  IC design similar to that shown in figure 1. Upon receipt of the


sample, a review of the ATE data logs indicated a high Rdson  condition for one of the high-side power FET output drivers. Based on the failure mode, it was determined that


microprobing of the gate and gate drive circuitry would be


necessary, making a backside fault isolation approach


unfeasible. For that reason, the device was topside


decapsulated. Subsequent topside microprobing in the output  power FET array identified a ~1.5kΩ resistive gate-source


leakage path in the FET array. For this particular device, each  high-side output driver is comprised of numerous large power


FETs in parallel. OBIRCH was first attempted with all metal  layers intact. Leakage bias levels were kept low (<20uA) so as  to not alter the failure site. First order analysis produced a


distributed OBIRCH signature covering approximately 25


gates. From past analyses, the impedance of the leakage


suggested a submicron issue; therefore better electrical


localization would be required to successfully locate the


failure mechanism.


The die was then extracted from the package. CAD layout


documentation was examined to understand the layout


characteristics and metallization of the output FET array. The


goal was to determine the maximum number of metal layers


that could be removed while still maintaining the functionality  of the FET as a whole. For this particular device with four


metal layer technology, it was determined that metal4 (top


blanket metal layer) was used to connect the common source


and drain nodes together. Completely removing the metal4


layer would electrically isolate each source and drain finger,


which was not desired. Therefore, the thick aluminum metal4


layer was mechanically de-layered leaving the thin underlying  arc-metal4 layer intact to maintain the functionality of the


output driver.  Microprobe techniques were used to bias the GS leakage path for OBIRCH fault isolation. OBIRCH at arcmetal utilizing the Seebeck effect (zero bias) [1] was able to


localize the leakage point to a single gate finger while utilizing  very low bias conditions.


Figure 3: OBIRCH with blanket metal intact (upper image) verses  OBIRCH with blanket metal removed (lower image). Removing the  thick blanket metal improved localization from ~25 gates to 1 gate.


After precise electrical localization of the leakage site, the


device was deprocessed layer-by-layer down to polysilicon


using both mechanical and chemical de-layering techniques. Optical inspection at each metal layer and at polysilicon


revealed no anomaly. Subsequent SEM (Scanning Electron


Microscope) inspection of the OBIRCH site location revealed  conclusive evidence of a process defect. The defect, which


was likely caused by CMP (chemical mechanical


planarization) related micro-scratch damage, produced a


localized weak point in the gate oxide eventually resulting in a  gate oxide rupture. See figure 4.


Figure 4: Physical evidence of a process defect which resulted in a


gate-source gate oxide rupture.


The second case study is also based on an IC design with


analog output drivers comprised of numerous power FETs in  parallel and covered in thick blanket metal. This particular


analysis utilized a combination of topside and backside


techniques [2] to identify the failure mechanism.


A review of the ATE data logs upon receipt of the sample


indicated that a single output on the IC was not functioning


correctly – the output failed testing for high Rdson as well as  various functional tests. Based on the failure mode and design


of the IC, it was determined that topside microprobing would  be necessary for electrical fault isolation. The device was


topside decapsulated. Subsequent microprobing in the output


driver FET array revealed a 3.3kΩ gate-drain leakage path.


This particular output driver consists of hundreds of power


FETs configured in parallel and covered in thick blanket


metal. OBIRCH with blanket metal intact was attempted first, but was unsuccessful. In order to achieve optimal fault


localization, the blanket metal layers covering the power FETs  would need to be removed.  As in case study 1, CAD layout


documentation was first studied to determine the maximum


number of metal layers that could be removed while still


maintaining the functionality of the FET as a whole. For this  particular device with four metal layer technology, it was


determined that metal2 was the lowest metal layer used to


connect the common source and drain nodes together and


maintain functionality as a single power FET. The die was


extracted from the package and metal4 and metal3 layers were  mechanically removed stopping on via2. FIB probe pads


where then deposited to via2 on the common gate and drain


nodes of the FET array.

Figure 5: Localized OBIRCH site at via2 after mechanically


removing blanket metal layers.


OBIRCH analysis was then performed utilizing the Seebeck


effect (zero bias). Analysis revealed an abnormal localized


OBIRCH site on one of the power FETs within the output


array. By removing the blanket metal over the power FETs


and repeating OBIRCH, it was possible to localize the leakage  site to a single gate while utilizing low level bias conditions


and preventing any alteration of the failure site.


Based on the gate-drain leakage signature and the OBIRCH


data, a gate level defect was suspected, therefore the decision  was made to proceed with a backside physical analysis


approach. In preparation for a backside bulk silicon etch, the  extracted die was mounted to a sacrificial substrate and then


encased in epoxy. The die was then mechanically thinned to  approximately 50 microns. A TMAH etch was then used to


remove the bulk silicon and expose gate oxide while keeping

the remaining metal1 and metal2 intact. Following removal of  the silicon substrate, backside optical inspection of the


OBIRCH location revealed evidence of an anomaly. See


figure 6. Due to the small size of the anomaly, SEM imaging


was necessary. Subsequent backside SEM inspection of the


anomaly revealed evidence of a possible patterning defect. See  figure 7.


Figure 6: Backside optical images showing an anomaly at the


OBIRCH site location.


TAZPAL 4.0KUX43,00011mm Figure 7: Backside SEM image showing a polysilicon patterning  defect.


In order to determine the root cause of the patterning defect, a  backside FIB cross-section was performed. Analysis


confirmed the presence of abnormal polysilicon extending into  the drain region creating a resistive leakage path between the


gate and drain contact. The defect is likely the result of a fallon particle after polysilicon deposition and prior to the gate


photo patterning process. The particle blocked the subsequent


polysilicon gate etch and resulted in a patterning defect. The  drain contact was formed during subsequent process steps and


shorted to the anomalous polysilicon resulting in gate-drain


leakage.

Finding small defects or subtle ESD damage in large power  FET arrays can be challenging due to the design, layout and  processing characteristics of current ICs. Backside fault


isolation techniques are typically preferred when analyzing


100nmF1 L01


power FET arrays; however they are not always feasible - a


topside approach is often necessary to achieve adequate bias  conditions for electrical localization. Topside techniques such  as OBIRCH however, can be challenging due to thick blanket

metal and multiple backend process layers which can obscure  signals and make electrical localization difficult. A key point


discussed in this paper is the strategic removal of power FET  metal layers for the optimization of topside OBIRCH. The


mechanical removal of as many blanket metal layers as


possible prior to OBIRCH analysis can significantly improve  fault localization. In some cases, strategic metal removal can


improve localization from dozens of gates to a single gate


relative to a traditional topside approach. Additionally,


strategic metal removal enables the utilization of low-level


leakage bias conditions which helps to prevent alteration of


the failure site. It is important to note however, that


understanding the layout and metallization characteristics of a  power FET array prior to de-layering is critical. The


inadvertent removal of metal layers which are used to connect  common source, drain and gates nodes can be detrimental to  an analysis, as hundreds of isolated FETs are created. The goal


of this technique is to remove as many thick metal layers as


possible while still preserving the functionality of the array as


a single power FET for biasing. The successful


implementation of this technique can significantly improve


electrical localization and increase the probability of finding


the needle in the haystack. Furthermore, combining backside  physical analysis techniques with optimized topside electrical


localization techniques provides an accurate means of root


cause failure analysis in large power FET arrays.
