Conversion of a D-mode FET to an E-mode FET via electrostatic discharge in a  GaAs Power Amplifier Duplexer Module


Rose Emergo and Steve Brockett


TriQuint Semiconductor, 2300 NE Brookwood Parkway Hillsboro, OR 97123


This paper outlines the systematic isolation of an electrostatic  discharge defect on a depletion-mode FET. The ESD damage  converted a small portion of the DFET into an enhancementmode FET and affected the logic circuit such that the device  was stuck in a single power mode at both band frequencies. The affected DFET is connected to the VMODE0 pin of a 2-in-1 GaAs Power Amplifier Duplexer Module. The module is  for Bands 2 & 5 for use with WCDMA, CDMA and LTE  modulations. The module is comprised of B2 PA, B5 PA, duplexers, couplers and voltage regulator circuits (Figure 1). Each PA operates in either medium or high power mode. The  voltage applied on the VMODE0 pin dictates which power  mode the device operates at. The device was fabricated using  TriQuint’s BiHEMT process and assembled using CuFlip (TriQuint's patented flip chip interconnect technique). The  GaAs BiHEMT die consists of the pHEMT technology used  for the control circuit; and the HBT technology used for the  PA circuit.

those of the HPM. This suggests that the device is stuck at the  HPM regardless of the chosen power mode.

Several 8M SRAM wafers suffered from zero yield with major  issue of entire block failure at the beginning stage of  technology development. Figure 14 shows a typical wafer map  with failure bitmap for a chip at right side. For this case, no  WL or BL pattern was able to be identified. Thus, without the  assistance of the SRAM designer, layout tracing was  impossible. In order to narrow down the suspected defective  area for physical failure analysis, three failing chips were  subjected to PEM analysis. PEM analysis on three failing  chips showed emission at a repeated particular circuit (See  Figure 15).  A reference chip was also done PEM analysis and  no any emission was detected at the same given circuit. The  100X PEM image showing the emission at the particular  circuit is displayed in Figure 16. It implied that a systematic  defect in this circuit caused the entire block failure. Based on  the PEM analysis, subsequent physical analysis found poly


broken at the all emission sites. Figure 17 is the SEM image of  an example of the poly broken.


Figure 14: A wafer map showing lots of entire block failures  with one chip-level failure bitmap at right side.


Figure 15: PEM image showing emission sites at a repeated  particular circuit for three failing chips and no emission at the  same circuit for a reference chip.


Unlike SRAM single bit, paired bit or quad bit failures, whose  defect can be located based on a tester bitmap, SRAM logic  type failures involving WL or BL patterns or entire blocks, are  much more challenging for failure analysis. Their defects are  often not at the failure locations and detailed fault isolation is  necessary prior to physical failure analysis. This paper has  demonstrated how to use SRAM decoder scheme knowledge, detailed layout tracing and Photon Emission Microscope


(PEM) analysis to deal with the challenges and find the root  causes for several cases of the SRAM logic type failures.

[7] K. Nikawa and S. Tozaki, “Novel OBIC Observation  Method for Detecting Defects in Al Stripes Under Current  Stressing”, Proceedings, ISTFA, pp. 303-310 (1993).

Circuit Edit Geometric Trends


Michael DiBattista, Martin Parley, Don Lyons, Roddy Cruz, Alan Wu,  Jamie Langley, Jonathan Lau, and Ray Stevens


Qualcomm Incorporated, San Diego, CA USA   miked@qti.qualcomm.com


Focused ion beam (FIB) tools for backside circuit edit play a  major role in the validation of integrated circuit (IC) design  modifications. Process scaling is one of many significant  challenges, because it reduces the accessible area to modify  transistors and IC interconnects in the design.  This paper  examines the geometries available for FIB nanomachining, via  milling/etching, and deposited metal jumpers by analyzing  polygon data from computer aided design (CAD) virtual layers  gathered across four process technologies, from 180nm down  to 28nm.  The results of this analysis demonstrate that the  combination of silicon nanomachining box length and FIB via  box length identifies the most challenging aspects of the FIB  edit.  The smallest geometries include a 300 nanometer silicon  access area with a FIB milled 200 nanometer via inside it.  More advanced technology nodes will require the ability to  make smaller geometries without the help of integrated design  features typically referred to as design for FIB/Debug.


Role and Capability of FIB Tools


The semiconductor industry has employed focused ion beam (FIB) tools to execute on-silicon design modifications for  many generations of technology nodes [1, 2].  This technique  has been a key design validation tool in the industry; primarily  used to fault isolate and debug integrated circuits (ICs), validate mask changes before tapeout, and create working  prototypes for hardware and software development. A  significant portion of circuit edits on advanced ICs are  performed from the backside of the silicon substrate due to flip  chip packaging requirements and increased numbers of  interconnect layers [3].  One of the recognized and significant  capabilities of focused ion beam systems is the ability to  operate across orders of magnitude in scale from hundreds of  microns to hundreds of nanometers [3], but it is important to  understand the impact of process scaling on the capabilities of  backside capable FIB tools.


Navigation and via milling are two of many challenging  aspects of backside circuit edit with a FIB.  The smaller silicon  process technology nodes lead to shrinking access areas in the  design to accomplish FIB modifications such as cuts and metal  deposited jumpers.  In this paper, approximately four years of  backside circuit edit data on advanced digital and analog


semiconductor ICs have been analyzed to examine key  geometry information, such as the length of metal jumpers and  the size of milled vias to different layers of IC metal  interconnects.  This data has been collected primarily from  silicon process technologies ranging from 180nm to 28nm and  includes a wide range of different design types (logic, RF/analog, and power) and foundries.  This data can be useful  to examine the XY geometries required for even more  advanced technology nodes with smaller transistor and metal  interconnect dimensions.


Polygon based FIB Instructions (Virtual Layers)


The circuit edit request data has been archived as virtual layers  polygons in the computer aided design (CAD) layout and  navigation software [4].  A virtual layer file can contain a  number of polygons containing different FIB steps such has  via milling, IC interconnect cutting, and FIB metal deposition.  Figure 1 shows one example of a completed backside circuit  edit (A), the virtual layer overlaid on the CAD layout of the  chip (B), and  the isolated FIB virtual layer polygons that serve  as instructions (C).


Figure 1: An example of a backside circuit edit (A), the  corresponding virtual layer superimposed on the CAD layout  of the IC design (B), and the isolated FIB virtual layer  polygon instructions (C).  The description labels and arrows  have been added separately to image C.


In order to accomplish this analysis on the large data set of edit  and polygon information, a PERL script was written to collect  and assemble the data from the virtual layer data files.  The  details of Figure 1 serve to demonstrate that the polygon  instructions contained in the virtual layer file are an accurate  representation of the actual FIB edit performed on silicon. The  goal of this work was to systematically examine a large  population of real laboratory XY geometric data to look at the


A


B


required scaling demands on FIB tools as the process  technology progresses.


Analysis of Circuit Edit Trends


Key Elements of FIB operations


The execution of successful backside circuit edit modification  requires many skillful steps that never be fully captured in the  literature, but the requests can be broken down to comprise of  a series steps involving navigation, silicon nanomachining, dielectric deposition, via milling/etching to expose IC  interconnects, metal deposition to create new connections, and  finally IC interconnect cuts.  Many aspects of this effort can be  captured visually as polygons in the CAD layout rather than a  series of coordinate information (data locations) and  corresponding FIB activity.  The polygon data can then be  overlaid with the GDS mask layer information to provide an  effective initial layout and strategy for the FIB activity  sequence.  In addition, this method minimizes transposition  errors that can occur during complex edit activities.


FIB Metal Deposition Analysis


FIB deposited metal jumpers are a key circuit edit capability  used for making new signal connections to power up circuits, ground signal paths, or move clocks/dynamic signals on to  new paths. In addition, probe pads can be built in order to  enable signal probing and measurement of specific voltages  and currents under different test conditions [5].  FIB based  metal deposition involves introducing a metal organic  precursor to the area of interest of the integrated circuit, and  rastering the ion beam in a defined pattern to grow the new  metal connection [6-8].  Some examples of metal depositions  completed during backside circuit edits are shown in Figure 2.  Based on the capabilities of the tool and the design  requirements for interconnect resistance and capacitance, the  length and width of these interconnects can vary from submicron to hundreds of microns long.


Figure 2: Backside circuit edit images of two different FIB  requests requiring multiple interconnect signals to be rewired  to enable test and validation of design changes.


In Figure 3, a histogram of the deposition data required on  180nm, 65nm, 45nm, and 28nm integrated circuits FIB  requests is shown.  The range of deposition lengths is shown  on the x-axis of the graph starting at 1um and continuing to  past 50 microns.  The occurrence shows a strong weighting of  depositions less than 1um, 10-12 microns long, and  depositions longer than 50 microns.  There seems to be little  dependence on the silicon process tech node.  With the  distribution of occurrences in the length bins equally spread  out on the graph.


Figure 3: Histogram of the deposition data from analysis of 4  process technology nodes (180nm, 65nm, 45nm, 28nm).


The sub-micron depositions represent the large number of  requests requiring inter-device shorting.  These types of  requests often involve removing the driving transistor and  tying the original driving transistor output to either Vss or Vdd  to permanently enable the logic state or modify the circuit  timing.  The 10-12 micron deposition lengths appear to be  outliers in the data trend of the graph, but upon further  examination of the types of edits, these two peaks indicate the  number and resulting usefulness of direct electrical probing of  signals independent of the technology nodes.  The FIB probe  pads are either 10 or 12 microns in length to allow mechanical  probing of internal signals that can’t be accessed through  direct test.


Even with advanced optical probing tools [9,10], FIB metal  probe pads are still requested at nodes as small as 28  nanometers, but in general, we have not scaled the size of the  FIB probe pad due to the optical limitations of the microscope  optics and the mechanical limitations of the probe tip.  Figure  4 shows an example of the virtual layer polygons for the FIB  probe pad request, and the corresponding FIB edit performed  on the backside of the silicon.


Figure 4: An example of the virtual layer polygons for the FIB  probe pad request, and the corresponding FIB edit performed  on the backside of the silicon.


There is some comparison data in the literature provided by  Rowlette et al. [11] analyzing FIB depositions for circuit edit  for the 90nm process technology.  This data shows some  similarity in the shape of the histogram even though the data  bins are 10X larger than the data presented in this paper.  The  figure shows there is a higher occurrence of relatively short  jumpers, and it also confirms that the depositions are required  over a significant range, with visible data points at the 190-200  micron lengths.


Figure 5: Histogram of FIB metal deposition length during  the debug of a 90nm logic process [11].


Silicon Nanomachining Requirements


In a backside circuit edit, trenching through the silicon  substrate is often required to gain access to the active region of  the IC. Often the trenching activity stops before or after the  active n-wells are visible from the backside [12].  These  backside trenches can be from tens of microns to full wafer  depth and are often accomplished by laser [13] or FIB based


[14] chemical etching.  Once this step is complete, the next  crucial step is to target specific locations to modify the  integrated circuit.  This process step often requires etching the  silicon and stopping on the shallow trench isolation (STI) in  between the transistors, or in advanced logic technology nodes  removing the gate and diffusion layers of the transistor.  Halogen gas chemistries such as iodine, chlorine, or bromine


are commonly used to provide chemical selectivity and etch  enhancement between the lightly p doped substrate and the  silicon oxide of the STI or active p+ diffusion in this step.  In  some cases, xenon diflouride (XeF2) is also used under  controlled conditions for this step.  The silicon  micromachining step has been called several names including  silicon access, silicon cut or node access hole.


Figure 6 shows an example of a silicon cut from the backside  of the integrated circuit.  The first image (A) shows the milled  area in the silicon after the edit is completed.  Close  examination shows the three contacts exposed in the silicon  cut hole as the active p+ diffusion is also removed.  Image 6 (B) shows the silicon cut with the contact CAD layer overlaid  to demonstrate the correspondence of the silicon to CAD  location.  Image 6 (C) shows the CAD layout without the  actual silicon showing the FIB edit virtual layer polygon  shown in blue.  This edit example was performed to remove  one polysilicon gate leg from the PMOS side to reduce the pull  up strength of the transistor and tune the circuit timing  resulting in an overall improvement in the system  performance.


Figure 6: Example of a silicon cut in the backside of the  substrate (A), the same cut with the contact CAD layer  imposed on top of the silicon image (B), and the  corresponding CAD layers with the cut location superimposed (C).


To enable further analysis of backside Si cut geometries, Figure 7 shows a histogram of the minimum length of the all  silicon cut dimensions across four process technologies.  The  x-axis of the histogram covers a wide range of geometric  length from less than 1 micron to greater than 50 microns.  The  graph shows that the primary silicon access hole geometry is 1  micron or less on the length side. The geometries on this scale  can represent real operational challenges for the existing tools. The occurrences of 1 micron or smaller silicon cuts are more  than 2x any other geometric length bin the graph.  This leads  to implications that the ability to successfully execute at even  smaller geometries is necessary for shrinking technology nodes  in the future.


There is also a peak in the histogram at the 10 micron length  side.  An examination of the FIB edit activities shows that this  geometric size represents a standard size of opening for  navigation landmarks in the edit.  These structures, features, and locations exist even at the 28nm node and represent predetermined locations for navigation or other structures of  similar size opportunistically used to better enable navigation.


Figure 7: A histogram of the silicon cut minimum length  geometry showing the predominance of the geometries below  1 micron.


Figure 8 is a detailed view of the data histogram in Figure 7  within the range of 0 to 5 microns; the smallest silicon cut  minimum length attempted is on the order of 200 nanometers. This represents the accessible area in the layout to remove the  silicon.  The data shows the primary data bin occurs at 300  nanometers for minimum length side.  Other than the 300  nanometer data bin, the data is relatively flat across the x-axis  with peaks at 900 nanometers and 4 microns.  This data  represents typical logic and speed path edits requests to debug  silicon products.  Some of the 4 micron data points represent  local alignment points, which can be used to verify the  accuracy of navigation before the edit locations are exposed.


Figure 8: A zoomed in histogram of the silicon cut data  showing the occurrences from 0 to 5 microns on the minimum  length geometry.


With further examination, the large data peak at 300  nanometers can be explained and further understood as a  specific data request.  In addition to fault isolation, logic fixes, and speedpath improvement validation, FIB based circuit edit  tools are also used heavily for yield improvement.  In this case, the FIB tool is used to inject defects from the backside into


specific silicon memory locations in different SRAM blocks


[14].  This activity helps to validate or determine the bit layout  and mapping of the cells in the block.  Using FIB defect  injection, test and yield teams can interpret design features  such as bit twisting, column and row addressing mis-match, and memory test timing issues.  Figure 9 shows an example of  a typical six transistor (6t) memory cell layout in CAD with  the corresponding diffusion layer overlaid on the actual silicon  backside.  The target defect location is the latch portion of the  6t cell comprised of four of the transistors in the cell.  This  often results in a single bit fail, but even multiple bit defects  provide additional information on the memory mapping.  With  multiple samples, targeted defect and multiple bit cell  locations can be targeted to prove the FIB location accuracy.  This method is often a gold standard of memory defect  validation for yield and test teams because of the level of  targeting accuracy that can be achieved repeatably.


Figure 9: An image of the virtual layer silicon cut box drawn  over the memory cell location of interest, and the  corresponding FIB milled box in the silicon to create the  defect.


Analysis of FIB milled Vias


Milling a via to the metal interconnects in the IC is often the  critical step.  It involves accurate navigation (x, y) to ensure  that the via will be in the correct location, and the ability to  endpoint on the correct layer (z), while controlling the etch  characteristics of the via (including chemistry as appropriate).  Vias are created to enable either cuts on the interconnect (to  disconnect a signal path) or to create new connections by  filling the via with a FIB-deposited conductive layer.


During backside FIB operations, connecting to the metal signal  of interest is often limited by the diffusion, poly, and metal  layers above it.  Due to geometry and aspect ratio restrictions, it is often very difficult to target metal layers deeper into the  device because the open access is very limited, and secondary  electrons are required to escape from the via to allow the  operator to stop at the appropriate time.  Visually identifying  the features inside the FIB is often difficult, and at smaller  geometries for the vias end pointing on a metal interconnect is  often just based on a graph of the secondary electron signal  coming out of the via as it is milled through the dielectric  layers.  Figure 10 shows an example of a secondary electron


plot and an example of a FIB via milled deeper into the device  at metal 3 (M3).


Figure 10: An image of the endpoint curve based on  secondary electron count with the corresponding image, and  an image of a FIB milled via to metal 3.


Milling vias to metal 1 (M1) has traditionally been more  successful than accessing deeper metal layers because the  aspect ratio of the via is larger and depth of the via shorter.  FIB tools are traditionally very effective at milling very high  aspect ratio vias, but the total number of secondary electrons  escaping the access hole may reach detectable  limits(depending on detector design and position relative to the  sample) making it challenging to stop at the correct layer.  Figure 11 shows a statistical breakdown of many of the  backside FIB via geometric characteristics.  The yellow bar  graph shows the occurrence of vias milled to different layers in  the IC.  Vias to M1 represent the largest number, but there is a  somewhat surprising number of vias milled to accessible M2  locations.  The number of vias to M3 begins to diminish, occurring about half the time as the M1 locations.  Then access  to deeper layers such as M4 shows an even greater drop off on  the number of vias made.


Figure 11: Graph showing statistics of the FIB milled via data  with the total volume of requests, the largest minimum side of  the via, and the smallest via side, and the median value of the  via milled to different metal layers.


The data from Figure 11 also provides the measurements for  the largest minimum length value of the via, the smallest via  length side, and the median value for the via length.  The  average value provided little insight since the occurrence of  very large vias in the data set skewed the values to something  that usually wasn’t meaningful.  A comparison of the data for  M1 and M2 vias yielded imilar values for the minimum and  median via geometries.  The minimum via length size is  slightly less than 200 nanometers, but the median via is  slightly larger than 1micron.  This indicates that depending on  the GDS layout, there exist opportunities to access the metal  interconnect layers, even if it has to be done through the  transistor.


Analyzing FIB Vias and Silicon cuts in Combination


While completing the FIB via milling step is challenging, the  effect of the silicon access area cannot be neglected.  This is  an important aspect of determining the difficulty or success  rate of a specific FIB activity.  For the analysis of this data set  including all process technologies (180nm, 65nm, 45nm, and  28nm), the most effective way to determine the difficulty and  challenge of a FIB edit is to examine the combination of the  minimum of the silicon access length and the minimum length  of the FIB milled via.


A graph of the data is shown in Figure 12.  The range of the  minimum length of silicon access hole geometry is quite  extensive showing the full range of circuit edit requirements; from 50 microns down to nearly 500 nanometers.  On the Y  axis of the graph is plotted the minimum length of the FIB via  milled geometry created inside the silicon access length.


Figure 12: A graph showing the analysis of the FIB silicon cut  minimum length versus the FIB milled via geometry for all  process technologies.


The data in the graph falls below the 45 degree line, because it  is impossible to FIB mill a via larger than the silicon access  length. For example, in the middle of the graph, the silicon  access length is 25 microns with a range of via sizes starting at


sub-micron but stopping at 20 microns. The data also shows  that FIB tools are required to operate across a large range of  geometries, with a skew in the data toward the much smaller  geometries.


Figure 13 is a plot of the same data, but zoomed into the  region of interest when the geometries are much less than five  microns in length.  This data set is also broken down by  process technology node, so that FIB edit geometries are  visible for each process node.  Surprisingly, the smallest  geometry edit performed was on 45nm silicon, but the cluster  of 28nm FIB geometry requests is closely related.


Figure 13: A graph of the smallest silicon access geometries  and the smallest FIB milled via geometries, with the  corresponding silicon process technology.


The smallest data point shows 300nm silicon access area with  a 200nm FIB via milled inside of it. There are data points from  all four process generations in the sub-micron area of the  graph.  This seems to re-enforce that circuit edit is really a  design driven activity because there are always circuit  modification requests that cannot be attempted due to FIB  technology limitations.


One of the recognized and significant capabilities of focused  ion beam systems is their ability to operate across orders of  magnitude in geometry, from hundreds of the microns down to  hundreds of nanometers.  For the first time, this paper has  provided data to show the range of FIB circuit edit capabilities  across four silicon process technologies scaling from 180nm, 65nm, 45nm, down to 28nm. The paper also identified that the  minimum geometric length tends to be a key parameter to  judging the FIB modification difficulty.  It appears to be a  better indicator than the geometric area.  For example, if one  side of the mill box is significantly longer, it makes it easier on  the navigation and end pointing.


The data shows that FIB metal deposition length does not  necessarily scale with process technology.  It is relatively  design centric with long jumpers being required for all process  technologies, and short inter-device jumpers being performed  most commonly.  The silicon access/cut data shows that FIB  systems are commonly pushing into the sub-micron region  with 300 nanometers sized defects being created specifically  for defect injection into memory arrays.  FIB milled vias  continue to be one of the challenging aspects of the circuit edit  activity.  This analysis shows vias created down to 200  nanometers for both M1 and M2 layers.  There were no  significant differences in the geometries for M1 and M2  access.  The geometries implemented for M3 and M4 were  measurable larger but the numver of attempts or requests were  fewer, apparently associated with actual or perceived  accessibility limitations.


The data has also been used to show the combination of the  silicon access hole and the corresponding FIB milled via  designates an important criterion for the difficulty of the FIB  edit.  The smallest combination of FIB work performed was  with a 300 nanometer silicon access and a 200 nanometer via  to M1.  Process scaling will dictate that smaller geometries  will be required in the future, and tools will have to be able to  work in these smaller regions with greater success.  Design for  debug features could play a significant role to accommodate  for shrinking dimensions in the future.

Implications of Helium and Neon Ion Beam Chemistry for   Advanced Circuit Editing


H. Wu, D. Ferranti, L. A. Stern and D. Xia,


Carl Zeiss Microscopy LLC, One Corporation Way, Peabody MA 01960   e-mail: huimeng.wu@zeiss.com


M.W. Phaneuf,

Figure 4: Storage of the electronic system racks for a wind  power generator before installing it into the tower engine pod. Under such conditions, components may store humidity, causing early life failures shortly after installation/ power-up


addition, frequently it can be observed that in such electronic  systems subsystems are used, which are successful on the  market for many years but not field-tested for such harsh  applications. This applies for instance for commercially  available standardized power supply blocks as used for  instance to charge buffer batteries or to supply subsystem  electronics. When looking into such devices, sometimes their  construction is reminiscent of consumer electronics: Cheap  capacitors, lack of derating, missing hermetic sealing, connector blocks with narrow current margin etc…


Still many failure analysis reports with EOS-typical failure  profiles conclude to ESD; sometimes even ESD and EOS are  associated to the same or similar failure root causes. However, if seriously splitted over, only few percent of EOS failures are  really related to ESD. In most of these few cases, electrostatic  charging is generated by the (sub-) system itself, discharging  into the electronics during operation. Typical examples are  Hall sensor devices to measure the rotation of motors etc. If  for instance the shaft is mounted in plastic bearings, charging  could be generated and discharge into closely neighbored Hall  sensors.


Considering PCB layout, one of the major problems is given  by narrow line- and line-distance-dimensions with respect to  current respectively voltage. Especially where at positions with  a risk of local heating (protection-resistors, high power  resistors, high power semiconductors, connectors) the PCB  locally may become dark over long time, which significantly  reduces its isolation capability. As a consequence, electric  arcing may start, resulting in severe destruction or even  burning of neighbored electronics. In case of PCB-internal  high field strength combined with even moderate humidity, whisker growth has been observed, causing PCB-internal  shorts. These failures described are also a consequence of  increasing miniaturization on PCB level, too.


With new packaging methods, test escapes increased, too. The  simplest reason is the fact that in case of multi-chip-modules


and chip-on-board constructions, the last functional testing  possibility is on wafer level. Thereafter a lot of specific  assembly process steps (partially with a high level of ESDrisks) happen but no test is possible anymore in-between. The  only “next-step” testing capability is given sometimes not  before the subsystem (PCB) has been completed. This  circumstance and the fact, that usually in these processes  numerous suppliers are involved in the chain, makes a  systematic failure analysis rather difficult – at the same time, in such cases, anamnesis is even mandatory to proceed.


Considering the anamnesis process in general, we had also to  cope with significant problems, which were substantially  caused by the complexity of supply chains. When following a  root-cause-brainstorming on possible influence onto failure  mechanisms of a specific problem, it turned out that a lot more  parties/ companies are involved (and distributed over half of  the world) than we could imagine and that rather complex and  sensitive vendor-customer-relationships significantly limited  an open flow of information through the whole chain which  frequently is affected by a nonspecific fear of losing the next  partner’s confidence. Our way to cope with this challenge is to  offer specific, case-related trainings across intercompany  boundaries, acting as a confidence-building support to the  actual F/A case.


How to Structure the Anamnesis?


The first goal of the anamnesis is to find out, where the failure  becomes obvious and evident. Basically it can be distinguished  between device manufacturing, assembly processing, final (sub-) system testing, application time-zero-failure and field  failure (at the end user). In many cases a certain data base must  be investigated since a process failure might be latent and  convert towards evident only under real load conditions or  only fails in specific applications. We accumulate such  investigations to the topic “Failure history”, focusing on the  following questions:


- When did the failure appear the first time?


- Where did it appear (component test/ subsystem/ system test/ life test/ field test/ customer or end user)?


- Are any comparable failure profiles known from  former cases or relative applications?


- Does the failure occurrence correspond to specific  supply chain profiles?


- Is the failure occurrence specific to a customer or to a  dedicated application or application profile?


If suspicious to it, we look at application- and circuitryrelated cross checks in the next step by considering the  following questions:


- What are the environmental conditions in the  application, also considering ramp-up and standby  phases?


- Could the problem be linked to an EMI (electromagnetic interference) problem? (Typical  problems are exposure of the circuitry to RF, neighbored high power wiring or –circuitry, missing  shields, unshielded long connections to other PCBs or  interfaces, sensitive bus lines.


- How about the component’s balance in load, duty  cycles, standby-, power-on- and -off time?


- Did circuitry simulation results correspond to real insitu electrical measurements considering critical  potentials or signals?


- Was the failing device sufficiently protected against  voltage responses/ spikes from (hidden?) inductive  circuit components?


- How about the ground (GND) concept of the system? Consider also risks of unstable power supplies, shifting potentials, inertial grounds or missing GND  reference.


- What about external input signal quality considering  amplitude, timing, clocking, triggering?


- Does a “killing path” exist, which allows concluding  on the root cause? (sometimes further components (resistors, coils, capacitors etc) along a signal- or  power line are damaged, too)


- Could worst-case operational conditions of the (sub-) system, for instance in case of emergency switchingoff, sudden power breakdown, auto-ramp-up promote  the failure? Were these aspects considered in  simulation results?


- Self-generation of ESD due to friction electricity and/ or electrostatic inductance within the system?


The topic leads us to the subsystem level, where mainly PCB  setups need to be carefully evaluated by the following  questions:


- When ceramic SMD capacitors are used: Were their  placement rules kept in mind?; Could a ceramic  capacitor short be the primary failure? Ceramic  capacitors are extremely sensitive against bending/ tensile stress; when they crack, they don’t show a  short immediately. Even the crack is invisible (hidden  under the solder terminals, fig. 5) in most cases. At  first, the capacitance is reduced, later on, penetration  of conductive material into cracks generates shorts.


Figure 5: ceramic capacitor cracking due to PCBplacement/ bending problems. The cracks became visible  after etching the solder terminals


- What about bending and tensile stress of the PCB in  operation? Check mechanical fixing points/ screws, vibration exposure etc. Specific attention should be  paid on terminal connectors etc.


- Were dark spots observed on the PCB?


- What about line dimensions and distances  considering voltage and current?


- Placement of components: distances between heatsensitive and heat-generating components?


- Plug- and interconnect-technology: Vibration  sensitivity?/ Suitable to voltage/ current load?/ Risk  of mixing-up the PCB with similar PCBs of other  functions within the same system?


The next section – the assembly – divides up into two  subsections: While the assembly means placing the  components onto the PCB or foil, the previous processing  steps (for semiconductors) from wafer level to packaged  device/ component is called preassembly.


- Can the failure be assigned to dedicated process tools  or manufacturing lots? – In most cases, a process step  is done in parallel on several more or less identical  tools. If one tool has a problem, only the devices  operated on this specific tool would show the failure. This item applies for both assembly and preassembly.


- Could ESD or ESDFOS (ESD From Outside to  Surface) explain the failure profile? In preassembly, many process steps are exposed to ESD and ESDFOS  risks, which sometimes hide themselves as latent  failures. In assembly process ESD risks are somewhat  less and limited to ESD (no ESDFOS) [4].


- Could ultrasonic cleaning cause the failure? Ultrasonic cleaning (sometimes inherent to processes  as wafer dicing) may cause small surface damage, partially as latent failures, too [5].


- Were handling risks causing the failure? Besides  ESD, manual processing results in wide variation of  process windows, regarding to mechanical stress, contamination and ESD. These risks must be  carefully evaluated with respect to the failure texture. Besides ESD, one of the most frequent problems  caused by manual processing of PCBs is ceramic  capacitor cracking.


- Could the packaged device be a faked one with lower  specifications/ quality than the original one? Specific  guidelines how faked devices could be identified [6, 7].


Figure 6 shows an example, where one would clearly think on  a wafer manufacturing problem. However, also thanks to a  sound anamnesis, it had turned out that the horizontal metal  shorts shown in this figure, were not wafer-process-related but  laser-induced: The devices didn’t work anymore when  assembled in micro-SIM cards for mobile phones; in the  former regular SIM cards, the space on the plastic besides the  chip position has been used to laser the card number etc. On  the micro-SIM card, this space was not existing anymore and  the numbering field crossed the (hidden under plastic) chip  surface. The laser was strong enough to cause the metal  damages shown in the figure.


Figure 6: Laser-scriber--induced metal shorts in a SIM card


We end up in the questionnaire with semiconductor-specific  wafer-manufacturing related items. These questions must be  posted with respect to wafer test results, too


- Is it a lot- or wafer-related problem?


- In how far is the failure temperature-dependent?


- Are other environmental conditions influencing the  failure appearance and have they been seen such  evidence, too, on the wafer level, for instance in  process control monitoring chips (PCMs)? Did  shmoo test plots give some evidence?


- Gives the process window statistics of monitored key  parameters some evidence to the failure mechanism?


- Is the failure signature or defect- or parameter-related  nature?


- When revising the wafer yieldmap, do the failed  devices relate to dedicated low-yield-spots? Or do  they correspond to reticle-type repeating failure  patterns?


- Does the failure profile point towards a notch-/ flatoriented wafer process problem?


- Was the failure already been observed on PCM  testing on wafer level, too?


- Does the failure show a radial failure distribution on  wafer level, probably pointing towards cleaning/ drying process problems or oxygen rings in the basis  material? Or could it be due to ionic contamination?


- Considering the process tools, did the tool statistics  give specific evidence?


Of course, this detailed questionnaire cannot provide all details  of any specific case. But it should help to focus the analyst’s  mind towards the background of the failure, leading him  towards the root cause. In principle, it is not too difficult to  work out the important questions, if the following main  questions can be regarded as “head sections”:


Is the failure observed in the device an obvious process-related  failure or must it originate from the application?


If it applies, what is critical in the application?


Does the failure correspond to a PCN (process change notice) in any of the participating supply chain levels?


Did an application criticality result from a primary subsystem  failure, singular or systematic EOS, ESD, EMI or a circuitry (design) issue?


In many cases it turned out that the access to the information  needed is not accessible due to missing links to participants in  the manufacturing chain. If this applies, it must be stated that  root cause findings are limited to the rather low numbers of  obvious process-related failures of the investigated device. This matter of fact is a principle weakness in the 8-D-reporting  system. A useful 8-D-procedure [8] should involve all  participants up to the step/subsystem/system where the failure  occurs and all parties should sign it. In present practice, every  participant has its own quality and failure-reporting/ escalating  systems with strict borders following internal company rules. Considering system-level-root cause related failure anamnesis  and analysis, in many cases this is a serious no-go to find the  root cause. On the long term, it will need the implementation  of new, standardized and recognized procedures for an  intercompany failure anamnesis to successfully approach  toward root-cause F/A. To arrive at this point in industrial, automotive and aeronautic electronics, still a long was has to  be gone.


Another advantage hasn’t been discussed, yet: In opposite to  electrical and physical failure analysis with its large and very  expensive tooling setup, anamnesis is comparably cheap. By  asking the right questions before starting physical FA, thus  better understanding the failure history, a lot of expensive and  useless F/A work could be saved. The virtual price for this, however, would be the generation of an open, intercompanywide accepted “failure culture” where the common-driven  technical problem solution is in the foreground versus  economical claims for compensation. As long as the latter  issue superimposes (and frequently limits) all open technical  discussion, a fruitful anamnesis will remain difficult.


To overcome this problem, a first normative step for cases  with greater economic damage could be the mandatory  implementation of a mediation team for an intercompany  anamnesis with an external proven specialist as an accepted  teamleader. Such team could also include legal service  functions to in-time define potential lines of interest conflicts  and to workout useful and binding solutions.


By means of a sound, purposive anamnesis before a physical  FA starts, many hidden system-related root causes can be  found, which never would be detected by device-related FA.


The paper redirected the analyst’s view from nano-scaled  failure signatures towards the operation environment and  circuitry-related failure sources, which need to be considered  in priority for real-root-cause-finding. Thus, useless FA  activities can be saved and learn-loops significantly shortened.

Failure Analysis for SRAM Logic Type Failures


Zhigang Song1, Felix Beaudoin, Stephen Lucarini, John Sylvestri, Laura Safran,  Manuel Villallobos and Richard Oldrey


IBM Systems and Technology, 2070 Route 52, Hopewell Junction, NY, USA


1. Email: zsong@us.ibm.com; Tel: 845-892-1691; Fax: 845-892-6094


Failure analysis for Static Random Access Memory (SRAM) is  the major activity in any microelectronic failure analysis lab. Originating from SRAM array structure, SRAM failure can be  simple as single bit, paired bit or quad bit failures, whose  defect is located at the failure location, or complicated as logic  type failure involving WL or BL patterns or entire blocks, whose defect is often not at the failure location. For such  SRAM logic type failures, failure analysis is more challenging  and detailed fault isolation is necessary prior to physical  failure analysis. This paper has demonstrated how to use  SRAM decoder scheme knowledge, detailed layout tracing and  Photon Emission Microscope (PEM) analysis to deal with the  challenges and find the root causes for several cases of SRAM  logic type failures.


Static Random Access Memory (SRAM) is often chosen to be  the process qualification vehicle during technology  development, and consequently failure analysis of SRAM is  the main feedback for process improvement and yield learning [1, 2]. It is because the SRAM high density and small feature  size make its yield be very sensitive to process variation and  the failing bitcells can be precisely localized by functional test  for physical failure analysis. It is true for single bit failure, pair  bit failure or quad bit failure etc. For such type of failure, since  the defect causing the failure is exactly within the failing cell  or at the shared stacked interconnects for pair bit failure or  quad bit failure, Passive Voltage Contrast (PVC) technique


[3], Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) inspection, Focus  Ion Beam (FIB) cross-section, and electric probing by Atomic  Force Probe [4] or SEM in-chamber probe [5] can be  employed to locate and image the defect. However, there are  some SRAM failures with various spatial patterns, for  instance, regular repeated bitline (BL) failure, regular repeated  word line (WL) failure or block failure, for which the defect is  often not at the failure location. Those spatially patterned  failures can be called SRAM logic type failure because they  are usually caused by a defect at SRAM address decoder logic  circuitry. For such SRAM logic type failures, failure analysis  is more challenging. Detailed fault isolation with layout  tracing, Photoemission Microscope (PEM) analysis [6] and  laser stimulation techniques such as OBIRCH or TIVA [7, 8]


prior to physical analysis is necessary. It is also worthwhile to  mention that as modern SRAM design includes Jtag and scan  chain concepts, failure analysis on SRAM logic type failures is  becoming not only necessary but also indispensable for SRAM  non-zero yield breakthrough and great yield improvement at  the beginning stage of technology development.


In this paper, we present several cases of successful failure  analyses for SRAM logic type failures to demonstrate how to  use SRAM address decoder scheme knowledge, detailed  layout tracing and PEM analysis to deal with the failure  analysis challenges of SRAM logic type failure and eventually  find the root causes.


SRAM Logic Type Failures and Failure Patterns


SRAM is organized as array structure of single bit storage  cells. Each cell can be selected and access through address  decoder logic circuitry and other circuitry, like sense amplifier, multiplexer, driver and control logic. Figure 1 is the simplified  block diagram of a typical SRAM design. A SRAM operates  in such a way that the row decoder selects a row, also known  as WL, by setting the WL at logic high for all the cells along  the selected row. The contents of these cells become available  to be transferred to their respective bitline and bitline-bar. The  column decoder is then used to select the particular column, also known as BL, to write or read the content of the cell at the  intersection point of the selected row and column. The data in  the bit is ultimately routed to drive an output pin. Modern  SRAMs are often organized so that 2m bits are accessed  simultaneously, for which the data from 2m columns are  selected and gated to 2m data output pins simultaneously. Therefore any defect in the address decoder circuitry will  result in an unique SRAM failing spatial patterns. With the  hierarchy decoder scheme in modern SRAM designs, the  spatially patterned failures can be even more complex. In  general, these various spatially patterned failures can be  classified into three categories, namely BL type, WL type and  entire block failure. Here, block failure is a loosely defined  term which can be referred to any rectangular shape with every  bit failing inside of it, resulting from the hierarchical grouping  of bits of the SRAM. A sub-block denomination is typically  used if the failure area corresponds to a portion of the  hierarchical block. Block or sub-block can be defined by its  numbers of bits in the WL and BL directions, such as  192BLx1024WL. For such types of failures, since the defect is


usually not at the failure location, the conventional failure  analysis method for single bit failure, pair bit failure and quad  bit failure is not effective. More detailed fault isolation works  such as layout tracing, PEM or OBIRCH analysis are  necessary before performing any destructive analysis work.

SRAM Logic Type Failure Analysis


In this section, failure analyses for several cases of SRAM  logic type failures are described. These failure analyses have  demonstrated that layout tracing with the knowledge of SRAM  decoder scheme is very helpful for failure analyses for BL-type  and WL type patterned failures. For entire block failure, where  layout tracing is difficult, PEM analysis is employed to narrow  down the suspected defective area.


(1) WL Type Failure


A 48M SRAM chip suffered from a WL type failure within  sub-block 192BLx1024WL. Figure 2 shows a chip level  failure bitmap and the WL type failure pattern to be analyzed, as shown at right side. It was noticed that there are 16 solid  WLs with regular interval. Considering an one fault only  assumption, the defect should be within the WL decoder  circuit, which controls these 16 WLs, leading to hard failure  for the 16 WLs. The other partially failing WLs were likely  secondary effect due to interference among WLs. So, the  failure analysis focused on the hard failure of the 16 WLs. After looking at the 16 WLs more carefully, it was found that  each failed WL in 64 WL group was 20 WLs from the  boundary and with mirror image in every two 64 WL groups. The WL type failure pattern is graphically showed in Figure 3. Based on the failure pattern, layout tracing was performed  starting from every failing WL and tracing up to WL decoder. Layout tracing from all 16 failing WLs ended up at the same  WL decoder. The traced layout was highlighted and is shown  in Figure 4. It was found that the WL decoder was located at  the middle of the sub-block 192BLx1024WL and two signal

only assumption, the defective area causing all 16 WL failure  in the sub-block 192BLx1024WL was highly suspected in the  WL decoder area, which is showed at the right side of Figure


4. After the suspected defective area was isolated, the chip was  de-processed layer by layer and SEM inspection was focused  on the WL decoder area. Finally, distorted and bridging poly  lines were observed, as shown in Figure 5. To further  understand the root cause, the defect was subjected to FIB  cross-section. FIB cross-sectional image in Figure 6 showed  that the defective poly was abnormally higher than normal  poly and its bottom was shorted to contact. It was  hypothesized that a big poly silicon particle dropped here  during poly deposition, which then affected the subsequent  poly patterning.

(2) BL Type Failure


Another 48M SRAM chip suffered from BL type failure within  sub-block 192BLx512WL. Its failure bitmap pattern is shown  in Figure 7. Analysis of the failure pattern found that there  were 2 solid BLs (BLs 3 and 4) failing at middle of every 8 BL  group, as shown at right side of the Figure 7. Similarly, the  other partially failing BLs were secondary effect due to  interference among BLs. Based on the failure pattern, layout  tracing started from these solid BLs and traced up to a BL  decoder. Figure 8 shows the layout tracing result, which  suggested that there were three possibilities causing the  reported failure: (1) the signal line shorting to adjacent lines, like Vdd and Vss, (2) the signal line having open interconnect  from the BL decoder, (3) a BL decoder malfunction. Bearing  these suspected defects in mind, the subsequent physical  failure analysis found an undersized contact within the  highlighted BL decoder by layout tracing, as shown in Figure  9 SEM image. FIB cross-section on the undersized contact  showed that the contact was actually under-etched (Figure 10).

Another case of the BL type failure showed a different failure  pattern for which every 8BL had failing BLs 1 and 6 within  sub-block 192BLx256WL, instead of sub-block  192BLx512WL, as displayed in Figure 11. Again, layout  tracing started from the failing BLs and identified 3 Vias (Via3, Via4 and Via5), which most likely caused the failure (Figure 12). Since the top suspected Via was Via5, the sample  was de-layered to layer Metal 6 and FIB cross-section walked  through these 3 Vias. FIB cross-section found Via5 underetch, as shown in Figure 13. The Via5 under-etch resulted in  an open failure to the re-buffer circuits for the reported failing  BLs in the sub-block 192BLx256WL.

(3)  Entire Block Failure


Gallium focused ion beams (Ga-FIB) have been used  historically in semiconductor industry for failure analysis, as  well as circuit edit (CE) [1-4]. Significant efforts have been  invested to improve the performance of Ga-FIB. These efforts  include but are not limited to the following: (1) optimizing ion  beam parameters to control nanomachining processes, (2) incorporating laser interferometer-based stages with CAD  overlay to improve navigational accuracy, and (3) studying a  wide array of precursors for gas assisted deposition (to  improve metal or insulator deposition qualities) and for gas  assisted etching (to increase selectivity and process latitude). However, in spite of the best of these efforts, as integrated  circuit (IC) dimensions continue to shrink, Ga-FIB induced  processes are being driven to their physical limits.


The latest gas field ion source (GFIS) column [5] in Zeiss  Orion NanoFab offers both helium and neon ion beams, with  significantly smaller probe sizes for each (helium at 0.5nm  and neon at 1.9nm) as compared to the traditional Ga-FIB  probe size (3~5 nm)). Also, the GFIS beams have ten times  lower energy spread (<1 eV FWHM) than the liquid gallium  ion sources (LMIS) used for Ga-FIB. These unique features  provide an alternative solution for the future needs of the  semiconductor industry’s shrinking scales and complex  packaging structures. Many research reports have  demonstrated the capability of the Zeiss Orion to fabricate sub  10 nm patterns at high densities using the He+ ion beam. Neon  GFIS has been studied regarding stability and imaging. With  the improved column design and higher vacuum environment, Orion Nanofab provides a more stable and reliable neon ion  beam. This has created significant interest for neon ion beam  nanofabrication.


Previous work at Zeiss has explored various kinds of metal  organic compounds for conductive metal deposition and has  optimized the deposition conditions to demonstrate the  ultimate line width possible for the GFIS microscope (using  either He+ or Ne+ ion beam) and to improve the deposition  purity. The choice of metal precursors for circuit edit is  determined by many factors, but the most important factors  minimize the deposit resistivity, the contact resistance, the  proximity deposition and the feature size, all while  maintaining the chemical and thermal stability of the interface  and producing high purity deposits. We have studied platinum


[6], tungsten and cobalt [7] deposition using trimethyl (methylcyclopentadienyl) platinum (IV) (PtC9H16), tungsten  carbonyl (W(CO)6) and dicobalt octacarbonyl (Co2(CO)8)  precursors, respectively. The narrowest line we have  demonstrated is about 10 nm wide with approximately 100 μΩ-cm resistivity.


The main purpose of this paper is to report the helium and  neon ion beams’ induced chemistry including metal  deposition, dielectric deposition and chemically enhanced  etching.


Two simple examples will be shown as proofs of concept  demonstrating GFIS development for circuit edit applications. We will summarize the general utility of He+ and Ne+ ion  beams for metal deposition, dielectric deposition, and  sputtering and etching processes, and we will discuss some of  the technical challenges associated with current GFIS  technology.


Results and Discussion


I. Metal Deposition. High-purity cobalt lines have been  deposited by He+ ion beam with metallic conduction within an  order of magnitude of the bulk value. Because of the  extremely small spot size of the helium ion beam, we are able


to deposit single cobalt lines as small as 10 nm wide or  multiple cobalt lines at high density with minimal overspray  around the deposits. Figure 1 shows multiple cobalt line  patterns with various line widths and pitch sizes.


Figure 1: Helium ion microscope (HIM) images of multiple  cobalt lines. a) a 45degree titled HIM image of an 8 line


pattern with a 90 nm pitch; b) a 4 line pattern with a 50 nm  pitch; c) a 4 line pattern with a 20 nm pitch.


Since the Zeiss Orion GFIS column offers both helium and  neon ion beams, we are able to compare the deposition rates  and resistivities of material induced by each beam. We found  that the mass difference between the He+ and the Ne+ ions  results in significant differences and trade-offs in the  deposition yield, sputtering rate and electrical properties of  each. For example, Pt deposits using the He+ ion beam have a  high deposition yield, but also a very high (  3.5×104 μΩ-cm) resistivity. In contrast, Ne+ deposited Pt has a low deposition  yield but also, a much lower resistivity (600 - 3.0×103 μΩ-cm)


[6]. Similarly, the Ne+ deposited W lines have lower resistivity  than the He+ induced W lines. The optimization of beam  parameters can further improve the purity and electrical  properties of metal deposition. The lowest resistivity of Ne+ induced W lines achieved was 160 μΩ-cm.


II. Insulator Deposition. Tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) and  penta methyl cyclo penta siloxane (PMCPS) have been used as  precursors for insulator deposition. In both cases, the  resistivity of dielectric deposits induced by the He+ or Ne+ ion  beam is significantly higher than those induced by Ga-FIB.


Figure 2: HIM images of PMCPS deposits induced using a He  ion beam. a) a 45 degree titled image of a 5×5μm PMCPS box  deposited on a gold pad. Top-view of PMCPS horizontal lines  space pattern (b) and horizontal and vertical line patterns (c). The 50 nm gap, marked in (b) has 5 fine lines, indicating the  pattern has a 10 nm pitch.


Figure 2a shows a titled HIM image of PMCPS deposition on  a gold pad, induced by a He+ ion beam. The significant  contrast difference between the background (gold pad) and the  deposit indicates the dielectric property. The deposit is very  dark. This means the deposition should be a high quality  insulator. Using similar gas flow and beam parameters while  changing the pattern and dose amounts, we were able to make  a 5 nm half pitch horizontal line space pattern (Fig. 2b). We  then deposited the second vertical line space pattern over the  horizontal lines without damaging them (Fig. 2c) due to the  minimal interaction of the He+ ion beam with the underlying  surface.  It should be noted that the lack of darkness of these  deposition patterns is due to their reduced thickness (only  several nanometer thick) and the highly topological nature of  their structure.


To measure the resistivity of our insulator deposits, we created  parallel plate capacitor test structures (Fig. 3a). The insulator  was first deposited with He+ ion beam on an existing gold test  structure, and then the top electrode (gold) layer was produced  by e-beam lithography. Fig. 3b is the optical photo of a 30 ×


30 μm insulator deposit covering the lower gold pad with an  18 × 18 μm smaller gold pad on the top of the insulator layer. The thickness of this insulator deposit is 80 nm. A two point  probing method was used for I-V measurements. These two  probes are also shown in Fig. 3b. The left probe was put on the  large gold area, where no deposits were performed. The right  probe contacted the top gold pad of insulator capacitor test  structure.


Figure 3: I-V measurements of insulator deposits. a) illustration of the  capacitor test structure; b) optical photo of  th capacitor test structure, and (c) typical I-V curves for  insulator deposits on the capacitor test structure.


Figure 3 shows typical I-V curves for insulator deposition. The gray and green-blue curves were measured on the same  insulator sample by repositioning the probe on the small gold  pad.  To confirm the I-V curves shown here actually came  from the leakage current through the insulator layer with good  probe-electrode contacts, we measured open air I-V curves as  a control. These open air curves are shown in Fig. 3 as bright  green and dark purple curves. The control curves were  measured by simply lifting the probe off the small gold pad  into the air and measuring twice. As expected, the I-V curve of  insulator resistivity was on the order of 1013 Ω cm, or roughly  one to two orders of magnitude higher than that of Ga-FIB  induced deposition [8].


III. Chemically Enhanced Etching.  We have demonstrated  the milling capability of the He+ and Ne+ ion beams to  fabricate fine structure patterns into various substrates, including silicon, graphene and gold thin film [9].  The He+ ion beam has a smaller probe size and is therefore the finer  and more precise nano-machining tool. And previous crosssectional analysis of Ne+ and He+ milled vias has shown  aspect ratios better than 10:1 [10].  The Ne+ ion beam has a  much higher sputter rate than the He+ ion beam.  However, compared with the Ga-FIB, even the milling rate of the Ne+ ion beam is relatively low.  To improve the material removal  rate, XeF2 was tested as chemical enhancement agent. The  XeF2 etching enhancement is dependent on many factors


including but not limited toXeF2 flow rate beam intensity, dwell time, pixel spacing, and nozzle position. Preliminary test  results show the dose enhancement factor, when milling SiO2  with the Ne+ ion beam and XeF2 gas assisted etching is about  7 times that of straight Ne+ ion beam sputtering on SiO2. Figure 4 shows 45 degree tilted HIM images of boxes milled  in SiO2 substrates.


Figure 4: 45 degree tilted Ne ion microscope (NeIM) images  of Ne+ ion beam milled 600× 600 nm boxes on an SiO2  substrate. a) milled using the Ne+ ion beam alone without  XeF2 gas; b) and c) the boxes were etched with XeF2 gas flow  at (b) 3.4E-6 Torr and (c)1.2E-5 Torr of chamber pressure.   The depths are (a)  94 nm,  (b) 290 nm and (c) 660 nm. The  enhancement in material removal rate due to XeF2  is  three  times that of the beam alone at 3.4 E-6 Torr and about 7 times  that of the beam alone at 1.2E-5 Torr.


IV. Two Examples of Circuit Edit Using the Orion GFIS  column. An Empire test chip (made by University of Albany) was used for both examples. This wafer has two metal layers  with a 100 nm low-k dielectric between two metal layers. The  metal-1(M1) layer is 150 nm thick and the metal-2 (M2) layer  is 200 nm thick. The Empire test wafer has many structures  but for our experiment we chose two similar structures as  shown as Figs. 5a and 6a. Both structures consists of a M1 and  a M2 line routed perpendicular to each other with a via  connecting them at the point where they intersect. Figure 5b  overlays the layout of the metal lines with an HIM image. The  blue line in Figs. 5a and 5b represents the M1 line and the  pink line represents the M2 line. The via connecting M1 and  M2 is at the intersection of these two lines. The differences  between Figs. 5a and 6a are the designed widths of metal lines  and the diameters of the vias. The designed line width in Fig. 5a is 100 nm with a via diameter of 70 nm, while the structure  in Fig. 6, has a 70 nm line width and a 48 nm via.


The first example shown here is to cut the top metal line (M2) and then reconnect. Electrical measurements were performed  before and after each step to check the results of our  modification. Two steps were involved in this process. First, two cuts were made on M2 line using a straight unassisted  5keV Ne+ ion beam. The boxes milled were 200 × 300 nm  each (see red boxes in Fig.5b). Then one of the cuts was filled  with cobalt. The resulting electrical measurements made at  each step are summarized in Table 1.


Here, R13-16 is the resistance measured on pads 13 and 16. This  is the resistance of M2 line. R14-15 is the resistance of M1 line. R13-15 and R14-16 are the sum of the resistance of a half M1 line, a half M2 line and the resistance of the interconnection via. A  two point probing method was used for all the electrical


measurements. Before beginning the modification, the  electrical measurements confirmed a solid connection existed  between the M1 and the M2 lines through the via. With two  Ne ion beam cuts, the M2 line became open, and M1 line  remained intact. After filling one cut with cobalt, the M2 line  was still open, but the lower half of the M2 line now filled  with cobalt was connected with the M1 line through the via  and an electrical path now existed from pads 14 to 16.. The  electrical measurement (in bold in Table 1) confirmed that the  resistance of R14-16 recovered once the cut was filled with  cobalt. It can clearly be seen that refilling the metal line with a  cobalt deposition did not significantly affect the conductive  property of that metal line. Given the low resistivity of cobalt  depositions, this result was expected.

The second example shown here is an application of the GFIS  ion beam for a simple circuit edit (Fig.6). Baseline electrical  measurements were performed first. IV. Future development.  Compared with traditional Ga-FIB, He+ and Ne+ ion beams have obvious advantages including  smaller probe size, more flexible process control and no  gallium contamination. With the relentless shrinking of IC  geometries and the increasing complexity of 3D packaging,


these advantages are becoming more critical to the success of  future circuit edit and failure analysis endeavors. Here we only  show some simple examples for proof of concept. For real-life  circuit edit in the semiconductor industry, several critical areas  need to be addressed. For example, we have to improve the  Ne+ ion beam stability over time. A stable ion beam is critical  to a reliable process. There is also much work to be done on  precisely controlling the etchant and deposition chemicals, on  improving the signal/noise ratio (SNR) for amplifying and  displaying images and on solid end-pointing of signals from  small and high aspect ratio vias. Finally, a large amount of  work still remains to be done to further our knowledge of the  FIB circuit edit process and to research more extensive  applications of the various techniques.


In summary, we have demonstrated the feasibility of  depositing high-quality metal and insulator materials. For  metal deposition, both 10 nm wide single lines and multiple  metal lines at high density have been achieved with minimal  overspray around the deposits. The metallic conduction of  these deposits is only an order of magnitude higher than their  bulk value.  For insulator deposition, ultra high resistivity (on  the order of 1013Ω-cm) has been achieved. We have also  shown nanofabrication capability by producing high density  patterns with a 5 nm half pitch and then depositing the second  layer without damaging the first layer.


Both He+ and Ne+ ion beams facilitate milling small holes and  other complicated fine structures in various substrates. To  improve the milling rate, XeF2 gas assisted etching was tested  and was shown to optimize the milling conditions. Preliminary  test results show a 7 times dose enhancement factor in terms  of material removal rate was achieved when milling SiO2  using the Ne+ ion beam with XeF2 gas compared to straight  Ne+ ion beam sputtering on SiO2.


Finally, using GFIS ion beams, we have demonstrated that we  can precisely cut the top and buried metal lines and then  reconnect them. The electrical measurements performed  demonstrated successful milling and deposition results. As  proofs of concept, these two circuit edit examples successfully  demonstrated the capability of He+ and Ne+ ion beam systems  for FIB circuit edit applications of the future.


The above results, together with high flexibility platforms  such as the Orion NanoFab, confirm that helium and neon ion  beam chemistries represent an attractive approach for precise  nanofabrication and may be well suited for future FIB circuit  edits at 22 nm and smaller.
