Silicon & Package Preparation Options for Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Circuit  Editing & General Packaging Failure Analysis


Steven B. Herschbein, Carmelo F. Scrudato


George K. Worth, Edward S. Hermann


IBM Systems & Technology,


2070 Route 52, Hopewell Junction, NY  USA


The Focused Ion Beam (FIB) technique of internal  modification for chip repair, layout verification, and internal  signal probe access has become an integral part of the process  for bringing advanced products to market.  The pervasive  switch from wire bond connections to single component flipchip solder bump mounting on high value products has greatly  aided the task of FIB editing by placing the bare backside  silicon of the die within easy reach.


FIB chip circuit access begins with task-specific sample  preparation.  The package opening and silicon prep process is  well defined and quite robust when full thickness chips are  mounted to simple ceramic carriers.  Unfortunately, the  introduction of flexible organic laminate substrates and the  development of stacked die packaging has further complicated  the process.  Multi-chip packages containing combinations of  full thickness and thinned chips may be present.  They could  be wire-bond connected, or use Through-Silicon Vias (TSV) for double sided attachment. Multiple heat treatment cycles  joining together materials with vastly different coefficients of  thermal expansion (CTE) may result in severe package  warpage and stress.  All of these conditions and possible  combinations have served to invalidate key elements of the  established sample preparation process, and made each  presented case unique.


As the FIB team works to develop new precision techniques  for internal circuitry access, the greater semiconductor  packaging development and failure analysis community has  benefited from the introduction of new tooling and  methodologies.


FIB editing is a laboratory technique in which an ion beam  and processes gases are used to selectively uncover internal  circuitry, rewrite the wiring pattern, and reseal the chip.  The  revised circuit functions essentially the same as if the revision  was made by way of a photomask change, except the results  can be obtained weeks or months earlier.  As devices became  more complex,  with added levels of dense,  thick  upper-level


power planes and tighter lower-level point-to-point wiring and  device geometries, primary FIB access through the backside  of the chip has become the only viable approach.  The  pervasive switch to flip-chip solder bump mounting of chips  to modules and chip to chip stacked die has made the backside  editing approach ever more sensible by placing the  unobstructed backside of the die within easy reach.


The complexities of the Focused Ion Beam (FIB) chip edit  process combined with the evolution in semiconductor  packaging technology has propelled innovation in sample  preparation for years.  A module prepared for editing must  remain robust and fully functional, as though it was a  purposely engineered assembly.  From this standpoint, the  unique requirements of FIB preparation have been driving a  level of precision that typically goes beyond the needs of most  conventional package failure analysis.  On the positive side, these techniques have proven to also be of great benefit to  those who are analyzing stress failures in more recent package  designs, especially those involving chip stacks.  Consequently  the team primarily responsible for developing package  disassembly/reassembly processes for FIB chip edit have  proven to be extremely well prepared for the challenges of  advanced packaging analysis.


The sample preparation landscape for backside editing is  changing as packaging evolves.  Mechanical thinning of the  silicon is desirable to speed FIB trenching time and reduce the  aspect ratio of the backside circuitry access hole.  However, silicon machining can be problematic on highly stressed chips  as there is a high risk of cracking [1]. In addition, there are  situations in which die strength and original thickness must be  preserved (edit and return in ‘as received’ condition) to meet  specific customer requirements.  Full thickness backside  silicon editing has been practiced for several years, but this  method is not appropriate in all cases and has a number of  layout limitations.    Ultrathin silicon preparation negates the  need for almost all trenching and can greatly simplify the  editing process, but the precision requirements of the  mechanical steps are still being refined.


Computer numeric controlled (CNC) and gravity fed milling  tools have long been used for FIB silicon prep, but in the past  they generally suffered from the inability to properly follow


the complex shape of stressed chips.  The ability of the new  generation of tabletop tools to accurately map and machine  contour shapes enabled them to not only satisfy advanced chip  edit needs, but to also be of aid in advanced package analysis  and new product qualification.  Milling entirely through either  the silicon or the package components in contour following  mode is now routine practice as an aid in being able to  examine the joining interfaces in their entirety.


The FIB tool’s internal XeF2 gas trenching apparatus has also  found new use in packaging and assembly analysis, stripping  away the silicon surrounding TSV and pad structures.


Modern Packaging


The term ‘packaging’ when used in conjunction with  semiconductor devices refers to any number of protective  enclosures that also allow for electrical connection to the next  level of assembly.  VLSI devices with low pin-count typically  relied on perimeter wire bond pads, with the backside of the  chip bonded to a header, paddle or similar internal structure  that provided mechanical support and substrate grounding.  This also placed the top surface of the chip and back end  wiring of the device ‘up’, within easy reach of the failure  analyst.  A progression of ceramic and metal structures gave  way to plastic encapsulated packages for pin-through circuit  boards and later surface mount applications, the majority of  which still relying on chip-up wire bonding methods.


The move to higher power consumption and high I/O pin  count assemblies accelerated the adoption of the distributed, full chip area solder bump direct attach connection system.  First introduced by IBM, the Controlled Collapse Chip  Connection (C4) flip-chip attach system is now a popular  alternative to wire bonding [2].  In this scheme the die is  directly and rigidly bonded to the package base, face down.


While a number of styles of electronic packaging co-exist  today, for purposes of discussion about FIB chip editing and  advanced packaging challenges we will concentrate on the  flip-chip style ball grid array (BGA) as shown in Figure 1  below.


Figure 1.  Typical metal lidded Flip-Chip BGA package  shown.  The package base substrate material can be either an  organic laminate or ceramic.


The C4 direct attach method replaces the conventional wire  bonding pad with a terminal metal pad surrounded by a  polymer solder resist material.  These pads can populate the  entire top surface of the chip, and are not just located around


the perimeter.  A reflowed solder ball resides at each location.  In the assembly process, the chips are placed upside down on  top of a package substrate populated with a matching pad  pattern, and the components are heated until the solder melts.  The temperature is then ramped down and the solder  solidifies, locking the two components together both  electrically and physically.  A final step is to fill the remaining  gap between the chip and substrate with an epoxy commonly  referred to as underfill.


The underside of the BGA substrate is populated with larger  solder balls, enabling the next level of assembly between the  chip package and a system board.  On top of the die is either  an integral heat spreader or more typically a metal lid.  Both  use a putty-like Thermal Interface Material (TIM) to transfer  heat away from the chip.  An edge seal attaches the lid to the  substrate.


The inversion of the die had several profound impacts on the  failure analysis community.  For one, it put the backside of the  die and thus the underside of transistors towards the viewer.  This re-enabled a variety of thermal, beam-based and  photoemission imaging techniques that had become  problematic with the advent of dense, multi-level back end  metallization [3].  It also enabled easy access to low level  interconnect wiring at the primary logic level for FIB chip  editing [4].  Again, this was a capability deemed lost when  upper level wiring became so dense that it dictated a routine  need for ultra-high aspect ratio access holes.


The back end of line (BEOL) wiring was now the primary  attachment plane between the chip and the package. While  this might aid analysis, it also can potentially put a degree of  mechanical stress on the entire chip wiring through the  interconnection metal and dielectric stack, also directly tied to  the active region.  Depending on the characteristics of the  materials involved, the stresses can be extreme enough to  cause internal cracks or layer separation [5].  But this was  rarely a problem with chips bonded to ceramic carriers.


Ceramic to Laminate BGA Package Transition


If the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) between the  silicon chip and the package material are nearly identical, the  components will expand, become bonded together, and then  contract in tandem.  This will result in very little stress  between the different materials, and this is the typical scenario  when a silicon chip is attached (or bonded) to a ceramic  carrier.  Metal lidded ceramic substrates were a popular  package style and are still preferred in some high end  applications, but have diminishing market share due to cost, electrical performance constraints, etc [6].


Ceramic carriers are hard and structurally ridged, and fully  supporting of the attached silicon.  They don’t rely on the  strength of either the chip or the metal lid to resist bending.


As a result, a full thickness silicon chip solder bump mounted  to ceramic and properly underfilled can be machined and  polished to most any final thickness, and still resist cracking.  In most cases, the total amount of bowing across the die  typically measures less than a few percent.  This greatly  simplifies the chip thinning process, as the milling tool can  operate in a single step per pass planar cut mode.


A package substrate design based on the organic laminate ‘printed circuit card’ is a common style today.  It is  inexpensive and relatively easy to manufacture, yet robust  enough for most commercial applications.  The liability, unfortunately, is that organic laminates have a very different  CTE from silicon, resulting in a high stress gradient after C4  joining. The board compresses at a faster rate than the silicon  as the assembly cools down to room temperature after the  solder bump attach process [7].  The result of this size  differential after cooling is a pincushion curvature in both  components.  On a large die / large board assembly the centerto-corner (C-to-C) deflection as measured across the chip can  exceed 125 µm (see Figure 2 below).  The bow along any side  of the base board can be great enough to be visible to the  naked eye, and can come close to the maximum acceptable  limits of industry standard coplanarity tests [8].


Countering some of this bending force may be a metal lid.  When bonded along the perimeter of the package and to the  top of the die, a metal lid adds physical protection, mechanical  strength and helps to keep the entire assembly rigid.


Figure 2.  Silicon on laminate center-to-corner ‘pincushion’ deflection can reach an extreme of 130 µm, impacting blind  navigation accuracy, mounting integrity (coplanarity) and can  even promote chip cracking during mechanical milling.


The Move to 3D Packaging


Just as chip technology is rapid evolving, so is package  density and integration.  The desire of the industry to reduce  path lengths by going to 3D assemblies adds significant  technical challenges to the term ‘Chip-Package Interaction’.  Fortunately, we have been able to apply a number of our  advanced CNC silicon milling techniques to aid those directly  involved in packaging qualification and failure analysis.


The variety of packaging styles that an analyst may encounter  can be broadly categorized by the following three terms [9]:


2D: Single or multiple chips connected to a substrate that  connects to a system board.  This configuration is the  traditional package assembly as shown in Figure 3 (top).


2.5D: Single layer of 2 or more chips connected to an  intermediate substrate (interposer) that can pass signals  between chips, while providing some passive component  buffering.  In the case of a double-sided silicon interposer, solder bumps on the underside connect to a substrate that  connects to a system board (Figure 3 middle drawing).


3D: An extension of the 2.5D description, in which additional  chips piggyback on top of the first layer of chips (Figure 3  bottom).  Now each chip may have a double-sided connection  as well.  There is no stated limit to the stack height.


First generation chip stack designs used tiered wirebonding.  Smaller chips or chips with different aspect ratios are placed  on top of larger ones, separated by adhesive films or spacers.  All chips are arranged wiring side up, and positioned so that  their perimeter wire bond pads are accessible during the  stacking process to allow connections to either each other, or  to matching package cavity pads.


Second generation assemblies are using direct attach double  sided solder bump technology.  In order to place pads and  bumps on both sides, the chips must have through-silicon deep  etched via technology (TSV) that connects front to back.  The  current practical limit for TSV drilling is around 50 µm, necessitating thinning of the die at wafer level prior to the  second side bumping [10].


Figure 3.  Top: 2D, Middle: 2.5D, Bottom: 3D package.


Single or Multiple Edits Required


The very nature of chip editing requests has changed  dramatically over the years.  Many of our designs employ  multiple cores, each with dozens of input channels.  There is a


reduced probability that invoking a single point wiring change  be adequate, unless the error happens to be in a singular  global support circuit.


A single logic error in the master layout often gets repeated in  each core of a multi-core chip, and may need to be fixed  independently at each location.  Individual edit sites might  have to be connected by long deposited wires.  Or, FIB editing  might be employed as an investigative tool, requiring several  iterations over a large geographic area to fully understand the  nature of a fault.  As a result of these potentially widely  spaced edits, multiple FIB trenches through the backside  silicon are often required.


Selecting a sample preparation method that is compatible with  the edit plan, specific customer requirements and which will  also work well with the package assembly can be a study in  compromise.


Silicon Thinning for FIB Chip Edit


In devising a strategy for a new FIB device modification, four  thicknesses are commonly referenced.  The decision on which  to use is largely based on the specifics of the circuitry revision  plan, how the FIB tool is equipped, any specific customer  mechanical requirements, and characteristics of the  component to be edited.  There are distinct pros and cons  associated with each starting point.


1) Reduction to about 100 µm remaining.


2) Reduction to around 30-40 µm remaining.


3) Work with as received: ranging from 20 – 775 µm thick.


4) Ultra-thin prep with about 10 µm remaining.


Mechanical Reduction to 100 µm


In an examination of the literature, 100 µm of silicon  remaining is often cited as a typical and safe starting point for  backside emission and stimulus injection, or for FIB chip edit.  At that thickness, backside IR imaging is suitably precise, yet  the chip remains physically strong and capable of dissipating  generated heat loads when external cooling is applied [11].


Multiple edits would certainly be easier after globally thinning  the silicon from 775 µm to about 100 µm, as the FIB work can  be performed in relatively low aspect ratio trenches.  See  Figure 4.  FIB tools that contained a dedicated trenching  nozzle (XeF2 concentrator) can clear a 200 µm diameter hole  down to the underside of the active region in about a half  hour.  An alternative to FIB gas trenching is the use of a laser  chlorine gas cell etcher which can produce an efficient  inverted pyramid-shaped removal pattern.  Both chemical  trenching systems generally rely upon mechanical milling and  may require fine surface polishing as a preceding step, especially if IR imaging verification of the layout is required.


Figure 4.  Pictorial representation - Typical profile of a die  mechanically thinned to 100 µm and FIB trenched (light blue  region) to the underside of the active region. Extra care must  be taken when flat milling bowed silicon on laminate  substrates to avoid stress cracking or the production of overly  thin regions.


If the die was bonded to a ceramic carrier, the chance of  cracking or otherwise damaging the silicon during the  mechanical milling and polishing step is low.  A basic flat  surface CNC mill program could be used, as the difference in  final thickness at any point across the die is well within  tolerance of the trenching procedure.  Subsequent testing  without relidding is possible, as the stiff ceramic prevents chip  bending during socket insertion.


The situation changed markedly when laminate carriers were  introduced. Applying the established parameters for silicon  machining and polishing often resulted in micro-cracks in the  substrate, rendering the product unsuitable for editing and  further use. A greater amount of care was required during the  entire machining and handling process to avoid damage.  Variables that were addressed included the lid removal  procedure, support under the module during cutting, bit  selection, spindle speed, feed and plunge rate, etc. [12].


But the issues went beyond simple survivability.  Two  dimensional flat-top cut methods could work with large die on  ceramic carriers, as the center-to-corner (C-to-C) variation in  thickness is typically well under 20 µm.  Practically, it is  simply not possible to achieve a uniform, sub-100 µm final  silicon thickness on a laminate carrier sample that starts with a  C-to-C variation as much as 130 µm.  The center will  approach zero and become unacceptably brittle long before  the corner target is obtained.  Even a gravity-fed system can  run into unacceptable thickness variation issues on a heavily  bowed unit.  And while it is possible to employ one of the  various elevated temperature temporary stress reduction  methods to flatten the module while milling (to be discussed  later), we found it unlikely that you can dial out curvature  completely, uniformly, or in a repeatable manner.  The typical  compromise approach was to aim for no less than 75 µm in  the center of the die and allow the corners to remain thicker.   A first generation approach to characterizing the initial  curvature of the die and CNC milling it following an  approximation of that contour was first demonstrated over 10  years ago [13].  Systematic error was introduced by the need  to execute the die level mill in quadrants, along with the  inability to account for stress relaxation in the sample during  that operation.  The resulting final thickness uniformity was a  great improvement over flat top milling and shown to be well  suited to producing samples in the range of 100 µm.


Internal development work with a modern CNC contour  milling tool designed for lab use is showing very good  promise.  It has the capability to either make the surface  measurements directly using a profilometer, or import optical  system measurements from another standalone tool. With  mapping and contour cutting a more uniform final thickness  across the die has been achieved with targets below 100 µm.


Thermal/Mechanical Restoration


With the lid off and the die thinned, there is little to prevent  laminate board flexing and die cracking during post edit  socket level module tests.  To prevent this, a whole new  approach to the package re-assembly process had to be  devised.  See Figure 4.  A sandwich of thermal compound  paste and metallic shims is used to replace the silicon  removed, and then the lid is reattached to the board around the  perimeter.  The entire assembly regained much of the bending  resistance of the as-received module, along with a suitable  thermal path.


An alternate approach is to leave the perimeter of the lid  attached to the laminate board to act as a permanent stiffener, and simply cut a window in the lid for die access.  This  method is shown in Figure 5 and Figure 6.  Working within a  confined cavity can complicate die thinning and polishing, along with certain FIB tool operations.  For example, we have  had difficulty inserting and positioning the process gas jet  nozzles safely and effectively in a reduced opening.    The  window may have to be oversized or even offset to remain  centered over the edit site.


After editing, a thicker slug and thermal paste is inserted into  the window to replace the volume of silicon and lid that was  removed, restoring the thermal path.  One advantage of this  method is that it reduces the thermal paste interface from two  to one.


With improved tools and processes die cracking associated  with the preparation of laminate packages has been  substantially reduced, and the overall uniformity of final  silicon thickness greatly increased.  But due to their delicate  nature, we still experiences a slightly higher loss rate for  laminate preparation over the more rigid and inherently flat  ceramic carriers.


Figure 5.  Two package reassembly techniques used to restore  both mechanical stability and thermal performance.  Left: whole lid removal, with a shim and thermal paste used to  replace the silicon. Right: partial lid removal, with the center  section replaced with a solid slug.


Figure 6.  Partial lid removal using a CNC picture frame cut.  The remaining portion acts as a stiffener to reduce further  board bending and die cracking.


Mechanical Reduction to 30-40 µm


This is a common starting thickness for those that operate a  FIB tool that is not equipped with a gas concentrating nozzle  designed specifically for rapid trenching. Machining an entire  bowed die to this final thickness can be difficult with a planar  cutting tool unless the edit happens to be near the center  region [14].  This juncture is where ‘pocket milling’ is a  sensible approach.


Shown in Figure 7 below, a pocket mill is a relatively small  area machine cut just over the region to be edited.  It works  particularly well in cases of stressed silicon.  As the area cut is  only a small portion of the entire die, the silicon tends to retain  greater resistance to cracking.  As the cut is confined to a  limited spot along the curved structure, the small area can be  made thin without resulting in global thickness uniformity  issues.  After editing, a small shim about 90% of the pocket  mill area is cut and sandwiched into place with thermal paste  prior to the lid restoration.


This approach works well if there is only a single location or  small region of edits to be attempted.  Individual pocket mills  may be less practical on multi-core chips in which an edit has  to be repeated in several places across the die.


Figure 7.  Pocket milling used to achieve a small region of  thinned silicon.  Left: prepared for FIB editing.  Right: milled  region replaced with a small shim set in thermal paste and  ready for lid reattachment.


As Received, from Full to Thinned Die


‘Full die thickness’ is a highly variable term, as it is dependent  on both the original source of the product and the condition of


the product as received by the analyst.   Traditionally it  implies the 775 µm thickness of a typical 300 mm wafer.  Those working exclusively in advanced package assembly  might only ever see thinned product.  A backside ground chip  bonded to glass intended for stacking could be as thin as 10 µm [15].  The decision to begin the edit process without doing  any further silicon thinning could be driven by unique  customer requirements, problematic structural integrity, or  simply advances in the FIB process that enable the skipping of  mechanical sample prep.


Early work on a FIB edit process that involved no mechanical  pre-thinning of full 775 µm silicon was in response to a  customer requirement that involved presorting die for speed


[16].  Each chip of a multi-core processor module used in a  massively parallel computing environment needed to be  prescreened and matched with like chips for uniform  performance. This constituted a level of testing that went  beyond what could be accomplished at wafer probe, necessitating a temporary module build.  Individual die were  solder bump mounted to reusable ceramic carriers but not  underfilled with the stabilizing epoxy, and then extensively  tested. Prime die were then hot wire sheared off of the  temporary substrate, and remounted on the final system multichip module processor assembly with others that tested within  the tight window [17].


The ability to successfully test chips that were destined for the  prototype systems might also require the inclusion of a single  or multi-point FIB edit.  Die that were mechanically thinned  for conventional backside FIB modification could not be  subjected to the mechanical stress of shearing without  suffering severe damage, especially if there are multiple edit  sites further weakening the structure.  The mixing of thin and  full thickness die on a dense assembly was also of concern to  the thermal management team, as the applied lid / heat sink  would not naturally contact all points uniformly.  The only  possible way to work with chips that had to be removed and  remounted was to edit them in a minimally invasive manner, leaving untouched as much of the base silicon as possible.


A process dubbed ‘Megatrenching’, shown in Figure 8, was  developed that helped make full thickness editing possible.  By greatly exceeding the spontaneous etch threshold of  disassociated XeF2 gas in a confined space, the isotropic  removal rate outside of the region actually scanned by the ion  beam increased almost 100x.    An initial vertical removal rate  of close to 100 µm per minute was achieved. Within about 25  minutes the upper bowl shaped region attained a diameter of  approximately 1,300 µm across and up to 300 µm deep, while  the inverted cone shaped trench branching out from the  bottom of the bowl extends down to the active device region.  The end result is a full depth trench with a wide angle for  material escape and visibility, with an adequate tapered profile  for good gas flux to reach the bottom.  Depending on the exact  parameters used, up to 3x108 µm3 of silicon substrate material


can be volatilized, resulting in an average removal rate of over  107 µm3 / minute [18].


Figure 8.  Pictorial representation – Typical profile of a “Megatrench” full depth access hole milled in less than 25  minutes using a method that concentrates disassociated XeF2  in a confined space.


Chips mounted on laminate packages that never receive a  conventional lid are another example of ‘difficult-to-FIB’ modules.  These units will remain lid-less through the system  board assembly process and only during final box level  construction will a radiator-like thermal transfer device be  mounted directly to the backside of the silicon.  This means  that during socket-level testing any thinned die would be  extremely vulnerable to stress cracking either from the  clamping force or from the application pressure of a cold  chuck or other thermal transfer device used to keep the  module cool.


A minimally invasive approach using full thickness FIB  trenching worked well in this situation. Several iterations of  editing were performed on multi-core processors in the last  product cycle, and all survived lidless test head insertion.


Edits will also need to be performed to chips mounted in 2.5D  and 3D packages.  As introduced in the section on advanced  packaging configurations, second generation assemblies will  stack chips on top of silicon interposers in a variety of  configurations.  Some of the chips will be traditional thickness  and ‘active side down’ with their bare backside silicon facing  up.  Others may be thinned, utilizing TSVs and double-sided  C4 attachment technology to allow other chips to be stacked  on top of them.  The stacked chips may be arranged with the  active side facing up or down, making some easy to FIB edit  and others nearly impossible.   The analyst may receive a  partially built assembly providing access to the edit site on an  intermediate chip, or may even have to remove a component  to get to one beneath.


Flip-chip bonded die are usually stabilized by the insertion of  underfill epoxy, although this might not be the case with  evaluation samples or partially built units.  If the assembly of  components is not underfilled, mechanical machining of any  kind may be too harsh and induce damage.  We have  successfully performed Megatrench editing on the top chip in  a non-underfilled 2.5D stack.


It is also possible to take a hybrid approach if the stack is  underfilled, as shown on a 2.5D module in Figure 9.  To speed  the editing process approximately one-third of the larger die


was mechanically thinned to 250 µm.  Eight edit hole using a  modified Megatrench process were milled across this region.


Figure 9.  Examples of “Megatrenching”.  Left: 2.5D module  with 3 die on a silicon interposer on a BGA substrate.  A  hybrid edit approach: 8 reduced sized trenches in a section of  the die thinned to 250 µm to speed the process.  Right: Single  chip module, full sized trenches on a 6x6 mm chip.


But as valuable as this all-FIB process has been to our chip  edit effort, it can only be applied to a subset of all possible  situations.  The basic concept could probably be improved  upon by reengineering the Megatrench process to work in the  high current Xe Plasma FIB, but it still has spatial limitations.  In reality, it represents just one of the tools in the Chip Edit  tool box.  Depending on the spacing relationships of  individual edits, or especially if these edit sites need to be  joined together by new interconnect wiring, improved low  profile methods are needed.


Ultra-thin Prep to 10 µm


The benefits of ultra-thin silicon preparation are well known, and in fact practiced regularly on a small scale during every  chip edit [19].  The challenge is to accomplish this over a  chip-level wide area, transferring it from a FIB chemical  process to one of mechanical milling.


The final preparatory step in any chip editing process is to  establish a flat, even edit floor a few microns above the target  region.  When working with a conventional bulk silicon  process, this insulated plane may be 10 µm wide.  With a  silicon-on-insulator transistor structure the buried oxide layer  can serve as this plane, and can be cleared several millimeters  across in the extreme [20].  See Figure 10.


We typically open up only as much buried oxide floor as  needed to execute the repair, as shown in Figure 11.  Less  exposed area helps limit implanted charge issues and reduces  the possibility of inducing local thermal discontinuity.  It also  reduces the potential loss of any deep trench decoupling  capacitors in the area. But the option to open up a larger area  increase targeting accuracy always exists.


Figure 10.  CAD drawing and FIB image of edit sites and 500 µm long lines deposited directly on the buried oxide floor of a  45nm device. Voltage contrast effect clearly shows the  circuitry below the interface.


Figure 11.  FIB image and drawing describing a trenching  process that opens up a portion of the buried oxide floor for  easy, low aspect ratio editing on a 32 nm device.  Ultra-thin  silicon prep would give this type of low aspect ratio advantage  across the entire chip.


The biggest benefit of a completely open floor is the ability to  place edits anywhere - infinitely close or far away, and yet  easily join them.  Secondary electron and IR imaging for  targeting is greatly improved, and n-well or capacitive  imaging, if the technology affords, is also possible with little  additional effort.  Gas processes work more efficiently when  there are no trenches, offering the freedom to position the  nozzles for optimum flow patterns.  In short, an ultra-thin  silicon approach enables unlimited circuit edit opportunities  without the vertical and horizontal constraints that working  within or near a trench presents.


The ability to mechanically contour a massive area or even the  entire chip to an even 10 um remaining would bring the  benefits we’ve experienced working on SOI to any silicon  technology.  One team has already reported significant  development work in this area, accomplishing the uniform  thinning with a gimbal mounted grinding/polishing assembly  rather than a CNC tool.  They reported their results at ISTFA  2009, noting that “Most significant is the improvement to  efficiency that the ultra-thin process provides by enabling a  high degree of flexibility in using circuit edits to solve  problems. The ultra-thin process enables iterative, unplanned  FIB work, maximizing the usefulness of an edited device”


[21].


Heat removal has always been a concern when thinning to the  buried oxide, and with only 10 µm of silicon remaining the  outcome will likely be similar.  We intentionally pack  conventional trenches with thermal paste, and remove it with  an appropriate solvent if subsequent edit work in the area is  required.  Similar to large areas of exposed buried oxide, a  whole die of ultra-thin silicon will likely have to receive equal  or even greater care during package reconstruction.  Refer to  Figure 4 for the two basic approaches to thermal and structural  management.  Conformal milled shims to match the contour of  the silicon, or soft metals that can be pressed into place will  likely be required.


One of the constraints in ultra-thin processing is the accurate  determination of remaining silicon thickness and the  uniformity across the area being prepared.  A simple infrared  microscope, either bench top or built into the FIB tool is  typically used for determining this.  Using the assumed index  of refraction of 3.5 for silicon, the values are reasonably  accurate down to around 25 um remaining, and when imaged  over a broad area.  Much below that, however, the accuracy  drops off due to various factors including too great an optical  depth of focus hampering actual surface determination, uneven reflections from circuitry features such as deep trench  capacitors, changes in doping density, etc.  More elaborate  methods such as reflectometry and interferometry offer great  promise, especially when combined with a conventional IR  imaging scope so that a measurement location free of  obstructions can be selected.  For instance, a bank of deep  trench decoupling capacitors can scatter the beam and give a  false or erroneous reading.


Despite the limitations in being able to use the in-chamber IR  microscope for accurate thickness measurements, its use as a  navigation and first order beam targeting aid is of utmost  value.  The image quality when looking through backside  silicon is a function of surface roughness, thickness and  doping density.  As can be seen in Figure 12, visual acuity and  fine feature resolving power is superior with ultra-thin sample  preparation.


Figure 12.  IR visual acuity comparison – full 775 µm left  verses thinned to 10 µm right [22].  Initial targeting accuracy  by either CAD overlay or ‘dead reckoning’ is greatly  improved with better feature resolving power.


CNC Milling Ultra-thin Prep


The development of a reliable CNC contour milling and  polishing procedure to enable ultra-thin preparation is  underway at IBM.  While a gimbal polishing system has been  shown to work, we don’t consider it to be a universal solution  easily adapted to our various chip/package configurations.  It  would be especially difficult to envision this method being  applied to a 2.5D or full 3D assembly.


One of the problems we have encountered is the changing  center to edge deflection value as the silicon is thinned.  Organic laminates are often cupped even before chip  mounting, and no two samples seem to be exactly alike or  respond consistently to thermal and mechanical cycling.  There is a natural tendency for stress relaxation and shape  change during the milling process.  Very large samples may  have to be remapped multiple times and the cutting program  adjusted, not just for curvature but for the evenness of silicon  remaining during the cutting process.   The goal is to develop  a predictive model that will allow us to map a component and  then apply a curvature shift to the cutting instructions that will  compensate for the natural change.


There has been some debate amongst CNC tool users and  manufacturers alike about the best conditions for actually  cutting stressed modules.  Some suggest to map and mill the  modules as-received, while others use a heated chuck to  promote relaxation [23].  The idea of heating is to drive the  CTE point back closer to the joining conditions when the two  components were a physical match.  Our experimentation has  followed a modified approach, using waxes of different  melting/solidification temperatures to lock in varying degrees  of relaxation.  It is also possible to apply a controlled amount  of pressure on the module as the wax sets to lock in an even  flatter contour.  There may be an ideal bending state for  cutting that will both retard creep and breakage during ultrathin prep.


To date we’ve mapped modules as received, after being  locked into several different melting temperature waxes, and  after various degrees of cutting.  We see positive trends with  the application of correction factors, but the outcome is  variable and to date has not produced totally acceptable results  at the 10 µm target.  One theory is that the board itself  undergoes a combination of elastic and plastic deformation  during this stress cycling, and is thus unlikely to completely  return to its original shape even after die, C4 ball and underfill  removal.


As discussed, stressed glassy materials do not stand up well to  rough handling, and silicon cracking is a likely outcome if the  milling process is not done in an exacting manner, or when  dealing with flawed materials.  This general statement is  amplified as the remaining silicon thickness approaches zero.  For example, a non-uniformly applied epoxy underfill


(variable density) can create regions of uneven pressure  sensitivity and a localized lack of support under the silicon.  These factors increase the risk of sudden punch-through and  fracturing when milling or polishing silicon in the ultra-thin  regime.  It may not be reasonable to assume that the underfill  process can be made 100% void free, so our machine  parameters may have to be adjusted for reduced feed or  plunge rate as we approach the final thickness target.


Packaging Level Analysis


The expertise developed by the FIB sample prep team has  been applied to helping the package development team  perform various investigative studies.


There was interest in developing the capability to remove  individual chips off of a 2.5D module. As shown in Figure 13, the four logic chips are mounted to a silicon interposer, which  is in turn mounted to the BGA laminate substrate.  The intent  was to be able to study details of the C4 joining process and  visually examine the uniformity of the injected underfill  epoxy.  Typical of modules that use an organic laminate as  their base board, this whole assembly is under stress and the  silicon interposer and the chips are bowed.  Conventional flat  top milling methods even when combined with hand grinding  could not uniformly remove components with acceptable  results.  By mapping and contour milling the chips right down  to the terminal metal connections and beyond, the entire  joining system could be examined in detail.


Figure 13. Four chips on a silicon interposer on a laminate  substrate. Two of four chip milled ultra-thin for visual  inspection, and then completely removed (milled into the C4  joining ball and epoxy region) for examination of ball  integrity and underfill application uniformity.


The cut direction through the module assembly can be  reversed, using concave shaping rather than convex.  In the  case shown in Figure 14, the C4 solder on the chip side after  reflow was of interest.  The underside of the Pad Grid Array  package was accurately mapped and milled away, leaving the  silicon separated from the assembly.  Visible is the chip with a  thin surface layer of ball joint solder and remnants of the  surrounding epoxy underfill lip.  If there was an interest in  proceeding with a chip-level failure analysis, the underfill  could be plasma ashed away and the remaining C4 bumps  stripped off.


Figure 14. A reverse direction cut used to separate the chip  from the package, but preserve the chip side C4 joints and the  underfill for inspection.


TSV Analysis Using FIB XeF2


TSV’s are ‘drilled’ (reactive ion etch milled) about 50 µm  deep and filled with copper during the BEOL wiring process.  After back lapping the wafer to expose the opposite end of the  deep via, another terminal metal layering is applied and a  solder bump formed [24]. TSV connections can put stress on  the surrounding connectivity and insulator stack, and an  alternate method of isolating and stripping away the silicon  for inspection was sought.


Figure 15.  TSV inspection - backside silicon cleared using  the chip edit FIB XeF2 trenching nozzle.


Existing wet chemistry methods like cesium hydroxide and a  commercial XeF2 gas cell stripping system are available, but  neither offers the ability to image the chemical silicon  stripping real time, be able to stop at any point for  examination, and even do a FIB cross-section at will.  As  shown in Figure 15, the XeF2 concentrating nozzle designed  for trenching during FIB chip edit provided the solution.  The  near spontaneous etch rate of 2x105 cm3 per minute clears the  silicon yet does negligible damage to either the TSV itself or  the buried oxide separating the via from the rest of the stack.  Applying a small amount of ion beam increased the rate  considerably while still doing only limited damage to the  embedded and underlying structures.


Despite significant advances in circuit modeling and extensive  use of automated layout and checking algorithms, simple  interconnect wiring errors and logic inversions continue to  happen.  As a result, FIB based circuit editing through the  backside silicon continues to be an important part of the timeto-market strategy for many chip makers and foundry  customers.


The established methods of sample preparation to support FIB  chip edit that worked well for single chip modules do not  always translate directly to the unique requirements of modern  packaging.  Flexible organic package base boards with  inconsistent bending characteristics, and the introduction of  stacked die packages with conjoined multiple thickness  components is prompting a complete rethink in the selection  of starting parameters.  The proliferation of multi-core or  multi-channel chips means that a single edit may have to be  replicated any number of times.  The chip preparation method  chosen must help enable a high edit yield, while also produce  a robust final assembly that will survive subsequent testing  and handling.  No single preparation technique works well in  more than a handful of applications, and this dictates that we  develop complementary techniques.


A truly uniform final thickness ultra-thin silicon preparation  technique offers tremendous promise for FIB editing, but a  reliable process remains elusive. We believe that the new  generation of CNC machining and polishing tools equipped  with the ability to map and mill complex shapes will  ultimately offer the solution.   Unfortunately we did not fully  appreciate the complexity of the need to remap and adjust as  the chip-package system stresses change the shape of the  assembly. Net is that it’s going to take a lot more work to  perfect a robust FIB preparation process.


The engineering labs responsible for qualification and failure  analysis of these new style packages are facing similar tooling  needs.  Fortunately, the team responsible for supporting chip  edit has been in an excellent position to help with this  development.  We have been able to apply our basic CNC tool  knowledge and recipes to help the package team better  investigate the bonding interfaces in highly stressed  assemblies.   The TSV analysis using the FIB gas trenching  was more to show the synergy and outcome of cross-team  pollination, and that tools designed for one purpose can be  applied to solving other problems.

Simulation Studies on Fluorine Spec Limit for Process Monitoring  of Microchip Al Bondpads in Wafer Fabrication


Hua Younan, Nistala Ramesh Rao, Yang Yanjing, Zhao Siping and Redkar Shailesh


GLOBALFOUNDRIES Singapore Pte Ltd, 60 Woodlands Industrial Park D, Street 2, Singapore 738406  E-mail: Younan.HUA@globalfoundries.com


In wafer fabrication, Fluorine (F) contamination may  cause fluorine-induced corrosion and defects on  microchip Aluminum (Al) bondpads, resulting in  bondpad discoloration or non-stick on pads (NSOP). Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES) is employed for  measurements of the fluorine level on the Al bondpads.   From a Process control limit and a specification limit  perspective, it is necessary to establish a control limit to  enable process monitor reasons. Control limits are  typically lower than the specification limits which are  related to bondpad quality. The bondpad quality affects  the die bondability. This paper proposes a simulation  method to determine the specification limit of Fluorine  and a Shelf Lifetime Accelerated Test (SLAT) for  process monitoring .Wafers with different F levels were  selected to perform SLAT with high temperature and  high relative humidity tests for a fixed duration to  simulate a one year wafer storage condition. The results  of these simulation results agree with published values. If the F level on bondpad surfaces was less than 6.0  atomic percent (at%), then no F induced corrosion on  the bond pads was observed by AES. Similarly, if the F  level on bond pad surfaces was higher than 6.0 atomic  per cent (at%) then AES measured F induced corrosion  was observed.


It is commonly known that Fluorine (F) contamination  may cause F-induced corrosion and defects on  microchip Al bondpads, resulting in bondpad  discoloration or non-stick on pads (NSOP). In the  authors’ previous studies (Hua and Ramesh et al, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], theories, failure mechanisms/characteristics  and methods for eliminating solutions of Fluorineinduced corrosion on Al bondpads have been presented.


In this paper, we will validate the industry accepted FSpec limit based on a study of F-induced corrosion on  Al bondpads using Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES) and Shelf Lifetime Accelerated Test (SLAT) simulation  methodologies.


In wafer fabrication, AES is widely used for controlling  and monitoring the F levels on Al bondpads after back  end of the line (BEOL) processes. X-ray photoelectron  spectroscopy (XPS), also known as Electron  Spectroscopy for Chemical Analysis (ESCA) is also  used for F analysis on bondpad. However, as compared  to  AES, XPS’s lateral resolution is poor due to its large  probe size (~10um-2mm). AES’s lateral resolution is  much better (~10nm-field emission). Moreover, AES  results are more stable. Therefore, we recommend using  AES for bondpad contamination monitoring in wafer  fab.


A simulation method is proposed to determine the  specification limit of F and a Shelf Life Accelerated  Test (SLAT).


The Spec limit, which is related to bondpad quality, impacts the die bondability. A Spec limit of F should be


6.0 at% (using AES as monitoring analysis), which is in  agreement with that reported in the literature. Results  showed that if F level on bondpad surface was less than


6.0 at%, no F-induced corrosion was found. However, if  F level on bondpad surface was higher than 6.0 at%, signature of F-induced corrosion defects were observed


As an off-line laboratory monitoring methodology, we  have to set up a control limit and Spec limit for OOC (out of control limit) and OOS (out of Spec limit) bondpad quality controlling. In general, the control limit  is process related and it can be determined by collecting  a group of real monitoring data from the process  monitored using the SPC methodology. Thus, the


control limit may be different for different process flow. Currently it is about 2.0 - 5.0 at% for Auger bondpad  monitoring.  However, it should be lower than the Spec  limit.


For the Spec limit, it is not process related, but it is  bondpad quality related. This means that if F level is up  to the Spec limit, bondpad quality will be negatively  impacted as the F level at the Spec limit will result in Finduced corrosion and defects, and then damage  bondpad surface and cause negative effect and even   NSOP issue at assembly processes. So it is very  important to validate a industry accepted F-Spec limit.


In this paper, we call it as “Industrial F Spec Limit”. What is value of “Industrial F Spec Limit”? How can we  determine it? According to the literature studies, George  G. Harman reported that if F level was larger than 6.0  at%, it might cause the negative effect on wire bonds in  his book titled “Wire Bonding in Microelectronics: Materials, Processes, Reliability and Yield” [7]. Jeanne  Pavio et al [8], J.F. Gaves et al [9] and J.K. Nesheim [10] also studied reliability effects of F contamination of  Al bonding pads on semiconductor chips and came out a  similar conclusion. In this study, a simulation method is  introduced to validate “Industrial F Spec Limit” on Al  bondpad surface. Here, we used the F-induced corrosion  as a signature of pass or fail criterion rather than wafer  bondability.


Experimental Results and Discussion


In this study, three wafers were prepared with different  F level on bondpad surface and they are labeled as  Wafer A, Wafer B and Wafer C. Auger Electron  Spectroscopy (AES) was used for the analysis of surface  F level on bondpads. AES results are shown in Table 1-3. From the results, one can see that the wafer A, which   is standard or control wafer, has F level in the range 2.5


- 4.0 at% on the five bondpads measured. B and C are


the engineering wafers and have F level of 4.0 - 5.5 at% and 6.5 - 8.0 at%, respectively.


After AES analysis, the three wafers were conducted  wafer storage simulation test using Shelf Lifetime  Accelerated Test (SLAT), which is patented test  methodology from GLOBALFOUNDRIES [11] and it is  used to perform in the laboratory in a special oven with  an accelerated high temperature (T) and relative  humidity (RH) test for a certain fixed duration (t) to  simulate one year of wafer storage in a controlled  environment at the storage area. The controlled


environment means that wafers should be stored either  in N2 cabinet or in vacuum package and kept in a  storage area maintained at suitable Spec values of T and  RH.

After wafer storage simulating test using SLAT, the  three wafers were conducted SEM inspection to check if  there were F-induced defects or not on bondpad surface.  High resolution SEM inspection results for both samples  before/after SLAT test are showed in Figures 1-3.


Based on the SEM inspection results, one can see that  no F-induced defects are found on bondpad surface of  the wafer A (F level: 2.5-4.0 at%) shown in Figure 1 and  the wafer B (F level: 4.0-5.5 at%) shown in Figure 2. But the F-induced defects (white dot-like) are found on  bondpad surface of the Wafer C (F level: 6.5-8.0 at%) shown in Figure 3.


Figure 1. SEM results showed that no F-induced defects  are found on bondpad surface of the Wafer A (F level:


2.5-4.0 at%), both before and after SLAT test.


Figure 2. SEM results showed that no F-induced defects  are found on bondpad surface of the Wafer B (F level:


4.0-5.5 at%,), both before and after SLAT test.


Figure 3. SEM results showed that the F-induced defects  are found on bondpad surface of the Wafer C (F level:


6.5-8.0 at%) after SLAT test


From the above experimental results, we can conclude  that after SLAT simulation test for one year of wafer  storage, no F-induced defect is found if F level is less  than 6.0 at% on bondpad surface (refer to the results of  wafers A and B shown in Figures 1 and 2).  However, the F-induced defects are found if F level is higher than


6.0 at% on bondpad surface (refer to the results of wafer  C shown in Figure 3).


Therefore,    we   can    confidently     recommend     that “Industrial F Spec Limit” of 6.0 at% as reported in the  literature [7-10] is valid if using AES as the monitoring  tool for bondpad surface analysis. This means that if F  level on bondpad surface is less than 6.0 at%, the risk of  F-induced corrosion will be lower. However, if F level  on bondpad surface is higher than 6.0 at%, the risk of Finduced corrosion and negative effect on bonding will  be higher.


In wafer Fab, we recommend to use Auger Electron  Spectroscopy (AES) for controlling and monitoring of F  level on Al bondpads as it has good lateral resolution

and relative stable results. The control limit is process  related and can be different for different processes and  should be lower than the Spec limit. The Spec limit is  quality related. In this paper, SLAT simulation  methodology is introduced for wafer storage evaluation  on F level on bondpad surface. According to our SLAT  simulation results, the “Industrial F Spec Limit” is 6.0  at% if using AES as monitoring tool for bondpad  surface F analysis, which is in agreement with it  reported in the literature. If F level on bondpad surface  is less than “Industrial F Spec Limit” 6.0 at%, the risk of  F-induced corrosion will be lower. However, if F level  on bondpad surface is higher than “Industrial F Spec  Limit” 6.0 at%, the risk of F-induced corrosion and  negative effect on bonding will be higher.

Surface Microstructure Evolution Upon Silicidation of Ni(Pt) and the Different  Responses to Metal Etch


Wentao Qin1, Dorai Iyer1, Mike Thomason2, Jim Morgan3, Carroll Casteel3, Robert Watkins1 and Rod Crowder1   1Technology Assessment and Characterization Lab, ON Semiconductor, 5005 East McDowell Road, Phoenix, AZ 85008  Wentao.Qin@onsemi.com


2 Fab10, ON Semiconductor, 2300 Buckskin Road, Pocatello, ID 83201


3 Product Engineering, ON Semiconductor, 5005 East McDowell Road, Phoenix, AZ 85008


Ni(5 at.%Pt ) films were silicided at a temperature below 400 ºC and at 550 ºC. The two silicidation temperatures had  produced different responses to the subsequent metal etch. Catastrophic removal of the silicide was seen with the low  silicidation temperature, while the desired etch selectivity was  achieved with the high silicidation temperature. The surface  microstructures developed were characterized with TEM and  Auger depth profiling. The data correlate with both silicidation  temperatures and ultimately the difference in the response to  the metal etch. With the high silicidation temperature, there  existed a thin Si-oxide film that was close to the surface and  embedded with particles which contain metals. This thin film  is expected to contribute significantly to the desired etch  selectivity. The formation of this layer is interpreted  thermodynamically.


Metal silicides are widely used as contacts, interconnections  and Schottky barriers in very large-scale integrated circuits. NiSi has replaced CoSi2 as the contact material in advanced  integrated circuits due to significant advantages including low  temperature formation, low consumption of Si, and  compatibility with SiGe [1]. The addition of Pt in the Ni film  increases the nucleation temperature of NiSi2 by  approximately 150 ºC, stabilizes the NiSi films, and enables  barrier height adjustment [2]. For silicides of near-noble  metals (Ni, Pd, and Pt), the barrier heights on n-type silicon  depend on the metal deposited and are relatively insensitive to  the silicide phase [3, 4]. Silicides formed from NiPt alloys  have barrier heights between those of Ni- and Pt-silicides [5], and there is a systematic increase of the barrier height from


0.66 eV for Ni to 0.75 eV for Pd, to 0.85 eV for Pt.


After formation of the silicide on Si and poly-Si, a wet etch is  performed to selectively remove the unreacted metal on  isolation (Si-oxide) and spacer (Si-nitride). Finally, a second  anneal may be necessary to form the desired silicide phase. The etch selectivity was believed to result from a passivation


SiO2 layer on the silicide [5, 6]. The same mechanism of etch  selectivity for the case of Pt-silicide was reported [7]; however, the presence of a nanometer thick SiO2 layer was  inferred based on characteristic Auger features of SiO2 without  confirmation through visualization of the morphology of the  surface microstructure [5].


The objective of this paper is to present microstructure data, including TEM images, of the silicides formed with Ni(Pt) on <001>Si as well as correlation of the microstructure data with  etch selectivity.


Experimental


70 nm of Ni(Pt) was sputter-deposited on n-type <001> Si


substrates with a Ni(Pt) alloy that contains 5 at.% of Pt, at the  temperature of 100 ºC. The Si substrates were cleaned with


diluted HF prior to the deposition.


Annealing was performed at nominally 400 ºC in an ambient  of N2 for 45 seconds; however, the temperature control of the  furnace was found to be inaccurate, and flakes of Si-oxide  were observed on the wafer surface after metal stripping with  aqua regia at 65 ºC. The temperature control was subsequently  restored, and the annealing was conducted at 550 ºC to ensure  a complete consumption of the Ni(Pt), which had led to  solving the flake problem.


The TEM samples were prepared with mechanical grinding  and polishing and finalized with ion-milling. TEM images and  EDS data were acquired with a Philips CM200 TEM operated  at 200kV and an EDAX EDS system, respectively. The  composition was determined based on EDS standardless  quantification and presented in the format of atomic percents. The AES data was acquired using a Physical Electronics 670A  Scanning Auger Nanoprobe with a probe beam voltage of


10kV. The samples normals were tilted 30º to the probe beam  to reduce sample charging. The depth profile data was  acquired by alternately collecting selected spectral data and


Figure 1. a)TEM image and b)Auger depth profiles of the wafer surface after Ni(Pt)  was deposited on Si.


sputter etching the surface. Sputter etching was carried out  with a 04-303A differentially pumped Ar + ion gun built into  the spectrometer. The approximate sputter rates were  determined by profiling through a 400 Å SiO2 film under  similar ion gun conditions. The atomic concentration values  were determined based on published sensitivity data and not  actual standards. Concentration values should only be used for  relative comparisons between samples.


Results


Figure 1 presents a TEM image (a) and Auger depth profiles


In the context of the increasing complexity of materials used in  semiconductor device processes, the STEM EDX technique is  now used routinely. It can be used to discriminate stacked  layers in advanced devices where STEM HAADF Z-contrast is  not sufficient. Moreover, it allows a new use of planar  preparation for layer investigation. The complexity of  analyzed structures drives a need for 3D information which  can also be obtained with the chemical information of the EDX  analysis.


Physical failure analysis of advanced technology nodes faces  two main challenges: ever shrinking dimensions require the  use of TEM imaging (and the requisite sample preparation) to  get sufficient resolution to observe the defects, while the  chemical complexity of the deposited layers may lead to a  misinterpretation of the analyzed faults.


Advanced technology processes require chemically complex  materials to improve performance and scale devices. This is  evident in the 28nm node that combines a high-K metal gate  stack, containing TiN and HfSiON layers [1], and Arsenic, Phosphorus, or Boron doping in the source-drain.


Three primary results are given in this paper. First, 2D EDX  analysis efficiency is demonstrated for cross-section and  planar extraction applications. Second, a volume rendering is  performed using only two observation directions (90° stereoscopy). Third, a complete EDX tomography analysis is  carried out on an exotic device.


Chemical analysis


Previously chemical analyses such as STEM EELS or EDX  have been used for line scan profiles [2] or in an uncommon  way for dopant mapping at nanometer scale [3]. These


analyses have been made using a FEG source and an EELS  spectrometer or Si(Li) EDX detector which implicates low  signal emission and detection. Consequently, these timeconsuming analyses are not adapted for full device  characterization when mapping acquisitions are mandatory. With the recent improvement of X ray emission and detection  using high brightness electron source and SDD detectors, morphological and chemical information can be efficiently  carried out.  In this work, a Tecnai Osiris is used [4] implementing these advanced technologies. The technique  offers both the spatial resolution needed to analyze a defective  device and the chemical information to discriminate elements  present in the stack, so as to better pinpoint the root cause of  the failure. This can be illustrated with Fig. 1, showing a  defective MIM capacitor (TiN/ Ta2O5/TiN), with a) STEM BF  imaging and b) corresponding EDX mapping.


Figure 1: STEM BF HAADF and EDX mapping of a defective  MIM TiN/Ta2O5/TiN capacitor (Ta rich particle re-deposition) The STEM EDX mapping was performed at 120keV with a  1nA probe current. The defect morphology is complex and the  STEM BF image showing only material density contrast does  not allow a complete understanding of the failure. The STEMEDX map gives all the materials composition allowing the  defect origin to be more easily interpreted. The MIM capacitor  failure is probably die to de-lamination and re-deposition of a  Ta2O5 thin layer during the Ta2O5 deposition process. The  EDX is a real asset for understanding this type of defect. It can  be used for section observation but there are numerous other  applications including planar observation and 3D analyses.


Planar Sample Preparation for Stacked Layers Analysis  with EDX Mappings


Conventional sample preparation for silicon devices physical  analysis is generally performed with cross sections (either for


FIB/SEM analysis or TEM lamellae preparation), as it offers  the ability to render how the process layers have been stacked  together. However, cross section TEM lamellae preparation  appears to be tricky for 28nm technology nodes and below: very thin lamellae have to be extracted (to avoid overlapping  structures), while being prepared at a unique location, i.e. at  the defect position. The latter highlights the tricky part for  TEM physical failure analysis: How does one extract a TEM  lamella at the right location? Planar TEM imaging eases  sample preparation, as the whole device can be included in the  TEM lamella [5]. Combined with EDX imaging, it is then  possible to discriminate process layers, and thus to determine  the process failure. Figure 2 evidences the interest of  combining this specific sample preparation and EDX imaging. While the defective SRAM does not show up any defect in  STEM imaging mode due to the overlaid process layers (left  image), EDX imaging of the same device (right image) discriminates layers by their chemical composition.


Figure 2: Left image: HAADF STEM image of the defective  SRAM cell. Right images: XEDS STEM elemental mappings, showing defective TiN and Hf oxide layers in the gate stack.


Thanks to the EDX mappings, a defect in the TiN layer and  hafnium oxide layer can be observed. These layers have  probably been consumed due to a patterning issue and  chemical attack (infiltration).


Toward 3D analysis


Although planar imaging identifies the defective layer through  the use of EDX imaging, topography remains unknown. In  specific cases, such as dealing with very thin layers, volume  rendering of a thin layer can be performed with only two views  of the same feature, a section one and a planar one (i.e. horizontal and vertical). Here again, EDX imaging allows  filtering of the chemical elements not involved in the stack  formation. Figure 3 shows such a 3D rendering of a thin layer  of TiN in the gate stack of the 28 nm SRAM.


Figure 3: a) cross section view, b) planar view, c) & d) 3D  reconstruction of the TiN layer using the two perpendicular  views.


This 3D view is created by binarizing the two Ti elemental  mappings and combining them with the Amira Software. Separately, theses mappings show the thickness (Fig. 3a) and  the width (Fig. 3b). When both are combined (Figs. 3c&d), the  global topology can be linked to the device process. Indeed, the most important fluctuations are localized at the silicon  active boxes limits, i.e. at height variations. This study  highlights the need for 3D information from advanced devices.


STEM EDX Tomography


Volume rendering with two views can be performed for  process monitoring, and here two different devices are  observed (one for each direction). Moreover, the observed  layers have to be stacked (e.g. MOSFET) to be considered as  invariant thick layers.


But, when analyzing a defective part, or when dealing with a  fully 3D object (e.g. multi-gate transistors with geometrically  complex layers), a complete 3D analysis is required for  volume shape characterization. Indeed, considering a 10nm  silicon nanowire surrounded by a gate stack of 7nm [6], a 3D  analysis offers the ability to observe all the parts of the same  device. The SEM image (Fig. 4 left) shows the 3D complexity  of the device hardly characterized with 2D lamella. A rodshaped specimen of 100nm of diameter was extracted in the  planar direction for complete device analysis (Fig. 4 right)[6].


Figure 4: SEM image of the Nanowire device (left image). Rod-shaped tomographic sample of the device prepared in a  FIB (right image)


Figure 5 presents the obtained results from a XEDS STEM  tomography [7] acquisition performed every 5° and over 180° to control all the process steps of the same device (SiGe pads  etching, silicon nanowire shape and the “all around” gate  deposition). Each 750*900 pixels EDX mapping was acquired  in 10min (800µs/px of dwell time). For the reconstruction  process, four elemental volumes have been reconstructed and  combined (Hf, Si, Ti and Ge).


Figure 5: 3D chemical representation of the device. Silicon is  in blue, germanium in purple, titanium in yellow and hafnium  in red. a) & b) Global rendering showing the geometrical  complexity of the device. c) Focus on the 10nm Si nanowire  and its high-K metal gate deposition all around the nanowire.


Comparison with a defective device can also be performed, to  determine the origin of the fail, with the emphasis that  conventional 2D analysis may not provide the correct  assessment. Indeed, two perpendicular cuts in the same device  are difficult to perform [5], and this approach is not always the  most relevant especially in presence of a singular fail. Moreover, for such a 3D device, the relevance of the analysis  stands on the ability to observe all parts of the device and their  combined effect during the process. Figure 6 shows two views  of the reconstructed volume. Two facts can be observed: The  SiGe pads are misaligned (Fig. 6a) and the gate is not  deposited all around the nanowire (Fig 6.b).


Figure 6: 3D chemical representation of a failed Si nanowire  device (Ge in purple, Ti in yellow).


a) Top global view of the device with dashed blue line  showing misalignment between the SiGe pads and the gate; b) View along the direction of the expected Si nanowire, showing  deposition failure.


The 3D visualization facilitates a full understanding of the  process steps interactions – the misalignment of the SiGe pads  and the consequent failure in the gate deposition. With a  conventional 2D analysis, this issue would have been  misunderstood. Therefore, the 3D analysis is a valuable asset  for specific applications especially when different directions  must be qualitatively observed.


The added value of in-TEM EDX capability was demonstrated  for physical failure analysis, as well as process monitoring. 2D  cross sections can be chemically analyzed over relatively large  area and at nanometer resolution. Thanks to EDX layer


discrimination, large sample preparation with planar extraction  can be performed to characterize defective layers. Moreover, if  a cross section view is added to the planar one, a false volume  can be rendered assuming a thin invariant layer. Finally, a  complete device can be analyzed by STEM EDX tomography  offering an in-volume (3D) analysis in all directions.

Automatic Registering and Stitching of TEM/STEM Image Mosaics


Chung-Ching Lin, Franco Stellari, Lynne Gignac, Peilin Song, John Bruley IBM T.J. Watson Research Center


1101 Kitchawan Road, Rt 134, Yorktown Heights, NY 10598


cclin, stellari, gignac, psong, bruley@us.ibm.com


Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and scanning TEM (STEM) is widely used to acquire ultra high resolution images in different research areas. For some applications,a single TEM/STEM image does not provide enough information for analysis. One example in VLSI circuit failure analysis is the tracking of long interconnection. The capability of creating a large map of high resolution images may enable signiﬁcant progress in some tasks. However,stitching TEM/STEM images in semiconductor applications is difﬁcult and existing tools are unable to provide usable stitching results for analysis. In this paper, a novel fully automated method for stitching TEM/STEM image mosaics is proposed. The proposed method allows one to reach a global optimal conﬁguration of each image tile so that both missing and false-positive correspondences can be tolerated. The experiment results presented in this paper show that the proposed method is robust and performs well in very challenging situations.


1. Introduction


Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)/scanning TEM (STEM) provides signiﬁcantly higher resolution images than reﬂected-light and laser-scanning microscopies(LSM), allowing scientists to examine structures as small as a single column of atoms. The high resolution image acquired by TEM/STEM is essential to many scientiﬁc research ﬁelds, e.g. cancer research, material science, nanotechnology, and semiconductors. The downside of such technique is that the Field Of View (FOV) of an individual image is usually very small. The capability of creating a large map of high resolution images can enable breakthrough development in some researches: tracking the connectivity of the neuronal circuit, automatically mapping and detecting process defects and process variations, and reverse engineering, etc. However, creating a large map of high resolution TEM/STEM images of VLSI chips, which involves image stitching, is difﬁcult because the images


contain a large amount of repetitive structures that may lead to registration issues, as shown in the high energy BSE images in Figure 1. As a result, existing methods [2] cannot provide good stitching results for this application. In this paper, we propose a new fully automated stitching method that can robustly create a 2D panorama of TEM/STEM images in a region of interest (ROI) for semiconductor applications.


Anderson et al. [1] proposed a registration pipeline for large TEM/STEM datasets using the intensity correlation of the images within an overlapping area. The relative translation of each pair of images can be obtained in an unordered image set. Then the images are concatenated using the relative translations. This method can ensure the continuity in adjacent images but it will easily propagate and accumulate the error in the sequential registration step, especially for very large datasets containing very repetitive structures.


Furthermore, this method allows only for rigid transformations and is not able to handle scaling, rotation, and more complicated transformations. In summary, the method using the intensity correlation works well for certain cases but it usually leads to high computational complexity in ﬁnding the rigid transformation when the images contain very distinct textures at different locations. Furthermore, the intensity correlation is not a very reliable measure for images with very similar structures but with slight changes in focus,and different levels of the average intensity.


Brown and Lowe [2] proposed a stitching method to provide a more reliable way of ﬁnding the relation between images using the corresponded feature points. This method can also ﬁnd the non-rigid transformations between images,but it was developed for the unordered daily-life images.


For stitching TEM/STEM images of semiconductor circuits, we need a robust feature point algorithm. Mikolajczyk and Schmid have [8] shown that the Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [7] is the most robust algorithm among competing techniques. Based on some characteristics of the SIFT work, we have developed a new stitching method that demonstrates very good performance in stitching large TEM/STEM images datasets, and it is ro-


bust to slight defocusing, translation stage errors, presence of repetitive structures, and missing and false-positive registration points.


In the next sections, we will discuss in detail our new proposed method and present several application examples.


Figure 1. Two adjacent high energy, 300 kev, Backscattered Electron (BSE) images taken of a bulk semiconductor sample in a TEM/STEM.


2. Problem Deﬁnition


The projection of a 3-D point i on a image plane can be expressed as a matrix form in homogeneous coordinates

Any two images from a same plane in space can be related by homography. A corresponded point i between image  and  can be expressed as:


ai = a ·ba ·b · bi

In this case, cameras are assumed to be ideal (no distortion).
