For mapping VLSI chips, the TEM/STEM tool is usually setup to acquire images at different locations by stepping the stage with a ﬁx constant value that guarantees a desired partial overlap of adjacent images, as shown in Figure


2(a). However, sample translation stages of a TEM/STEM tool are not perfect and usually introduce translation and repeatability error in acquired images. As a consequence,the actual poses of the dataset looks more like Figure 2(b).


For this reason, each related transformation between each couple of adjacent images is different and it needs to be estimated individually. To solve this problem, we use the detected correspondences to estimate the global transform matrix  for each image tile. Then, the transformation matrix is used to create a panorama of the dataset.


Figure 2. (a) desired sampling constellation, (b) actual sampling constellation.


3. Overview


The block diagram of our proposed method is shown in Figure 3. For our application, we ﬁrst acquire a twodimensional array of partially overlapping TEM/STEM images of a region of interest (ROI) using an automated software script. Once the feature points are detected using the Harris corner detector and histogram of oriented gradient(HoG) is extracted as the descriptor of a feature point, the corresponded points between adjacent images are then obtained with our new group matching method. The correspondences are reﬁned using RANdom Sample Consensus(RANSAC) [3]. All the correspondence of the dataset are then used to estimate the global optimal conﬁguration using bundle adjustment [11] with Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm [9]. Finally, to generate the panorama, the estimated conﬁgurations are used to transform all pixels to their global positions, and the pixel values in the overlapping regions are averaged.


4. Corresponded Points


Unlike other types of images, the TEM/STEM images from semiconductor chips contain circuit elements that usually show a large amount of repetitive structures. Therefore,stitching this type of TEM/STEM images is very challenging and requires a strong feature point detector. Mikolajczyk and Schmid [8] have shown that SIFT [7] is a robust method for feature point detecting and matching. There-


Figure 3. Block diagram.


fore, the histogram of oriented gradient (HoG) used in SIFT method is a strong descriptor of a feature point.


In our method, we use the Harris corner detector to ﬁnd the locations of the feature points, and then use the HoG as the descriptor of a feature point. The nearest neighbor of the descriptors is used to ﬁnd the corresponded points.


To identify the distinct matching points, the second nearest neighbor is compared to the nearest one: the higher the nearest neighbor ratio is, the more distinct the corresponded point is. The corresponded points with high ratio are then selected as detected feature points.


However, even with this methodology, estimating stitching parameters using the matched feature points in TEM/STEM images of semiconductor chips is still difﬁcult because the matching results contain many false correspondences. One way to improve positive correspondences is to increase the size of the descriptor that may lead to quickly overwhelming computational complexity for large datasets. Therefore, we propose here a new group matching method to reduce the false correspondences without increasing computational complexity. After the feature points are detected using the original proposed size of the descriptor, the feature points are separated into groups with partial overlapping regions. These overlapping areas are necessary to compensate the stage translation errors when taking sample images with the TEM/STEM tools. The matching is then performed between the corresponded groups. The new


group matching technique can increase the nearest neighbor ratio, reduce the searching area, and even reduce the computational complexity.


5. RANSAC


Even though the new group matching method reduces signiﬁcantly false correspondences detection, the matching results still have a signiﬁcant number of false ones. To re-ﬁne the correspondences, we use random sample consensus(RANSAC) [3]. RANSAC is typically used to ﬁnd the majority of the correspondences that agree to the same model within acceptable error. However, in our case, we have found that the majority is not always consistent with the true transformation due to the repetitive structures. For this reason, after the majority is obtained, we further verify that the model ﬁts the majority consistently within the overlapping area between adjacent frames. Since the exposures of the adjacent frames may not be at the same level, the overlapping areas in both frames are adjusted to the same average illumination level (see Algorithm 1) before we evaluate the consistency.


6. Tile Conﬁguration


After all corresponded points between every adjacent image couples are obtained, all corresponded points are used to estimate the optimal conﬁgurations for all tiles. Instead of estimating each tile conﬁguration iteratively, we estimate all conﬁgurations altogether. In this way, all corresponded points in four neighbors of a single tile are considered for optimizing the conﬁguration. This step is achieved by using bundle adjustment with Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) algorithm [9] to estimate the conﬁgurations.

The ﬁrst  iterations correspond to the burn-in step. That allows us to set all initial value of stitching parameters to zeros. After the burn-in step is completed, all the conﬁgurations are close to the optimal ones. Then, the weighting is applied based on the residual k in every iteration. 7. Experiment Results


Applications of our new stitching algorithm to reallife experimental data will be shown in this section. For these examples, we used high energy, 300eV, Backscattering Electron (BSE) images of semiconductor chips [4, 5].


The BSE images were taken of a bulk sample using a microchannel plate detector in a JEOL 3000F TEM/STEM. A BSE detector in a TEM/STEM can produce images with information from layers several microns below the surface.


Gatan Inc. Digital Micrograph Montage software was used to automatically acquire a matrix of BSE images near a region of the chip containing a memory array. The size of each image is 512 x 512 pixels with 14.9 nm/pixel resolution leading to a FOV of approximately 7.6  x 7.6 .


Precisely mapping memory arrays may be considered one of the most challenging tasks for an automated panorama algorithm because of the highly repetitive structures that makes the correct registration very difﬁcult. Experiments show that the proposed method is indeed robust to register each image tile and provide good stitching results.


In our analysis, no initial value of each tile is needed.


The number of groups in every tile for matching corresponded points is two.


Figure 4 shows the stitching results of the dataset corresponding to the memory array. This particular dataset consists of 16 x 8 tiles. Figure 4(a) shows a set of images corresponding to a small portion of the memory array dataset.


The size of ﬁnal stitched images is about 100  x 50 (6651 x 3396 pixels). As one can see, repetitive structures are very common among adjacent images, which makes the

(b) of the Ni(Pt) as-deposited on the Si substrate. A glass slip  was bonded to the sample surface using M-bond 610 from  Allied High Tech. In addition to Ni(Pt), an approximately 9  nm thick layer that exhibits some diffraction contrast exists  between the Ni(Pt) and Si. In the reactions of near-noble  metals (Ni, Pd and Pt) with Si below 300ºC, the sequence of  silicide phase formation is the metal-rich silicides, M2Si (where M stands for the metal), and the monosilicides after the  metal is entirely consumed for the M2Si [8 - 10]. Such a Ni2Si  that is 3-4 nm thick on [001] Si after the deposition of a Ni(5% Pt) film was observed by TEM imaging [11]. On the other  hand, simultaneous growth of NiSi and Ni2Si after deposition  of Ni(5 at.%Pt) on Si <001> was also observed. Even this 9  nm-thick polycrystalline layer is likely Ni2Si, since EDS  analysis (with a small enough electron probe) of the layer has  not been performed, no composition information about the  layer is available. As a result, this layer is labeled “NiSix” in  Figure 1. Presence of this layer indicates a sufficiently clean  surface of the Si substrate prior to the Ni(Pt) deposition. A  very thin layer of oxide very likely was present on the Si  surface before the Ni(Pt) deposition. A small-probe analysis in  the format of EDS/EELS profiling can help verify the presence


of the oxygen and determine its location between the Si  substrate and the Ni(Pt).


A TEM image of the wafer surface after annealing in the  furnace without accurate temperature control is presented in  Figure 2a. The image shows a stack of two layers on Si. A  glass slip was bonded to the sample surface using M-bond 610, after the sample surface was coated with Cr. EDS  quantification yields a composition of Ni 65% and Si 35% for  the layer on Si, which is consistent with the Auger depth  profiles presented in Figure 2c. The EDS and Auger depth  profiles indicate that the stack is [unreacted Ni(5% Pt)]/Ni2Si  on Si. The identifier “Ni2Si” used here denotes the  composition inferred from the EDS and Auger depth profiles, and serves another purpose of brevity. Verification of the  Ni2Si phase(s) via crystallographic information that is to be  inferred from electron diffraction patterns is currently ongoing  but the data is not presented in this article, although the  primary phase is likely Ni2Si based on studies by others and  discussed earlier [8-10]. The use of another identifier “NiSi” further in the article is within a similar context.


The Auger depth profiles presented in Figure 2c also indicate  that the Pt concentration is higher in the unreacted Ni(Pt) than  the Ni2Si. This is because Pt was expelled from Ni2Si due to  the low solubility of Pt in Ni2Si, in a process referred to as  snowplowing [12, 13]. Pt exists in grain boundaries of the  Ni2Si, and acts as a barrier for the Ni diffusion from the Ni(Pt) through the Ni2Si layer, which in turn suppresses the growth  kinetics of Ni2Si. With 3% of Pt, the onset temperature of  simultaneous growth of NiSi and Ni2Si on Si <001> was 350 ºC [13]. For 5% Pt in the Ni(Pt) alloy on <111> Si, this  temperature was reported to be 400 ºC [12]. The higher  content of 5 at.% Pt is expected to further slow down the  formation kinetics of Ni2Si, and subsequently increase the

After metal stripping, the wafer surface is covered with a Sioxide layer that is about 120 nm thick as shown in Figure 3a. Regarding the sample preparation, a glass slip was similarly  bonded to the sample surface using M-bond 610, after the  sample surface was coated with Cr. Some residual silicide is  left on the Si. EDS spectra of the Si-oxide and the residual  silicide are presented in Figure 3b. Auger depth profiles of the  wafer surface, presented in Figure 3d, have verified the stack  of SiO2/residual silicide/Si. The SEM image presented in  Figure 3c shows flakes of Sioxide in a patterned area of the wafer.


Etching of un-reacted Ni(Pt)/Ni2Si on Si (annealed at < 250 ºC) and Ni2Si on NiSi/Si (annealed at < 350 ºC) using  Hydrochloric Peroxide Mix (HPM, consisting of  HCl/H2O2/H2O), with Si-oxide as an etch product, has been  reported [14]. The etch was stopped when the NiSi layer was  exposed. Consequently, NiSi formation after the first RTA was  deemed necessary to prevent the loss of silicide during the  selective etch by HPM. The higher etch rate of Ni2Si, compared with that of NiSi, was interpreted in terms of the  following two factors. 1) Ni2Si possesses a higher density of  Ni-Ni bonds and a lower density of Ni-Si bonds than NiSi. The  bond energies are 2.1 eV for the Ni-Ni bond, and 3.3 eV for  the Ni-Si bond. The difference in the volume fractions of NiNi bonds and Ni-Si bonds would make Ni2Si more easily  decomposed by HPM than NiSi. 2) Pt has a lower solubility in  Ni2Si than in NiSi. Consequently, the distribution of Pt in  Ni2Si is more inhomogenous than in NiSi. The difference in  the Pt distribution homogeneity would make Ni2Si more  vulnerable to the HPM etch.


In our case, both the residual Ni and the underlying Ni2Si were  etched by the aqua regia, leaving Si-oxide on the wafer.


Figures 4a and 4b present TEM images  of the wafer surface  after annealing at 550ºC, and EDS spectra (4c) acquired from  films in the stack on the wafer surface. On Si, there are two  layers of monosilicide with very close Ni/Si ratios, and the top  monosilicide contains about 2 at.% of Pt. The bottom silicide  exhibits a slightly higher Si/Ni ratio than the top silicide, which is consistent with its proximity to the Si.


A stack configuration of


NiSi(Pt/Ni=1%) / NiSi(Pt/Ni=6%) / NiSi / (interface with Si  characteristic of a ratio of Pt/Ni=0.3%) / Si <001>


was reported after Ni(Pt 3 at.%) was annealed at 450 º for 20  minutes [13]. The configuration was attributed to the  formation of NiSi at both the top and bottom interfaces of NiSi  with Ni2Si and Si, as well as the expulsion of Pt from Ni2Si  toward NiSi due to the low solubility of Pt in Ni2Si. Specifically, at the Ni2Si-NiSi interface, Ni2Si decomposed  into NiSi + Ni. The Ni diffused to the NiSi-Si interface and  formed NiSi with Si of the substrate. In our case, the annealing  temperature was higher; hence, a higher degree of silicidation  is anticipated. Since the temperature window for the NiSi is  about 350 ºC – 650 ºC [1], the primary phases in the top and  bottom silicide seen in Figures 4a and 4b are both expected to  be NiSi, which is consistent with the EDS and Auger  quantification data. A hypothetical interpretation of the layer  sequence is described as follows. First, the Ni(Pt) was entirely  consumed to form Ni2Si. Subsequently, the Ni2Si decomposed  into NiSi + Ni. Due to the high solubility of Pt in NiSi, some  Pt was retained in this top layer of NiSi. On the other hand, the  Ni from the decomposition of Ni2Si diffused to the interface  with the Si substrate and reacted with Si which eventually led  to formation of the bottom NiSi with a lower Pt content.


On the top silicide there is a layer containing Si and O, and  there are particles containing Ni and Pt and embedded in the  layer. Further up is another layer that contains Ni and O.

The stacking sequence of thin films on the wafer surface


shown in Figures 4a and 4b and Figure 5 can be interpreted in  terms of thermodynamics as follows.


After the complete consumption of Ni(Pt) for silicidation, there were Ni and Si atoms diffusing to the silicide surface. Although Ni is the major diffusing species in silicidation, Si  diffusion is already evidenced by silicide bridging over


oxide and nitride at high temperatures. The out-diffusion of


both Ni and Si to the silicide surface leads to the following two  possible stacking sequences of:


Silicide / Ni-oxide / Si-oxide, and


Silicide / Si-oxide / Ni-oxide.


The first possible sequence of


Silicide/Ni-oxide/Si-oxide


is unstable and un-favored thermodynamically, since the Nioxide can be reduced by the out-diffusing Si spontaneously via  the reaction of


Si + 2NiO = 2Ni  + SiO2, ∆F =-84 kcal/mol at 500 C. Consequently, Ni-oxide ends up being outside of Si-oxide and  further away from the top silicide.


Based on the discussion of the mechanism to form the surface  Si-oxide, it becomes obvious that from the process point of


view, the Ni(Pt) on Si needs to be entirely consumed, after


which monosilicide forms. An additional annealing in an


oxidizing ambient ensures the formation of a Si-oxide layer on  the top Ni-silicide layer [7, 15]. The stack of Ni-oxide / Sioxide / monosilicide is believed to be more resistant to the etch  than that of unreacted Ni(Pt) / Ni2Si. This resistance can


prevent catastrophic removal of the unreacted Ni(Pt), as well  as the subsequent reaction of the stripping chemistry with


Ni2Si to produce Si-oxide on the wafer. No Ni(Pt) is to be left  unreacted on Si. Any unreacted Ni(Pt) shall only be present on  Si-nitride and Si-oxide, and will eventually be removed by


aqua regia.


If, on the other hand, the Ni(Pt) is not entirely consumed, the  kinetics of Si diffusion to the surface of the residual Ni(Pt) is  likely too slow; hence, cannot lead to sufficient formation of


Si-oxide on the residual Ni(Pt). In addition, Ni2Si, rather than  NiSi, forms under the unreatced Ni(Pt). The stack of


Ni(Pt)/Ni2Si is less resistant to the metal stripping chemistry


than that of Ni-oxide/Si-oxide/NiSi, and therefore will be


etched and Si-oxide forms on Si.


In short, the silicidation shall be driven to the point of


complete consumption of the Ni(Pt), with formation of NiSi as  the top silicide layer. Additional anneal in an oxidizing


environment promotes the growth of a stack of Ni-oxide/Sioxide on the NiSi layer, which provides a buffer that can


prevent the catastrophic etch of the underlying NiSi.


With 70 nm of Ni(5% of Pt) deposited on Si <001>, about 9  nm of polycrystalline NiSix forms on Si. After being annealed  at nominally 400 ºC in a furnace with an inaccurate  temperature control, the Ni(Pt) film was not entirely silicided  and about 20 nm of residual Ni(Pt) was left unreacted on  Ni2Si. Subsequent metal stripping with aqua regia at 65 ºC had  removed the residual Ni(Pt) and etched the underlying Ni2Si, leaving a Si-oxide film on the wafer. With a higher annealing  temperature of 550 ºC, the Ni(Pt) was entirely consumed, which allowed out-diffusion of both Si and Ni to the silicide  surface. The out-diffusion resulted in a Ni-oxide layer on a  stack of Si-oxide/NiSi. The stacking sequence stemmed from


Si-oxide being thermodynamically more stable than the Nioxide. The Si-oxide layer, nonetheless, is not homogeneous  but has instead embedded particles that contain Ni and Pt. Nonetheless, the stack of Ni-oxide/Si-oxide/NiSi is more  resistant to aqua regia, and therefore produced the desired etch  selectivity of the metal etch. The enhanced etch resistance is  believed to result from the buffer provided by the stack of Nioxide/Si-oxide/NiSi, the higher volume density of the Ni-Si  bonds in the NiSi than those in the Ni2Si, and a more  homogeneous distribution of Pt in NiSi than in NiSi2.

Satish Kodali and Wayne Zhao

With increasing complexity involved in advance node  semiconductor process development, dependability on  parametric test structures have also increased significantly. Test structure characterization plays a predominant role  throughout the entire development cycle of a product. They are  used to understand the process windows and also help to  monitor the health of line (HOL).


We would like to present characterization work on one such  test structure in 20 nm bulk technology. Replacement metal  gate process technology has been implemented for the first  time at this node. Process complexity cause significant  challenges in understanding root cause of various fail modes. It is very important to design test structures to deconvolute  various process signal to identify and address the root cause of  fail modes in a much organized and timely fashion. This  approach enhances dependability on electrical inline signals to  address and plan for key process changes as needed. For  example, one of the key concerns upon the development of the  20 nm node is to identify unique replacement metal gate stack  process issues. Understanding those fail mode requires the  existence of test structures which monitors gate leakages due  to gate stack faults only. The gate leakage in these structures  could be from gate to gate and gate to substrate, provided there  are no gross gate fill metal under polish issues.


One of the key principles in successfully monitoring the HOL  is to establish passing and failing electrical criteria to various  test structures. In the current work, electrical and physical  characterization of one such test structure is shown. Further, we are proposing a novel way of establishing electrical  signatures to specific defect fail mode finger prints for early  identification and monitoring of process related defects.


Test Structure:


The test structure under consideration is intended to measure  gate leakage fail modes due to gate stack issues only. Figure 1  shows the schematic of the structure.  A Comb–Serpentine  configuration of gate runs all the way across the test structure  of active area (AA) islands. No source or Drain contacts are  present in the structure to eliminate any other potential fail


mode introduced by them. Thus, the test structure addresses  the gate leakage mechanism due to gate stack processing issues   only. During Inline Test (ILT) a preset voltage is applied to  the Serp while grounding the comb and substrate. The  resistance due to the leakage current is reported as an output.


Figure 1: Schematic of the test structure.


Electrical Characterization


A key process development lot has a wide spread electrical  distribution for resistance reported on the structure; Figure 2  shows the distribution. Any value below resistance of 1E+06  and above 1E+08 ohms are considered the two tails of the  distribution. The integration team wanted to understand the  failing tail of the distribution to take necessary corrective  actions. To understand the root cause of the fail mode, three  distinct populations of the defects, namely 1E+05, 1E+06 and  1E+07 ohm resistance sites, are chosen for characterization. The chips for all the three categories are bench tested by  applying ground on the comb while sweeping the serpentine  from -0.8V to +0.8V. The AA is held at ground during the  measurement. Extreme caution is used to choose relatively low  voltages, compared to the ILT, to protect the defect’s electrical  Gate

and physical signatures. The I-V curves measured with the  bench test setup are shown in Figure 3.  The corresponding log  scale data of Figure 3 is shown in Figure 4

Even though the raw data shows the leakage is higher on E+05  ohms sites; it doesn’t provide any additional information about  the characteristic comparison between the three populations. Figure 4 suggests that the characteristic of E+05 and E+06  ohm sites are very similar except for the extent of the leakage. E+07 ohm sites have a different characteristic compared to the  other two populations.


To localize the defects in the test structure, XIVA (eXternally  Induced Voltage Alteration) is used.  The technique is based  on laser scanning by applying a constant voltage and constant  current simultaneously by a current choke for improved signal  detection efficiency [1]. A 1340 nm laser is used for scanning  the test structure in order to locally inject heat. The resulting  power signal variation is monitored using a Lock-in amplifier  to improve the signal detection efficiency.


On a E+05 site, a voltage of 0.07 V is applied on the  Serpentine pad, while the comb and substrate pads are  grounded, generating a current of 500 nA in the defect. XIVA  analysis is done under those conditions. Figure 5 shows the  raw signal identified by XIVA. It is important to note the two  distinct flavors of spots that can be seen in the image. Firstly, the two spots identified by arrows have a distinct second band  of signal around the primary spot; while the others do not  exhibit such a second band characteristic. Further, the intensity  of the double band primary spot is considerably higher than  the others. Figure 7 shows the threshold adjusted image to  show the most intense signal spots only. They correspond  perfectly to the identified double band primary spots in Figure


5.


Similar XIVA analysis is performed on a E+06 site. A voltage  of 0.4 V applied on Serpentine pad while the comb and  substrate pads are grounded generated a current of 210 nA in  the defect. XIVA analysis is done under those conditions. Fig  8 shows the raw XIVA signal. A similar double banded spot is  identified with a strong primary spot signal along with several  single babded spots. Figure 9 shows the overlay image. E+07  sites exhibited very high resistance characteristics. A voltage  of 1V had a leakage of 1 nA. The leakage current was too low  to detect any fail modes with XIVA. We assumed absence of  gross hard fails in this population. Physical characterization is  done to identify the difference between the two distinct  populations identified by XIVA analysis namely the double  banded and single banded spots.

Physical Characterization


The failing chip was deprocessed to remove metal fill patterns  on top of the test structure. Top-down inspection was then  performed to identify  anomalies. No physical fail modes could  be identified in both secondary (SE) and back scattered (BSE) electron modes of SEM inspection. The dimension of the test  structure is approximately 30 um x 45 um. The SEM top down  inspect images are used to calibrate the XIVA optical and  signal overlay image. The position of the signal spots is  estimated from the calibrated XIVA image within 1 um  accuracy. The limited extent of the test structure can thus be  used to our advantage to precisely locate the failing site  without mandatory use of advanced isolation techniques like  solid Immersion Lens (SIL). A FIB dual beam section is done  through the failing sites.


Double banded XIVA signal spots:


The FIB section through the double banded spots identified the  fail modes shown in Fig 10. It is believed that a stacking fault [2-5] generated during the very early steps of processing


surfaced to the top of AA. Subsequent gate processing steps


filled the defect with gate material.


Figure 10: SEM image of  a FIB cross section of a double


banded spot


Single banded XIVA signal spots:


FIB section through the single banded XIVA spots revealed no  sign of defects. A TEM analysis is done on the defects to  identify the root cause. Fig 11 shows the TEM image of the  fail mode.  It is identified that due to poor spacer oxide  integrity of the gate material a wet clean generated a key hole  to the substrate. Subsequent processing steps led to migration  of gate material into the substrate. Fig 12. shows the elemental  map confirming the gate material is actually migrated into the  substrate


Figure 11: Single banded spots TEM analysis.


Figure 12: Elemental map showing that gate material  migrated into the substrate.


The test structure is intended specifically to identify gate to  gate and gate to substrate leakage mechanisms. Three distinct  populations from the inline data namely E+05, E+06 and E+07  are chosen for analysis. Electrical bench sweep  characterization attributes similar signature to E+05 and E+06  populations but different to E+ 07 population. XIVA analysis  identified two distinct categories of fail signatures on both  E+05 and E+06 sites; namely the double banded and single  banded spots. The double banded spots are due to metal filled  stacking fault originated defects. The reason for double  banding signal in the XIVA system is not fully understood. We  identified this signal for first time in the 20 nm technology  node. The single banded signal spots are due to gate metal  leakage to the substrate. Even though both kinds of spots are  identified in E+05 and E+06 sites, the greater incidence of  stacking faults, identified by dual banded spots, caused higher  leakage. Thus an electrical defect signature is established to


the XIVA spots for this specific gate stack test structure. The  resulting XIVA map provides invaluable information to the  integration team in terms of defects across the test structures  and also across the wafer without actually performing physical  failure analysis on individual sites.


Adjusting the spacer oxide thickness and gate etch process  eliminated gate material migration into the substrate defect fail  mode. Stacking fault defect are eliminated by addition of  anneal steps in the process post Si etch.


Attributing electrical bench test and XIVA signatures to  physical defects on various parametric structures provides  valuable information. This methodology enables faster yield  learning during process development for instance by cutting  short the turnaround time analysis of subsequent lots affected  by known defects.


As the semiconductor device geometries continue to shrink, process development challenges are increasing significantly. Dependability on various parametric test structures to evaluate  the process window and electrical functionality is becoming  more and more important. In the present work, novel test  structures on advanced 20 nm technology to deconvolute  process complexity to pin point process issues and address  them is illustrated. Further, a novel way to establish electrical  signatures to defects from Inline Parametric characterization to  identify and monitor health of line (HOL) is presented.

8. Discussion


We proposed a new fully-automated robust method for stitching TEM/STEM image mosaics. In this method, weﬁrst acquire an image matrix, and then the correspondences between adjacent images are detected and reﬁned. The reﬁned correspondences are considered altogether to estimate the global optimal conﬁguration of each image tile for stitching. Our experimental results show that the proposed method is robust and performs well in very challenging semiconductor applications. Although HoG is a very robust descriptor to ﬁnd correspondences, the match-


Figure 5. Zoom-in results of the memory array dataset: (a) the stitching result using the proposed method in [10], Figure 4(b),


(b) the stitching result of the proposed method without weighting,Figure 4(c).


ing method using HoG may still provide too many false correspondences in semiconductor chip applications due to the high repetitiveness of device structures. Our new method overcomes this drawback. Moreover, there is no need to know correspondences between every couple of adjacent images since our method can tolerate both missing correspondences and false-positive correspondences.


We have also presented experimental validation of our method using a VLSI chip fabricated in IBM 90 nm bulk technology. This method provides a comprehensive solution to register and stitch TEM/STEM images with highly repetitive structures.

AFM-based Chemical and Mechanical Property Characterization of Interconnects  and Defects


Michael Lo, Eoghan Dillon, Qichi Hu, Kevin Kjoller, Roshan Shetty, Craig Prater

Spectroscopic characterization of interconnects and circuits in  semiconductor devices has become increasingly complicated as  dimensions for breakthroughs and failure analysis are  continuously shrinking.  Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) and  infrared microspectroscopy (IRµs) are popular for basic device  analysis due to ease of operation and readily available  spectroscopic data in the literature.  Since typical defects are  smaller than the IR probe beam, the IR spectra would be  dominated by the signal from the surrounding material.   This  deficiency may be compounded with distorted band shape due  to optical interferences in the various materials which typically  compose a semiconductor device.   In addition, the spatial  resolution of IRμs is in the order of 3 – 10 µm due to the long  wavelengths of the radiation.  Hence, these sub-micrometer  defects create a significant challenge in spatial resolution and  reasonable signal to noise for IRµs.   Raman spectroscopy  potentially provides a sub-micrometer spatial resolution due to  the short excitation wavelength.  Good quality Raman spectra  could be obtained in this manner but this will depend on the  excitation wavelengths, the depth of penetration and the  transparency of the microelectronic circuits [1].   For instance, should visible excitation be used for Raman spectroscopy, devices coated with visible-transparent low-k dielectrics would  be saturated by Raman signals from silicon-based material  underneath [1].


To achieve high spatial resolution IR spectroscopic  information, a broadly tunable, pulsed infrared laser can be  coupled to an atomic force microscope in the AFM-IR  technique (Fig. 1) [2,3]. Here, pulses of the IR laser impinge  onto the sample co-located with the AFM tip.  At an absorption  of the sample the rapid expansion due to heating would cause  vibrations of the AFM tip that is directly in contact with the  sample.  The amplitude of the ringing motion of the AFM tip  can be recorded as the same tip scans over an area of interest.  By detecting only the perturbations directly underneath the  AFM tip, spatial resolution below the optical diffraction limit  of IR radiation is achieved.


To complement the AFM-IR technique, and to provide another  means to map the variation in composition of the sample is to  determine the local mechanical stiffness using the AFM probe.  A number of techniques have been developed to accomplish  this with most being limited to materials with low modulus  values due to the low amount of force which can be applied by  a typical AFM probe.  One technique which has demonstrated


value on stiffer materials (>10 MPa) is Contact Resonance  Atomic Force Microscopy (CR-AFM).  In CR-AFM, the AFM  probe or sample is oscillated, typically vertically, to interrogate  the mechanical properties of the sample by monitoring the shift  in the resonant frequency or quality factor of the AFM  cantilever.  As the AFM probe moves from less stiff to more  stiff materials the contact resonance frequency will increase  because the cantilever and sample create a two spring system in  which the characteristics of the AFM cantilever are impacted  by the sample.  By making use of a number of the oscillation  modes of the cantilever a range of modulus values can be  analyzed.  In order to accurately monitor a large number of  modes in an AFM cantilever a clean drive mechanism must be  employed.  In contrast with the typical piezoelectric drive  mechanisms, the Lorentz Contact Resonance AFM (LCRAFM) used in this work makes use of the Lorentz force to  oscillate the probe.  This force is created by flowing an AC  current through a specially designed two legged probe.  When  this probe is put in an external magnetic field with the right  orientation, the AFM tip will oscillate vertically allowing  determination of the contact resonance.  The spatial resolution  of the LCR-AFM technique is limited by the contact area of the  probe/sample.  This can allow a spatial resolution in the 10 nm  or less range.


Fig. 1. Principle of AFM-IR operation


Result and Discussion


AFM-based chemical and mechanical characterization  techniques provide resolution allowing analysis of submicrometer scaled features and defects.  As a demonstration of  the benefits of high spatial resolution IR spectroscopy, a  semiconductor device patterned with a low-k dielectric was  analyzed.  These devices are typically characterized using  transmission FT-IR on blanket (interlayer dielectric) ILD films.  There is some concern that there is local variation in the


chemical structure of the ILD material which could not be  analyzed on the non-device blanket films.  As illustrated in Fig. 2, the region where the ILD material is highlighted when the IR  laser is tuned to 2960 cm-1.  Such observation is caused by  absorption due to the methyl groups in the SiCOH low-k  dielectric having an absorption causing an increase in the  amplitude signal at this wavenumber. Alternately, upon  collecting the ringing amplitude of the AFM tip as the IR laser  is tuned across a range of wavenumbers, local FT-IR-like  spectra are generated (Fig. 3Error! Reference source not  found.).  This way, the methyl C-H stretching band is readily  observed from an individual ILD layer instead of an average of  multiple layers, as in conventional IRµs.

In these experiments, by initially collecting broadband  mechanical spectra the frequencies characteristic of the  different materials was determined.  Then the frequency of  oscillation of the probe was fixed and the amplitude was  mapped across the sample surface.  As the tip scans the surface, the amplitude of the AFM tip vibration would change from the  ILD, Cu and Ta/TaN layers (Fig. 4).  This is due to the change  in the mechanical stiffness from one material to another [4].   Here at 948 kHz, the copper would have a maximum amplitude  but the ILD and Ta/TaN layers would have smaller amplitude


since their maximum is away from the 948 kHz resonance.  This  allowed characterization of the relative modulus values from  the three materials and also high spatial resolution maps of the  different materials.

The advent of the AFM-IR technique opens the possibility of  analyzing surface features that are smaller than the wavelength  of interest.  Sub-micrometer-scaled imperfections could be  detected spectroscopically and chemically identified.  Preliminary data from a strand-like, 150-nm thick contaminant  on a liquid crystal display surface (Fig. 5) suggests the AFMIR technique could provide sensitivity for defect analysis on a  surface and a complementary piece of information to allow  more rapid and complete surface analysis.

The combination of AFM-IR and LCR-AFM has great potential  for providing high spatial resolution chemical and mechanical  analysis.  To demonstrate the feasibility of the AFM-based  techniques, AFM-IR spectrum and images were obtained from  the interlayer dielectrics of a test structure at a length scale  shorter than the IR wavelength.  In addition, using the LCRAFM technique, the relative mechanical properties of the  components could be mapped distinctively by simply observing  the contact resonance of the AFM probe.  Finally, preliminary  data suggest there may be AFM-IR spectral differences  between contamination and the bulk material on a liquid crystal  display.  Such data will provide useful correlation to other  analytical technique.

Direct surface bonding of wafers in 3D integration  requires perfectly smooth surfaces, with roughness  values below 1 nm, usually characterized with Atomic  Force Microscopy. An alternative technique, Digital  Holography Microscopy is evaluated here and shown to  be precise enough to differentiate adequate wafers, that  is chemical mechanical polished, from non treated ones.


According to Moore's Law, downscaling of Integrated  Circuits devices has led to the development of 3D (threedimensional) integration technologies which enables the  stacking of heterogeneous devices [1]. Potential benefits  of the exploitation of the third dimension do not only  concern size reduction but also resistivity, power  consumption, delay, etc. A large range of technologies  and processes based on the 3D stacking of crystals have  been and are still explored. Thus, new types of  interconnections had to be developed, such as Through  Silicon Vias. Among them, direct surface bonding  appeared to be a very promising route and has been  deeply studied in order to understand its physical  principles [2]. It was demonstrated that the quality of the  surface of the wafers, in terms of roughness, was a key  point to ensure a good bonding. Thanks to an appropriate  chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) step of the copper  top layer, surface roughness could be lowered from 15  nm to 0.4 nm. Such low roughness values could only be  characterized with Atomic Force Microscopy, which is  the most precise non-destructive technique enabling such  fine characterization. Its drawback is that it is a slow and  local measurement technique (such roughness  measurements are usually performed on 25x25µm² areas), which makes it difficult to integrate in a wafer


production control process. Optical 3D characterization  technique might be an interesting alternative, which  exhibit in the best case, near sub-nanometric vertical  resolution [3]. It is quick and allows 3D measurements  as well at short ranges (roughness) as at long ranges (waviness, wafer warpage). Due to optical limitations (wavelength, optical aperture of objectives…), the lateral  resolution of such systems (about 400nm) is poor  compared to that of AFM. Nevertheless, considering the  sub-micronic size of objects to be characterized, that is  of the same order as the nominal resolution of our optical  system, measurements should be indicative of the true  surface roughness [4]. It appeared worthwhile to  evaluate the capabilities of our optical 3D system, a  Digital Holography Microscope (DHM) and compare to  those of an AFM.


AFM 3D measurements


Topographic measurements were performed with a  Digital Instruments Dimension 3000 in tapping mode, with standard Nanosensors non-contact probe (force  constant 42 N/nm) and 512 measurement points. The  distance between two successive measurement points  will then depend on the scan size (97.7nm for  50µmx50µm and 19.5nm for 10µmx10µm).


DHM 3D measurements


Digital Holographic Microscope (DHMR2200, Lyncee  Tec) captures holograms resulting from the off-axis  interference between two coherent monochromatic laser  beams a "reference" one and that reflected by a sample (Figure 1). The beam source, laser diode, is separated in  two: an object beam O, and a reference beam R. The  object beam illuminates the sample via the condenser. The retro diffused wavefront is collected by the  objective, and then recombined with the reference beam  to form a hologram in the camera. The length of the


reference beam must be adjusted to be the same as that  of the object beam by moving the mirror


ensuring the coherence of both beams to form the  hologram. The acquisition time of this hologram varies  between one and one hundred microseconds depending  on the object observed and the configuration of the  microscope. Digital treatment allows real-time imaging  of the entire complex optical reflected wavefront (amplitude and phase) [5, 6].

When considering only the 2pLADA results, and to  serve as a direct qualitative comparison, Fig. 5(a) and


(b) illustrate the imaging capabilities of an optimized  conventional CW 1064nm LADA system and  2pLADA system, respectively. The optical power  incident before the 2.45NA GaAs SIL (for both  configurations) was only 0.35mW (peak power =


16.4W for the pulsed laser), the number of averaged  images was 200, the optical zoom was set to 8X, the  pixel dwell time was 32μs, the LSM resolution was  512 × 512, the fail rate was set to 50%, and the laser  pulses (separated by 10ns) were synchronized to start  arriving 3.06ns after the test loop trigger.  It is  immediately clear from Fig. 5(a) that the traditional  CW 1064nm LADA methodology is unable to  localize its weak signal to individual transistor sites, offering instead a global single polarity (i.e. predominantly passing) signal distribution which  cannot be overlaid with accompanying CAD details. 2pLADA on the other hand overcomes these  limitations and can produce a plurality of highly  localized LADA signatures which, when the incident  laser pulse is accurately synchronized to the  inverter’s switching event, emanate from vertically  displaced PMOS and NMOS transistors comprising a  simple inverter structure that is not limited by PMOS  dominance.  Moreover, with only 0.35mW incident at  the device, and with only 200 averages performed per  imaging technique, it is clear that 2pLADA  outperforms its CW 1064nm LADA counterpart in  terms of signal acquisition rate. The high peak power  of the pulsed laser interrogation makes it possible to  perturb and visualize weaker LADA spots to a larger  degree without damaging the device – laser damage  is of great concern as transistor size shrinks with  scaling.


For the purpose of evaluating the lateral fault  localization performance of our 2pLADA scheme, we  offer the following argument: Conventional spatial  resolution metrics, such as Rayleigh’s criterion for  example, were derived by defining the minimum  resolvable separation distance between neighboring  point sources, which assume an isotropic signal  distribution when observed. Therefore, for LADAbased evaluations, were physical circuit features (assuming an extended geometrical distribution) are  involved, an identical comparison simply cannot be  made. As a result, since measured LADA signals  occupy a digitized (i.e. either pass or fail) 2D  physical area, we argue that the more appropriate  methodology to adopt is a direct measurement of the  electronic response representing the physical distance  between the critical structures under test. Therefore, in terms of quantitatively evaluating the 2pLADA  isolation resolution performance from this data, it


was decided that the vertical gap separating the two  neighboring 2pLADA signatures in Fig. 5 (b) should  be used as the defining spatial metric. This gap  between the active PMOS and NMOS nodes of this  simple inverter was measured to be 117nm from the  computer-aided design (CAD). For this analysis, a  total of 630 2pLADA images were accumulated as a  running average and a collection of 4 neighboring  vertical line-cuts were extracted which suitably  traversed the 2pLADA signatures in Fig. 5 (a). These  4 line-cuts were then averaged and plotted. However, due to the opposing polarities of the neighboring  2pLADA sites, it was difficult to accurately  determine their separation. Therefore, the absolute  value of the averaged line-cut was plotted. This  enhanced the measurement since an all-positive data  set revealed a more distinct separation between  adjacent signatures. However, before measuring the  physical separation between the neighboring pass/fail  2pLADA signatures, we first need to determine the  magnitude of the 50% fail rate biasing fluctuations, since this variance represents our reference point. Anything above or below this 50% threshold will  represent clear laser-induced delays to the switching  transistors. This result is shown in Fig. 6(a) and a  magnified section containing only the 2pLADA sites  is given in Fig. 6 (b). From this data, it was possible  to measure a 2pLADA isolation resolution  performance approaching 100nm.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated a custom  ultrafast nonlinear optoelectronic probing platform  for the purpose of advanced IC debug and  characterization. Datasets qualitatively evaluating  CW 1064nm LADA, 2pLADA and 2pSEU  generation have been discussed with a quantitative  evaluation of lateral signal localization (2pLADA) and signal response rate  (2pSEU), deducing  approximately 100nm and 40nm lateral  resolution  performance, respectively. By way of a simple  comparative analysis, it was possible to deduce


2.25X to 4X improvements in rise/fail time response  rates when utilizing 2pSEU over 2pLADA. This  work demonstrates a new LADA-based evaluation  opportunity for modern SEU analysis and offers a  complementary toolset for other SIL-enhanced TPAbased IC characterization techniques [13-15]. We  have now set the standard in optoelectronic  microscopy of silicon ICs in terms of localized  volumetric resolution performance, invasiveness, and  opportunity. In addition to the impressive spatial  performance of both 2pLADA and 2pSEU, the  temporal performance of this technique also offers a  significant advantage which has yet to be fully  explored.

A Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detector (SnSPD) System for Ultra  Low Voltage Time-Resolved Emission (TRE) Measurements of VLSI Circuits


Franco Stellari, Alan J. Weger, Seongwon Kim, Dzmitry Maliuk*, Peilin Song, Herschel A. Ainspan, Young Kwark, Christian W. Baks, and Ulrike Kindereit


IBM T.J. Watson Research Center, 1101 Kitchawan Rd, Yorktown Heights, NY - stellari@us.ibm.com, 914-945-3223


Vikas Anant


Photon Spot Inc., 142 W Olive Ave, Monrovia, CA 91016


Ted Lundquist


DCG Systems, 45900 Northport Loop East, Fremont, CA 94538


In this paper, we present a Superconducting Nanowire Single  Photon Detector (SnSPD) system and its application to ultra  low voltage Time-Resolved Emission (TRE) measurements (also known as Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis, PICA) of scaled VLSI circuits. The 9 m-diameter detector is housed  in a closed loop cryostat and fiber coupled to an existing  Emiscope III tool for collecting spontaneous emission light  from the backside of integrated circuits (ICs) down to a world  record 0.5 V supply voltage in a few minutes.


Time-Resolved Emission (TRE) measurement, also known as  Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis (PICA) [1-9], based on  the collection of near infrared light (NIR) emitted by hotcarriers in the transistor channel, is an invaluable method  that has been widely adopted by the test and failure analysis  communities. This technique enables one to non-invasively  probe the switching activity inside VLSI circuits to measure  skews, propagation delays, duty cycles, etc [1-9]. Over the  years, its capabilities have been continuously extended by the  use of Light Emission due to Off-State Leakage Current (LEOSLC) [10-15] to completely new applications, such as  logic state mapping [10], pattern debugging [12], latchup  ignition study [16,17], power supply noise [14,18,19] and  slew rate measurement [20], self heating estimation [21], systematic and random device variability characterization


[15], security and counterfeit detection for ICs [22], etc.


However, the continuous trend of the semiconductor industry  towards smaller devices and lower supply voltages [23] has  caused significant changes in the intensity and spectrum of  light emitted by ICs [24]: the detectable light decreases  exponentially with the electric field in the transistor, and  linearly with the lateral dimension of the FET. Furthermore, the reduction in circuit voltages has also caused a progressive  shift of the spectral distribution of the emitted light towards  longer wavelengths as shown by previous work [25-28].


For all these reasons, detectors superior to the current state of  the art InGaAs SPADs (Single-Photon Avalanche Diode)


[29], with higher sensitivity at these longer wavelengths, as  well as lower intrinsic noise (dark counts), are needed.


About a decade ago, IBM was an early adopter of the  Superconducting Single Photon Detector (SSPD) technology  as a single point/pixel alternative to InGaAs SPADs and 2D  PICA cameras [30]. At that time, we demonstrated a 4X  improvement in SNR compared to the InGaAs SPAD, notwithstanding the poor (<4%) System Detection Efficiency (SDE) and the thermal degradation of the cryostat at the time  the comparison was performed. This improvement is  equivalent to a reduction of ~90 mV in the supply voltage of  the circuit while still guaranteeing a SNR similar to the  InGaAs SPAD [31,32]. In recent years, advances in the  understanding of the detector physics, material fabrication  processes, lithography, and cryogenic cooling technology  have allowed the manufacture of significantly better SSPDs, detectors and systems, that promise significant improvements  for TRE applications in VLSI testing [33-35].


In this paper, we will discuss the performance of a new  Superconducting nanowire Single-Photon Detector (SnSPD) system developed by Photon Spot [33-35] and its integration  at IBM into an existing Emiscope III PICA tool from DCG  Systems. In the following sections, we will use a custom-

designed IBM 32 nm SOI test chip for performing a detailed  characterization of the detector using realistic operating  conditions for VLSI circuits. We will show excellent  detection sensitivity down to a record low 0.5 V supply  voltage as well as detailed comparisons with the current  InGaAs SPAD [29].


Setup


The detector described in this paper consists of a niobium  nitride-based (NbN) 9 m diameter SnSPD fabricated without  any anti-reflecting coating or resonant cavity [33-35]. The  detector is housed in a closed-loop cryogenic system that  allows operation down to ~3 K, below its critical temperature (Fig. 1). Photons are delivered to the detector through a 9 m  Single Mode Fiber (SMF) and a collimator lens that are  mounted on an adjustable piezo-electric stage inside the  cryostat. Custom electronics biases the SnSPD, detects the  electrical spikes due to the absorbed photons, and generates  NIM (Nuclear Instrumentation Module) signals suitable for  the electronics used by the PICA tool. The described system  has a detection efficiency of about 8% at 1550 nm, a low jitter  of 32 ps-FWHM (Full Width at Half the Maximum), and low  intrinsic noise (Dark Count Rate, DCR) of less than 100 cps. The newly developed SnSPD system is integrated at the IBM  lab into an existing Emiscope III PICA tool from DCG  Systems, as schematically shown in Fig. 2. The original


62.5 m Multi Mode Fiber (MMF) used to optically couple  the Phase II+ InGaAs SPAD is disconnected from the base of  the microscope and replaced by the new SnSPD 9 m SMF. Unfortunately, this results in a reduction in collected signal  strength for most gates, and a more challenging positioning  of the collection spot on the gate of interest, leading to an  estimated SNR (Signal to Noise Ratio) degradation of about  2X in measured TRE waveforms. It should also be noted that, although the new SnSPD detector is sensitive to emission at  much longer wavelength than the InGaAs SPAD [33-35], the  optics of the current Emiscope system were not originally  designed for that range and therefore they do not allow  capture of the additional emission observed in previous


papers [27,28]. From the electronics point of view, the NIM  signal generated for each detected photon is directly fed to the  existing Ortec Picosecond Timing Analyzer (pTA) electronics. Additional software is used to control the SnSPD, such as its bias and fiber alignment.


A custom designed test chip, fabricated in IBM 32 nm SOI  technology, was used to characterize the performance of the  new detector. This chip contains many partitioned  experiments, such as delay lines, ring oscillators, complex  circuits, and discrete transistors. Each structure is  implemented in multiple variations covering different device  sizes, spacing, and threshold voltages. The chip allows for  separate and versatile evaluation of the detector sensitivity, jitter, and lateral spatial resolution, respectively. For the  purpose of this paper, the majority of the data was collected  from dedicated inverter-based delay lines using high Vt (threshold voltage) devices of different size and spacing (see  Fig. 3). Circuits may be controlled directly or via scan chains. The stability and repeatability of the new system performance  was first evaluated to guarantee a reliable characterization  and comparison of the detector over time. Notwithstanding  the vibration of the cryostat, the alignment of the 9 m SMF  was found to be quite stable over time with a degradation of  only few percent over several weeks of usage (Fig. 4(a)). As  expected the detector base temperature displayed a slow  increase of ~1 mK/month (Fig. 4(b)) due to the degradation of  the cryostat displacer, but no noticeable degradation could be  noticed in our measurements. Finally, by taking particular  care in landing the SIL (Solid Immersion Lens) and by  adjusting the focus for maximum emission collection every  time, very good repeatability of TRE waveform measurements  was demonstrated over time (Fig. 4(c)).

Novel SnSPD vs. state of the art InGaAs SPAD


Initial characterization of the system, consisting of the SnSPD  and Emiscope III optics with a centric SIL lens, showed good  performance. The jitter of the system during a real  measurement (which includes the circuit, pulse generator, timing electronics, and detector jitter) was shown to be less  than 50 ps-FWHM (Fig. 5(a)), significantly below the ~70 psFWHM of the existing InGaAs SPAD. For a typical bias  current of 19 A used in our experiments, the intrinsic DCR  of the detector was also measured to be below 10 cps in free  running conditions (Fig. 5(b)), a more than three order of  magnitude reduction compared to the InGaAs SPAD.


A detailed comparison with the existing Phase II+ InGaAs  SPAD was also performed under real-life measurement  conditions, using the 32 nm SOI test chip. In order to  guarantee the fairest comparison and the collection of the  most significant data, the analysis was performed collecting  waveforms with both detectors using the same operating  conditions for the circuit under test. In particular the same  physical chip was used and waveforms from the same  switching gates were acquired. To simplify the analysis, a  simple inverter with a 5 x 650 nm n-FET, switching at a fixed  10 ns (100 MHz) period was used (Fig. 6). The same SIL  objective and fiber coupling optics of the Emiscope III were  also used for both experiments. However, different fibers were  needed to connect the microscope to the detectors: a smaller  9 m core SMF was used for the SnSPD compared to the  InGaAs SPAD 62.5 m MMF. The timing electronics was  setup for a 2.5 s trigger loop (limited by the InGaAs SPAD), an acquisition window of 300 ns (for good time resolution), and a 5 min acquisition time (a good compromise for all  operating voltages). Even with all these precautions, an exact  comparison cannot be fully guaranteed due to remaining  small differences in collection area and intrinsic behavior of  the detectors (such as after-pulsing and slight differences in  the window gating) that cannot be easily quantified.


Fig. 7 shows waveforms acquired with both detectors at a  nominal (1 V) and reduced (0.8 V) supply voltage. All  waveforms show an initial high LEOSLC condition of the  inverter n-FET, followed by a switching transition peak due  to the output of the inverter dropping. The LEOSLC remains  low while the output is low and it finally returns to the  elevated state when the inverter output becomes high again. For all the measurements only one clock period is shown  without any data folding, but with an ideal ~10 GHz low pass  filter (LPS) applied. One can qualitatively observe that the  switching peaks in the SnSPD waveforms are smaller in  amplitude but significantly better identified, thanks to the  much smaller noise band. Furthermore, the InGaAs SPAD  already shows poor waveform quality at 0.8 V supply voltage. For the purpose of the paper, the switching signal strength is  defined as the amplitude of the switching emission peak over  the low emission state of the inverter. Furthermore, the noise  is defined as the standard deviation of the counts calculated in  the low LEOSLC region of the waveform, while the Signal to  Noise Ratio (SNR) is the ratio between the two previously  described values. Fig. 8 shows an analysis of these quantities  for both detectors for a more extensive set of measurements at  different supply voltages. By looking at the switching signal  strength in Fig. .8(a), one can quantitatively confirm the  lower detected signal strength of the SnSPD due to the lower

During this study, Digital Holography Microscopy was  used to characterize the topography of copper top layer  of wafers prepared for direct surface bonding. Though  this technique is optically limited in lateral resolution, it  allowed to differentiate CMP treated wafers from non  treated ones and could be a good alternative to AFM  microscopy. In an attempt to quantify the discrepancies  between these two techniques, studies on calibrated  samples were performed. Unfortunately, these samples  are supposed to exhibit the same surface texture, which  is true when characterized using stylus–type  profilometer. They exhibit scratches, some very deep  and steep, which make the DHM observations more  difficult. Nevertheless, obtained images with both  techniques were qualitatively very similar and  measurements follow the same trends. Furthermore, the  fine study performed on our AFM and DHM systems  evidenced their differences in surface texture, which  could be quantified through waviness and roughness  parameters. This study emphasizes the common idea that  surface texture measurements should be adapted to the  expected surface properties, this in relation to their  functionalities. Under this point of view, our purpose  being to evaluate the finishing quality of copper wafer  surface for direct wafer to wafer bonding, DHM system  was successfully used.

Pump-Probe Imaging of Integrated Circuits


David Stoker1, Michael Bruce2, Eric Lavelle1, Erik Matlin1, James Potthast3, Christopher Sakai1, Neil Troy1  1SRI International, Sensor Systems Laboratory  333 Ravenswood Ave. MS-301-01, Menlo Park, CA, 94025 2 Independent Consultant  3 Averna Test Systems


e-mail address: david.stoker@sri.com


Abstract: We present a new method of imaging integrated


circuits (ICs) using a dual-laser scanning confocal


microscope. In this method we introduce physical and/or


functional changes to the integrated circuit using the first


‘pump’ laser and then image the response of the circuit


using the second ‘probe’ laser. We propose several novel


applications of this imaging method. Specifically, we show


how to image the flow of injected charge carriers and use


the derived images to improve the resolution of material


interfaces. We also show how to image changes to activity


and laser voltage-probed waveforms and use the


information to discover electrical connections between


logic cells.


INTRODUCTION


Laser microscopes are used routinely in failure analysis (FA) labs to image integrated circuit (IC) devices with  resolution close to 230 nm [1].  In addition to passive  imaging, they can also be used to localize faults by  injecting charge carriers [2], or via local heating of the IC


[3]. They can also be used to directly measure electrical  waveforms via laser voltage probing (LVP) [4]. An  interesting question can then be asked, ‘what happens when  these methods are used simultaneously?’ For example, one  could apply Laser Assisted Device Alteration (LADA) or  Light Induced Voltage Alteration (LIVA) [2] and then  image the functional response using LVP at a different  location within the IC. If it were possible to locally activate  or deactivate logic cells within an integrated circuit and  then simultaneously detect LVP signals in other parts of the  circuit, one could potentially develop automated methods to  non-invasively identify design details of circuits when  layout or netlist information is unavailable.


In this paper, we address the above question by  demonstrating a simultaneous dual-laser scanning system  capable of imaging the response of an integrated circuit to  laser-induced changes by directing a pump laser at a feature  of interest while concurrently imaging the localized effects  of the pump laser with a second, scanned probe laser. If the  pump laser is pulsed, we are able to observe motion of the  charge carriers by locking on to the pump laser signal. Similarly, if the device is active, we are able to detect


changes in device function by measuring changes in laser  probed waveforms. In this paper, we describe the  experimental setup used and demonstrate these two  examples. Some discussion of the theory behind each  example is provided throughout.


FIG. 1.  (Color online) The two laser scanning setup. Both  lasers are arranged in confocal modes. The arms are  coupled together using a dichroic beamsplitter and filters  are used in each detector to reject back reflections from the  other laser. Simultaneous laser focusing is achieved via  movable scan lenses.


EXPERIMENTAL SETUP


The setup used for our experiments is shown in FIG 1. For  the pump laser we used a continuous wave (CW) 1064 nm  laser from CrystaLaser. The output of the pump laser was  amplitude modulated (AM) by sending it through an  electro-optic modulator (EOM), which modulated the  polarization from 0-90 degrees, before passing through a  polarized beam splitter (PBS). In this way we could AM the  pump laser from 1-10 MHz. The laser was then raster  scanned +/-3 degrees in vertical and horizontal directions  using a galvanometer based optical scanner (Cambridge  Tech.), and the light scattered from the scanned spot was  recorded as a function of scan angle using a microscope


objective lens (Seiwa, 50x, 0.6 NA) and a pair of 100 mm  focal length scan and tube lenses. A half wave plate (HWP) was used to depolarize some of the light reflected from the  IC for optical detection. The pump laser was coupled to the  probe arm with the reflective surface of a polarizationsensitive dichroic beam splitter (CVI-Melles Griot). The  probe arm was arranged similarly, although the laser was a  1319 nm CW laser from JDSU and no amplitude  modulation was used. The focus of each laser arm was  aligned onto the sample by adjusting the relative positions  of the scan lenses. In this way, chromatically corrected infocus images could be taken simultaneously at both  wavelengths or one laser could be directed to a target  location while the other scanned over the surface to detect  small changes in the device reflectivity. In the tests here we  used a semi-custom device built on a 0.8 micron process, imaging with a 50x air gap lens, which is equivalent to  probing a 160 nm process using state-of-the-art solid  immersion lens (SIL) technology. In both cases the  minimum feature size is smaller than the diffraction limited  spot size.


PUMP-PROBE IMAGING OF CHARGE  MOTION


It is known that device function can modulate the local  reflectivity of the device through free-carrier induced  changes to the real and imaginary part of the index of  refraction [5]. In the FA community this effect has been  used to detect electronic waveforms via Laser Voltage  Probing (LVP) and modulation activity through frequency  mapping (FM) [6]. Microscopically, these voltage signals  are transduced from variations in free carrier density as  they collect and screen the small changes in the electric  field of a field effect transistor.


Similarly, it is possible to observe excess carriers directly  following injection by a pump laser. However, without the  local potential well created by the active transistor gate, these excess laser-injected free carriers move away from  their local injection until recombination occurs. In  crystalline materials this effect has been studied, even on  ultrafast time scales, and it is understood that the electrons  stream out until they scatter from the lattice and decay back  into the valance band [7].


Our experimental setup allowed us to very clearly observe  the laser-generated carriers while simultaneously rejecting  signals from the native device reflectivity. What is  observed depends on the time scale and magnification of  the observation. If the pulse duration of our 1319 nm probe  laser  is much longer than the free carrier recombination  time , the charge motion is temporally unresolved.  FIG. 2 shows a characteristic image taken with a 50x  magnification objective. When the pump laser is off, as in


FIG. 2 – Pump-probe imaging of charge flow. a-left) 50x  probe image at 1 MHz with pump off showing no activity. a-right) pump on showing charge flow over approximately  50 m diameter within the field of view. b) zoomed  reflectivity image vs. charge-flow image. c) close up of poly  gates (dark vertical lines) in reflectivity image (b-left). d) close up magnitude of lock-in signal in blown up area of (c). e) close up color-phase image in blown up area of (c).  FIG. 2 a-left, the image appears dark. When the pump laser  was turned on, as in  FIG. 2 a-right, the image contained a  large, bright spot with detectable charge activity against a  dark background. The diameter of the spot D is given by  twice the product of the charge velocity v and the  recombination time . We measured the diameter of the  charge area to be approximately D=50 microns.


If the recombination time were known precisely, it would  be possible to determine the speed of the carriers in the  device from the magnitude of D. It is difficult to know the  precise recombination time in this CMOS device due to the  varied interfaces and doping in the region of the 1064 nm  pump laser. The transit time of the charge wave is bounded  on the upper side by the minority carrier lifetime in  crystalline materials (1 ms), and bounded on the low side  by the saturated drift velocity (250 ps). It is known also that  carrier lifetimes are strongly related to material doping and  defects [8]. Experimentally, we observed the spot size to  maintain the same shape and intensity for all pump  repetition rates below 10 MHz. Even after temporarily  replacing the EOM and pump laser with a mode-locked  laser with a pump repetition rate of 75 MHz, the spot did


not change diameter, which is consistent with a charge  density wave transit time of less than 10 ns. If we assume a  1 ns lifetime for the charge wave, then it indicates a drift  velocity of close to 50 km/s, which is 50% of the saturated  drift velocity in silicon and is very similar to the results  obtained by other researchers in similar experiments (20-80  km/s) [9]. The physical mechanism of the charge wave is  strongly related to transit time. If the charge wave dynamics  were driven by diffusion then the transit time would be  given by


/


, where D is the diffusion constant. Assuming electron diffusion, D=(kT/e)*u=37 cm2/s and the  transit distance of L= 50 m, implies diffusion time of  170ns. Since we observed no change in the charge-flow  image for the range of pump laser modulation frequencies, we must conclude that the charge density dynamics are a  drift effect. Therefore, local electric fields must play a role  in models of laser-injected charge carrier dynamics.


Once the drift velocity is known, it is possible to estimate  the local electric field strength. The drift field


is the  sum total of the time-dependent electric field created by the  concentration of charge carriers


and the timedependent electric field due to the laser


. These excess  laser-injected free carriers drift away from their local  injection region at a speed given by


, where  is the carrier mobility and E(t) is the time-dependent, local  electric field induced by the excess charge carriers and  laser. Using the approximated value for the drift velocity of  5x106 cm/s and mobility of 1000 cm2/V/s , we estimated the  local electric field causing the drift to be 5x103 V/cm [10]. At higher zoom, we were able to resolve further details in  the integrated circuit. The probe signal was detected at the  pump frequency using an RF lock-in amplifier which  allowed us to record both amplitude (magnitude) and phase  signals. A comparison of the charge flow image shown in   FIG. 2b reveals the surprising result that fine integrated  circuit details are preserved even though the time-scale of  temporal blurring would suggest otherwise. Moreover, the  zoomed charge-flow image in  FIG. 2d contains finer  details than the corresponding reflectivity image in  FIG. 2c. ‘Phase images’ such as the one shown in  FIG. 2e were


created using a red-white color map that color-codes the  phase of the detected charge oscillation with respect to the  pump laser. The red regions of the image display charge  oscillations that are in phase with the pump laser. The white  areas have a phase shift of 180 degree with respect to the  pump laser. The gray scale intensity of the image directly  relates to the magnitude of the detected charge flow. When  the phase image in  FIG. 2e was overlayed with the  standard reflectivity and CAD layout images it became  clear that additional details were the polysilicon gates. In a  standard reflectivity image, the polysilicon appears dark  against a bright n-well. On the contrary, in the phase image  both the n-well and polysilicon are bright and their regions  are distinguished by a phase inversion at the boundary of  the two materials. Phase inversions of this type can result  from conductive materials as their local field reverses to  cancel an external field. Additional phase inversions were  also noted near the heavily doped contacts to both the gates  and the source/drain regions of the transistors. The zero  intensity point at the phase inversion is consistent with  there being no charge flow across the interface of the two  materials.


PUMP-PROBE


IMAGING


WITH


“WAVEFORM SUPPRESSION”


In the second example, we apply the pump laser-injected  free carriers to alter the function of a working device. We  then image the change in activity as a function of pump  laser position and show that the resulting probe waveform  is altered only when the pump laser is directed to a  connected logic cell. In FIG. 3 we summarize this new  method which we call ‘waveform suppression’, whereby  we turn off a logic cell’s output using the pump laser.


In the experiment, we examined two different test regions  of the same test article. First, we decreased the operating  voltage of the device until the device performance was  marginala similar setup to LADA. The VDD level was  decreased until we observed some failures in the output  test vectors and then increased slightly until no errors were  observed. We then navigated to the first test

connected logic cells. (below): ‘Activity image’ of test region 2 showing changing activity of device for different pump laser  locations. Purple arrow indicates where activity has been altered (schematic shows circuit location of pumps and altered  activity)


region shown in the CAD layout in FIG. 3a, which was


known to contain a NAND gate where one input was


connected to the output of the neighboring inverter. In the


reflectivity image in FIG. 3b, it is not possible to observe


the electrical connection between the gates. We then


measured the waveforms shown in FIG. 3c corresponding


to the enumerated pump laser locations in FIG. 3b. Only


when the pump laser was placed on the inverter did we see


full suppression of the probed waveform. This effect is


similar to LADA, only instead of monitoring the pass/fail


state we selectively suppress the output of logic cells


within the device with a 1064 nm laser and observe the


change locally through the LVP signal.


We then navigated to a second region of the same test


article (see the bottom half of FIG. 3) which contained two


NAND gates connected in series. We carried out a similar


experiment, only instead of measuring waveforms at a  single probed point, we collected what we call an ‘activity  map’ for three different locations of the pump laser. These  activity maps, analagous to photoemission images, display  the RF power contained in the probe reflectivity in a  frequency band between 1-100 MHz. In the activity map  images, it is also possible to see the reflectivity of the  inactive sample as a result of laser noise contained in the  frequency band; however, we are interested in bright spots  in the image that correspond to RF power due to device  activity in the RF detection band. Moreover, as shown in  FIG. 3(below), the activity map was found to change as a  function of the pump location. As in the case of the first test  region, only when the pump laser was positioned near the  output of the gate connected to the probe location did the  activity at the probe become suppressed.


CONCLUSIONS


In this paper we introduce pump-probe imaging as a new  approach to integrated circuit analysis. We provided two  examples of how the setup can be used to extract new and  pertinent information from both passive and active  integrated circuits. In the first example, we show that it is  possible to increase the resolution of reflectivity images by  phase-resolving the response of the probe laser. Where  charge density changes are essentially zero, the probed  images are dark. Where they are bright, there is strong  charge density oscillation at the pump laser frequency. We  observed dark nodes in the charge density oscillations at the  boundary between poly gates and doped wells which  suggests that highly conductive materials may introduce  image charges that counters the drift energy of free  electrons. We also observed the pump laser energy to  spread out beyond the nodes in the charge density  oscillations which suggests near-field coupling may be  responsible for the long-range transport of energy within  the IC and methods similar to those described here may be  useful to better understand the local capacitance of  integrated circuits. The magnitudes and phases of the local  index changes are directly related to the local potential  environment of the free carriers and the size of the charge  density fluctuation region was used to extract the local  electric field experienced by the charge in the laser. It is  clear from the data that local field effects models are  necessary to fully explain the dynamics of photo-generated  free carriers within the device. In the second example, we  used the same free carrier injection method to alter  functionality of logic cells. The physical mechanism for  logic cell suppression appears to be related to the local  electric fields created by the freely moving charges. The  magnitude of the local estimated field in the neighborhood  of the charge density wave (5x103 V/cm) is 20% of the  magnitude of the local field created by the transistors  during operation (2.5x104 V/cm). When the charge wave  interacts with a marginally operating logic cell, it is enough  to critically alter the local transistor bias so that it no longer  functions. We then applied the ability to control the logic  cell function to non-invasively detect electrical connections  between logic cells. Using this or similar approaches it  could be possible to reverse engineer a design without the  need to destroy the sample.


There may be other useful pump-probe imaging setups. In  the discussion here we focused on the steady state effect of  charge injection by the pump laser. However, it is also  possible to develop an ultrafast pump-probe setup, which  would enable the ability to record the transient response of  a LADA or LIVA test. In that case, it may be possible to  infer process-related details, such as wire impedance or the  delay between two points on a chip, by recording the  temporal response of a waveform suppression  measurement.

Two-Photon-Absorption-Enhanced Laser-Assisted Device Alteration  and Single-Event Upsets in 28nm Silicon Integrated Circuits


K. A. Serrels, N. Leslie, T. R. Lundquist and P. Vedagarbha


DCG Systems Inc.


45900 Northport Loop East, Fremont, California 94538, USA

K. Erington and D. Bodoh


Freescale Semiconductor


6501 West William Cannon Drive, Austin, TX 78735
