Table 1. Characteristics of common analytical techniques.


Identification of failing electrical behavior


during Electrical Test and Characterization (test), may


pinpoint a greatly reduced area within the chip where a defect  can exist. For example, a single cell fail in memory indicates a  very small fraction of chip area. However, in other cases, large  fractions of chip area must be analyzed due to the large size of  nets or the lack of electrical access to internal circuit nodes.


Power supplies, for example, can span the entire chip area.


Integrated circuits that are Designed For Test may greatly


reduce the pinpointed area in some cases, but in many cases


further analysis must still begin at the chip scale, even after


further diagnostics. Thus the localization provided by test


varies greatly depending on the class of defect and the circuit  design.


As scaling continues and device complexity  increases, visually finding smaller defects in larger circuits


with PFA techniques has become increasingly difficult and


often impossible for several reasons. The spatial resolution of  many PFA techniques has not kept pace with scaling, so many  defect classes that were once visible are now invisible.


Finding the fails that are still visible also takes longer and


costs more, because of increased chip area and device count. Optical Inspection Microscopy and Scanning Electron


Microscopy (SEM) are surface techniques, so planar


preparation of samples prior to localization has also become


more challenging. Focused Ion Beam tools used for for sitespecific cross sectioning now incorporate an SEM to improve  the resolution (Dual Beam). Thus, all of these factors


contribute to longer turn-around-time, higher cost, and higher  No Defect Found rates for PFA localization.


Electrical signatures of defects, on the other  hand, have remained measurable in spite of scaling and


increased device complexity, since their existence triggers


analysis in the first place. Thus, EFA techniques have become  the critical path that analysts increasingly rely on, because


EFA follows failing electrical behavior from the chip scale to  the defect scale. For leading edge process technologies, PFA  results of all but the grossest defect are only successful if EFA  has identified the actual cause and precise location of the


defect prior to PFA data generation and analysis.


The capability to access every node in a


circuit must be maintained for EFA to be successful. There are  three types of electrical nodes in modern integrated circuits:


external, microscale internal, and nanoscale internal. External  circuit nodes, including the power supply, input and output


channels, are designed for external electrical connection


during testing and product use. A probe card or socket is used  to connect to the external circuit nodes, at the wafer or module  level, respectively. The number of external circuit nodes is


roughly a thousand, when the total number of circuit nodes is  near a billion.


In the twentieth century, every internal node   in a circuit was microscale and could therefore be accessed


with microprobers. However, with current leading edge


process technologies, only upper level metal interconnect


layers are microscale. At present, the number of microscale


internal circuit nodes is roughly a million, when the total


number of circuit nodes is near a billion. Microprobing's lack  of access to lower level metal interconnects severely limits an  analysts ability to control or measure voltages and currents


deep in the design, thereby limiting the range of defects that


are detectable. For this reason Nanoprobers were developed


more than a decade ago to maintain non-destructive electrical  access to every node in a circuit, including Nanoscale internal  circuit nodes. It is well known that Focused Ion Beam (FIB)


Wiring is damaging to sensitive front end structures.  FIB


Wiring local circuits to pads and then contacting the pads by


Microprobing is destructive, complex, and costly, and thus


rarely used in EFA.


In Scanning Probe Microscopy (SPM)


measurements, a probe is scanned over a small field of view


containing several transistors, while measurements with the


probe are conducted. Atomic Force Microscopy is the most


commonly used type of SPM in analysis, and achieves the


highest spatial resolutions, which are necessary for


measurements on leading edge process technologies.


Typically, Scanning Probe Imaging techniques such as


Scanning Capacitance and Scanning Conductance, localize


defects to a single transistor or interconnect, and then the the  probes are held in place (Nanoprobing), while the defect is


electrically characterized.


In Optical Electrical Microscopy (OEM)


measurements, both photons and electrons interact with a


circuit to localize defects. OEM techniques include optical


absorption, emission, and scattering techniques, such as Laser  Stimulation, PICA, and Optical Probing, respectively.[1-3] For  emission measurements with a camera, the entire optical


image is acquired simultaneously, in a massively parallel


nature. For absorption measurements with a scanning optical  microscope, the optical image is acquired sequentially, in a


serial nature. OEM is a core EFA capability used to localize


defects over five orders of magnitude in each lateral direction, thereby moving from the chip scale to the device scale.


However, the spatial resolution of OEM is currently limited by  the diffraction of light.[4-6] In most cases at least several


transistors along a particular circuit node or within a


diffraction-limited spot are identified as possible locations for  a defect.


Common sequences of techniques in EFA


are illustrated in Figure 1. In some cases, such as a single cell  fail in memory, information from test, targets a small enough  area that SPM is sufficient to capture the fail in its field of


view, so the resulting sequence is test > SPM > TEM. In other  cases, test yields non-local failing electrical signatures, so


OEM is used to bridge from the chip scale to the device scale, so the resulting sequence is test > OEM > SPM > TEM. In


some cases, FIB Wiring of local circuits is currently necessary  to gain better electrical access for OEM, so the resulting


sequence is test > FIB Wiring > OEM > SPM > TEM. The


EFA process has a serial nature, so barriers encountered in a  sequence may often lead to analytical failure with No Defect  Found.


Figure 1. Common EFA work-flow with current tooling.


Though they will not be examined in this


work, another important set of EFA techniques employs beams  of high energy particles that interact electrically with an


integrated circuit, such as in voltage contrast and specimen


absorbed current. Acceleration voltages of the high energy


particle beam typically range from hundreds of volts to tens of  kilovolts for electrons in a SEM or ions in a FIB.


Figure 2 illustrates the incomplete coverage  of current EFA techniques in the range of defects that may be  easily found. Thus, random sampling with high resolution


techniques, such as Nanoprobing or TEM is often the only


way of finding a defect. The cost and time associated with this  lack of capability is often ignored, and thus allocation of funds  for equipment and new technique development are limited.


Unless this trend in resourcing is reversed, the cost to find a


fail will continue to increase, with No Defect Found rates.


Figure 2. Incomplete coverage of defect space by current EFA.


The essential EFA capability of electrical


access to every node in a circuit has been maintained by the  introduction and continuous improvement in Nanoprobing


techniques for more than a decade. However, systems with


OEM capabilities were never equipped with SPM and


Nanoprobing capabilities, so the fraction of circuit nodes


accessible during OEM measurements has continued to


plummet. In this work, new concepts in equipment and


measurement techniques that integrate OEM and SPM


capabilities in a single tool will be described under the


umbrella of Optical Nanoprobe Electrical (ONE) Microscopy. Table 2 shows the level of optical and electrical access to the  integrated circuit available with current and future


technologies. ONE microscopy provides full electrical access  to a circuit, while also providing full optical access, in a nondestructive manner both electrically and physically.


Electrical


Optical


Standard Probing


1,000 pads &


1,000,000 upper level  metal interconnects


Nanoprobing


1,000,000,000  transistors and all  metal interconnects


No Optical  Channels


Scanning Probe  Microscopy


Diffraction  Limited


1,000,000,000  pixels


Optical Electrical  Microscopy


Optical  Nanoprobe  Electrical  Microscopy


Table 2. Optical and Electrical Access to Integrated Circuits.


As formerly illustrated in Figure 2, ONE


Microscopy techniques can be broadly divided into two


modes, depending on how the image is formed. In Scanning  Probe mode, an optical or electrical probe is scanned to form  the image. In Optical Imaging mode, conventional OEM


techniques are used to generate the image, while the


Nanoprober electrically accesses the circuit.


Optical Imaging ONE microscopy permits  non-destructive measurement capability, that was lost more


than a decade ago, when the early metal levels became


electrically inaccessible to Microprobers. Examples include


probing a local bit line in memory or a local signal net in


logic, while collecting optical electrical images. Reconfirming  previous OEM measurements at the local level by Optical


Imaging ONE microscopy in the SPM tool environment also  significantly increases confidence and avoids costly errors in  analysis. Similarly, reconfirmation of electrical test results is  always the first step in OEM localization, and regularly


catches artifacts and errors in the test and OEM equipment.


Optically Imaging ONE microscopy can also  significantly improve the accuracy of defect localization prior  to Nanoprobing. The spatial resolution of OEM is currently


limited by the diffraction of light. However, the defect density  in analyzed circuits is typically low, so features in optical


electrical images tend to be sparse, with a single diffraction


limited hot spot in the entire field of view. On the other hand, the layout of modern integrated circuits, by design, is certainly  not sparse, so reflected light images tend to be very dense in


features. The sparse nature of optical electrical images would  make super-resolution techniques attractive, if the optical


electrical images also had sparse design features that could be  directly correlated to the circuit layout. Unfortunately, the


optical electrical images usually have no design features, so


reflected light images taken with the same optical microscope  are used to correlate to the circuit layout, as illustrated in


Figure 3 in green. This indirect approach is necessary, but


leads to a second error in defect localization that can't be


easily overcome with super-resolution techniques. For this


reason, localization at leading edge technology manufacturers  now relies heavily on the use of solid immersion microscopy  with annular stops.[6] Annular stops provide better


localization by improving the longitudinal resolution and


thereby significantly decreasing the density of features in


reflected light images.


Optical electrical images can be registered to  a high-resolution SPM topography image, instead of a lowerresolution reflected light image, as illustrated in Figure 3 in


blue. Thus, an accuracy well beyond the diffraction-limited


resolution of the optical microscope is generated when using  properly aligned and calibrated Optically Imaging ONE


microscopy with super-resolution techniques.


Figure 3. Super-resolution Optical Imaging ONE microscopy.


In Scanning Probe ONE Microscopy, the


SPM provides the acquired images. For electrical probe


scanning, the image may be formed either by applying an


optical input and measuring an electrical probe output while


scanning or by applying an electrical probe input while


scanning and measuring an optical output. For example,


carriers produced by optical absorption in semiconductor


junctions can be measured during scanning probe current


imaging. Another example, would be collecting optical


emission from the backside of the chip while scanning with a  probe at constant voltage. For optical probe scanning, the


probe enhancement of the optical field by a factor of one


thousand in the confined region at the tip can provide spatial


resolution well beyond the diffraction limit.[7] Scanning Probe  ONE Microscopy measurements provide the range of defects  available to OEM techniques at a spatial resolution defined by  SPM.


Figure 4. Optical Nanoprobe Electrical (ONE) Microscope.


The  prototype  ONE  microscope  shown  in  Figure 4 was built to collect optical emission while electrically  nanoprobing integrated circuits. Nanoprobing with a Scanning  Probe Microscope requires  tight  control  of  temperature  and  vibration.  The  thermal  instability  and  vibration  levels  associated with the microprobe stations found in most OEM  tools  are  far  too  high  for  high-resolution  SPM.  Standard  mechanical functions such as switching mirrors and changing  objectives also introduce too much vibration for SPM. In ONE  microscopy, though, a single objective may be used since only  high-resolution  and  magnification  are  required  at  the  local  circuit  level.  Designing  an  Optical  Microscope  around  the  SPM  requirements  thus  proved  to  be  the  simplest  path  to  systems  integration.  High  resolution  Scanning  Probe  Microscopes  use  active  Vibration  Isolation  between  the  microscope  Platform and  floor  mounted  Base.  The  Sample  Stage, SPM heads, and infrared Optical Microscope were all  mounted  on  the  Platform.  However,  the  640x512  InGaAs  Camera was mounted to the Base because it was both a source  of vibration and temperature variation via thermal conduction. The Camera remained detached from the rest of the Optical


Microscope, but optical quality remained ideal because of the  large diffraction-limited spot size and depth of  focus of  the  image after the tube lens. Dividing the microscope into two  was therefore necessary to maintain SPM performance while  using standard OEM equipment.


ONE Microscopy was first conducted on


integrated circuits manufactured in a leading edge process


technology to demonstrate the most challenging application,


with obvious extension to older technologies. Figure 5 shows  emission measurements from an SOI integrated circuit at


contact level, with electrical excitation of a single NFET


transistor in a scan latch by nanoprobing. The SPM


Topography image of a three by three micrometer field of


view in Figure 5(a) demonstrates a typical five nanometer


resolution. Green probes and a blue bar indicate the redundant  gate, source, and drain contacts in Figure 5(a) that were


electrically excited to yield the optical emission image from


the same field of view, shown in Figure 5(b). Diffraction


limited spatial resolution of one micrometer was obtained with  the Mitutoyo M PLAN NIR 50X HR objective (0.65 NA).


Figure 5. (a) SPM Topography image and (b) Optical


Emission Image of integrated circuit at contact level.


Figure 6 shows emission measurements from  an SOI integrated circuit at the first metal level, with electrical   excitation of two different NFET transistors in the periphery  of  SRAM by nanoprobing.  The  two blue  bars  in  the  SPM  Topography image in Figure 6(a) represent the positions of the  two transistors separated by 1.6 micrometers. Emission images  from exciting the left and right transistors are shown in Figure  6(b) and 6(c), respectively.


Figure 6. (a) SPM Topography image of integrated circuit at first metal level with two nanoprobed transistors marked with blue bars. Optical Emission Image of (b) left and (c) right transistor.


To the  best  of  our  knowledge,  we  believe  this  is  the  first  experimental  demonstration  of  ONE  microscopy on integrated circuits. The capability to access any  electrical node in modern integrated circuits while acquiring  Optical Electrical images has been recovered, after more than  a decade in the dark. Current SPM Imaging techniques do not  have sensitivity to many types of defects, and Nanoprobing all  of  the  transistors  in  an  area  pinpointed  by  OEM  is  often  impractical. Thus, in many cases, ONE microscopy capability  will permit analytical success instead of failure.

Device Characterization using AFP Nanoprobing for the Localization of   New product Design Weakness


Ang Ghim Boon, Quah Alfred, Chen Changqing, Zhao Si Ping, NAGALINGAM Dayanand, Li Yan, Neo Soh Ping, Shailesh Redkar  Failure Analysis, Quality and Customer Enablement (QCE) department,


GLOBALFOUNDRIES Singapore Pte Ltd


Email Address: anggb@globalfoundries.com


This paper illustrated the beauty of AFP nano-probing as the  critical failure analysis tool in localizing new product design  weakness. A 40nm case of HTOL Pin Leakage due to  Source/Drain punch-through at a systematic location was  discussed. The root cause and mechanism was due to VDS  overdrive testing issue. This paper placed a strong emphasis  on systematic problem solving approach, deep dive and use of  right FA approach/tool that are essentially critical to FA  analysts in wafer foundry since there is always minimal  available data provided. It would serve as a good reference to  wafer Fab that encountered such issue


In wafer Fabrication, a quick root cause identification and  process fix particularly on the new product design weakness in  advanced tech node is essential to ensure 1st silicon success  and quick time to market. However, as semiconductor  technology approaches advanced nano technology together  with increasing complexity of integrated circuits, the number  non-visual defects related to design weakness has increased  and the success of finding these defects are slim with  traditional failure analysis flow of curve tracing, electrical  fault localization and PFA [1][2]. It is even more challenging  particularly in wafer foundry industry where foundry FA  engineers are required to work on limited information and test  support.


For new product design weakness related to front end issues, generally, electrical characterizations on prime die transistors  using nano-probing has played a critical role in the  localization of these design issues [3]. In this paper, a case of  such design issue engaging Atomic Force Probing (AFP) by  using Multiprobe MPIIB system is discussed.  The AFP  includes both the current imaging mode as well as nanoprobing mode for electrical characterization of the family of IV curves for probed transistors. It has been proved to be very  useful as compared to the traditional Passive Voltage Contrast (PVC) technique. With enhanced sensitivity, the MPIIB  system is capable of scanning at smaller tip landing force. This  allows for nanoprobing device analysis at Cu level without


smearing using slower scan speed. This was critical for  probing at Cu Via in this discussed case.


A new product was reported suffering from HTOL Pin leakage  failures in wafer fabrication with majority of units having  leakage levels of <20uA as compared to good unit of ~1uA. IV curve tracing was first performed to verify the reported  failure. As shown in Figure 1, leakage of few uA was  observed on the bad analyzed units.


Figure 1: IV curve tracing showing leakage in uA on the  HTOL failed units


Figure 2: Electrical Fault Localization revealed repeatable spot  on a particular block on these failed HTOL units


Upon electrical verification, electrical fault localization by  EMMI was then conducted. Upon analyzing of few bad units, it was observed that all bad units showed a repeatable spot on  a particular location. There was no such repeatable spot seen  on good units (Figure 2)


Based on the EFA results, there are 2 obvious questions from  the analysts namely:


• Is there a systematic defect connected to the failed pin?


• Is this a defect mainly from front end since low level  leakage was seen?


Upon all metal layers removal, PVC analysis was performed  on contact layers of the suspected transistors in the emission  spot site. However, there was no obvious contrast. Thereafter, another effective FA approach is to perform AFP current  imaging and nano-probing on contact layers to check for any  obvious anomaly. Instead of observing leakage as expected, surprising, there was no leakage seen. As shown in Figure 3, the Ioff was in pA range from the Id-Vg curves.


Figure 3: PVC, AFP current imaging and nano-probing  showed no obvious leakage at the suspected transistors at the  emission spot site


This AFP nano-probing result immediately brought a new  insight into the analysis.


 Is the emission spot genuine?


 If the emission spot is genuine, could the defect be related  to backend issue since no obvious leakage seen at contact  layer?


 Was the leakage triggered/ induced?


Figure 4: Schematic layout of the suspected block labeled A2  that showed repeatable emission spot for all failed HTOL  units.


To understand whether if the emission spot is genuine, a  understanding of the circuitry of the emission spot is required. Based on the provided schematic layout of the suspected block  labeled A2 that showed repeatable emission spot for all failed  HTOL units in Figure 4, a cut is required to disconnect all  other circuitry connected to A2 block. The exact location of  the cut is shown in Figure 4.


Figure 5: FIB circuit edit was engaged to disconnect A2 from  other circuitry for further probing and electrical fault  localization.


With careful study of the GDS layout of the suspected block  A2, FIB Circuit Edit was engaged to disconnect the suspected  block A2 from other circuitry as shown in the Figure 5.  Subsequent probing on the Circuit edit pads showed that the  leakage remained dominant at A2 block with emission spot  remained identical to that prior to the FIB circuit edit (Figure  6)


Cut


Figure 6: Subsequent probing on the Circuit edit pads showed  that the leakage remained dominant at A2 block with emission  spot remained identical to that prior to the FIB circuit edit


Figure 7: Overview of the A2 block showing that transistors  nodes (S/D/G) are not isolated


Upon confirming the emission spot at A2 is genuine, AFP  nano-probing was again engaged in the analysis in order to  allow us to identify the source of the leakage How was this  analysis done? Instead of the typical application of AFP on W


contact layer, it was used in Via Cu layer. As shown in Figure  7, device probing and analysis was challenging as transistors  nodes (S/D/G) are not isolated. The A2 block that shown  emission spot was actually consists of left PMOS and Right  PMOS transistors labeled in Figure 7. At metal2, the drain of  both PMOS was connected together while the gate of the left  PMOS was connected to the source of the right PMOS


AFP nanoprobing was first conducted at Metal2 layer. It  showed that there is Source-Drain leakage seen at the right  PMOS. Concurrently, on the left PMOS, gate to drain leakage  and gate to source leakage was seen. Thereafter, metal2 layer  was removed and AFP nanoprobing was then conducted on  Metal1 layer. For the right PMOS, source to drain leakage  continued to be seen. However, for the left PMOS, there was  no gate to drain or gate to source leakage seen. As mentioned  earlier, at Metal2, the gate of the left PMOS was connected to  the source of the right PMOS. Thus, source drain  punchthrough leakage on the right PMOS will result in the  gate to source or gate to drain leakage seen on the left PMOS. Upon, probing at contact layer, the leakage was gone. This  observation is similar to the earlier analysis (Table 1).


Table 1: Device characterization at Metal 2, Metal 1 and  contact using AFP Nanoprobing


Failure Mechanism


Based on the FA finding from the AFP nanoprobing, several  questions evolved namely:


 Why is Leakage disappeared at CA?


 Why leakage only existed when probing at Metal layers?  Is there any weakness on the good unit?


In order to have a better understanding of the failure  mechanism, other analysis were engaged and showed the  following:


 Top down PFA and XTEM at BEOL weakest point check  showed no anomaly.  Metal 1 pitch not at minimum  design rule  Not Process related.


 Good units: Can also be easily stressed to suffer pin  leakage with same EMMI spot as bad units   Marginal  good units  Further indicated overall routing or testing  induced failure

At this stage of analysis, the AFP nanoprobing has clearly  provided a strong indication that it was SD leakage on PMOS  on those HTOL failing units. It existed at Metal2 and Metal1  but disappeared at Contact. Good units also showed similar  leakage once stressed. There was a high suspect that there  could have been a testing issue.


With all these strong supporting data from AFP nanoprobing, a request was made to the customer on the availability of more  detailed schematic diagram (besides the initial version  provided).  This request was made earlier during the start  of analysis but was rejected.


Upon receiving the detailed schematic diagram, it was  immediately confirmed the earlier suspect and hypothesis  is true. The HTOL pin leakage due to VDS overdrive causing  SD punch-through across the IO PMOS. For PFA sample  preparation, since it was treated with RIE for dielectric  removal, the UV could result in punch-through leakage  recovery.


A simulation was conducted by having the transistor stressed  with 4-5V VDS. It showed a significant increase in Ioff  leakage. This verified that the PMOS could not withstand 4-5V HTOL stress condition. Besides that, by baking the  leakage units for 1 to 4 days, it was observed that the leakage  has partially or fully recovered after bake (Figure 8). This  further verified the recovery hypothesis.


Figure 8: Significant increase in Ioff leakage after stress. Leakage partially/fully recovered after bake.


A case of device characterization using AFP Nanoprobing for  the localization of new product design weakness was  discussed in this paper. It clearly illustrated the importance of  AFP nano-probing as the critical failure analysis tool in  resolving this HTOL pin leakage issue in prime die level. It  had enabled the analyst to confirm the cause of the HTOL  leakage was caused by a Source/Drain punch-through at a  systematic location. Subsequent investigation confirmed it was  due to VDS overdrive issue. This paper also placed a strong  emphasis on the right FA approach /tool that are essentially  critical to FA analysts in wafer foundry since there is always  minimal available data provided. It would serve as a good  reference to wafer Fab that encountered such issue

SEM-based nanoprobing on 40, 32 and 28nm CMOS devices  Challenges for Semiconductor Failure Analysis


Erik Paul*, Holger Herzog, Sören Jansen, Christian Hobert and Eckhard Langer


GLOBALFOUNDRIES Dresden Module One Limited Liability Company & Co. KG  Wilschdorfer Landstraße 101, 01109 Dresden, Germany


* Erik.Paul@globalfoundries.com, Phone: +49-351-277-4203


This paper presents an effective device-level failure analysis (FA) method which uses a high-resolution low-kV Scanning  Electron Microscope (SEM) in combination with an integrated  state-of-the-art nanomanipulator to locate and characterize  single defects in failing CMOS devices. The presented case  studies utilize several FA-techniques in combination with  SEM-based nanoprobing for nanometer node technologies and  demonstrate how these methods are used to investigate the  root cause of IC device failures. The methodology represents a  highly-efficient physical failure analysis flow for 28nm and  larger technology nodes.


Semiconductor IC products have to withstand external  influences like electrical, thermal and mechanical stress during  their lifetime. The quality and lifetime of those products  strongly depends on the performance and reliability of their  individual components, like single transistors.


In case of field returns, root cause analysis needs to focus on  the entire product but in some cases, the failure needs to get  traced back to single transistors. Therefore the electrical  behavior of single CMOS transistors by SEM-based  nanoprobing belongs to the portfolio of methods required by  modern PFA laboratories.


This paper contains three case studies using the common  Failure analysis methods Optical Beam Induced Resistivity  Change (OBIRCH) and Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in combination with the nanoprobing technique. These  studies will show the efficiency of this failure analysis method  to investigate the root-cause of failing IC devices. Electrical  failures, which lead to yield drop in Semiconductor Fabs, can  be located effectively by SEM-based nanoprobing.


The first case study in this paper presents the verification of an  OBIRCH-finding within a 40nm node nFET-test array. The  second case study is an investigation of pFET degradation of a  32nm device due to high-temperature stress. In the final case  study, high-resistive behavior within a 6T-cell was analyzed  for a 28nm CMOS device.


Case studies


1)  Verification of OBIRCH finding (40nm)


Significant nFET junction leakage was observed within  several 40nm node test arrays (approximately 6000 nFET  transistors). The OBIRCH technique was applied and  narrowed down the failure location to an area which included  4 transistors.


Figure 1 (a) illustrates the OBIRCH spot from wafer backside (left) and an overlay of an OBIRCH image and a CAMELOT  GDS sketch (right). During OBRICH the surface of device  backside was scanned by using an infrared (IR) laser.


The number of transistors which had to be analyzed was  minimized significantly due to the high sensitivity of the laser  to detect changes in resistance values as shown in Figure 1 (b).


Figure 1. (a) OBIRCH image from wafer backside (left) and  overlay of an OBIRCH image and a CAMELOT GDS sketch;


(b) Precise nFET fail location


The previously identified fail location within the affected test  array was extracted as a planar FIB-lamella and analyzed in a  TEM. That analysis did not show any obvious root cause for  the leakage behavior. Figure 2 illustrates a high resolution  planar TEM image of affected 40nm nFET devices.


Figure 2. High resolution planar TEM image of affected NMOS devices.


To determine exactly the root cause for the OBIRCH spot a  further SEM-based nanoprobing analysis was done to  investigate the conspicuous nFET transistors. Figure 3 shows  an SEM image of fail location after top-down polish to contact  level with tungsten probe tips.


Four single nanoprobe tips were landed on mentioned  transistors by contacting gate-source-drain region including  bulk contact at 0.5kV SEM acceleration voltage.


Figure 3. SEM image of 40nm bulk Si devices with tungsten  probe tips.


Figure 4. I-V characteristics of 40nm devices within OBIRCH  fail location.


The electrical characterization of the conspicuous nFET  devices was carried out by sweeping the gate from 0 to 1V in  forward (FWD) and backward (BWD) mode to clarify the fail  mechanism. Figure 4 shows drain current properties of the  nFET transistors within OBIRCH fail spot. The ID-VG curves  of nFET device no. 3 showed a significant electrical offset  with a leakage current of ∆ID~20µA comparing to neighboring  transistors.


Possible Missing Pocket (Halo) Dopant


Because the pocket implantation is coupled with LDD  implantation, the defect root cause may block pocket implant  process besides LDD implant. Therefore, the possible missing  pocket doping around S/D regions would be considered for  current increasing from punch-through mechanism. Regarding  the competition between higher channel resistance and more  punch-through current, we use the TCAD to simulate the  current. In general, the current should be dominant by missing  LDD above 40nm process. However, as seen in figure 5, missing pocket doping could be more significant than missing  LDD doping beyond 40nm products. Thus, the signature 1 of  missing LDD, low channel current, could be violated at the  conditions of missing LDD/Pocket dopant at the advanced  technologies with much smaller critical dimension of channel  length. Therefore, the supposed output of the first condition is  not necessary for all missing LDD. Nevertheless, the high  channel resistance still is satisfied in the unique conditions but  not measureable in the current value.


Fig.5 TCAD Simulation to the missing LDD/Pocket  implantation for 40nm NMOS


Combining the possible issues of missing LDD/Pocket dopant, the measured current at the drain could be written as equation (4,5) below, a variation of equation (1,2):


δ Id=δ Idrift,s+δ Ipunth,s+δIleak,b                                  ---- (4) δ Is=δ Idrift,d+δ Ipunth,d                                                     ---- (5)


Strategy of post-Nanoprobing


How to proceed in the following analysis with the sufficient  Nanoprobing data and analysis based on the postulates? Simulation is the first way to be suggested with the advantage  of fast result and low cost. Missing Pocket dopant has been  demonstrated in this content and in referenced papers [2,7]. We  all select TCAD to enhance the FA capability. Table II shows  an example for the properties of missing pocket. In this  simulation, the one-side missing pocket dopant would exhibit  asymmetric current of Source/Drain biasing like missing LDD. Regarding PFA, we need more aggressive investment to reach  to the outstanding level of capable microscopy or spectroscopy  for the tiny structure or doping issues, such as pocket dopant  inspection.


Table-II: TCAD simulation reveals missing S/D Pocket alone  in one side would exhibit asymmetrical property. Biasing the  missing side exhibits smaller current than the other one.


In the example of missing LDD, owing to the very small  dimension of missing LDD, using chemical wet stain to prepare  sample for SEM/TEM inspection is the standard way of PFA. It  has been successful applied for real cases, see figure 6 and  other papers [5,6], and should become mature Labs for the fast  analysis of N-type doping. Nonetheless, the reference [6] demonstrated an effective way to delineate P+/PLDD profile  but the exhibition is not significant as N+/NLDD profile. However, the chemical stain/S-TEM is a destructive way and  ineffective for quantitative analysis, or moreover non-available  for the original dopant profiling.    Considering advanced  spectroscopy, the EDS/EELS in STEM can well detect NLDD [8,9] profile with acceptable sensitivity in the modern  instruments. However, the techniques are not likely available  for Boron (P-type dopant) until now due to the too low  sensitivity for light element in EDS [10] and severe signal


interference in the EELS [11]. Besides, the SCM/SEM  techniques of dopant profiling are not well capable for the  LDD missing due to the too small CD. Besides, the modern  Holography in TEM [12] and Atom Probing Tomography (APT) [13] should be capable for the N/PLDD inspection and  more in-depth investigation for other dopant profiling. However, TEM-Holography needs dedicated TEM and  knowledgeable and skillful Analyzer for the application and  APT is not common in the analytical lab due to ultra-high cost  and complication.


Fig.6 TEM imaging is easy to inspect the missing NLDD for  the sample with proper preparation using chemical stain.


The first postulate claims the limitation of highly manual  operation. The second postulate proposes the existence of  completed measurement. The third postulate tries to link the  electrical signatures to physical characteristics. Based on the  power of detailed interpretation of the unique characteristics of  a full collection of measurement data, it can be valuable for the  Nanoprobing analysis. Due to highly challenge of PFA, the  exact conclusion from Nanoprobing to missing LDD or other  physical defects become useful and valuable for the FA  methodology.


For the strategy of post-Nanoprobing analysis, there are two  approaches suggested. First is simulation. The assistance from  TCAD may become useful due to the fast output and low cost. The example of missing pocket has been demonstrated. However, is the resource of TACD able to be available for FA  purpose because of the possible heavy loading of Technology  Development? So, how to achieve the method? The second is  PFA for the end-point of debug. However, the analysis for the  doping profile and gate oxide loop are highly challenged. The


modern TEM [14] and the latest SPM & APT would become  essential in the deeply subtle PFA.


I believe the analyzers can find the unique characteristics for  missing Source/Drain (N+/P+) with the same idea as missing  LDD. Furthermore, we can push the methodology to the other  physical abnormal features, e.g. Gate loop, channel doping or  others. When the FA community can prove the unique postulate  as fundamental principle and achieves the common knowledge  database, Nanoprobing techniques will step up the contribution  for the advancing technology development not only failure  analysis.


The affected n-channel transistor was coated with e-Beam  Platinum and a lamella was prepared for further TEM  investigations. That FIB cross section was analyzed by using a  tilted “two-beam” condition. A dislocation under the channel  of failing nFET transistor was found as shown in Figure 5.


Figure 5. Dislocation defect under the channel of affected  nFET device no 3.


The combination of several physical failure analysis (PFA) methods and SEM-based nanoprobing clearly identified the  transistor weakness caused by a lattice defect due to a specific  implant process. That information was transferred to the Fab  for process modification.


2)  Investigation of pFET degradation (32nm)


A 32nm node pFET transistor suffered from degradation due  to poly line thinning effect which was detected during inline  defect control. Several lots during production process showed  this phenomenon.


Figure 6 illustrates the poly line thinning phenomenon within  pFET device detected via inline inspection (left) and layout of  device schematic (right).


Figure 6. SEM image showing poly line thinning within pFET  device (left); CAMELOT schematics (right)


In order to determine whether the thinning of poly lines of  pFET devices could lead to degradation within the transistor  an electrical investigation under elevated temperature was  performed.


Therefore, after final polish to contact level the device was  mounted on a thermal stage to ensure homogeneous  temperature distribution on device surface during  nanoprobing.


The affected pFET transistor was operated with a gate voltage (VG) of 1.25V and constant temperature of T=125°C (257°F). The nanoprobe needles stayed on the tungsten contacts for a  time (t) of 380 seconds before losing electrical contact.

The process parameters for this production step were modified  when the explicit results of the SEM-based nanoprobing  analysis were forwarded to the responsible Production  Engineer. This invaluable method of physical failure analysis  in combination with high-temperature nanoprobing helped to  significantly reduce the feedback-time to the production  engineers.


3) Bit cell nanoprobing - high-resistive 6Tcell (28 nm)


During reliability testing of a fully assembled 28nm device, the final test result showed a single bit cell (6T-cell) which  failed during the high temperature operating life test (HTOL). This single bit (SB) showed a high-resistive behavior during  the mentioned burn-in test, as well as, under electrical stress of  high-voltage (VHIGH=1.25V). Figure 9 shows high resolution  SEM image of the affected SB-fail after final polish to contact  level and CAMELOT schematics of that cell which consists of  4 nFET and 2 pFET transistors.


Figure 9. SEM image showing poly line thinning within pFET  device (left); CAMELOT schematics (right)


SEM based nanoprobing was used to characterize the  complete failing 6T-cell. The investigation shows no fail issue  regarding the nFET transistors (pull-down and pass-gate). As  illustrated in Figure 10 the right pFET pull-up device (PU) within failing SB shows a significantly lower current flow in  combination with leakage behavior (red curve) in FWD-mode  while sweeping the gate from 0 to -1V.


Both pFET transistors were electrically analyzed in  FWD=Drain (CAREC) and BWD=Source (CA) direction  regarding drain voltage of VD=-1V.


Figure 10. I-V characteristics of pFET pull-up device within  failing 6T-cell (logarithmic scaling).


Figure 11. p/n junction characteristic (diode test) of   pFET PU devices.


An additional electrical test was performed to verify the  leakage current regarding the right pFET PU device (red  curve) shown in Figure 10. Therefore the p/n-junction (diode  test) of each source/drain contact (CA/CAREC) within both  pFET PU transistors was investigated by sweeping  source/drain contact from -1V to +1V while keeping gate, bulk and source or drain fixed on 0V.


The analysis showed a high-resistive behavior regarding  CAREC contact of pFET PU (right) which is shown in Figure


11. This nanoprobing methodology confirms clearly the  assumed high-resistive properties of affected pMOS 6T-cell. The leaky p-channel transistor especially the source-drain-area  was prepared via lamella lift-out for further TEMinvestigations including energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to analyze the fail mechanism in combination with  material analytics.


Figure 12. TEM cross section incl. EDX of affected CAREC  contact in comparison to reference.


Figure 12 clearly illustrates the affected contact (CAREC) with missing silicide at contact bottom as physical root cause  for high-resistive contact within failing single bit.


This method of physical failure analysis to investigate a highresistive 6T-cell via nanoprobing was also verified  successfully on a low-voltage single-cell fail. As shown in  Figure 13 the physical root cause was a nickel (Ni)-protrusion  in combination with thin nickel silicide under the contacts.


Figure 13. Ni-protrusion shown in TEM cross section incl. EDX-mapping.


In this paper three case studies were shown for 40, 32 and  28nm CMOS devices. SEM-based nanoprobing was combined  with other physical failure analysis techniques to yield a  highly-efficient and successful methodology within  semiconductor industry. The nanoprobing of a single device  was the only way to find the root cause of technological issues  within the production process.

LiLung Lai

The Nanoprobing technique has become a popular tool for the  Failure Analysis. This paper tries to establish the fundamental  postulates for the following improvement of the technique. After description of the postulates, the application to missing or  blocked LDD is claimed. Meanwhile, the following strategy of  post-Nanoprobing is discussed by the case of missing LDD and  for general conditions.


The Nanoprobing measurement for Metal or Contact (CT) levels has become a standard way of Semiconductor Failure  Analysis in recent years. As the size of devices shrink for  newer technologies, the following physical failure analysis (PFA) is getting challenged to reveal the true problem. Especially, the standard microcopies and spectroscopes, e.g. SEM/TEM/AFM/EDS/EELS, are hard to exhibit doping profile  for the real-world devices, down to 20nm and smaller. The  developing methodology of electrical measurement needs to  push the Nanoprobing to identify the accurate location for the  failure device. The application to advanced SRAM analysis, from 90nm to 20nm and below, will become more useful for  failure analysis (FA). In this article, I demonstrate several  postulates of Nanoprobing including the completeness and  uniqueness for the electrical behavior to physical characteristic. The case of missing LDD is an example to be implemented, and followed by discussion of missing Pocket (sometimes  called halo) implant.


Postulates of Nanoprobing Analysis


As Nanoprobing is getting higher demand in the field of  semiconductor failure analysis (FA), I would like to push the  capability of device measurement to extend the depth of the  analysis. I propose three postulates be supposed and attainable  in the Nanoprobing analysis in the following description.


I. “Localization”: The only effective data for the  comparison are restricted in the finite domain of operator, tool, prober, time and sample.


It claims the Nanoprobing measurement is fully manual  operation and pursues the technology of Nanoprober system  with higher efficiency. Therefore, the comparison between  reference and target is only effective for these confined  conditions.


II.  “Completeness”: There are completed ways of taking  Nanoprobing measurements to reveal all kinds of physical  variation of the process.


It encourages a more powerful Nanoprobing methodology to  more fully cover its analytical purpose. These ways of  measurement include DC and AC signals, plus current – voltage (I-V) and capacitance – voltage (C-V), etc.


III. “Uniqueness”: The full electrical characteristics of  Nanoprobing measurements uniquely correspond to each  physical structure.


It gives the ultimate capability of Nanoprobing to become the  technique with precise electrical signatures. Postulate III of  Nanoprobing in failure analysis (FA) performs not only the  electrical measurement for device but also physical localization  for following PFA. However, to achieve the full power of  Nanoprobing for nano-devices, it would need a very high cost  of technology and methodology. Thus, the simplified process  should become necessary for the real analysis.


Postulate I.  Manual Operation


The concept of Postulate I. claims the effectiveness has been  limited in the finite domain of sample, tool, time and operator  because the fully manual operation for the measurement and  sample preparation. The desired analysis, a comparison  between Nanoprobing and Wafer Acceptance Test (WAT) data  from a tester, won’t likely be supported by the postulate. An  improved Nanoprober system, skillful technician and wellcontrol facility become crucial to increase the available  window of data comparison.


Postulate II.  Nanoprobing Measurements


There are several ways of obtaining Nanoprobing measurement  to get different information for device performances. In the  example of MOS measurement, the following is the list of  methods:


1. Diode I-V Behavior using Two Probes (N+ to P-well or P+


to N-well), or One Probe and the chuck;


2. Gate Insulator C-V Behavior using Two Probes (Gate to


Source, Drain, or Well);


3. Bipolar Behavior using Three Probes (Source, Drain, and


Well) or Four Probes (device held in its off state).;


4. MOS Transfer Curve Characteristics (Id vs Vg, fixed Vd)


and Output Curve Characteristics (Id vs Vd, fixed Vg) each


using Four Probes with Vs and Vb at a constant ground


voltage;


5. Back-Transfer Curve Characteristics (Id vs Vb, fixed Vd) using Four Probes with Vs and Vg at a constant ground  voltage;


6. MOS AC Transfer Curve Characteristics (Id vs high  frequency Vg, fixed Vd) and AC Output Curve  Characteristics (Id vs high frequency Vd, fixed Vg) each  using Four Probes with Vs and Vb at a constant ground  voltage.


7. Extended AC measurement replacing of DC signal.


In general, most application use method #1, 4 as standard DC  measurements. Method #1 measures the junction behaviors of  Drain/Source (N+/P+) to the well. Method #4 measures the  transistor characteristic, including transfer curves (Linear and  Saturation conditions) and output curves (On and Off states). Is  all the data independent information for the analysis? It is not  at all. In general, the family of transfer curves includes the  richest information with linear & semi-log scale and become  the most popular data for the FA. See figure 1.


Fig.1 Typical transfer curves (Id-Vg) of NMOS from a failing  and passing address.


The output family curves do not contribute additional  information beyond transfer curves for the channel property. Nevertheless, the Off-state Output data exhibits the bipolar  characteristic seen in Method #3. See the figure 2. The idea is  not typical yet for the FA application but it would become  valuable after in-depth investigation. Meanwhile, the On-state  Output curves can reveal some mechanisms beyond transfer  curves and will be shown in the case of missing LDD or high  contact resistance CT loop.


The other methods need to be developed for the applicable in  the real FA cases. The postulate claims the existence of a set of  measurements is able to cover the whole electrical behaviors. This is the belief. Therefore, the mission of technical FA is to  find the methodology of Nanoprobing for the required  applications.


Fig.2 The same case as Figure 1, Off-state (Vg=0) Output  curves (Id-Vd) reveal the direct short with Drain-side biasing  but not in Source-side biasing.

Example of Postulate III.  - Missing LDD


The third postulate is proposed for the linkage between  electrical measurement and physical analysis. This paper will  not show rigorous proving with the mathematic derivation. However, if the uniqueness is real, then all measurements  would be applied for the deduction and make the analysis much  more complicated and harder to be worked. From postulate to  principle, we need the support of more data and later on the  deductions based upon the assumptions to get accurate physical  fault localizations. The paper takes missing LDD as a typical  example for the first discussion.


Fig.3 The figure of missing or depleted LDD in the example of  NMOS


Id =Idrift,s +Idiff,s +Ipunth,s +Ileak,g +Ileak,b +dQ/dt  ---- (1)  Is =Idrift,d +Idiff,d +Ipunth,d +Ileak,g +dQ/dt            ---- (2)


There are lots of papers [1-5] for missing, depleted or blocked  LDD to describe the FA cases as lessons learned. According to  the figure 3 and equation (1,2), assume biasing at drain and  ground at source, we propose the six independent unique  characteristics of Nanoprobing data as sufficient conditions of  the missing LDD.


1. High resistance of channel in the MOS


- Supposed low channel current and high Vt measured;


2. Asymmetric channel current by Source or Drain biasing


- Asymmetry of Id-Vd & Id-Vg behaviors, see exampled curves  in the figure 4, in fail MOS between Source/Drain biasing; (General assumption for different level of LDD missing in  Source and Drain side.)


3. Low/Normal channel current for common contact in  between Fail/Pass MOS (see figure 3);


4. No gate current leakage;


5. No bulk current contribution - No junction leakage via  problematic contact; (No VC in SEM/FIB imaging).


6. No GIDL [1] - No contribution from GIDL for drain/bulk  current for defect-side biasing.


Ioff,d=Ioff,s (No GIDL effect in both sides)    -- (3)


Fig.4a Output curves (On-state, Vg=Vdd) show the asymmetry  behavior and saturation/non-saturation characteristics for  missing/depleted NLDD in NMOS (same characteristic of  missing/depleted PLDD in PMOS)


Fig.4b Transfer curves (Saturation mode, Vd=Vdd) show the  asymmetry behavior for missing NLDD in NMOS (same  characteristic of missing PLDD in PMOS)


According to the theoretical derivation and examination for the  real cases, we propose the above conditions are necessary to  missing LDD. The following explanations are for the above six  conditions:


1. Missing LDD results in high resistance in the current path  and therefore low current should be measured. The smaller  current observed becomes the first reason of bit failure in  SRAM. If the current is not low, missing LDD could be  ruled out at first sight for the root cause.


2. One side of missing LDD should cause the asymmetry of  S/D biasing. It has been described and confirmed by  several reference papers. If not, you may suspect the low  current resulted from the channel issue under the MOS  capacitance effect, e.g. gate/oxide/channel doping. See  figure 3.


3. The missing LDD only affects the channel current of  transistor in one side of Contact (CT). Therefore, the  transistor on the other side won’t be affected by the  missing LDD. If not, you should suspect the root cause  from CT-loop, such as high-Rc interface/open or Sacilide  shortage.


4. No gate to Source/Drain/Well interaction for missing  LDD. If not, the oxide defect or thickness would be the  root causes.


5. Even with a missing LDD, the N+/P+ in the Source/Drain  sites still fully cover the current path from CT to channel. So, there is no junction leakage current measured in the  transistor without LDD implantation. If not, it may  encounter the problematic sacilide with high Rc  encroaching into LDD region causes junction leakage [4] or incomplete doping profile of N+/P+ (Source/Drain).


6. As with missing LDD, the overlap of Source/Drain with  Gate disappears and transistor won’t exhibit GIDL [1] (Gate Induce Drain Leakage) along the part of missing  LDD. If not, it may suffer the partial missing sacilide  inducing asymmetrically electrical behavior of items 2 &


3.


However, we need to more precisely review the outputs for the  above conditions. Let’s see the following abnormal example  which breaks the first condition.

A Study of Electron Beam Irradiation Influence on Device Contact Junction  Characteristics of Advanced DRAM Using Atomic Force Probing


Physical Failure Analysis Department


Inotera Memories, Inc.


No.667 Fushing 3 RD. Kueishan, Taoyuan, Taiwan, Republic of China  E-mail:waynewang@inotera.com. Tel: 886-935-350-186


In this paper, we revealed p+/n-well and n+/p-well junction  characteristic changes caused by electron beam (EB) irradiation. Most importantly, we found a device contact side  junction characteristic is relatively sensitive to EB irradiation  than its whole device characteristic; an order of magnitude  excess current appears at low forward bias region after 1kV  EB acceleration voltage irradiation (Vacc). Furthermore, these  changes were well interpreted by our Monte Carlo simulation  results, the Shockley-Read Hall (SRH) model and the  Generation-Recombination (G-R) center trap theory. In  addition, four essential examining items were suggested and  proposed for EB irradiation damage origins investigation and  evaluation. Finally, by taking advantage of the excess current  phenomenon, a scanning electron microscope (SEM) passive  voltage contrast (PVC) fault localization application at n-FET  region was also demonstrated.


In today’s semiconductor industry, EB analytical methodology  has been widely used in both FAB and failure analysis (FA) lab for defect inspection, critical dimension (CD) measurement and fault localization, such as defect review  scanning electron microscope (SEM), CD-SEM, passive  voltage contrast (PVC) fault localization. At present, EB  irradiation induces modern device to get an unexpected  electrical change has become a non-negligible issue due to the  extremely small device dimension. Regarding to prior studies, influence factors of the EB damage can be categorized into  two main parts; the first part is device physical dimensions  such as interlayer dielectric (ILD) height…, the second part is  EB conditions, such as electron acceleration voltage (Vacc), dose of electron to the sample (Dose)... and so on. Nevertheless, the awareness of the maximum permissible EB  irradiation conditions of your own products is very important  and it is because the improper EB irradiation condition can  produce additional dielectric charge traps and unexpected  SiO2/Si interface states creation to a device [1-3]. Consequently, these will lead to the circuitry marginality test


failure or the product reliability poor performance, such as  device hammer test, DRAM variant retention time test (VRT) and device charge pumping issue [4-7]. In addition, if this  anomalous creation happens before the FA LAB nano-probing  analysis, it will be an artificial result and it can mislead the  process guy to come up with a wrong corrective action. Thus, trying to prevent EB damage no matter during semiconductor  manufacturing process or before FA LAB nano-probing  analysis is quietly important. As above mentioned, try to keep  the EB Vacc and dose as low as possible during your  utilization and a thicker ILD of a device are two main factors  of the EB damage. However, technology node keeps shrinking  is a must for a DRAM company to keep being competitive and  profitable. Therefore, trying to keep the EB Vacc and Dose as  low as possible is an advisable way for EB damage  prevention. Regarding to previous literatures [8-11], researchers had studied and revealed that how variant kinds of  EB irradiation conditions cause device parameters shifts, but  rare of them reported the device contact side junction  characteristic changes. As a result, regarding to above  statement, we convert these into three research questions and  set up a series of experiments to get the answers.


1. How does the EB irradiation affect a device contact side  junction electrical behavior?


2. Which electrical parameter of a device is relatively  sensitive to the EB irradiation?


3. Which examining items are essential for EB damage  evaluation and the origin investigation?


In the end, by taking advantage of EB damage result, we  demonstrated a FA fault localization application at n-MOS  device. By this method, the difference between good and bad  gate contacts contrast can be effectively enhanced and the  faulty gate contact is more easily identified.


The advanced DRAM product peripheral p/n-MOS planar  devices (gate oxide ~2nm) and their p+/n-well and n+/p-well  contact side junctions were chosen for the following study. An  atomic force prober (AFP) system which equipped with  Agilent 4156C parameter analyzer was used to acquire all


electrical data. System current (leaky current) of each probe  was less than 0.1 pico-Amperes. A Hitachi S-4800 SEM  system provided the variant EB Vacc and Dose irradiation  conditions and the beam current was examined by Faraday  cup. The EB Dose was calculated from the beam current, scanned area and EB exposed time and it ranged from 3.08E-9  to 1.23E-8 Ampere second/μm2. Before and after EB  irradiation, the same device transfer characteristic and its  contact side junction characteristic were compared for the EB  irradiation influence analysis; electrical parameters such as  on-state current (Ion), threshold voltage (Vth), sub-threshold  slope (S), contact side junction forward current (IF) at 0.35V  and reverse current (IR) at 1.3V were calculated for data  comparison.


As to the repeatability of the measurement in this study, Figs. 1 and 2 illustrated the relative standard deviation (RSD) values of two and four probes measurements, respectively; and the data was calculated by repeated scanning and probing  at same transistor by the same operator. Regarding to these  low RSD (two probes: 3.02%; four probes: 3.2%), our AFP  measurement system is acceptable for the qualitative analysis  in this study.

Figure 2: A diagram illustrates the RSD value of two- probe  measurement (voltage=1.3V).


Device Parameters Shift


Figures 3 and 4 described p-MOS and n-MOS device transfer  characteristics, before and after 1 minute EB irradiation at  variant Vacc (1, 1.2, 1.5, 3 and 5kV) conditions; the  percentage of device parameters shifts were calculated and  summarized in Table I. From the Table I results, as we can see  the result showed no significant change until we increased EB  Vacc above 3kV. While EB was above 3kV, the suppressed  Ion, higher Vth and sub-threshold slope degradation all  appeared in both p-MOS and n-MOS devices.

Contact Side Junction Characteristic Changes


Figures 5 and 6 showed p+/n-well and n+/p-well contact  junction characteristics before and after 1 minute EB  irradiation at variant EB Vacc (1, 1.2, 1.5, 3 and 5kV) conditions. Table II summarized p+/n-well and n+/p-well  junction characteristic changes at 0.35V forward bias (IF) and


1.3V reverse bias (IR) conditions. From the results, both p+/nwell and n+/p-well junction characteristics showed an excess  current in the low forward bias region while EB Vacc was  above 1.5kV. Besides, the lowest data dot of junction  characteristic begin to shift toward to x-axis origin, however, this result represented the higher diode switching speed (voltage sweeping from forward bias to reverse bias  condition) and the mechanism will be further discussed in the  following pages. While the EB Vacc was at 3 and 5kV, the  excess current became more severe and it appeared in both  forward and reverse bias regions.


Figure 5: A diagram illustrates the p+/n-well contact junction  characteristics before and after 1minute EB irradiation at  variant EB Vacc (1, 1.2, 1.5, 3 and 5kV) conditions.


Figure 6: A diagram illustrates the n+/p-well junction  characteristics before and after 1 minute EB irradiation at  variant EB Vacc (1, 1.2, 1.5, 3 and 5kV) conditions.

By Table I and II data comparison, we could realize that EB  irradiation changed contact side junction characteristics earlier  than shifted its whole device parameters; an order excess  forward current appeared at EB Vacc 1.5kV condition. While  the EB Vacc was above 3kV, two orders of magnitude  forward excess current appeared at 0.35V and more than one  order of magnitude excess reverse current appeared at 1.3V. Simultaneously, the device parameters showed a significant  shift. In addition, this excess reverse current can be interpreted  as the device contact to well leakage path formation as well as  explained the device suppressed on-state current result. Regarding to above observations, it illustrated that device  contact side junction characteristic (low forward bias region) is relatively sensitive to EB irradiation than its whole device  parameters. Nevertheless, we were wondering that “how the  EB dose affect device contact side junction characteristic?” Therefore, we set up another experiment for further  investigation and these were under variant EB irradiation  Dose conditions (D1: 3.08E-9 AS/μm2, D2: 6.17E-9 AS/μm2, and D3: 1.23E-8 AS/μm2). As shown in Fig. 7, even the EB  Vacc was low (1kV), the excess forward current can also be  produced by higher EB Dose (D1: 3.08E-9 AS/μm2)


irradiation. Besides, this excess forward current was  permanent and it was demonstrated by the re-measurement  results which was after a period of time, as shown in Fig. 8.


Figure 7: A diagram illustrates the n+/p-well contact junction  characteristics before and after Vacc 1kV EB irradiation at  variant Dose (D1: 3.08E-9 AS/μm2, D2: 6.17E-9 AS/μm2, and  D3: 1.23E-8 AS/μm2) conditions.


Figure 8: A diagram shows the n+/p-well junction currents  after EB irradiation for one day, three days and one week.


For further studying the mechanism of the “EB irradiation  caused junction characteristic change earlier than its whole  device parameters shift” result, Monte Carlo simulation at  variant EB Vacc (1kV, 3kV, and 5kV) conditions were  performed on our device. As shown in Fig. 9, Fig. 9 (a) illustrated the p-MOS device physical dimensions; Figs. 9 (b) and (c) presented the incident electrons’ penetration depth (PD) in the device gate dielectric region and the nearby  contact side junction region, respectively.


From the results, it could easily find that incident electrons  can always penetrate deeper in the nearby contact region than  gate dielectric region at every EB Vacc condition. In  accordance with previous studies [1-3.], it is believed that  perform EB irradiation to SiO2/Si sample can apparently  produce dielectric hole traps and SiO2/Si interface state


creations through electron beam bombardment, plasmon  excitation, hole hopping and hole trapped steps. Thus, the  deeper penetration depth result in the nearby contact region  indicated a shorter hole hopping distance and a higher  possibility of interface state creations. Therefore, it explained  why junction characteristic change appears earlier than its  whole device parameters shift. While EB Vacc was at 3 and  5kV, the incident electron distribution became deeper and  even more it’s covered with SiO2/Si interface. Under this  circumstance, the SiO2/Si interface states can be intensely  created and the creation mechanism would be not only by hole  hopping effect, but also the direct creation of interface states.


Monte Carlo Simulation


Figure 9: (a) A diagram illustrates our p-MOS device  physical dimensions. (b) Monte Carlo simulation result in the  device gate dielectric region and (c) in the nearby device  contact side junction region at EB Vacc 1, 3 and 5kV  conditions.


As for the surface charges that induced by EB irradiation, it  was wondering that “Does the device contact voltage potential  caused by the induced charges has some contributions to this  excess current result?” In order to clarify this, an electrical  stressing experiment to the device p+/n-well contact junction  was conducted and the voltage stressing program contains 1  minute six voltages forward biasing then subsequent with 1  minute six voltages reverse biasing. As shown in Fig.10, it  illustrated that there is nothing change after the voltage  stressing and it indicated that surface charges induced by EB  irradiation has nothing to do with the junction characteristic  changes in this study.


Figure 10, A diagram illustrates p+/n-well junction  characteristics before and after the electrical stressing.


Mechanism Discussion


As for the consequences of EB irradiation to a MOS  transistor, there will be two creations, one is dielectric layer  hole traps and the other is device SiO2/Si interface states  creation. For a n-MOS device, the gate dielectric hole traps  tend to decrease device threshold voltage (in absolute value) while SiO2/Si interface states tend to increase it. For a p-MOS  device, both gate dielectric hole traps and the interface states  tend to increase the threshold voltage (in absolute value). In  addition, these SiO2/Si interface states creation can  particularly degrade device channel carrier mobility and lead  to the depressed sub-threshold slope.


Regarding to the device parameter shifts in Table I, higher Vt  and degraded sub-threshold slope appeared in both p-MOS  and n-MOS devices after EB Vacc 3 or 5kV irradiation and  these device parameter shifts led us to concluded that the  SiO2/Si interface state creations dominate the device  parameter shift in this study and these SiO2/Si interface state  creations have closely related to the junction characteristic  changes and it will be further illustrated in the following  section.


Excess Current Enhanced by SiO2/Si Interface States


Before further interpreting how the SiO2/Si interface state  creation related to the junction characteristics changes, Shockley-Read Hall (SRH) recombination model and four  carrier generation-recombination (G-R) processes were briefly  introduced and will used for results explanation [3]. The four  processes meant “electron capture”, “electron emission”, “hole capture” and “hole emission” steps, and these steps can  significantly enhance the electron-hole (E-H) generation and  recombination rate at space charge region (SCR) of p-n  junction of a semiconductor material by a G-R center traps  assistant such as crystalline defect. Particularly, the SiO2/Si  interface states behaved like G-R centers in SRH bandgap  diagram and it help to enhance carrier G-R rate (less carrier  lifetime) in the SCR and it implied that there will be an excess  recombination and generation current under the forward and  reverse bias conditions, as shown in Fig. 11 (a) and (b). In


Fig.11 (a), the diagram illustrated how the G-R centers assist  electron capture and hole capture processes in SCR under the  forward bias condition and Fig. 11 (b) presented the electron  emission and hole emission processes enhancement under the  reverse bias condition. As for the mechanism interpretation of  junction characteristics changes, it will be separated into three  different voltage bias conditions; at large forward bias  condition, at medium/low forward bias condition and at  reverse bias conditions.


Figure 11, this bandgap diagram describes SRH processes  and how the G-R centers enhance recombination current and  generation current in the (a) forward bias region and (b) reverse bias condition.


At large forward bias (greater than built-in voltage):


Under this condition, the recombination current caused by  SiO2/Si interface state creation was negligible and it was  because the rather small SCR width at this bias condition. Therefore, diffusion current dominated the total junction  current at this large forward bias condition. However, this  hypothesis showed a good agreement with our results in both  p+/n-well and n+/p-well contact junction characteristics, as  shown in Fig. (5) and (6) larger forward bias region.


At medium and low forward bias:


Under this junction bias condition, junction current was  consisting of diffusion current and SCR recombination current  Eq. (1). Even more, recombination current was the dominant  current at low forward bias condition. From Eq. (2) and (3), they illustrated that the density of G-R center was directly  proportional to the G-R rate (U) and recombination-generation  current density in the SCR (JRec/Gen). Thus, higher density of  SiO2/Si interface state creations nearby device contact region  can earlier alternate the contact side junction characteristic  than its whole device parameter. However, these SiO2/Si  interface states behaved like G-R centers can improve electron  capture and hole capture processes in the SCR, as shown in  Fig. 11 (a).   Hence, G-R centers creations enhance more  recombination current at low forward bias conditions and this  statement is consistent with the result in this study, as shown  in Fig. (5) and (6) medium/low forward bias region.

Q: Magnitude of electronic charge.


U: Generation-recombination rate.


W: Space Charge Region Width.


U =CnCpNt(np-ni2) / Cn(n+n1)+Cp(p+p1) ∝ Nt                            (3) Nt: Density of recombination-generation centers or traps.

At reverse bias:


JR=JDrift + JGen + JThermionic                                                        (4)


Under this condition Eq. (4), total current consisted of drift  current, generation current and thermionic emission current. Similarly, the G-R centers induced by EB irradiation could  enhance the electron emission and hole emission processes, as  shown in Fig. 11 (b). Thus, excess generation current was  produced at reverse bias condition and as the higher density of  G-R traps created, more SCR generation current would also be  produced at the reverse bias condition.


To sum up, the higher amounts of G-R traps (SiO2/Si interface  traps) enhanced the carrier G-R rate and produced more  recombination and generation current in forward and reverse  bias conditions, respectively. However, for further illustrating  the SiO2/Si interface state creations of a device under EB  irradiation, Fig. (12) presented the SiO2/Si interface state  locations and the enhanced device leakage current path.


Figure 12: This diagram illustrates how SiO2/Si interface  states enhance the reverse excess junction current and the  current path. (X represents the SiO2/Si interface states)


As to the result of the lowest data dot shift toward x-axis  origin of junction characteristics after EB irradiation, it  implied that the irradiated junction had a higher switching  speed of the diode (switching from forward to reverse bias) and it is due to the SiO2/Si interface states creation and  enhancement. Specifically speaking, these interface states  creation shorter carrier life time (higher G-R rate) and quickly  eliminates the minority charges at two sides of SCR (lower  junction capacitance storage time). However, there are many  applications in semiconductor power devices by using this  result [12].


A Case Application


To apply the findings (reverse excess current) of this study, a  SEM PVC fault localization application was demonstrated in a  real case. As shown in Fig. 13 (a), the n-MOS device drain  contacts and gate contacts always showed grey and dark  contrast under regular SEM  PVC inspection (EB Vacc 1kV). However, it was very hard to identify the faulty gate contact  which caused by gate to drain resistive short (poly short) and  it was because the minor contrast difference between the


faulty and normal gate contact. Therefore, we conducted the  high EB Vacc (5kV) irradiation to intentionally induce the  excess reverse current at suspicious n-MOS region. As a  result, the contrast difference was effectively enhanced and  the faulty gate became easier be identified (brighter in faulty  gate contact), as shown in Fig. 13(b). The mechanism of this  method is, the leakage current of the faulty device gate to  drain contact to well were dramatically enlarged after high EB  Vacc irradiation. The faulty gate contact surface positive  charges can drain off through the resistive short to the drain  contact then to the well. In comparison with the normal nMOS gate contact, the surface potential of faulty gate contact  can not be charged up so positively during SEM PVC  inspection, therefore, the faulty gate contact showed much  brighter. In other words, the intentional reverse excess current  creation enlarges the contrast difference between the faulty  gate contact and the normal one. Therefore, the faulty gate  contact became more obvious (brighter) and easily be  identified, as shown in Fig. 13 (c) and (d). About some  fundamental passive voltage contact theorem and application, few literatures are recommended [13-14].


Figure 13: These diagrams illustrate the application of PVC  fault isolation method by taking advantage of the reverse  excess junction current caused by EB irradiation. (a) A  diagram shows the n-MOS device region PVC image before  EB irradiation. (b) A diagram shows the n-MOS device region  PVC image after high EB Vacc irradiation. (c) A diagram  describes n-MOS contact contrast and their surface potential  status before high EB Vacc irradiation. (d) A diagram  describes n-MOS contact contrast and their surface potential  status after the high EB Vacc irradiation. (Red arrow points  out failing gate contact and green arrow points out the  reference)


As to the answers of our initial three research questions, the  first one would be, the improper EB irradiation condition can  significantly induced excess current at device contact side  junction characteristic at low forward bias region, moreover, this excess current can appear at reverse bias condition if the


EB Vacc or dose is high enough. For the second answer, the  device contact side junction characteristic at low forward bias  region is relatively sensitive to EB irradiation; however, this  finding can be used to be an indicator of EB irradiation  damage monitoring. For the answer of third question, device  contact side junction current at low forward bias condition, reverse bias condition, device threshold voltage and subthreshold slope are the four essential items for an EB damage  evaluation and the maximum permissible EB Vacc  investigation. Besides, each examining item has its  implication; an excess forward current appears indicates  certain amounts of SiO2/Si interface states creation; and a  reverse current happens represents the certain higher amounts  of interface states creation; device threshold voltage shift  direction and sub-threshold slope results can provide us the  information to identify the dominant origins of the whole  device parameters shifts; dielectric layer charge traps or the  SiO2/Si interface states.


In conclusion, a planar device contact side p+/n-well and n+/pwell junction characteristic changes caused by different EB  Vacc,  dose conditions are successfully illustrated. The  mechanism, a SEM PVC case application, four essential  examining items for EB damage evaluation and its  implications are favorably revealed in this paper. And it is  believed that EB irradiation damages are becoming a  negligible consideration whether an advanced planar device or  a 3D FinFET device. Awareness of the maximum permissible  EB irradiation condition of your own product is necessarily  important and it is suggested to take good notice of this and  prevent it happened no matter during a wafer manufacturing  process or before a nano-probing analysis.
