In-situ Characterization of Switching Mechanism in Phase Change Random  Access Memory (PRAM) Using Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM).


Sungkyu Son, Seungjoon Jeon, Jangwon Oh, Won Kim, Hojoung Kim,  Jonghak Lee, Seungho Woo, Sungjoo Hong, Gapsok Do*, Seungyun Lee*


DRAM Development Division, * R&D Division, SK Hynix Semiconductor, Ichon-si, Korea


Kyungjoon Baek**, Sangho Oh**


** Dept. of Materials Science & Engineering, POSTECH, Pohang, Korea


It is important to understand the switching mechanism of phase  change material for failure analysis of PRAM device. In this  study, the real time observations of phase transition and void  formation mechanism of confined GST structure were  investigated using in-situ TEM with multi-pulse AC biasing  technique. In-situ SET switching behavior between amorphous  state and crystalline state with continuous structural change  was successfully observed. Volume shrink of GST, due to the  phase transition, induced voids at grain boundary of crystalline  phase. Excess Joule-heating after crystallization caused  coalescence and migration of voids. These results may give us  a crucial clue for endurance failure analysis of PRAM.


Keywords: PRAM, GST, FIB, nano prober, in-situ TEM


PRAM is one of the most promising candidates to replace  conventional Flash memory in the near future because of its  non-volatile, high speed and high density characteristics [1]. The operation of PRAM is based on rapid switching of phase  change material between a crystalline phase (low resistance, SET(0) state) and an amorphous phase (high resistance, RESET(1) state) induced by electrical Joule-heating (Fig. 1(a)). Recently, Ge–Sb–Te (GST) chalcogenide alloys are  being used as phase change materials and confined GST  structures have extensively been developed because of its  excellent thermal efficiency (Fig. 1(b) and 1(c)). It is important  to understand the switching mechanism of GST in terms of  phase change or void formation to improve the device  performance or to prevent the void induced reliability  degradation [2]. Furthermore, it is critical to understand the  micro structural changes in the intermediate resistance status  for the reliable multi-bit operation [3].


Despite some observations of phase change process using insitu TEM technique [4,5], there are no reports about the direct  observation of continuous structural change of GST in a single  cell during AC pulse operation, because of its fast transition


time (sub microsecond range). In this paper, we report an  analytical technique to observe continuous phase transition and  void formation process of single confined GST cell by multipulse AC biasing test of the thin foil specimen using in-situ  TEM.


Figure 1: (a) AC switching pulses for Joule-heating. (b) SET  state (crystalline phase). (c) RESET state (amorphous phase).


Figure 2 shows the schematic diagram of TEM sample for  electrical nanoprobing and in-situ observation of  confined  GST cell. GST films were deposited on a confined hole  surrounded with nitride spacer and metal electrode. TEM  samples were prepared from special test pattern consist of  parallel line type top electrode and bottom electrode for testing  and observation of single GST cell. Focused ion beam (FIB) with lift-out method was used for site-specific sample  preparation and a low accelerating voltage (5kV) with a low  beam current was used for the final thinning of the samples.


The TEM samples were attached to a Cu grid and then, Pt  lines were deposited using FIB to connect bottom electrode  and Cu grid. SEM nano probing system (HITACHI N-6000) was used to confirm the electrical circuit of TEM samples. Insitu TEM observation technique with STM-TEM holder (NanofactoryTM) and AC pulse generator (Keithley 4200) was  used to characterize phase change and void formation in real  time.


Figure 2: Schematic diagram of TEM sample for nano  probing analysis and in-situ observation of confined GST cell.


DC test using SEM nano prober was very efficient technique  to confirm the electrical paths of in-situ TEM samples. Leakage problems or open failures of TEM samples due to  FIB sample preparation were easily screened by this technique. As shown in Fig. 3(a), one probe tip was connected with top  electrode metal to apply bias voltage and the other probe tip  was connected with Cu grid for ground forcing. I-V curve in  Fig. 3(b) shows a clear transition from amorphous (high  resistivity) to crystalline (low resistivity)  phase, which means  that there was no leakage current or open failure problem due  to ion beam contamination or ion beam damage during FIB  sample preparations.


Figure 3: (a) DC test of in-situ TEM sample using SEM nano  prober. (b) I-V curve showing a SET switching from  amorphous (high resistivity) to crystalline (low resistivity) phase.


Figure 4 shows the two different types of AC bias pulses used  in our in-situ TEM experiments. One is RESET pulse (Fig. 4(a)) with a 50ns falling time for fast quenching, and the other  is SET pulse (Fig. 4(b)) with a 600ns falling time for slow  quenching. Fig. 5 shows in-situ phase transition from initially  amorphous phase to crystalline phase when a single SET pulse  with height of 3.5V was applied. Fig. 5(b) shows an in-situ  TEM image of a SET state, and its crystalline structure with  voids was confirmed by HRTEM lattice image. However, it


was impossible to observe the detail crystallization or void  formation process due to the fast AC pulse rate (sub  microsecond range).


Figure 4: (a) AC RESET pulse for fast quenching.  (b) AC SET  pulse for slow quenching.


Figure 5: In-situ phase transition from (a) amorphous phase  to (b) crystalline phase, when a single SET pulse with height  of 3.5V was applied.


Instead of single AC pulse, periodic multi-pulses with a  reduced voltage height of 2V were used to decrease GST  thermal from Joule-heating. As shown in Fig. 6, continuous  crystallization and void formation process were observed  successfully with our modified multi-pulse AC biasing test  condition. At the beginning of the multi-pulse test, crystals  nucleated in the top area of confined hole, and voids nucleated  at the interface of crystals (Fig. 6 (a) ~ (c)). During the multipulse test, crystals grew until the cell was fully crystallized, which induced migration and coalescence of voids (Fig. 6 (d) ~ (e)). At the end of the multi-pulse test, crystal orientations  were changed and large single void migrated from the bottom  area to the top area of confined hole (Fig. 6 (f) ~ (h).


Figure 7 shows the schematic diagrams of crystallization and  void formation mechanisms of confined GST cell suggested by  our in-situ TEM observations. (ⅰ) High interfacial energy  between GST and top electrode might give a nucleation site  for crystallization. (ⅱ ) Volume shrink of GST due to the  transition from amorphous to crystalline phase might induce  voids at grain boundary. (ⅲ ) Excess Joule-heating after  complete crystallization might cause coalescence and  migration of voids to reduce their surface energy.


Figure 6: In-situ TEM observations showing (a) ~ (c) nucleation of crystal and void, (d) ~ (e) crystal grain growth  with coalescence of voids, and (f) ~ (h) migration of void.


Figure 7: Schematic diagrams of crystallization and void  formation mechanisms of confined GST cell.


We established an analytical technique to observe real time  phase transition and void formation processes of single  confined GST cell using modified multi-pulse AC biasing test  with in-situ TEM. For the first time, the continuous SET  switching behavior between amorphous and crystalline state  was successfully observed. We suggest that GST material or  confined structure should be optimized to reduce or release  volume shrinkage during SET switching. We expect that our  study will become an important reference for understanding  the characteristic phase-change behaviors and void induced  endurance failure mechanism of confined GST cell.


We acknowledge technical support for in-situ TEM  experiments by POSTEC in Korea.

[3] Gang Zhang et al., “Multi-level cell storage with a  modulated current method for phase-change memory  using Ge-doped SbTe,” Current Applied Physics, Vol. 11 (2011), pp. e79-e81.


[4] S. A. Song et al., “In situ dynamic HR-TEM and EELS  study on phase transitions of Ge2Sb2Te5 chalcogenides,” Ultramicroscopy, Vol. 108 (2008), pp. 1408-1419.

Failure Analysis due to Slightly Unetched Hard Mask using Nano Probe


Jong Hak Lee, Jong Eun Kim*, Chang Su Park*, Nam Il Kim*, Jang Won Moon*, Jong Chae Kim*,  Soo Yong Son, Kyung Dong Yoo*, Sung Joo Hong


DRAM Development Division, * Image Development Group System IC Division, SK hynix Inc, Icheon-si, Korea


In this work, a slightly unetched gate hard mask failure was  analyzed by nano probing. Although unetched hard mask  failures are commonly detected from the cross sectional view  with FIB or FIB-TEM and planar view with the voltage  contrast, in this case of the very slightly unetched hard mask, it  was difficult to find the defects within the failed area by  physical analysis methods. FIB is useful due to its function of  milling and checking from the one region to another region  within the suspected area, but the defect, located under contact  was very tiny. So, it could not be detected in the tilted-view of  the FIB. However, the state of the failure could be understood  from the electrical analysis using a nano probe due to its  ability to probe contact nodes across the fail area. Among the  transistors in the fail area, one transistor’s characteristics  showed higher leakage current and lower ON current than  expected. After physical analysis, slightly remained hard mask  was detected by TEM. Chemical processing was followed to  determine the gate electrode (WSi2) connection to tungsten  contact. It was also proven that when gate is floated, more  leakage current flows compared to the state that the zero  voltage is applied to the gate. This was not verified by circuit  simulation due to the floating nodes.


Keywords: FIB, TEM, Nano Probe, Floating Gate, Leakage  Current


In general, there is an increasing need to change the basic  analysis method for faulty structures in devices due to  increased component density in IC chips. Historically FIB, SEM and TEM are used to analyze devices; however, it is  getting harder to use only physical means in IC analysis  because of process scaling and increasing number of marginal  failures [1]. In these circumstances, nano probing analysis is  getting more and more important for analysis of marginal  failures by probing a specific layer to gather electrical data. The analysis of the bad cells is categorized into 2 basic types: Easy Failure Analysis and Marginal Failure Analysis [2]. While Easy Failure Analysis identifies Hard IDD failures such  as hard bridge or leakage failures, the purpose of Marginal  Failure Analysis is to distinguish bad sectors in particular  specifications of electrical test [3, 4]. Semiconductor process  technology will continue to scale dimensions and thus, Failure  Analysis will become increasingly difficult. In this paper, we  will discuss how the failure caused by a tiny unetched hard  mask affects device characteristics and how to find the failure  phenomenon by nano probing and chemical processing.


Experiment and Results


The fail bit map was obtained and shown in Figure 1, in this  image the two black squares show the fail location and green  squares show the normal regions. The unit square means the  output of one pixel.


Figure 1; Fail bit map (two black squares)


Because the output of two failed pixels is identical, it is likely  that the suspicious area is within the dashed line in the  schematic and its simplified layout as shown in Figure 2 (a) and Figure 2 (b) respectively. In Figure 2 (b), for simplicity, it  was indicated from active to contact layer.


The brightness of pixel is determined by the difference  between reset voltage and signal voltage. If the difference is  large, pixel is shown more brightly, on the other hand, if the  difference is small, the pixel is shown more darkly. The reset  voltage is fixed to “HIGH” by the reset transistor and the  signal voltage varies by the amount of incident light. The more  light enters the photodiode, the more signal voltage falls. The  determination of brightness of pixel is shown in Figure 3.


(a) Suspicious failed area in the schematic


(b) Layout corresponding within dashed line, from Active to


Contact Layer


Figure 2; Schematic and layout of the suspicious failed area  consisting of 3 transistors and 7 contacts


Figure 3; Brightness of pixel


Several chips, classified with the same failure phenomena, were analyzed with FIB milling and checking method but did  not identify any defects. Because all of the transistors and  contacts in Figure 2 (b) were not aligned in a row and they  were not far-off sufficiently, TEM lamella could not be  prepared at the same time within the failed area. To find the  failed transistor or contact, nano probing was used. The  current-voltage relationship graphs of each transistor were  measured as shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.


Because there was no contact between B gate and C gate as  shown in Figure 2 (b), when C transistor was measured, B gate  was kept in the ON state. Similarly, C gate was kept ON when  B transistor was measured. Three chips were measured. Among them, the two chips, named as #01 and #02 are  classified with the same failure phenomena and the rest one, name as #03 was a normal chip for reference. Figure 4 shows  the OFF current characteristics of the each transistor and  plotted on logarithm scales and Figure 5 shows the ON current


characteristics of the each transistor and plotted on linear  scales. The threshold voltage of the A Transistor is smaller  than that of B and C Transistor. The A Transistor was  fabricated intentionally for the operation of circuit. The  measurement results show that the B transistor was proven as  failure and the failed transistor had higher OFF current and  lower ON current compared to the normal transistors. Particularly, Figure 5 shows that the channel located under the  gate and between source and drain was controlled somewhat  by the gate voltage.


(a) Measurement Results of A Transistor


(b) Measurement Results of B Transistor


(c) Measurement Result of C Transistor


Figure 4; OFF Current results of each transistor


(c) Measurement Results of C Transistor


Figure 5; ON Current results of each transistor


If the voltage was not directly applied to the gate at all through  the floated contact from the gate electrode, the curve of ON  current was not plotted linearly as shown in Figure 5 (b). So, we analyzed and found that the contact connected to the gate  electrode was slightly separated. Figure 6 shows the cross  sectional images of the failed and normal transistors at dark  field of TEM, because remained hard mask was not as clearly  distinguished at bright field. In the failed case, the remaining  hard mask (Si3N4) is observed as a dark fine line between  contact (W) and gate electrode (WSi2) within the dashed line  in the zoomed in image as shown in Figure 6 (a).


While in the normal case, Figure 6 (b) shows that the contact  and gate electrode were clearly connected to each other.


To confirm more clearly, the failed samples were dipped in  chemicals to remove contact, barrier metal and gate electrode. If a contact and a gate electrode are connected to each other, the gate electrode must be removed by chemical processing. However, if the contact and the gate electrode are separated  each other, the gate electrode should not be removed because  of the hard mask existing between the contact and gate  electrode. Figure 7 shows the chemical processing results. In  the failed case, the gate electrode was not removed because of  the remaining hard mask blocking the invasion of chemical  that can remove the gate electrode composed of tungsten, so  the gate electrode was seen brightly as shown in Figure 7 (a) (Don’t be confused.). While, in the normal case, the gate  electrode was partially removed by the invaded chemical so  the fraction of the gate electrode is displayed darkly within  dashed line as shown in Figure 7 (b). The sequence of the  removing each layer by chemical processing is explained in  Figure 8. Because the failed area corresponds to the gate of B  transistor in Figure 2, it could be explained that the circuit was  open. The modified simple schematic due to the failure is  shown in Figure 9. The B transistor acts as a source follower. Because the input of source follower is open, no signals from  the pixels can be transferred to the next stage. So the output is  also undefined and the output is displayed blackly as shown in  Figure 1. Although the failed phenomenon described above  can be detected by cross sectional view, the failure was not  detected by FIB-SEM because of the remaining very thin hard  mask under the contact in tilted view as shown in Figure 10. In  this case, it looked like that the contact and the gate electrodes  are connected well to each other due to the optical illusion.


In this paper, it was proven when the voltage was not directly  applied to the gate due to the described failure mechanism, the  transistor had more higher OFF current. This phenomenon  could not be explained by circuit simulation. If floated nodes  exist in the drawn circuit, an error message window appeared  when simulation command is executed. In this case, the  floating gate node phenomenon occurred only for one bit or  one pixel. However, if many floating gate nodes were present  in the logic circuit such as defocus of contacts, open backend  metallic line, it is possible that a soft standby current failure  was detected.

A slightly unetched hard mask was detected by nano probing, TEM and chemical processing. The electrical analysis was  performed using nano probing to localize the specific failing  transistor. To identify the root cause, TEM and chemical  processing were both used. The combination of two or three  methods was useful and effective to find marginal failures.

Physical and Electrical Performance Comparison of Identical 28nm Qualcomm  Telecommunication Die produced by Samsung and TSMC


Anton Riley, Sean Zumwalt


Multiprobe Inc., Ca, USA,


(anton@mulitprobe.com, sean@multiprobe.com)


Sinjin Dixon-Warren, Gary Tomkins,


Chipworks, Ottawa, Canada, (sdixonwarren@chipworks.com,)


In today’s competitive semiconductor environment, product  performance and market timing has never been more valuable. Design IP, speed to market, and taking advantage of the most  advanced technology are three ways fabless companies can  maintain an advantage over the competition. Foundries target  these demands by offering superior support, competitive  technology, and rapid development cycles. Using the advanced  tool suites of SEM, FIB, TEM, and Atomic Force  NanoProbing (AFP) the failure analysis community now has  the ability to investigate and compare foundry performance on  the device level.


The 28 nm LP Qualcomm “SHELBY” die is dual-sourced  from both Samsung and TSMC, and is the primary die in the  MDM9215 4G/LTE modem used in several smartphones. This  represents a unique case of leading technology, available to the  public, to qualify for electrical performance on the device level  using the AFP and the corresponding physical differences  using SEM and TEM. These advanced FA techniques were  employed and were able to identify manufacturing differences  between foundries. They were then used to relate the physical  variations with the electrical device performance.


The HG11-N3877 fabricated by TSMC and the HG11-N9204  fabricated by Samsung were the subjects of this comparison (see Error! Reference source not found.). The investigation  located spatial and geometric variations of the SRAM devices  using cross sectioning and TEM imaging. This was followed  by Electrical Characterization of multiple SRAM Cells using  the AFP. The electrical measurements showed clear differences  in device parameters.  These differences highlight  manufacturing process differences between the two companies  that could directly relate to chip performance.


Physical Inspection


Top down SEM inspection at the contact layer revealed  the 6T-SRAM Cell Area of the Samsung 28nm LP process was


0.14um2 compared to the TSMC 28 nm LP process of 0.15 µm2 (see Figure 2).  However, the contacted gate pitch of the  6T-SRAM is the same as the TSMC 28 nm LP process at 120  nm (see Figure 3). Cross-Section through the substrate shows  consistent STI geometries between foundries. Minor variations  in CESL SiN thickness did not play a key role in the device


performance. Gate Lengths for both manufacturers were  measured in a TEM cross section as 50 nm and 53 nm for  PMOS and NMOS transistors respectively. The Gate widths  inside the SRAM also measured identically for both  manufactures at 60nm and 150nm for the PMOS and NMOS  transistors.


Figure 2: SEM image showing the 6T-SRAM Cell Area on  TSMC fabricated HG11-N3877.  Note this is 7% larger than  Samsung 28nm LP design for the same die.

The SRAM was also evaluated for Alpha (α), Beta (β), and  Gamma (γ) values.  These values represent the ratio of drive  currents between the 3 different transistor types.  α represents  the ratio of the Pullup transistor’s Ion and the Pulldown  transistor’s Ion.  β represents the Pulldown to Passgate Ion ratio  and γ represents the Ion ratio of the Passgate to the Pullup.


These 3 values (seen in Figure 6) are indicators for how  resilient an SRAM cell will be to soft defects like read disturb  and write fails.

Threshold Voltage Evaluation for TSMC and  Samsung SRAM process


For many devices, the current draw during operation is a  critical parameter for device performance.  This is especially  important for chips destined for mobile applications.


In SRAM operation, the majority of the current draw will  occur during read and write operations – very little current  draw occurs as static dissipation.  The amount of current draw  will be determined by how well the threshold voltages are  matched for the 3 transistor varieties.  For inverters and latches, the ideal scenario would be that the thresholds would be  matched such that very little time is spent the high-currentdraw transition zone.


As seen in Figure 4 and Figure 5, TSMC and Samsung are  not closely matched for Vt for Pulldowns – 0.33V and 0.38V  respectively. For Pullup transistors, TSMC devices run “cooler” at -0.32  V vs. -0.26V for Samsung.


The 120 mV difference between Pullup and Pulldown Vt for  the Samsung SRAM vs. a 10mV (see Figure 4 and Figure 5) difference for TSMC could indicate a process that uses


significantly more power during write operations.


While switching performance is important, read performance  is also critical.  The NMOS Passgates (Access Left and Access  Right) need to be matched such that the Passgate can pull a Bit  Line low relative to Bit Line Bar - therefore triggering the Bit  Line sense amplifier.  The longer it takes to pull the Bit Line  low, the more read fails can occur.[3]  This read stability is  effected by the ratio of the Passgate current draw to the  Pulldown current draw [4].


For the TSMC part, the Passgate transistor has aVt of 0.39V  while the Samsung Part registers a Passgate Vt of 0.38V.  Both  of these are closely matched with similar standard devitations, meaning they should see similar read characteristics.  However, the Pulldown Vt for TSMC measures at 0.33V while the  Samsung Pulldown measures at 0.38V.  This means that the  TSMC Pulldown devices will turn on sooner in a switch  operation and their higher Ion will make them more resilient to  read stability issues [4].


TSMC Cell Stability Concerns with Pulldown  and Pullup Variations


Shifts in the Pullup threshold voltage can result in a type of  soft fail known as a “write fail”.  A shifted threshold voltage  can result in an increase or decrease in drive current or Ion.


In write operations, the Passgate must pull the input of the cell  from “1” to “0”.  In order to do this, the Passgate must have  sufficient drive current to overcome the Pullup transistor’s  ability to maintain the internal node at “1”.  If the γ (gamma) ratio of Passgate strength to Pullup strength is too low, then  write operation will not be able to pull the internal node down  far enough to flip the cell.  This will result in the cell returning  to a “1” state after a “0” write operation.[5]


Figure 7 highlights a process outlier where the targeted Pullup  transistor had higher drive current then the reference device.  A  device like this would be more susceptible to the previously  mentioned write failure.


Figure 7: Voltage Threshold plot a of targeted “hot” TSMC  Pullup transistor (Solid line) compared to reference (Dotted).


In an SRAM cell, a Vt shift in the “hotter” direction for the  Pulldown transistors (closer to 0 Vgs) could adversely affect  device stability – especially if a “hot” and a “cold” Pulldown  are in the same cell.  This scenario could result in a cell  flipping during a read operation (also known as access disturb  or read disturb).


In this situation, a weaker Pulldown drive current (associated  with the Pulldown with a “cooler” Vt) will see a higher node  voltage during a read operation.  This higher node voltage can  overcome the Vt for the “hotter” Pulldown on the opposite side  of the latch.  When this happens, the latch will flip and the  previously written “0” will be switched to a “1” during the  read.


Figure 8 shows an outlier device that is significantly stronger  than the reference Pulldown.  This type of device would make  the cell more susceptible to read disturb failures.


Figure 8: Voltage Threshold plots of a targeted “hot” TSMC  Pulldown transistor (Solid Line) compared to reference (Dotted).


Samsung Cell Stability Concerns with


measured variations on Pulldown and Passgate  Transistors


For both the TSMC and Samsung parts, the β ratios were very  low.  The Pulldown and Passgate Ion for Samsung were 0.31  and 0.68 mA/µm respectively.  This type of drive current  relationship can result in a third type of soft fail in SRAM.


In a read operation for a “0” bit, the Bit Line and Bit Line Bar  are precharged and the Passgates turned on. If the Pulldown  transistors are weak or too slow to turn on, then the Bit Line  will not see a significant enough drop versus Bit Line Bar to  trigger the sense amplifier circuit – and the read will fail. [3]


Figure 9 highlights one of these process outliers measured  from the Samsung die and plotted against a reference  Pulldown.


Figure 9: Voltage Threshold plots of a targeted “cold” Samsung Pulldown transistor (Solid Line) compared to  reference (Dotted).


A fourth type of SRAM soft failure is characterized by a weak  Passgate transistor.  In this scenario, a weak Passgate transistor  can fail to overpower the Pullup transistor causing a “0” write  operation to revert back to a “1” state.[4]  This tendency is  indicated by a low γ ratio.  Figure 10 shows a weak Passgate  on the Samsung part with over 150mV of threshold voltage  shift. [5]


Figure 10: Voltage Threshold plots of a targeted “cold” Samsung Passgate transistor (Solid Line) compared to  reference (Dotted).


dC/dV is a measure of change in capacitance and  does not give an absolute capacitance value. CV on  the other hand gives the absolute capacitance value. dC/dV can be a localization technique and has  higher throughput and imaging sensitivity than any  other capacitance measurement techniques. CV  allows for direct comparison to design targets and  process assumptions. Both dC/dV and CV analysis  times are similar or slightly longer than regular DC  device characterization. Both techniques identified  the resistive gate defect.


In this particular analysis the CV measurement of  the failing device has a slight slope to it and this is in  agreement with the dC/dV analysis. On the passing  device the CV in accumulation (Vg = -1 to -0.4V) appears to be flat. However, the dC/dV suggests that  there would be a slope larger than the fail. The onset  of inversion, at Vg = -0.4V is consistent between the  two sets of measurements. Full inversion seems to  occur at Vg = 0.4V on dC/dV and at Vg = 0.7V for  CV. The complementary nature of these two  techniques helped paint the complete picture for this  fail.


Root Cause Analysis


High KV FIB Voltage Contrast imaging was  performed on this sample after nano-probing. FIB  Voltage Contrast image (Figure 10) showed a darker  contrast on the failing gate compared to a reference  gate. This indicates that there is high resistance on  the failing gate and is consistent with the DC  NanoProbing.


A cross section TEM analysis was performed on the  failing contact and an insulating interfacial layer was  found between the CA and the gate silicide layer.


Fig 10: FIB Voltage Contrast Image of the failing  location (performed after nanoprobing) shows  contrast difference on the failing Gate.


Follow-on process split experiments indicated that  this eDRAM bitline fail signature was completely  dependant on a contact RIE Split.  This is also  consistent with the PFA results. The contact RIE  process was optimized further to fix this defect  mechanism.


This paper is an extension of prior work [4] on  dC/dV from bulk semiconductor technology into  eDRAM circuits and SOI technology. A  combination of advanced localization and  characterization techniques, especially utilizing  dC/dV and CV measurements, were demonstrated in  the understanding of a resistive gate defect. These  techniques were instrumental in bridging the DC  NanoProbing data and the process root cause.

Applications of Nanoprobing for Localization of Design for Manufacturing Issues  on Analogue-to-Digital Converter on Advanced Technology Node


A.C.T. Quah, C.Q. Chen, G.B. Ang, D. NAGALINGAM, Y. Li, J. Zhu, S.P. Neo, S.P. Zhao


Failure Analysis group, Quality and Customer Enablement (QCE) department,  GLOBALFOUNDRIES Singapore Pte Ltd


alfredquah@globalfoundries.com,


This paper describes 2 case studies where device  characterizations using Atomic Force Probe (AFP) nanoprobing, allow for the localization and verification of  design weakness and process variations on the Analog-toDigital (ADC) block that resulted in degraded device  performance and severe yield loss. In these cases, the sensitive  resistor structures in the ADC block was impacted due to  design pattern density interaction with process fabrication  steps. In addition, close collaboration with customer was also  essential for quick root cause identification, design and  process fix.


As semiconductor technology continues to scale towards submicron miniaturization, transistor devices are approaching the  scale of silicon lattice. Together with the increasing  complexity of integrated circuits, these have significantly  increased the impact of process variations and design and  process interactions on the manufactured device performance  and yield. Thus, design for manufacturing is critical to ensure  1st silicon success and shorter yield ramp cycle. For analogue  circuitry, variations could result in device mismatch thereby  resulting in analogue failure due to comparator offsets, bit  inaccuracy or degraded signal-to-noise ratio [1].


For wafer fabrication, process variations are monitored  primarily by measuring the parametric from Electrical Test (ET) structures along the scribe lines. However, the ET  structures would be insensitive to pick up systematic device  parametric drift that are due to design pattern density  interactions with fabrication steps. Thus, characterizations on  prime die transistors and passive devices using nanoprobing [2, 3] play a critical role in the localization of these design  issues. In this paper, 2 case studies involving ADC failure on  40nm new products due to pattern loading effects on sensitive  resistor structures are discussed. The 1st case study describes  on the oxidation of metal liner connecting to polysilicon  resistors, at low metal pattern density region, resulting in  abnormal high interconnect resistance and ADC failure. The  2nd case study describes on an ADC failure issue due to pattern  density induced resistance variation on a group of poly resistor


array during Laser Spike Annealing (LSA). For both case  studies, AFP nanoprobing was performed using Multiprobe  MPIIB System. With enhanced sensitivity, system was capable  of scanning at smaller tip landing force. This allows for  nanoprobing device analysis at Cu level without smearing  using slower scan speed. This was critical for resistance  measurement at Cu via level on one of the case studies.


Case Study 1 : ADC Failure due to Oxidation of Metal 1  Liner


The first case study was a 40nm new product which suffered  severe failure in the ADC block in the prototype lot. Fig. 1  showed the wafer sort map with passing die in white and ADC  failure units in maroon. It is evident from the sort map that the  failure is gross with almost whole wafer failed. However, all  failure units passed other bins like continuity, scan, MBIST  and leakage. This indicates that the issue is specific to  analogue ADC block and probably is design or structure  related.


Figure: 1 Wafer sort map showing severe ADC failure  highlighted in maroon


Customer debug team identified that ADC failure was due to  problematic poly resistor in the ADC block highlighted in Fig  2(a). Customer engaged external FA analysis which  subsequently observed broken poly contacts as shown in the  FIB cross-section in Fig. 2b(i). However, our internal FA  analysis, from multiple FIB cross-sections on several bad units  with different severity, observed no anomaly. No broken  contacts were observed as shown in Fig. 2b(ii). Thus, it was


suspected that “broken contacts” were induced from sample  preparation.

Figure: 2(a) Layout of suspected problematic resistors, highlighted in blue, in the ADC block. FIB cross-sections on  resistors showing b(i) “open” contacts from external FA and  b(ii) no anomaly from internal FA


To characterize the failure, 2 points AFP nanoprobing was  performed at contact level on the suspected poly resistors. Both bad and good units showed comparable resistance  between 31KΩ - 32KΩ as shown in Table 1. The resistance  values correlated well to the design specification. It also  verified that there is no anomaly at the contacts level and all  the FIB cuts that showed no broken contacts were valid. Next, nanoprobing was performed at Cu via 1 and Table 1 showed  that both good and bad units observed high resistance in Mega  Ohms except that bad units were worse in severity with  resistance at 2 orders of magnitude higher. After metal 1 was  removed, further resistance measurements at contact level on  both good and bad units showed that the resistance had  reduced from Mega Ohms to between 31KΩ - 32KΩ level. Based on this critical electrical finding, it was suspected that  the defective layer was between Via 1/Metal 1 to Contact  interface. In additional, results also indicated that “good” units  were also not good.


Table 1: Resistance comparison between bad and good unit at


contact and via level.


Subsequent TEM cross-section analysis showed that via 1  profile was normal. However, STEM analysis from Fig. 3(a) revealed that but abnormal metal 1 barrier profile was  observed. EELS Oxygen map verified the presence of oxygen


at the bottom metal liner as shown in Fig. 3(b). Semiquantitative EDX analysis in Fig 3(c) showed that the O/Ta  atomic ratio was much higher at the bottom liner (~1.5) as  compared to the sidewall liner (~0.25) . Thus, it was evident  that the oxidized TaOx barrier was the root cause for the  abnormal high resistance resistors.

Analysis did not stop there. It was discovered that there was  another group of poly resistors of the same dimensions within  the ADC block that was not reported failing as shown in Fig. 4(a). Similar resistance measurements at via 1 level showed  surprisingly that the non-reported resistors had much lower  resistance at ~ 98 KΩ as compared to the bad resistors as  shown in Fig. 4(b). TEM EDX showed that non-reported  resistor’s O/Ta atomic ratio at the bottom barrier was much  smaller than the bad resistor within the same failure unit.


Figure: 4(a) Layout of showing the reported bad resistors and  non-reported resistors in the ADC block of the same critical  dimensions. 4(b) IV resistance comparison between reported  bad resistors and non-reported resistors within bad unit


Layout study was engaged to investigate the difference in the  environments of the 2 sets of resistors. It was observed that the  good resistors were located in dense metal 1 region while the


bad resistors were placed in sparse metal 1 region (blue) as  shown in Fig. 5. Thus, the liner oxidation was correlated to the  metal density loading effects. The ADC failure was due to  Metal liner oxidation in low metal density environment due to  thermal cycling and dielectric out gassing. The design  weakness was improved and the issue was resolved with  increasing metal density at the resistors environment. This is  thus a design issue instead of process flaw. Further process  improvements were also made for out gassing prevention.


Figure: 5 (a) Bad resistor in sparse metal density location  and (b) good resistor in dense metal density location

As the specific ADC functional  performance was not tested in wafer sort, the issue was  surfaced only in the final test. It was suspected that failure was  due to the poly resistor mismatch. Detailed resistance variation characterization was performed  on a LSA design of experiment (DOE) splits. Short loop  wafers were processed to contact level for characterization on  the ADC poly resistors using AFP 4 point nanoprobing  resistance measurement. Table 2 showed the summary of  resistance variation. It was evident from the Skip LSA and  Normal LSA measurements that the resistance variation was  introduced from the LSA step. Without LSA, the resistance  variation was < 0.5% but with LSA, the variation was > 3%. In  addition, a change in the wafer rotation during LSA would  reduce the resistance variation by approximately 50%. Further  investigation observed that variation was correlated to both the  laser beam orientation to the structure and pattern density  loading effect in the resistors environment.


Figure: 8 Division of resistor array surrounding areas into 4  regions


Table 3: Pattern density comparison across regions  surrounding resistor array


The area surrounding the resistor block was divided into 4  regions as shown in Fig. 8 and the polysilicon (PC) and STI  pattern density differences across various regions were  computed and shown in Table 3. During LSA, region with  denser PC tends to be colder due to higher reflectivity and  region with denser STI tends to be hotter due to lower thermal  conductivity. As hotter thermal surrounding results in lower  resistance, the decreasing resistance trend observed with  normal LSA from Fig. 7 suggests that region 1 is colder than  region 4. From Table 3 it was observed that the pattern  differences between regions 2 and 3 are similar with < 3 % delta. The thermal effect from denser PC is compensated by  denser STI.  However, comparison on regions 1 and 4 revealed  the greatest STI pattern density difference of close to 10% delta. This would results in colder region 1 than region 4. From these studies, the local resistance variation correlates


stronger to STI pattern density difference [5]. During normal  LSA, the beam scanned the resistor array from left to right. At  the instance of annealing, the laser beam covered all the  surrounding regions from 1 - 4. The thermal difference  between region 1 and 4 from STI pattern loading effects would  result in a decreasing resistance trend. With wafer rotation, the  beam scanned the array from the top to bottom. At the  annealing instance, the array saw a similar thermal surrounding  from regions 2 and 3. As the coverage on region 1 and 4 was  reduced, the pattern loading effects from region 1 and 4 were  also significantly reduced. Thus, the resistance variation was  smaller as compared to the normal LSA. With the adoption of  the optimized wafer orientation in LSA with the minimum  resistance variation, issue was resolved with enhanced ADC  performance.


In conclusion, 2 case studies of ADC failure due to design  pattern density loading effects on sensitive resistor structures  were discussed. In both cases, AFP nanoprobing plays a  critical role in the localization and characterization of the  parametric resistance drift of the failing resistors. These case  studies also indicate that in the design and layout of highly  precise components in the analogue circuitry, attention has to  be given to the pattern density surrounding these components  and of the interconnect layers to minimize design interactions  with the fabrication steps.

Electro Optical Terahertz Pulse Reflectometry - a fast and highly accurate nondestructive fault isolation technique for 3D Flip Chip Packages


Stephane Barbeau


IBM Microelectronics, Bromont, Qc, Canada  sbarbeau@ca.ibm.com


Jesse Alton, and Martin Igarashi


TeraView Limited, Cambridge, United Kingdom


Electro Optical Terahertz Pulse Reflectometry (EOTPR), a  terahertz based Time Domain Reflectometry (TDR) technique, has been evaluated on Flip Chip (FC) and 3D packages. The  reduced size and complexity of these new generations of  advanced IC products necessitate non-destructive techniques  with increased fault isolation accuracy. The minimum accuracy  achievable with conventional TDR is approximately 1000µm. Here, we show that EOTPR is able to differentiate all of the  critical features in a 3D FC package, such as µC4 and Through  Silicon Via (TSV), and is capable of producing distance-todefect accuracy of less than 20µm, a significant improvement  over conventional microwave based TDR techniques.


The challenges within failure analysis are increasing with the  continued miniaturization and greater complexity of advanced  IC devices. Key among these challenges is the non-destructive  pre-localisation of electrical failures, prior to the destructive  investigation. Defect pre-localisation has become increasingly  important in the new generation products, such as 3D packages  where the package geometry is both highly complex and fragile. Until recently, an accuracy of 1000μm was acceptable for most  defect pre-localisation in IC package failure analysis.  However, this is no longer the case for the new generation of  products. Consider the typical stacked dies on a 3D package, the distance between two interconnects can be less than 80µm  in a FC package with TSV technology and a thinned die. Thus, non-destructive fault isolation techniques with an accuracy of  much less than 80µm are required today.


TDR is an essential non-destructive technique for IC package  failure analysis. This technique sends a high frequency  electrical pulse into the defective circuit in order to detect  impedance variations related to the defect in the device under  test (DUT). In this paper the performance of a conventional  TDR system is compared with EOTPR, a terahertz time domain  reflectometry technique which offers greatly increased  distance-to-defect accuracy.


What is the required accuracy?


The required accuracy for isolating a fault is directly related to  the density of features, such as interconnects, within the  package. The miniaturization of IC packages has resulted in a  higher circuit density with smaller features. Non-destructive  techniques must be able to differentiate between the critical  structures around the defect area, as the smaller the suspected


area, the faster the destructive investigation and the lower the  risk of missing the defect.


Consider a typical laminate flip chip circuit as illustrated in  Figure 1, several components around the C4 could be  responsible for an electrical failure; the Under Bump  Metallization (UBM), the die circuit, the Flip Chip Array (FCA) pad, the via underneath the FCA pad, or the electrode on the top  layer. If the accuracy of the non-destructive technique used to  locate the defect is inadequate, the destructive investigation will  need to be performed over a larger area, and thus will become  extremely time consuming. With conventional TDR, which  typically has an accuracy of around 1000µm, it is not possible  to isolate the fault to only the region around the C4, as the  dimensions of the C4 (~ 80µm) are significantly smaller than  the available distance-to-defect accuracy of the technique. At  this point a destructive investigation could be undertaken to find  the fault location. But, this requires several steps to check all of  the components in the suspected area, and risks destroying the  defect or introducing further defects in the process. In order to  minimize the area of investigation, several other nondestructive techniques can be combined with the TDR  technique, such as acoustic microscopy and 2D/3D X-Ray  inspection.  However, some defects are very difficult to isolate  even with these techniques, and those that can be isolated can  take hours, or in some cases days, to accurately identify the  location of the failure.


Figure 1: Typical laminate circuit in a Flip Chip package.


In a 3D package the difficulty level is greatly increased as  several C4 interconnects are present in each net. Considering a  3D package with silicon interposer and TSV technology (Fig. 2), the distance between the top side of the laminate and UBM  of the top die is typically less than 200µm. In this small area, two C4s, a TSV, and interposer circuitry can all be present. Moreover, this type of package is more sensitive to destructive  analysis than conventional FC packages, further justifying the  need for a non-destructive technique that can differentiate  between critical features. The µC4s used in this type of package  could be less than 20µm in height, thus a fault isolation  accuracy of better than 20µm is ideally required.


Figure 2: Cross section of a typical 3D package.


Overview of TDR technique


In conventional TDR, the incident pulse is generated by a diode. This technology can reach a spatial resolution of approximately  750µm, using a 70GHz plug-in module, and a rise time of 9ps  in a microelectronic circuit with an effective dielectric constant  of 3.5 [1]. Here, the fault detection accuracy is a function of the  rise time of the incident pulse, the time based jitter, and the  signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The smaller the rise time and time  based jitter and the greater the SNR the better the distance-todefect accuracy of the system [2]. Presently, no commercial tool  using a standard diode can reach a higher frequency than  70GHz. Thus, the spatial resolution is limited to 750µm with  this technology and the distance-to-defect accuracy is limited  by the time base jitter to several hundreds of microns. Another  parameter to consider is the effective dielectric constant of the  package. Microelectronics manufacturers are reducing the  dielectric constant of their package materials in order to  improve electrical performance. However, as seen in Figure 3, spatial resolution degrades with decreasing effective dielectric  constant for a given rise time.


Table 1: Comparison of EOTPR and TDR system properties


Figure 3; Impact of effective dielectric constant ( eff ) on  spatial resolution


(C is the speed of light in air - 3.0x108 m/s)


Overview of EOTPR technique


As in conventional TDR, the fault detection accuracy of  EOTPR is a function of the rise time of the incident pulse, the  time based jitter, and the SNR. The EOTPR system generates a  terahertz pulse using an ultrafast laser and pair of  photoconductive switches for generation and detection  resulting in a system with (i) high measurement bandwidth, (ii) low time base jitter, and (iii) high time base resolution. Compared to conventional TDR, EOTPR has a faster rise time, a greater SNR, and a much reduced time base jitter (Table 1), system properties that offer the potential for a significantly  increased distance-to-defect accuracy.


A schematic diagram of the EOTPR system is shown in Figure  4 [3]. During operation pulses are launched into the DUT via a  110GHz circuit probe. Portions of the pulse are reflected back  as it encounters changes in impedance within the integrated  circuit such as dead opens, resistive opens, and short circuit  defects. Reflections are recorded as a function of time and result  in the EOTPR waveform. EOTPR generates an impulse  response rather than the step response of conventional TDR. Therefore, for EOTPR, high impedance discontinuities in a  DUT result in positive peaks and low impedance discontinuities  result in negative features in the reflected signal. The magnitude  of the reflected peaks indicates the size of the impedance


change encountered by the pulse and the peak position gives the  location of the fault.


Figure 4: Schematic of an EOTPR system.


Flip Chip package: TDR versus EOTPR comparison


In this section the impedance profiles obtained with a 50GHz  TDR system and an EOTPR system are compared for an  electrical open signature in a FC package, as shown in Figure


1. The module was composed of an FC die joined to an organic  substrate. The C4 interconnects, between die and the substrate, are approximately 80µm high, while 750µm diameter solder  balls are attached to the Bottom Side Module (BSM). In order  to optimize the defect location, a substrate with solder balls on  BSM was used to identify the laminate extremity in the  defective net.


Using the TDR system, the electrical defect was localized in the  C4 area by comparing the impedance profiles from a known  good module, a substrate and the defective module, as  illustrated in Figure 5. The impedance profiles from the  substrate and the fail modules diverge from the good module in  the same area, suggesting that the defect is located close to the  FCA pad. However, it is not possible to conclude if the defect  is in the laminate, before the FCA pad or in the C4 bump after  the FCA pad, due to the accuracy limitations of this technique.


Figure 5: Impedance profiles obtained using a TDR system  with 50GHz incident pulse.


Using the EOTPR system, the FCA pad and the defect give two  distinct resistive peaks, as shown in Figure 6. These two peaks  indicate that the defect is not located in the laminate, but after  the FCA pad, close to the top of the C4 bump. The magnitude  of the peak indicates that the defect is a dead open circuit.


Figure 6: EOTPR Impedance profile and the schematic  drawing of defective circuit.


Based on this information, no further investigation is required  to localize the defect, and the destructive investigation can be  limited to a single cross section of the suspect C4. The results  of the destructive investigation are shown in Figure 7, confirming that the fault was in indeed located at the top of the  C4, in the UBM via. Without a clear indication of the location  of the defect the investigation would be more complicated and  more time consuming. Other non-destructive techniques must  be used to reduce the size of the suspected area or the  destructive investigation would require more steps (e.g. zsections and cross sections) to check all of the components in  the suspected area.


Figure 7: Optical image obtained after cross section of the  suspect C4. A rupture in the UBM via is responsible for the  electrical open failure detected in the defective module.


3D Package


In the following section EOTPR is used to investigate faults in  3D FC packages. This package type presents a significant  challenge for failure analysis as they are both more complex  and fragile. Contrary to a conventional flip chip package where  a destructive investigation can be performed by following the  defective net in the laminate to the C4, 3D packages employ a  silicon interposer between the laminate and top die. Silicon  interposers are more sensitive to destructive investigations than  organic laminates, and hence non-destructive techniques with  the ability to distinguish between the critical features of a 3D  package are urgently required. The most important components  to characterize in this type of package are the C4 interconnects  and the TSVs.


To assess the ability of EOTPR to differentiate between critical  components, a 3D FC package with TSV was selected for  evaluation. The module was composed of a silicon interposer (bottom die) and IC die mounted on a substrate (Figure 2). The  thicknesses of the top die and interposer were 750µm and  70µm, respectively and 50µm long TSVs were embedded in the  interposer. The C4 interconnects, between substrate and  interposer, were 80µm high and the µC4, between interposer  and IC die, were 20µm high.


Defects were simulated by mechanically grinding a module  from the top die side (Fig. 8a). The first defect was created by  removing the top die, but keeping the µC4s. Subsequent defects  were created by removing the µC4s, and then grinding to the  top and bottom of the interposer TSV. After each grinding step, the module was measured with an EOTPR system and the  acquired waveforms are shown in Figure 8b. For each defect, a  distinctive resistive peak is observed. These peaks reveal the  distance-to-defect accuracy of the EOTPR in a real 3D package. In this case, the equipment exhibits a distance-to-defect  accuracy of better than 20µm, shown by the separation between  the resistive peaks “without die” and “without µC4” (Fig. 8b), a peak to peak distance equivalent to 20μm, the height of a μC4.


Figure 8a: Schematics showing the position of the simulated  defects in the 3D module.


Figure 8b: EOTPR waveforms


Accuracy of the defect localization


In order to optimize the defect localization accuracy of the  EOTPR technique several key elements are required. The first  element is to have a reference module. This reference module  is used to compare the defect localization with a known feature  from within the package and must be selected to facilitate the  defect localization in the critical areas of the package. For  example, a substrate could be used as reference for a Flip Chip  Package to enable the differentiation between laminate, C4, and  die related failure. For a 3D package, as discussed previously, a substrate and a module without the top die would give a  similar result for this package type and enable differentiation  between the two C4 interconnects.


Using AFP PicoCurrent Imaging to Target  Process Variations


A large standard deviation in the VT,lin and VT,sat parameters  was observed for both the Samsung and TSMC parts. The  AFP’s PicoCurrentTM imaging mode was used to survey large  blocks of the SRAM.  PicoCurrentTM microscopy is a  continuous image map of the surface locating subtle or gross  variations in current flowing between the imaging probe tip  and the grounded chuck or adjacent probe.


Several systemic variations were identified on both parts. For the Samsung HG11-N9204 over 5% of the Cells  depicted a triplet NMOS anomaly signature. Here three  contacts shared between the passgate and pull down  transistors showed a higher current draw during imaging.


Figure 11 shows the AFP PicoCurrentTM and Topography  image for one of these 5 um x 5 um survey scans highlighting  more than 8 of these triplet features.


In the PicoCurrentTM image, the purple contrast is related to  negative current draw.  The green contrast is related to positive  current draw.  In both cases, “brighter” features signify high  current measured for that node.


Figure 11: (a)AFP PicoCurrentTM Image locating NMOS  triplet anomalies (purple features). (b) Associated AFP  topography Image


Four probe measurements were performed on several of these  triplets measuring the Transfer and Output Characteristics of  the two Passgates and the two Pulldown devices involved.


Figure 12: AFP PicoCurrent Image locating triplet anomaly.


Each of these targeted transistors associated with the  PicoCurrentTM anomaly showed a Vt shift of 50-100 mV  compared to a reference. Figure 13 shows the transfer  characteristic for one targeted PullDown device showing a “cold” Vt,sat compared to a reference device. This device  behavior matches the outlier performance discussed prior with  the Samsung Read fails.  With a PicoCurrentTM signature now  matched with a “cold” transfer characteristic it is trivial to  identify the global frequency this process variation.  Systemic  device variations like these contribute to the large standard  deviation for the device performance.


Figure 13: Samsung Pulldown Transfer Characteristics  showing Vt shift on two curves (Solid Lines) versus reference  device (Dotted).


Similar PicoCurrentTM variations were seen across the TSMC  HG11-N3877. In this case clusters of PMOS devices were  highlighted in about 3% of the cells. Figure 14 shows a 4x4um  PicoCurrentTM scan with several of the anomalies circled.  In  this image, the green features represent the positive current  draw of the P-type nodes.


Figure 14: PicoCurrentTM  survey scan of TSMC HG11-N3877 SRAM array  The green features represent P-type  nodes.


These PMOS devices were targeted with four probe  measurements. There was no increase in Ioff but there was a  consistent shift “hotter” in the VT,lin and VT,sat. Figure 15  shows one example of the transfer output characteristic plot  comparing one of these Pullup devices against a reference.


Figure 15: Voltage Threshold plots of targeted Pullup  transistor (Solid line) compared to reference (Dotted).


This transfer performance correlates with the TSMC write fail  concerns identified before. The PicoCurrentTM survey image  has quickly targeted the devices having “hotter” VT,sat values. With this PicoCurrentTM signature fully characterized we were  able to routinely target hotter Pullup devices throughout the  millions of transistors in the arrays and at the same time  quantify their frequency and density.


In this paper, SRAM from two predominant foundries, TSMC  and Samsung, was evaluated for quality, consistency and  performance. A complete suite of FA characterization tools  were used to evaluate key physical parameters and the  electrical performance of discrete SRAM devices. Physical  measurements of the Gate lengths and widths were used to  normalize the electrical data for both manufactures. Significant  variation was measured electrically within the memory cells of  both parts.  Threshold voltage impact on power draw and read  operations was discussed along with possible Read and Write  failure modes.


A PicoCurrentTM signature was identified for two of the  process variations discussed. This signature combined with the  fast refresh rate of the AFP’s PicoCurrentTM imaging mode  allowed significant portions of the SRAM cell to be qualified  in just minutes. This technique allowed the targeting of  systemic process variations to investigate for yield detractors.


Further work would explore the root cause of the identified  systematic process variations.

Nanoprobing As An Essential and Fast Methodology in Identification of Failure’s  Root Cause for Advanced Technology


Ma Yinzhe, Oh Chong Khiam, Nyi Ohnmar, Chuan Zhang, Donald Nedeau, Lim Seng Keat and King Ming Chu


GLOBALFOUNDRIES


400 Stone break Road Extension  Malta, NY 12020


Yinzhe.ma@globalfoundries.com


This paper highlights the use of nanoprobing as a crucial and  fast methodology for failure analysis (FA) in sub 20nm with  an improved semi-auto nanoprobing system. Nanoprobing has  the capability to localize as well as characterize the electrical  behavior of the malfunctioning device for a better  understanding of the failure mechanism. It provides a valuable  guide to choose a proper physical FA technique to identify the  root cause of the failure. This established methodology helps  to accelerate the FA turnaround time and improve the success  rate. Its application to a few of the front end of line and one  back end of line issues is highlighted in the paper.


As current technology advances by shrinking the minimum  critical dimension to 20nm and below, combined with the  growing complexity of SoC design, the traditional physical  failure analysis method faces serious challenges due to the  increase in non-visible defects and limited resolution of SEM.  The non-visible defects result in lower success rate as  conventional FA tool and method are not efficient in  identifying root cause of the failure. Conventional physical FA  rely heavily on the use of passive-voltage contrast (PVC) for  defect localization, but the variation in the scanning electron  microscope (SEM) contrast is often not sensitive or conclusive  enough to localize the defective site or identify the defects  when the device is down to the size of 20 nm [1]. Hence  employing other advanced electrical FA techniques such as  conductive atomic force (C-AFM) probing and nanoprobing  are required to provide more information to understand the  failure mechanism [2] – [5].


With the improved efficiency of a new semi-auto nanoprobing  system which greatly reduces the preparation time, we can use  nanoprobing techniques as an essential and fast fault isolation  and diagnostic method to analyze the failure. After fully  understanding the failure mechanisms of the defects by  nanoprobing, an appropriate guide to the required physical  analysis can be carried out to “visualize” the defects. In this  paper we will discuss several case studies in which


nanoprobing techniques play a key role for root cause  identification. We will demonstrate the understanding of soft  failures by butterfly curve analysis, six transistors probing  isolation methodology and electron beam absorb current (EBAC) analysis to enhance deficiencies in Passive Voltage  Contrast.


In this paper a total of four 20nm technology node devices, namely device A, device B, device C, and device D  respectively, were analyzed. Two devices were analyzing  SRAM single cell fail (SCF), one device was analyzed a logic  chain failure, and one device was analyzed a electrical test  structure short failure. Figure 1 shows a circuit diagram of a  standard six transistor SRAM cell. A single memory cell is  made up of six transistors, two cross-coupled complementary  metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) inverters and two pass  NMOS transistors that connect the cell  to the bitline and  bitline bar (BL and BLB). All samples were delayered down  to contact (CA) level, then 1keV E-Beam energy was used to  inspect for any abnormal PVC using SEM. A DCG nProber  system was used to carry out the nanoprobing jobs. A DCG  nProber is comprised of high precision nano-manipulator  integrated to a high resolution SEM, capable of imaging with  500eV and low beam current. A Keithley 4200 parameter  analyzer was used to acquire the device parameters. From the  measured electrical data, the defect can be pinpointed to a  single transistor or a much smaller localized area of interest  and appropriate physical analysis can be carried out  accordingly to visualize the defect.


Figure 1: a circuit diagram for a standard 6-T SRAM cell. [6]


Case Study I. Metal Gate filling Material Replaced


Figure 2(a) shows the SEM PVC image of a 20nm device A at  CA level. The failed single bit was highlighted in the dashed  box in the center. From the bitmap data, this cell failed all the  testing corners thus it is a hard fail. However, there is no  abnormal PVC observed at CA level and there is no clue  where to do a TEM analysis for root cause identification. As  process technology shrinks down to 20nm and below we  found a lot of failures inspected by SEM do not contain  enough resolution and detail to help the process integration  team to fully understand the failure mechanism and implement  a proper fix to the process flow. In order to further isolate the  failure for TEM analysis, nanoprobe measurements are carried  out at each individual transistor of the fail bit cell. Nanoprobing is also carried out on a reference bit cell that  passes all the testing corners. Figure 2(b) and Figure 2(c) shows the Ids-Vgs curve of a defective NMOS and reference  NMOS transistor.

The NMOS transistor in the bad cell exhibits extremely low  on current due to high threshold voltage (Vth), two orders of  magnitude lower on current than the good transistor at 1V  bias. Cross-section-view TEM analysis is carried out at the  defective NMOS transistor with focus on the region of  source/drain and channel. Figure 2(d) shows a dark-field TEM  micrograph obtained from the sample. Figure 2(e) shows the  elemental analysis results collected on the TEM sample. Case Study II. SRAM Single Cell Soft Fail Understanding  by Butterfly Curve


Figure 3(a) shows three probe tips landing on the gate, drain  and source of device B. Device B passes functional test at the


1.05V test corner but fails at the 0.85V test corner. This kind  of failure is normally described as a “soft fail”. Furthermore, a  more detailed test confirms device B fails disturb at 0.85V. In  order to understand the failure’s static noise margin (SNM) and what is the root cause of the soft fail, nanoprobing tests  were carried out including six individual transistor probe  measurements to check the read margin of device B. Figure  3(b) and Figure 3(c) shows SNM test results of device B and a  reference bit during a read operation.

From SNM measurement results we can see that during a read  operation device B doesn’t have any read margin at 0.85V Vdd  bias, which means data stored in the SRAM cell will be  corrupted after one read cycle. Table 1 shows the individual  transistor measurement results at 0.85V Vdd bias. From this  table it can be seen the weak pull down left NMOS transistor  is the root cause for the bit cell to fail disturb.

Case Study III. High Resistance CA to TS Interface


Figure 4(a) shows a SEM PVC image at CA level from a logic  device C that fails the logic chain test. After volume  diagnostics identified the failing chain, physical FA was  carried out using layer by layer inspection through CA level. There was with no visible defect found or anomaly found  between fail cell 1 and the reference cell. Nanoprobing was  carried out to measure all the transistors in the fail cell.

Figure 4(b) and Figure(c) show Ids-Vds curves of a defective  transistor and a reference transistor in the failing cell. The  saturation current of the reference transistor is four orders of  magnitude higher (nA range versus uA range) than the  defective transistor. This electrical charasteristic  indicates a  very high contact resistance exists in the source/drain of the  defective transistor.

Case Study IV. Via2 to M2 Open in ET Structure


Device D is a 20nm technology back end of line M3-V2-M2  chain electrical test (ET) structure. The device fails the opens  test, and similar to other case studies, conventional method of  FIB grounding of one pad followed by PVC inspection didn’t  work for this case. EBAC analysis with nanoprobing was  carried out using nProber. Figure 5(a) and Figure 5(b) show an  EBAC image and an EBAC and SEM superimposed image for  the failed ET macro. From the EBAC results, two bright to  dark contrast boundaries can be observed in the macro. The  EBAC result indicates there are multiple V2 to M2 defects  presents along the chain and each open is not fully open. TEM  analysis was carried out at the right most contrast change  location.

Figure 5(c) shows the dark-field TEM cross-sectional view  image obtained according to the EBAC contrast change  location. From this result we can observe an unlanded Via2.


Figure  5(c):  Cross-section View TEM image of the unlanded   V2 in the ET macro


Nanoprobing techniques are capable of isolating the faulty site  precisely in a relatively fast manner compared to the  conventional SEM PVC method. Moreover, it enables more  thoroughly analysis and understanding of the failure  mechanism. Most importantly this can be used as a guide to  choose a proper method for the subsequent physical FA so that  the process of identifying the root cause of a failure can be  escalated. Hence nanoprobing is an essential FA technique  needed for yield improvement for the current and next couple  of technology nodes.

dC/dV and CV Characterization of Gate Resistance Defects in eDRAM Circuits


Sweta Pendyala, Dave Albert, Katherine Hawkins and Michael Tenney


IBM, Hopewell Junction, NY, USA

Resistive gate defects are unusual and difficult to  detect with conventional techniques [1] especially on  advanced devices manufactured with deep submicron SOI technologies. An advanced localization  technique such as Scanning Capacitance Imaging is  essential for localizing these defects, which can be  followed by DC probing, dC/dV, CV (CapacitanceVoltage) measurements to completely characterize  the defect. This paper presents a case study  demonstrating this work flow of characterization  techniques.


Problem Statement


Process split experiments are essential in a research  and development environment for qualifying a  technology. Parametric or functional tests are  performed on variety of electrical structures, including SRAM and eDRAM arrays.


The eDRAM Bit Line (BL) fail described in this  paper was an unexpected result of a contact (CA) RIE (Reactive Ion Etch) process split experiment. The inline functional array detected a low density of  bit line fails, failing the 0's pattern corner and the  wafer was submitted for physical failure analysis (PFA). This fail signature indicated a problem in the  sense amp circuit that controls the failing BL (as per  design) and all the PFA efforts were focused on the  sense amp circuit.


Fig 1: Inline test data


Top down scanning electron microscope (SEM) inspections at the backend metal levels and front end  device levels, plus focused ion beam (FIB) cross  sections at different levels were performed in the  sense amp circuit to isolate the fail. Both analyses  were inconclusive and a sample was submitted for  nano-probing to isolate the fail at the device level.


Scanning Capacitance Imaging


Atomic Force Probe (AFP) Scanning Capacitance  Imaging (SCM) is a localization technique useful on  SOI devices [2] where current imaging localization  is not possible as there is no direct path to ground. The AFP SCM module consists of a resonant sensor  and a lock-in amplifier (Figure 2). An AC bias, dV, applied via the probe relative to the sample moves  carriers resulting in a change in capacitance, dC. The  capacitance variation, dC, measured by the sensor is  amplified with the aid of a lock-in amplifier. Output  from the lock-in amplifier in the form of dC/dV  amplitude and/or phase is then displayed as an  image.


Fig 2: Concept of Scanning Capacitance Imaging


The sample was de-layered to CA level and scanned  with the AFP. Scanning capacitance imaging [3] was  used to localize the fail to one device in the sense  amp circuit. Figure 3 shows the SCM image of the  failing circuit. The n-type devices have a blue  contrast and the p-type has a yellow contrast. A clear  contrast difference can be seen on the failing gate.

DC NanoProbing (IV Measurements)


Scanning Capacitance Imaging is a useful  localization technique, but to fully understand the  device characteristics of a failing device DC  nanoprobing is required. To obtain the extended Vt  lin (linear threshold voltage) and Vt sat (saturation  threshold voltage) characteristics of the failing  device, the gate was swept from -0.5V to 1V while  the drain was held at 50mV and 1V, respectively.


In linear mode, the failing device showed low drive  current, higher Vt, and higher device resistance  compared to a reference device (Figure 4). In  saturation mode the failing device showed  anomalous behavior with very high Ioff and little to  no gate control on the channel with varying gate bias (Figure 5). It appeared as though there was a fixed  voltage (around 0.6V) on the gate. The slope of the  gate leakage current of the failing device appeared to  be a decade lower than the reference device, indicating a possible anomalous barrier within the  gate terminal (Figure 6).


The anomalous nature of this defect warranted a  deeper dive to understand the device characteristics  and a possible root cause mechanism. The DC  probing was supplemented with AFP dC/dV  measurements and nProber CV measurements to  completely characterize the defect.

dC/dV Measurements


If the tungsten probe tip, oxide, and sample are  considered to be MOS capacitors (Figure 7), then the  variation in capacitance can be approximated as a  result of a change in the separation of the plates of  parallel-plate capacitors. The capacitance between  the plates is given by,


C = εA/d


where, ε is the dielectric constant, A is the area, and  d is the distance between the plates.

The capacitance is highest when the plates are the  closest.  Under accumulation, the charge is attracted  towards the surface. A very simple analogy would  be the bottom plate moving upward and the  capacitance increases as the plate separation  decreases. For n-type material the measured  capacitance is highest when the applied voltage is  positive.


Conversely, the capacitance is lowest when the  plates are the farther away from each other.  Under  inversion, the charge is repelled from the surface. For n-type material, the capacitance decreases when  the bias is shifted negative, resulting in free carriers  being pushed away from the surface (Figure 7).


Fig 7: MOS Capacitor Approximation and resultant  CV curves


For SOI samples, there are three capacitors in series  during the dC/dV measurement.  Each has its own  response to the applied AC Bias.  The Contact  Capacitance, between the probe and the CA, is  metal-oxide-metal in nature and does not vary as a  function of voltage.  The Substrate Capacitance, across the BOX, is a semiconductor-oxidesemiconductor capacitor and due to the nature of the  dopants does not respond significantly to voltage.  The Device Capacitance, between the silicide and  the n dopant, does respond to the applied voltage and  dominates the dC/dV measurement. This principle is  used to obtain AFP dC/dV measurements on the  failing device.


Figure 8 shows the dC/dV characteristics of the  failing device compared to a reference device. The  dC/dV plot of the failing device (pink plot) shows no  difference in accumulation and inversion when  compared to the reference device. This indicates the  failing gate capacitance is not significantly  modulated by a change in voltage. The reference  device has the expected dC/dV response.


dC/dV is a measure of the change in capacitance and  does not give an absolute capacitance value. As a  result, dC/dV measurements were followed up with  CV measurements.


Fig 8: dC/dV Characteristics of the Failing Device


CV Measurements


CV characterization is based upon the same MOS  capacitor principles which were described  previously.  However, there is a difference.  The AC  Bias (dV) is now replaced with a DC Bias (V) and  capacitance (C) is measured directly.

The failing  device (pink plot) has reduced inversion capacitance, and the capacitance does not change significantly  under accumulation biasing. However, the  capacitance seemed to increase by 20 aF when the  voltage was swept from -1V to 1V.
