Similarities and Differences between dC/dV  and CV Measurements


The second element is to know the effective dielectric constant  for the analyzed module. This value can be determined using  the EOTPR waveform from a specific circuit for which the  length is known. If the substrate is used to determine this key  value, the dielectric constant will be an average of all the circuit


length in the laminate. However, it is important to know that the  dielectric constant value is not uniform in an organic substrate, since diverse materials and components are used. The build-up  layers and the core are not made of the same material, and the  circuit density is not constant throughout the package, thus  some difference in the dielectric constant value can be  observed. To improve the EOTPR accuracy, the effective  dielectric constant must be determined in the most significant  areas of package. For the 3D package, these areas are the  substrate, the C4/µC4 areas and the silicon interposer where the  TSV are located.


The third element is to use a de-convolution function for the  data analysis. As for the Z-line function included in most TDR  software, the de-convolution process removes the system  response from the waveform and aids data interpretation.


In order to illustrate these key elements in the accuracy of the  EOTPR system, defects were manually created in the organic  substrate of a FC package (Fig. 9). Two electrodes, on the  laminate top layer, were cut close to the FCA pads using a  blade. The first step was to localize the FCA pads in the  defective circuits using a laminate without die. These two  EOTPR waveforms were used to measure the distance between  the defects and their FCA pads. The second step was to evaluate  the effective dielectric constant for the defective circuits. With  knowledge of the circuit length and by measuring the required  time for the EOTPR signal to travel the distance between the  BGA and the FCA pad, the effective dielectric constant was  calculated. The third step was to compare the defect localization  with and without the de-convolution process. For circuit AH25, the de-convolution was not used to evaluate the defect  localization from the FCA pad, while in circuit AH26 the deconvolution was used to evaluate the defect localization from  the FCA pad. Results are shown in the table 2. In both cases, the accuracy is impressive, with localization errors of less than  24µm and 3µm for the raw data and de-convoluted data  respectively.


Table 2: Defect localization


Figure 9: Schematic showing the position of the defects


generated in an organic substrate. Circuits AH25 & AH26 are  shown in green and red. In the bottom image the top and FC2  layers superimposed.


The experimental results presented in this paper have  demonstrated the capability of the EOTPR technique to meet  the fault detection requirements in the new generation of  microelectronic packages, such as 3D FCs. Under appropriate  conditions, this technique can reach a distance-to-defect  accuracy of less than 20µm in a real package. The EOTPR  technique is a significant improvement over conventional TDR  and a critical solution to mitigate the failure analysis challenges  in advanced IC packages.

In the past couple years, Space Domain Reflectometry (SDR) has become a mainstream method to  locate open defects among the major semiconductor manufacturers. SDR injects a radio frequency (RF) signal into the open trace creating a standing wave with a node at the open location. The magnetic field generated by the standing wave is imaged with a SQUID sensor using RF electronics. In this  paper,  we show that SDR can be used to non-destructively locate high resistance failures in Micro  LeadFrame Packages (MLP).


Micro LeadFrame Package (MLP) has become  a common package technology used by the semiconductor industry due to its small size and  weight as well as excellent thermal and electrical  performance. These make MLP an ideal choice  for handheld portable applications such as cell  phones and Personal Digital Assistants (PDAs) or any other applications where size, weight and  package performance are critical factors [1].


Due to the compacted package design and difficulty getting non-destructive access to the  backside of silicon, many existing Fault Isolation (FI) techniques such as thermal and laser  techniques [10], [11], cannot find failure locations in MLP.  Magnetic Field Imaging (MFI), on the other hand, is uniquely suited for such  application due to ability of magnetic field to  penetrate most materials [4].


2. Magnetic Field Imaging (MFI)


A current carrying conductor generates magnetic field according to the Biot-Savart law [2, 9]. Magnetic Current Imaging (MCI) is a sub  technique of MFI. MCI has been used by the  semiconductor industry for more than a decade  to find shorts and leakages due to its capability  to “look through” any types of materials physically covering the signal, thereby allowing for  global imaging without physical deprocessing


[3], [4], [5]. MCI utilizes two types of sensors: Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) sensor for low current and large working distances and a Giant Magneto Resistance (GMR) sensor for sub micron resolution current  imaging at wafer/die level [6].


A newly developed technique based on MFI, namely Space Domain Reflectometry (SDR), has been successfully used to non-destructively  localize opens defects in microchips [7]. SDR  injects a continuous wave (CW) radio frequency (RF) signal typically at 40-60MHz (can range  from 30MHz to 200MHz) into the defective  trace. Modeling the trace as an open circuited  transmission line (see Fig. 1) shows that the  open reflects entire sampling signal due to substantial impedance mismatch between the trace  characteristic impedance (~50 ) and the open  impedance. A superposition of the incident and  reflected waves forms a standing wave, in which  the current fist node coincides with the open location.


Figure 1. A standing wave formed in defective  trace due to the open.


Since for typical Integrated Circuit (IC) the  RF radiation wavelength  is much longer than  the trace, the standing wave current decays linearly in close proximity of the open defect [8]. Due to relatively low operating frequency, the  SDR signal travels much further than the GHz  signals employed in Time Domain Reflectometransmitted=0

3. Microcontroller failing Resistive Open


A 32 bit microcontroller used for various applications ranging from automotive to hand held  mobile devices, was designed in an MLP and  was attached to a Printed Circuit Board (PCB) to  run advanced chip testing (Fig. 2).  The PCB  was approximately 1 inch by 1 inch and the pin  connectors were located close to the edge of the  PCB with the MLP located in the center of the  PCB. The sample went through thermal cycling.


Figure 2a. Optical image with dimensions of the  MLP sample attached to the PCB.


Figure 2b. X-ray image of the MLP chip on top  of the PCB.


The first step in the FA procedure was IV  curve test (Current I versus Voltage V) to check  for continuity (Fig. 3). A standard curve tracer  was used for the IV curve testing on the failing


pin and Ground.


Figure 3a. IV Curve for Good sample


Figure 3b. IV curve of the high resistance defect  sample


The sample showed resistive open failure between a data pin (IO) and a Ground (GND) pin (Fig. 3).


4. SDR applied for FI on the failed sample


SDR’s sampling signal at 60 MHz was applied  via PCB to the IO pin while the GND pin was  left floating (not connected).


Figure 4. SDR setup during raster scanning the  failed sample.


The failing sample was mounted onto the xyzstaging stack to position the sample close to the  sensor for optimizing resolution (resolution for  MFI is affected by the distance between the sensor and the signal trace) and to raster scan the  entire sample. The RF signal was injected into  the failing IO pin about 1 inch away from the  MLP sample.


The current density image obtained by SDR  was overlaid with the optical and X-ray images  for accurate fault isolation, as shown in Figs. 5a  and 5b, respectively.


Figure 5a. Overlay of the SDR current image  and optical image.


Figure 5b. Overlay of the SDR current image  and X-ray image.


The fact that we s observed a clear decaying  signal close to the open location indicated that  even if the sample failed resistive open, and not  fully open, the impedance change was large  enough to create the standing wave with a node  at the open location which was needed for SDR  to localize the open failure.


Overlay of the current image to the Xray image showed the failing location was close to  where the wire bond was attached to the die (Fig  5b).


5. Physical Failure Analysis (PFA)


To confirm that the defect location was at the  end of the wire bond located in the upper left  corner (Fig. 5b), Physical Failure Analysis was  performed. The first step in the PFA process was  to use a mechanical polisher to cut the PCB and  MLP from the left side towards the open wire  bond location as shown in Figure 6.


Figure 6. The area for conducting PFA.

After cross-sectioning with mechanical polisher, the part was brought to the Focused Ion  Beam (FIB) for more accurate localization of the  failure. The FIB cut was done at the location  indicated by the SDR.


Figure 7a. Cross-section of the wire bond attachment to the die after mechanical polishing  and FIB cut.


Figure 7b. High resolution SEM image of the  high resistance location where the wire bond has  been attached to the die.


The image taken using Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) showed consumption of all of  the aluminum during the formation of the intermetallic caused a higher resistance in the wire  bond when attached to the die surface (Fig 7).


6. Conclusion


The failing location was found using SDR


non-destructively. The technique can be applied  not only on fully open (“dead open”) defects but  also on high resistance defects caused by a partial open. SDR is a simple technique capable of  locating the open failure even without the sample layout.

Nondestructive analysis solution using combination of Lock-in  Thermography(LIT) and 3D oblique X-ray CT technology


Naoki Seimiya, MARUBUN CPRPORATION

We developed the non-destructive failure analysis method that  is combination of Lock-in thermography (LIT) and high  resolution 3D oblique CT. It made possible to complete the  total analysis efficiently, because we can distinguish the type  of failure by this non-destructive method.


Failure analysis process flow of semiconductor can separate  the non-destructive to the destructive. Final investigation is


done by destructive analysis but this work has no second


chance so it can’t afford to fail. In order to totally succeed with  failure analysis, destructive analysis technique is of course


important, but defect localization and observation through


non-destructive method are very important. In order to achieve  success with the total failure analysis, making accurate


tentative theory from non-destructive analysis result is very


important.


For non-destructive failure analysis tool, X-ray imaging


equipment is common, but in the past many people thought


that the resolution of X-ray imaging equipment for


semiconductor analysis wasn’t enough. Recently the


performances of X-ray imaging equipment and X-ray CT


function have dramatically improved by the progress of new


X-ray camera, X-ray generator and development of new CT


algorithm and its resolution becomes better than before. With  this detecting micro failure which was thought impossible to


be detected by X-ray, becomes available.


On the other hand there is a new problem that the more the  X-ray resolution is improved, the more field of view of X-ray  image becomes small in size. This means it is difficult to


locate the accurate position for X-ray imaging. So now, we  are proposing the combination method of Lock-in IR


Thermography (LIT) and High resolution X-ray CT analysis. This method is done before going to X-ray CT analysis, locate  the defect point by Lock-in IR thermography(LIT), by  doing  this the X-ray analysis shooting point is already located


accurately and X-ray analysis becomes more efficient.


In this report I will introduce the successful case example  of the defect IC package analysis. This non-destructive  analysis was tested by combination method of Lock-in  thermography and High resolution X-ray CT. By using this  combination method, we could distinguish the failure mode by  non-destructively. As a result of this, the next step of  destructive analysis becomes very easy. And we could identify   the cause of the defect.


Failure analysis of the semiconductor device


The failure device that we tried to analyze this time is QFP  Package. This package sample had a leak current between two  neighbor pin and there was temperature property. We tried Xray imaging using the old type of X-ray equipment, but we  couldn’t detect the cause of the leak current by old type of Xray. Fig 1.


Phenomenon that high temperature brings on the neighbor pin  leak is thought that there is some contamination between the  two pin. If the contamination is the cause of leak current, we  thought Lock-in IR thermography is useful to localize the  defect point, and we tried.


Advantage of Lock-in IR thermography is the possibility of  non-destructive measurement from plastic mold surface. Measurement method of Lock-in IR thermography is shown  below. Apply a pulse of voltage to leak pin and detect the  infrared information from the surface of plastic mold by high  sensitive IR camera. In this time, IR camera and Lock-in  source are synchronizing each other and camera detects the IR  information that is occurring frequency. This makes it possible  to narrow down the hot point. Fig 2 is the image of defect  localization by Lock-in thermography.


It took about 10minutes to take this Lock-in IR thermography  image. Applied voltage was 16V, and current value was


2.2μA. Fig 3 is the overlay image of X-ray and Lock-in IR  thermography. This image is showing that the defect point is  located near the wire bonding pads.


After the Lock-in IR thermography analysis, we tried high  resolution X-ray imaging. At this point, we have the


information of Lock-in  thermography; it means the viewing  point was already located. And we got the Fig 4 image. This  image was taken by 45 degree oblique angle of X-ray camera, and it defined that some kind of contamination is present  between wire bonding pads.


By using X-ray imaging, we detected the contamination


between the pads, but level of the contamination is not defined. To decide the way of destructive analysis, it is important to


know how high the contamination is. So we tried 3D oblique


CT analysis. 3D oblique CT is suitable for high magnification  CT analysis. Fig 5 is the 100X slice image of 3D oblique CT. Slice pitch is 0.5μm and shooting time is about 30minutes.


3D oblique CT slice image cleared up the height of the  contamination. As a result, the contamination was suspended


6.5μm upper of the pads. Fig 6 is the failure image of this  sample.


Fig 7 is SEM image of polishing this package. Previously the  failure point was localized by Lock-in IR thermography (LIT) and high resolution 3D oblique X-ray CT, so it was very easy  to go the destructive analysis.


Fig7 SEM image


Both Lock-in IR thermography and X-ray CT is nondestructive analysis method. Before going to destructive


analysis, if there are information of location of the defect and  high resolution X-ray CT image, success rate of destructive


analysis becomes almost 100%. The combination of this


advanced equipment is very powerful tool for semiconductor  failure analysis.


For this failre analysis, we used Lock-in IR thermography  model:ELITE produced by DCGsystems and X-ray CT system  model:XVA-160α produced by UNI-HITE system.


Fig8 and Fig9 are picture of these tool.

Sub-mohms Resistance Characterization of Conductive Interfaces on


Automotive Power MOSFET to Determine the Origin of On-Resistance Drift


Yann WEBER from Freescale Semiconducteurs France SAS


Freescale Semiconducteurs France SAS, Toulouse, France  yann.weber@freescale.com, Phone: +33(0)5 61 19 11 85


Philippe ROUSSEILLE from Freescale Semiconducteurs France SAS


Freescale Semiconducteurs France SAS, Toulouse, France  philippe.rousseille@freescale.com, Phone: +33(0)5 61 19 15 60


This paper presents an original approach allowing  determining the failure mechanism at the origin of onresistance (RDSon) drift on vertical Power N-MOSFETs, dedicated to automotive application. The studied devices  failed after Temperature Cycling (TC) qualification  stress. The originality of that paper concerns the  necessity to use strategic Failure Analysis (FA) approaches to determine the origin of the defect, without  any localization possibilities. In that perspective, an  original microprobing sub-mohms resistance electrical  characterization of the different conductive interfaces  was performed in order to determine the failing layer. Then, physical destructive FA techniques (backside  SAM, leadframe peel-off and mechanical cross-section) were combined in order to finely characterize the defect. As a result, problems in die attach layer were  highlighted, confirming the electrical probing  characterization. At last, root cause of this abnormal die  attach will be discuss through review of assembly  process parameters. These results allowed implementing  corrections and improving product stress resistance.


The qualification and robustness validation of power  devices are big challenge in automotive applications; it  can affect package, metallic connections, silicon die, solder [1]. To understand rejects and improve overall  technology process, accurate characterizations need to  use new methodologies.


This article presents a new method for RDSon drift  characterization applied on automotive power devices. The technique uses an original microprobing sub-mohms  resistance electrical characterization to discriminate the  different conductive interfaces at the origin of the  failure. Then, accurate physical analyses demonstrate the  failure mechanism at the origin of the RDSon drift. Finally, root causes of this abnormal die attach are  discussed through review of assembly process  parameters.


Problem Description


Device presentation


The device is a smartpower switch used to drive bulbs in  automotive applications. It is encapsulated in a SOIC54  plastic package and is constituted with two separated  dice: one mixed signal control die processed in 0.25um  technology and one power die made of 5 independents  high side trench VDMOS transistors (Fig.1a). Two  families of transistors are designed in silicon die (Fig.1b): transistors with nominal RDSon of 15mΩ for the  type I (small transistor) and 6mΩ for the type II (big  transistor).


Figure 1: a) Schematic cross-section of the trench Power  MOSFET; b) top picture of the device with output


naming.


The top die metallization (Al, Cu) is the source of the  transistors and the drain is connected to the leadframe of  the package, soldered with a conductive die attach for  the power die. Aluminum wedge bondings (15mils) are  used to connect Source to external pins. An exposed pad  leadframe on the backside of that product is connected to  the external battery voltage (VBAT), nominal at 12V, corresponding to the drain of the power die. The RDSon  characterization implies that silicon die resistance (Rch, Ra, Rd, Rsub in Fig.1a) and package resistance (pin, top  metallization, bondings, leadframe, die attach) are  a)


Type I


Type II


included. In this study, the wafer fab process data  analysis indicates that there is no process excursion, excluding potential failure inside the silicon. Therefore, the different package interfaces are investigated as  contributor of the RDSon drift measured after stress.


Failure report


The failure occurred after reliability stress of  Temperature Cycling (TC), using 1000 cycles (TC 1000) between -50°C and 150°C. The qualification process  requires that the RDSon are measured before stress and  after stress. The comparison of these RDSon values, measured at final test with Automatic Tester (ATE), reveals high number of outlier parts, presenting  abnormally high RDSon drift. The standard acceptable  RDSon drift values are lower than 1m. Based on the two  classes of transistors present on the product, the limits of  detection are established at 17m for type I and 7m for type II.


It is well known that RDSon drift are normal consequence  of material aging during different kind of electrical and  thermal stress [2]. However, it is observed here that too  many outlier parts presented abnormally high RDSon drift  after TC 1000 stress as compared to a standard drift (Fig.2). The percentage of type I transistors rises around  the 17m limits is too important. When the RDSon  variation before and after stress are compared in Fig.3, it  is clearly observed that distribution is not normal on the  transistor Type I, who are emphasize the phenomenon.


Despite these parts are considered as “good parts” (just  under the limit), the countless proportion of high RDSon  drift exposes all the difficulty and interest to work on  this kind of disparity, in order to improve product  reliability.


Failure Electrical Characterization


Failure analysis approach


The challenge for failure analyst is to localize the origin  of the 1.5mΩ drift. Based on these small variations, standard failure analysis techniques (Light Emission, OBIRCH...) are not applicable. Thus, microprobing  technique is chosen as selective response to explain this  RDSon increase. For a packaged device, the total RDSon is  the sum of the resistivity induced in several interfaces: Pins/Wedge


bonds,


Wedge


bonds/Metal, Metal/Leadframe. Two main failure mechanism  phenomenon’s can contribute to the RDSon degradation: metal layers and/or conductive interfaces degradations.


Electrical characterization


The four wires resistor measurement principle with  force/sense was not directly usable due to the limitation  of surface characterization and also to the low current  which can be applied with needles to measure each  interface [3]. The solution with the use of only two sense  needles and the device in conduction (“ON-state”) was  preferred. To have the best accuracy, the highest possible  current is forced in the transistor, in order to have the  highest voltage drop and then, deduct the resistance. First, the samples are chemically frontside decapsulated. The use of microprobes is mandatory to have the access  to each interface.


Sample Drains were biased at 12V with a high  current capability source. The load for the selected  transistor output was done with a current source. The  measurement principle follows this strategy: one sense  needle is fixed on the leadframe and the second needle is  moved between each interface (Fig.4). Both sense  needles were connected to a voltmeter, allowing the  measurement of the voltage drop for each interface. It
